22351-publisher-s-advertising-1872: Publisher's Advertising, dated 1872, is trade matter bound to sell a line of books. It praises those books in their familiar brown covers. The Boston Transcript is quoted on how far the covers had spread by then. They could be seen in railway cars and steamships, in studios and libraries, on verandas. All classes enjoyed the books, the quote claims, and new ones kept coming in a steady stream. In subject and style, it says, they offered wide choice. The pages show how a publisher sold a whole series.
22959-political-recollections-1840-to-18:
George W. Julian gathers Political Recollections covering 1840 to 1872, decades that remade his country. In his preface Julian concedes that he has restated many familiar facts of American politics. Still, he hopes his memories add something to the record of a movement known around the world. His aim, he says, is to save the fragments before they vanish.

Julian served in Congress as an abolitionist and Radical Republican, and his memories carry that fight's heat. Slavery's fall, the Whigs' collapse, and Reconstruction's battles pass through a participant's eyes. Memoirs like his are quarries for historians, rich and partial at once. Readers get both record and argument, from a man who helped make the events he judges.
alchemical-writings-1472:
Alchemical Writings is a late fifteenth-century manuscript on paper, now Lehigh Codex 10 in Lehigh University's Special Collections. It was made in Naples, Italy, between about 1472 and 1490, and it contains a compilation of alchemical texts assembled and copied by Arnold of Brussels. Dates written at the ends of works in the volume anchor its making in those years.

A group of works fills the codex, gathered by its scribe from the medieval alchemical tradition. Such compilations were how the art traveled: one practitioner's handbook of copied treatises, recipes, and authorities. The manuscript preserves alchemy as it was actually read and used in Renaissance Naples, in a working paper book rather than a luxury volume.
allibone-critical-dictionary-english-lit:
Volume Two of Allibone's Critical Dictionary appeared in 1872, fourteen years after the first, covering K to Q. Samuel Allibone had spent the interval gathering still more notices. The delay shows in the volume's fullness.

Entries continue the pattern: brief lives, full lists of writings, and quoted opinions from the press. American authors receive generous space beside their British cousins. Allibone's own judgments are plain and sometimes sharp, in the manner of a working bookseller. The middle volume carries the dictionary through the heart of the alphabet, a reference no literary library of the age lacked.
andersen-fairy-tales-1872:
Hans Christian Andersen's Fairy Tales appear here in the classic English translation of his immortal Danish tales. The mermaid, the snow queen, the ugly duckling, and the steadfast tin soldier people this beloved set of stories. Andersen, a shoemaker's son from Odense, published his first tales for children in 1835.

The Little Mermaid trades her voice for legs and dissolves into sea foam for love of a prince. The Snow Queen sends Gerda through seasons and robbers to melt Kai's frozen heart with her warm tears of love. The Ugly Duckling, read as Andersen's own life, turns scorn and winter into a swan's spring at last. His tales, unlike the Grimms', were invented, not collected, and their melancholy is a poet's own in every line. In the classic English dress here, they formed the nursery canon of the English-speaking world.
arxiv-2510-00072:
Chenhui Xu and a large team of co-authors published this 2025 paper presenting Geo-R1, a way to teach AI models geographic reasoning. The models at issue read both images and text, and they often falter on map and place questions. Geo-R1 trains them in two stages built around clear, step-by-step thinking. The team released their trained model openly for others to use.

In stage one, the model learns from made-up examples that show geographic thinking in steps. In stage two, it practices with reinforcement learning on paired views of the same place. Matching views across angles gives a reward signal that is easy to check. Geo-R1 then topped rival models on the standard geospatial reasoning tests used in the paper. The work shows that training for reasoning, not just facts, lifts place-based skills.
arxiv-2510-00172:
Amirhossein Abaskohi and colleagues at ServiceNow Research published this 2025 paper introducing DRBench, a benchmark for AI research agents. Companies want agents that can answer hard, open-ended questions using private files plus the public web. Older benchmarks test only simple lookups, so they miss that enterprise reality. DRBench builds fifteen deep research tasks across ten business domains.

Each task is grounded in a realistic employee persona and a mixed search space. Sources span email, chat threads, cloud files, office software, and the open web. Human reviewers checked every synthesized task before release. Scoring rewards recall of key insights, factual accuracy, and clear report structure. The team ran leading open and closed models through the benchmark and mapped their failure modes. The results chart what enterprise research agents still cannot do reliably.
arxiv-2510-00272:
Odichimnma Ezeji and four colleagues published this 2025 robotics paper on making a fast control method safer. Model Predictive Path Integral control steers robots by sampling many candidate trajectories and averaging the best. It handles nonlinear tasks quickly, yet offers no hard promise that limits will be respected. The authors bolt on a probabilistic safety layer called BC-MPPI.

The layer attaches a learned surrogate to every state and input constraint. At each replanning step the surrogate estimates the chance that a candidate path stays feasible. That chance scales the path's weight, quietly suppressing rollouts likely to collide or break limits. The surrogate was trained on one thousand offline simulations beforehand. On a simulated quadrotor dodging still and moving obstacles, the controller kept its safety margins. The design needs no hand-tuned penalty costs and fits certification workflows well.
arxiv-2510-00472:
Ben Abramowitz wrote this 2025 theory paper introducing capital games, a twist on classical game theory. In a standard game, each player's payoffs feed a fixed utility function. In a capital game, payoffs are known but need not behave like von Neumann-Morgenstern utilities. Instead, each player's own payoff dynamics generate what utility means for them.

Different players may run different dynamics, driven by their actions and interactions over time. Abramowitz makes no assumption about where those dynamics originate. He defines a solution concept called growth equilibrium for these games. The main theorem shows growth equilibria correspond exactly to Nash equilibria of standard games. That bridge lets decades of game theory machinery transfer into the new setting. The paper reframes familiar strategic analysis around growth, a natural language for wealth and capital problems.
arxiv-2510-00572:
Ahsan Farabi, Muhaiminul Rashid Shad, and Israt Khandaker published this 2025 paper on catching network intrusions with deep learning. Attack traffic evolves constantly, and benchmark datasets bury rare attack types under normal flows. Their framework, IntrusionX, pairs convolutional layers for local patterns with memory networks for timing. A squirrel-inspired search algorithm tunes the model's settings automatically.

Careful preprocessing, stratified splitting, and dynamic class weights fight the imbalance problem head-on. On the NSL-KDD benchmark, binary detection reached about ninety-eight percent accuracy. The harder five-class task landed near eighty-seven percent accuracy overall. Rare classes saw the biggest recall gains, with one jumping above ninety percent. The rarest attack family still resisted, reaching only about seventy-one percent recall. The authors stress reproducibility and release their code for other teams to test.
arxiv-2510-00772:
Li and Tringali study global isomorphisms between semigroups in this 2025 arXiv paper on algebra. A semigroup's subsets can themselves be multiplied setwise, forming a larger power semigroup. Two semigroups are globally isomorphic when their power semigroups match, which is weaker than being isomorphic directly. A class of semigroups is globally closed if nothing outside the class can be globally isomorphic to a member inside it.

The authors prove that three important classes are each globally closed: groups, torsion-free monoids, and numerical monoids. The group result extends a theorem of Shafer from 1967. The numerical monoid result is the hardest, leaning on the torsion-free case and on a classical theorem of Kneser from additive number theory. Their arguments track how cancellative elements behave under global isomorphisms, forcing the two semigroups to be genuinely isomorphic.
arxiv-2510-01072:
Le Blanc and Lam report lessons from the community effort to verify the Rust standard library, in this 2025 paper for the Verified Software conference. Rust promises memory safety, but its unsafe escape hatch reopens the door to undefined behaviour, and the standard library uses unsafe code for speed. Amazon convened a community project to prove the library's unsafe parts safe. At least fifty contributors have joined, giving the authors a record to learn from.

The paper reviews what has been verified and compares the tools in play. Bounded model checking proved the community favourite where it applies, though no tool covers everything. Obstacles remain: functions with generic inputs, complex preconditions, and concurrency all resist techniques. The authors propose directions for better tooling and invite formal methods researchers to join. They frame the effort as a field guide for verifying unsafe Rust anywhere.
arxiv-2510-01272:
Jha and co-authors model other minds as computer programs instead of belief-desire puzzles. Predicting people matters for safe collaboration, but rational-agent assumptions break and data-hungry clones stay brittle. Everyday behavior follows scripts, the team argues, like waiting for the green light before crossing.

Their algorithm, ROTE, asks a language model to propose candidate behavioral programs. Probabilistic inference then weighs those programs against sparse observations of what someone actually did. Tests in grid worlds and a household simulator beat behavior cloning and direct model prompting. Accuracy and out-of-sample generalization improved by as much as half in some comparisons. Programs, once guessed, predict cheaply because running code costs little. Gridworld tasks gave controlled tests before the messy household world. Beliefs and desires drop out of the model entirely. Social prediction becomes program synthesis, a reframing with legs for other labs.
arxiv-2510-01472:
Zhu, Zhang, and Huang ask language models to design neural networks for specific hardware, then fix the models' habit of proposing the same safe designs forever. Supernet search burns GPU days, while model-driven search is fast but suffers exploration bias. Latency ranges across the space go unexplored when the proposer keeps revisiting favorites.

Their framework partitions the search space by complexity, forcing coverage of every niche. A prompt co-evolution loop updates design heuristics from each round's results. Guided evolution then breeds architectures inside each partition in parallel. Accuracy and latency both improve while search cost drops. Hardware awareness means latency budgets shape the search from the start. Design heuristics accumulate in a knowledge base across rounds. Diversity is enforced structurally, not requested politely. Training-free search avoids the supernet's enormous upfront cost. Familiar architectures are comfort zones models retreat to.
arxiv-2510-01572:
Sellers revisits a family of number patterns about splitting whole numbers into colored parts. The counting function tracks partitions where even parts wear one color and odd parts may wear five. Two recent authors proved striking divisibility patterns for this count using heavy machinery from modular forms.

Short elementary proofs replace that machinery here, using generating functions and basic series manipulations. The results then widen into endless families of related divisibility statements. The original congruences reappear as single members of these larger families. Elementary routes matter because they expose why the patterns hold, not just that they hold. Ramanujan-style congruences hide at scattered indices, which makes spotting them a small triumph. Dissection splits a series into residue classes until the pattern shows itself. Colored parts sound whimsical, but the arithmetic is fully serious. Infinite families turn curiosities into theory.
arxiv-2510-01672:
Chiang and four co-authors present a 2025 particle physics study on finding triple Higgs boson events at large colliders. Their target signal decays into six bottom quarks, which appear as six b-jets in a detector. Pairing those jets back into three Higgs bosons is a hard puzzle. The team tests whether deep learning can solve that puzzle and sharpen the search.

The authors use a network called Spa-Net, which respects the pairing symmetry of the jets. Spa-Net assigns jets and classifies whole events inside one system. It separates signal from background far better than older dense networks. In their tests it tightened limits on the production rate by up to forty percent. Stronger limits would help future collider runs probe how Higgs bosons interact with each other.
arxiv-2510-01972:
Marziani and eleven co-authors synthesize evidence that accretion disks shape quasar emission lines, using the jet-loud quasar 3C 47 as their showcase. Thin disks around supermassive black holes should stamp a clear rotating signature on broad emission lines. Real line profiles usually deviate from that textbook picture, especially in radio-loud quasars. The report pulls three earlier studies into one coherent reading.

Broad hydrogen and magnesium lines lean redward in most quasars, and the most powerful radio-loud ones lean furthest. For black holes above a few hundred million solar masses, gravity and transverse motion explain those red shifts naturally. In 3C 47, the low-ionization lines fit a relativistic Keplerian disk glowing between one hundred and one thousand gravitational radii. The high-ionization lines need the disk plus a failed wind that hides part of it.
arxiv-2510-02172:
Yu and eleven co-authors teach reasoning models to distrust their own majority votes in this 2025 machine learning paper. Label-free reinforcement learning often trains on whatever answer the model produces most often. Those spurious votes can be confidently wrong, and training on them collapses. Their framework, RESTRAIN, turns missing gold labels from a dead end into a usable signal.

Self-penalization reads the model's whole answer distribution on each problem. Overconfident rollouts and low-consistency examples get penalized during training. Promising reasoning chains are preserved rather than flattened by the vote. The mechanism plugs directly into policy optimization methods such as GRPO. In their experiments, competing self-training runs destabilized or collapsed as training proceeded. RESTRAIN's accuracy stayed stable and kept improving. The authors frame restraint as the missing ingredient in experience-driven learning. Models can improve on unlabeled data if they learn when not to believe themselves.
arxiv-2510-02372:
Gupta proves a DDVV type inequality for maps out of quaternionic space forms. Her 2025 geometry paper extends a famous family of estimates. The DDVV conjecture began with Wintgen work in 1979. It links the bending of a shape to its internal geometry. Later authors widened the claim to higher dimensions. Gupta studies Riemannian maps, which preserve lengths in chosen directions. Her source spaces are quaternionic, built on four part numbers. She derives the inequality for maps into general curved targets.

The paper also settles when equality can hold. Equality cases reveal the rigid shapes behind the bound. An application section shows where the estimate can work. Such bounds constrain how maps can distort space. They also connect quantities that look unrelated at first. Pure geometry results often feed physics and data tools later. This extension completes another cell of the DDVV map.
arxiv-2510-02472:
Cai and Jelovica turn stiffened engineering panels into rich graphs for neural prediction. Their 2025 structural mechanics paper builds surrogate models for design. Stiffened panels appear in ships, aircraft, and bridges. Full finite element runs are accurate but slow. The authors split each panel into structural units. Stiffeners and the plates between them become graph pieces. Each unit carries geometry, boundary, and loading nodes. Edges encode local orientation and spatial relations. A heterogeneous graph transformer reads that structure. It predicts stress and displacement fields across the panel.

Tests used patch loaded panels and box beams. Predicted behavior matched finite element results closely. More graph heterogeneity improved prediction accuracy further. The cost was greater compute demand. Mixed materials and varied shapes stayed manageable. Non-uniform loads and supports fit the scheme naturally. Fast surrogates let engineers explore more designs.
arxiv-2510-02572:
Stewart, Robinson, and Banerjee survey the software libraries behind geospatial machine learning. Their 2025 review chapter maps a fast growing ecosystem. Earth observation data has exploded in recent years. Library support for its quirks has lagged behind. Satellite data mixes resolutions, spectra, and revisit rhythms. Coordinate systems and file formats vary wildly too. The chapter traces how domain libraries evolved to cope. TorchGeo, eo-learn, and Raster Vision get detailed profiles. Their architectures and framework links are compared side by side. Shared methods for preprocessing and benchmarking also get covered.

A crop mapping case study shows the tools at work. Pretrained models for Earth data feature in the survey. Design, licensing, and testing advice rounds out the guidance. Foundation models for geospatial data loom as the next wave. Newcomers can pick a stack with open eyes. Reproducible Earth AI depends on this plumbing.
arxiv-2510-02972:
Kumar and co-authors link neutrino mass to dark matter through flavor symmetry. Scotogenic models tie the two puzzles in one loop diagram. This team adds a discrete flavor symmetry called A4. Breaking that symmetry leaves a leftover parity rule. The parity keeps the dark matter particle stable. It also shapes how neutrino masses arise.

The model fits the two known mass gaps from sun and air data. It prefers the normal ordering of neutrino masses. A mirror-like rule between muon and tau flavors sculpts the mixing. The setup sets a floor under the lightest neutrino mass. It also predicts which octant a key mixing angle falls in. Fermion dark matter gains a lower mass bound from the mass gaps. Scalar dark matter stays open across a wide mass range. Light dark matter near fifteen giga-electronvolts survives through partner annihilation.
arxiv-2510-03172:
Zonneveld, Urbach, and Adam model how mid-scale ripples on a lens blur its images. Mid-spatial frequency errors sit awkwardly between smooth and fine. They scatter light in ways that are hard to quantify. Polynomial expansions need extreme orders to capture them. Those expansions turn numerically unstable and imprecise. The authors build their model on diffraction integrals instead. Fresnel integrals carry the surface structure straight to the image plane.

The model computes the point-spread function under such errors. Grids for the lens plane and image plane stay independent. That freedom costs extra computation, which parallelizes well. A lab setup then tested the predictions directly. A spatial light modulator imprinted custom test structures. Measured and simulated images agreed in the trials. The validation ran at low numerical aperture, a stated limit. Higher aperture tests will need phase retrieval tricks.
arxiv-2510-03372:
Heras Rivera, Neher, and Kurt present a 2025 arXiv paper on making brain elasticity maps in real time. Magnetic resonance elastography shakes the brain gently and images how waves move through tissue. Turning those waves into stiffness maps normally takes a slow, complex inversion step. The team trained an operator learning system, oNLI, to copy that slow step almost instantly. Training data came from sixty one volunteers scanned in three dimensions.

The learned system beat convolutional network baselines across the whole brain and every subregion tested. Its error on the storage stiffness measure ran near eight percent, half the error of the rival networks in the study. Matches with the reference maps stayed high in white matter, cortex, and deep structures alike. A built in structural prior helped keep fine detail sharp. Real time stiffness maps could aid brain surgery planning and studies of diseases that soften or stiffen tissue.
arxiv-2510-03572:
Sinha and Kooloth present a 2025 arXiv paper proposing an entropy based way to spot symmetry breaking in dynamical systems. Symmetry breaking marks turning points in physics, from magnets to the early universe. Their framework tracks information transfer, the directional flow of entropy between a system's observables. That flow can hint at a break before it fully arrives. The authors treat local breaks, both spontaneous and dynamical, and then extend the analysis to global breaks as well.

As a system loses symmetry locally, they show, its paths slow down markedly. At the same time, its Shannon entropy jumps upward. The pairing of slowing and entropy growth gives a measurable signature of the transition. Worked examples confirm that information based measures act as reliable early warnings and diagnostics. Engineers and physicists who watch complex systems could use such signals to anticipate tipping points instead of only explaining them afterward.
arxiv-2510-03772:
Miszczak presents a 2025 arXiv paper asking whether letting agents switch groups helps cooperation survive in a public goods game played on a lattice. Cooperation is puzzling because free riders should undercut it, yet it flourishes without punishment or reputation in systems. The model extends work on interaction diversity by letting a subpopulation of roaming agents reevaluate and change their neighborhoods. The rest play with fixed neighbors. The author varies how many agents roam.

Reevaluation by roaming agents boosted the emergence of cooperation in the simulations. Too much switching, however, turned destructive, and participation of roamers undermined the cooperative clusters. Tuned to the level, roaming reproduced behavior seen in scale free network models. The dial between stability and churn is the paper's contribution: neighborhoods must last long enough for reciprocity to pay, but not forever. Community programs and online platforms manipulate this dial when they set group sizes and mixing rules.
arxiv-2510-04072:
Wang and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on stabilizing reinforcement learning for language model reasoning. The popular GRPO algorithm trains on fresh rollouts, but early rollouts are weak, so their noisy rewards destabilize updates. Reusing each batch for several steps helps, yet naive reuse drifts off-policy and degrades performance. The authors split every training step into three stages to get reuse without the drift.

First, a short fast trajectory takes several inner steps on the same batch. Next, a reposition mechanism pulls the model back and controls how far it has strayed. A final slow correction then applies the real update, with the objective and rollout process unchanged. On math reasoning benchmarks, it beat GRPO by up to a few points of average accuracy. It also needed several times fewer rollouts and far less wall-clock time to match GRPO's best results.
arxiv-2510-04172:
Li and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper revisiting a key correction in the tau-lepton route to the muon's anomalous magnetic moment. Tau decay data can substitute for electron-positron collision data when computing the hadronic vacuum polarization contribution. That substitution needs isospin-breaking corrections, and the long-distance electromagnetic correction from real photon radiation is decisive. 

The authors recompute the radiative tau decay amplitude within resonance chiral theory. The single unknown coupling is redetermined from omega meson decay, now counting vector and scalar resonance contributions together. Combining everything with the remaining inputs from the 2025 muon g-2 White Paper shifts the final value noticeably. It lands nearly three standard deviations from the newest world average after Fermilab's measurement. The tau-based determination thus remains a live source of tension in this precision test of the Standard Model.
arxiv-2510-04472:
Baber Jan and four coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on finding objects that hide in plain sight. Camouflaged objects blend with their background in color, texture, and broken edges. Standard vision models miss them, since they evolved or were built to avoid notice. Older detectors stacked many add on modules, one for edges, one for attention, and so on. The stacks grew heavy and forced low resolution work that erased fine detail.

Their network, SPEGNet, replaces the stack with one unified design. It merges features across scales with channel calibration and spatial enhancement, so boundaries arise from rich context directly. A refinement stage adjusts edges with the strongest effect at middle resolutions. The design balances boundary precision against regional consistency in its masks. On three public benchmarks, the network posted top scores among rival methods. It handled tiny objects, large pattern matched ones, occlusion, and unclear edges.
arxiv-2510-04872:
Ercolino and five coauthors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on the census of exploding stars. A supernova keeps the imprint of the envelope its star wore at death. Stars with partners swap mass before exploding, which reshapes those envelopes. The team computed grids of binary star evolution in detail. They synthesized populations and varied the rules for which stars explode.

With an interacting binary share of two thirds, the mix matched surveys. Two thirds of explosions came out as hydrogen rich type II events, and one third as stripped type Ibc. Three quarters of the stripped progenitors had donated mass to a partner. Hydrogen rich progenitors had instead gained mass from a companion. Interacting explosions, where collapse hits during or after mass transfer, made up five percent. That share matches the interacting supernova classes seen in the sky. Binary life lowered the ejected mass of stripped events below star predictions.
arxiv-2510-05372:
Karen L. Collins and four co-authors ask which graphs are algebraic squares in this 2025 arXiv paper. Under the gluing algebra, a graph is square when it equals a graph glued to itself. Such squares feed into homomorphism density inequalities like Sidorenko's conjecture. Prior work chased those applications rather than the property itself.

The authors reframe squareness through butterfly involutions and symmetry. They derive necessary and sufficient conditions for a graph to be square. Applying them, they classify several classical families as square or not square. Joins and four kinds of graph products preserve squareness when one factor is square. Circulant examples mark the boundary, with some small cases square and larger ones provably not.
arxiv-2510-05872:
Nakamura and Ankerhold simulate two-qubit gates under realistic non-Markovian noise. Each superconducting qubit couples to its own reservoir with memory effects. Standard master equations miss the subtle qubit-reservoir correlations involved. Their 2025 study uses a numerically exact technique to capture them.

First, the rotating wave approximation is checked against disentanglement dynamics. Earlier work imposed it on the qubit-reservoir coupling without full validation. Second, entanglement creation and destruction are tracked through a square-root iSWAP gate. Reservoir memory effects shape both processes during and after the gate. Third, a Hadamard-plus-CNOT sequence is compared across decomposition schemes. Guiding device improvement is the stated purpose of the precision. As fidelities climb, minute residual effects become the limiting factor. Gate decomposition choice emerges as a practical design lever. Different noise types and qubit parameters run through all three studies.
arxiv-2510-05972:
Mantenoglou and colleagues benchmark language model planning under temporal constraints. Models are increasingly tested on planning tasks phrased in natural language. Real deployments add safety and timing constraints that benchmarks usually omit. Their 2025 LexiCon benchmark imposes temporal constraints on existing planning environments.

Constrained problems are translated into natural language for the model. New environments can be added through generators with automatically constructed constraints. Hardness can therefore scale as model planning improves. Experiments include frontier reasoning models such as GPT-5 and o3. Performance deteriorates steadily as the degree of constrainedness increases. Principled evaluation design is the benchmark's stated contribution to the field. Safety-critical settings motivate testing constraints explicitly rather than assuming compliance. Formal specification languages made such constraints hard for non-experts before. Natural language communication lowers that barrier for users. Constraint adherence, not raw planning, is the capability being isolated.
arxiv-2510-06072:
Muppidi and Radfar teach a network to read emotions from speech in a 2025 paper from Stony Brook University. Their model, EmoHRNet, adapts a high-resolution network design built for image analysis. Audio clips are first converted into spectrograms, which are pictures of how sound energy varies over time.

Most networks shrink their input early and lose detail. EmoHRNet instead keeps high-resolution features alive through every layer and fuses them with coarser views at several scales. That design preserves small vocal cues and broad emotional patterns. The model scored about 92 percent accuracy on the RAVDESS and EMOVO speech collections in the authors' tests. It reached about 80 percent on the harder IEMOCAP collection and beat the models they compared against. Results like these support emotion-aware interfaces that respond to how people sound, not just what they say.
arxiv-2510-06172:
Huo and four co-authors present Anchor, a technique for stabilizing quantum program output. Today's noisy intermediate-scale quantum machines suffer output-corrupting hardware noise. Worse, one program's output fidelity swings between machines and between days. Users cannot get consistent results even when rerunning the same program.

Existing tools attack average error rates but ignore variability. Anchor uses linear programming to choose how a program runs so performance stays steady. In evaluation, Anchor cut variability by about seventy-three percent on average versus a state-of-the-art error-reduction implementation. The authors call Anchor the first technique aimed squarely at variability over mean accuracy. For cloud users, predictable output matters almost as much as raw fidelity. A program behaving the same on Tuesday as on Monday is easier to debug, benchmark, and trust.
arxiv-2510-06472:
Rhodes and Woolley use speculative design fiction to imagine citizen-curated virtual museums in a 2025 human-computer interaction paper. Professional curators have monopolized museum-making for centuries. Cheap virtual reality and 3D capture could hand that power to citizens. The paper explores that future from inside.

Their scenario follows citizen curators designing and sharing immersive virtual museums. Galleries mix tangible heritage artifacts with intangible virtual elements and interactive experiences. Visitors take home asset packs. Each pack bundles 3D artifact models, curation assets, and interactive experiences. An envisaged visit shows physical and virtual experiences interplaying. The fiction then weighs consequences. Institutional resource demands could shift sharply. Traditional museums face competition and new partnership models. The value lies in surfacing these questions while the future museum is still cheap to argue about.
arxiv-2510-06572:
Seyed Sajadi and Supakchai Ponglertsakul study gravity in three dimensions, a simpler setting that still contains black holes. Their 2025 paper examines warped anti-de Sitter space, a twisted version of a standard curved spacetime. A proposed set of boundary rules was meant to make the Cardy formula work for such spaces. The authors test those rules inside new massive gravity.

They work out the allowed solutions, the symmetries at the boundary, and the related charge algebra. The surface charges turn out to be finite, which is a good sign. However, the charges are not integrable across the full solution space. Restricting to a smaller sector fixes that problem. Finally, they prove the Cardy formula correctly reproduces the entropy of a warped BTZ black hole. That check supports the boundary rules as a sound description of these warped spacetimes.
arxiv-2510-06772:
Alex Kerin, Barbara Dietz, and Joachim Brand find a puzzle in the energy levels of three trapped particles. Their 2025 paper studies quantum chaos, where energy levels push each other apart in patterns. The strongest known pattern belongs to the symplectic symmetry class, which is rare in nature. That class also forces every level to come in a doubled pair.

The team simulated identical bosons and uneven-mass fermions in a harmonic trap. With weak contact interactions, the levels repelled each other as strongly as the symplectic pattern predicts. Yet the doubled levels were absent, so that symmetry cannot explain the result. The measured repulsion follows the quartic pattern named in the title. With strong interactions, the statistics turn regular instead, matching known exact solutions. A Rosenzweig-Porter model describes the switch between the two regimes. The setup could be built with cold atoms in microtraps or optical lattices.
arxiv-2510-06872:
Frederic Gmeiner, Kenneth Holstein, and Nikolas Martelaro develop a better way to prototype proactive AI assistants. Their paper describes agents that watch a user's screen and offer help in real time. Such agents must react to speech and screen activity instantly. Ordinary prompt testing cannot capture that situational complexity well.

Their case study built SocraBot, an assistant for people doing hands-on domain tasks. Two methods drive their prototyping pipeline. Counterfactual video replay lets them rerun a recorded moment after changing a prompt, to see if the new behavior improves. A hybrid Wizard-of-Oz method mixes live human control with the model during trials. Together, the methods exposed prompt problems that static tests missed. The team shifted toward separate prompts for distinct tasks and clearer message wording. Designers of real-time agents gain a practical recipe here. Replaying the exact moment that failed beats guessing from logs alone.
arxiv-2510-07372:
Marin Guzman and co-authors propose experiments for quantum gates that run themselves. Their 2025 paper concerns autonomous quantum machines, which act without time-dependent external control. Classical controllers limit coherence and geometry in today's quantum hardware. A recent experiment showed autonomous reset of a qubit can work. This team extends the idea to logic gates on three platforms. For Rydberg atoms, a blockade interaction or an ultrafast jump can drive an entangling gate on its own. Passive lasers supply the control without timed pulses.

For trapped ions, sculpting the trap shape or using a ring trap enables mostly autonomous gates. Superconducting circuits can host autonomous phase and exchange gates through circuit quantum electrodynamics. One worked example reaches fidelity very near perfection for a quarter-turn rotation. The authors present the designs as building blocks for circuits that need far less classical oversight.
arxiv-2510-07472:
Adhikari and a large team characterize the solar wind where it crosses the Alfven speed, using Parker Solar Probe data. Their 2025 paper extends an earlier turbulence study from two encounters to encounters eight through nineteen. Deep in the Sun's atmosphere the wind flows slower than magnetic waves can travel; far out, it outruns them. The probe now samples the slow, sub-Alfvenic regime often as it dives lower. The team compares turbulence amplitude, magnetic anisotropy, intermittency, and switchbacks, the sudden field folds common near the Sun, across the three regimes, isolating intervals right at the transition.

Sub-Alfvenic wind shows smaller normalized fluctuation amplitude than its faster counterpart. Its turbulence is also more anisotropic, stretched along the field. Intermittency barely changes across regimes, while field deflections weaken on average in the slow wind.
arxiv-2510-07772:
Zhou and five coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on breaking tasks into pieces that language models can solve. Models fail on complex, multi-step problems. Ways to split tasks rely on rules of thumb or expert design. The authors want a method guided by a complexity measure. Their framework, ACONIC, recasts a task as a constraint problem. Graph measures on that problem then say where the difficulty sits.

ACONIC splits tasks so local complexity drops while the task stays satisfiable. The measure is treewidth, a gauge of how tangled the constraint graph is. On a logic benchmark and a database querying benchmark, guided decomposition helped agents substantially. Completion gains reached up to fifteen points on the logic tasks. On the database tasks they reached up to forty points. The results map difficulty frontiers for model reasoning and hint at more reliable systems built on theory.
arxiv-2510-07872:
Lee, Gross, Fukami, and Jiang wrote this 2025 quantum algorithms paper on the state hidden subgroup problem. That problem generalizes a classic task. Instead of a function hiding a subgroup, a quantum state carries the symmetry. The authors solve the problem for many copies of the dihedral group of the square, a non-abelian group. Their interest includes exotic stabilizers.

The algorithm runs in polynomial time, using constant-depth circuits. It extends work on abelian groups. As a special case, it also solves the ordinary hidden subgroup problem on this group. The authors point to Hamiltonian spectroscopy. Their takeaway is that the representation structure decides solvability here. Some non-abelian cases may yield to representation-specific methods even when the general problem stays hard. Weak Fourier sampling is the technique adapted for the job. The paper gives a foothold here.
arxiv-2510-07972:
Jiao and eight coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on teaching language models to judge product relevance for Taobao search. Shoppers type a query, and the system must decide which products truly match. Chain-of-thought reasoning makes such judgments explainable, but training recipes lag. Supervised tuning and preference optimization generalize poorly on rare queries. Reward-only reinforcement learning gives feedback too sparse to fix bad middle steps.

Their framework, TaoSR-SHE, grades reasoning step by step. A generative reward model scores each step, checked against a human-annotated offline verifier. Training concentrates on the steps that matter most, right or wrong. Data filtering keeps exploration diverse, and a curriculum grows task difficulty in stages. On real Taobao benchmarks, the framework beat supervised, preference, and group-relative baselines on accuracy. Reasoning quality and interpretability improved as well. The work shows how stepwise examination can discipline model judgment in production search.
arxiv-2510-08172:
Vassallo, Bolland, and eleven coauthors wrote this 2025 energy systems paper proposing a market where households trade their grid usage limits. Rooftop solar, electric vehicles, and batteries strain low-voltage networks built for one-way flow. Operators increasingly assign dynamic operating envelopes, time-varying caps on each customer's injection or withdrawal. Their system, SecuLEx, lets customers exchange parts of their envelopes through a market after the operator sets secure initial limits.

The authors formalize the paradigm and test it on a small low-voltage network. Both allocation and trading proved computationally tractable. Compared with traditional approaches, the market reduced renewable curtailment and improved grid utilization and social welfare. Security stays guaranteed because trades only reshuffle certified limits. If it scales, such markets could squeeze more clean energy through existing wires, delaying expensive upgrades.
arxiv-2510-08272:
Cédrick Austa, Jan Tobias Mühlberg, and Jean-Michel Dricot assess cache timing flaws on RISC-V chips in a 2025 arXiv paper. RISC-V is an open chip design that more makers now adopt. Attackers can exploit cache timing, where memory access speeds leak secret data. Test tools exist for Intel and ARM chips, but RISC-V lacked a matching suite.

The team ported a known Intel benchmark suite for cache timing flaws to RISC-V. They ran it on three commercial cores: the T-Head C910 and the SiFive U54 and U74. The C910 showed more distinct timing types than the other two cores. That pattern suggests code on the C910 faces more sources of leakage. About 65.9 percent of benchmark flaws appeared on all three processors, the team found. Only 6.8 percent were absent from every core tested.
arxiv-2510-08472:
Alvan Arulandu, Ilias Diakonikolas, Daniel Kane, and Jerry Li give the first efficient agnostic tomography for mixed product states in a 2025 arXiv paper. Tomography means reconstructing a quantum state from measurements on many copies. Agnostic tomography assumes the target is only close to a chosen family, here product mixed states. Prior algorithms handled only pure-state families like product or stabilizer states.

Their algorithm takes copies of a state near some product mixed state and returns a near-optimal product approximation. The output error scales mildly with the distance to the family, they prove. It uses polynomially many copies, runs in polynomial time, and needs only single-qubit measurements on single copies. The key step reduces the quantum task to robustly learning binary product distributions, a classic statistics problem. A nearly optimal solver for that classical task completes the algorithm.
arxiv-2510-08572:
Rocktim Jyoti Das and co-authors bootstrap robot manipulation training data with language model planners in a 2025 arXiv paper. Robotics lacks the internet-scale demonstration libraries that powered progress in vision and language. Collecting manipulation examples by hand is slow and costly. Their framework, BLAZER, generates its own training demonstrations automatically in simulation.

Zero-shot language model planners produce candidate demonstrations for diverse manipulation tasks. Successful examples then fine-tune the language model itself, improving its planning without human supervision. Although training uses the simulator's internal state, the learned skills transfer to sensor-based manipulation. Extensive experiments showed large gains in zero-shot manipulation in simulated and real environments. BLAZER also improved on tasks outside its training pool. It even enabled downscaling to smaller language models while keeping performance, the authors report.
arxiv-2510-08672:
Alex Meiburg, Leonardo Lessa, and Rodolfo Soldati machine-check a major quantum information theorem in a 2025 arXiv paper. The Generalized Quantum Stein's Lemma gives relative entropy an operational meaning in quantum hypothesis testing and resource theories. Its original proof contained a gap, prompting a search for a corrected argument. The authors formalize the 2024 Hayashi-Yamasaki proof in the Lean theorem prover.

They call it the most technically demanding physics theorem with a computer-verified proof to date. The formalization builds side results in topology, operator algebra, and analysis along the way. Minor imprecisions in the published proof surfaced and were rectified during the work. A sharper definition of what a quantum resource theory is also emerged from the effort. Their Lean-QuantumInfo library gains a robust foundation for a broader collaborative program. Formalizing quantum theory at this depth is the long-term goal.
arxiv-2510-09072:
Tiwari, Chakraborty, and Kopparapu make speech emotion recognition hold up outside the clean lab, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A system that reads anger or joy from a voice degrades quickly in noisy rooms, and it often stumbles on recordings from a different source than its training data. The team's answer works in two steps, both aimed at the internal features the system learns from speech.

First, a disentangling step pulls out features that separate the emotion classes while keeping the similarities that neighboring emotions honestly share. Next, an alignment step projects those features into a shared space chosen to stay maximally tied to the original speech. A classifier trained on clean recordings from public datasets then runs on these refined embeddings. Tested on speech it had never seen, both noisy and from foreign corpora, the system performed better than before under exactly the conditions that usually break it.
arxiv-2510-09172:
García-González proposes a rule-based recipe for describing research software so other scientists can find, cite, and reuse it, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Experiments increasingly depend on code, and reproducibility demands that the code itself follow the FAIR principles: findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable. CodeMeta is a shared vocabulary for software metadata, but the facts about a program are scattered across different formats and places. Existing generators handle only narrow cases.

His approach uses declarative mapping rules, written in a language called ShExML, stating how each scattered fact becomes CodeMeta. He built three mapping sets, called crosswalks, then merged them to produce metadata files for two real software packages. Outputs were checked automatically with two validation languages, and the workflow reruns with minimal human help when a new version ships. The paper doubles as a worked example other developers can copy into their own repositories.
arxiv-2510-09372:
Križan Jurinović, Merry Mitra, Rakesh Mukherjee, and Thomas Ouldridge review the design of DNA strand displacement reactions in a 2025 arXiv paper. In such a reaction, one DNA strand pushes another off a shared partner strand. These reactions power many synthetic DNA systems, including molecular circuits, sensors, and tiny machines built from DNA.

The review surveys recent design frameworks that serve different goals, starting setups, and conditions. It focuses on single reactions and asks what controls their speed, which structural features matter, and where current models fall short. Predicting reaction kinetics, meaning how fast the swap happens, remains a key challenge. The authors point to promising innovations and lay out what is still blocking accurate prediction. They close with directions toward DNA systems whose behaviour is more robust and more programmable.
arxiv-2510-09472:
Manuel Vargas Guzmán, Jakub Szymanik, and Maciej Malicki test how well language models handle logic in a 2025 arXiv paper. Two skills matter for generalisation: compositionality, the grasp of single rules that combine into complex inferences, and recursiveness, the repeated application of rules to build deep reasoning. The two are often lumped together, and the authors set out to separate them.

Their benchmark extends classical syllogisms, the old two-premise argument forms, into more complex structures that still allow controlled testing. Models proved reasonably good at recursiveness but struggled with compositionality. Performance also varied sharply by syllogism type, from near-perfect accuracy to far lower scores. To get a reliable prover, the authors propose a hybrid architecture that pairs neural computation with symbolic reasoning. The neural parts speed processing while the symbolic parts keep inference robust and efficient.
arxiv-2510-09672:
Kalin Dimitrov, the sole author, proposes a tiny text symbol for sharing locations in a 2025 arXiv paper. People already write at-signs for identity and hashtags for topics, but plain text has no standard way to mention a physical place. Pingmark fills that gap with a two-character trigger, an exclamation mark followed by an at-sign, that compliant apps interpret as a spatial mention.

When an app sees the trigger, it generates a standard resolver link carrying latitude, longitude, and an optional timestamp. No registration is required, and the design leans on open mapping technologies. Location data is produced locally and ephemerally, which protects privacy by never sending it to a central service by default. The paper lays out the Pingmark Protocol Specification, version zero point one, covering its motivation, syntax, and design, along with its reference resolver, aiming at an open internet standard.
arxiv-2510-09772:
J Bätz, M Mugrauer, and six co-authors check whether selected middleweight stars are single or multiple in a 2025 arXiv paper. They monitored thirteen intermediate-mass stars, between two and six times the Sun's mass, with radial velocity measurements at the University Observatory Jena in Germany. Radial velocity tracks a star's wobble along the line of sight, revealing unseen companions.

Observations ran from late April to early September 2024 with an échelle spectrograph called FLECHAS. Eight stars held constant velocity throughout, showing no sign of a close companion in that window. Five stars varied significantly, and for each the team fitted Keplerian orbits and derived the elements of these spectroscopic binary systems. They also searched the Gaia mission's third data release for wide companions of all targets. The work adds to the census covering bright, nearby multiple stars, a basic input for understanding how star systems form.
arxiv-2510-09872:
Srivastava and co-authors introduce WARC-Bench in this 2025 arXiv paper on AI web agents. The benchmark tests agents on subtasks, the short steps inside web use, such as picking the right date in a date picker or scrolling a panel to find hidden text. It is built from web archives rather than live sites.

The set holds 438 tasks drawn from real websites. Each task isolates one interaction skill, so failures point to a clear cause. The authors argue that mastering such subtasks is a required step before agents can handle full, complex browsing jobs. WARC-Bench gives labs a shared way to measure that skill in multimodal agents, which work from both screen images and text.
arxiv-2510-09972:
Smith-Perez and co-authors study aromatic molecules in the planetary nebula NGC 7027 in this 2025 arXiv paper in astrophysics. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, large carbon ring molecules, hold a big share of the universe's carbon. They dominate the mid-infrared glow of many space environments.

These molecules are thought to form in the outflows of dying stars, but their formation and growth remain poorly understood. NGC 7027 is a young nebula where the process can be watched closely. The team examines the diversity of PAH spectra there, the fingerprints that reveal which aromatic carriers are present. Tracing how those spectra vary shows how the carbon carriers evolve as the nebula ages.
arxiv-2510-10072:
Cai and co-authors introduce Unilaw-R1 in this 2025 arXiv paper on language models for law. Reasoning models are advancing in many domains, but their skill at complex legal problems is little explored. Unilaw-R1 is a model tailored for legal reasoning at a lightweight scale of seven billion parameters.

The authors target three core challenges: gaps in legal knowledge, unreliable reasoning logic, and weak generalization to real legal business. They train with reinforcement learning and iterative inference, letting the model refine its answers over rounds. The small scale cuts deployment cost for law firms and courts. The paper tests whether a focused, modest model can beat general models on the reasoning lawyers actually need.
arxiv-2510-10172:
Kolountzakis, Nir Lev, and Máté Matolcsi study the Turán and Delsarte problems in this 2025 arXiv paper in harmonic analysis. Both problems optimize over positive definite functions on Euclidean space, with limits on where the function may live and where it must keep one sign. They connect to tiling and packing questions in geometry.

The authors also study the dual problems, the mirror optimization problems that bound the originals. In finite group settings, weak and strong duality between these problems hold automatically. The paper examines how much of that duality survives on Euclidean space. Progress here feeds bounds on sphere packing and related extremal problems, where Turán and Delsarte type estimates are standard tools.
arxiv-2510-10572:
Byeongchan Lee offers a theory of why contrastive learning works, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Self-supervised methods learn useful features from unlabeled data and perform well, yet theory lags practice. Lee frames this learning as an approximation to supervised learning objectives, where labels would be known. From that framing he derives a loss close to popular contrastive losses such as InfoNCE.

The derivation brings out two ideas. One is prototype bias, a distortion tied to the reference points used in training. The other is a balanced contrastive loss, which adjusts how strongly positive and negative pairs pull on the learned features. Lee shows how parts of the framework match common practice in the field. He also tests the effect of balancing positive and negative pairs, confirming the framework's predictions.
arxiv-2510-10672:
Md Nahid Hasan and three co-authors model how rumors spread through a network when people hesitate and forget, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Rumor dynamics resemble epidemics, and several rumors can circulate at once, like cross infecting diseases. Their I2E2S2R model sorts people into compartments, including the ignorant, the exposed, spreaders, and the recovered, with hesitation and forgetting built in. The network is homogeneous, meaning members have similar numbers of contacts.

From the model's mean field equations, the authors compute the rumor free equilibrium and the basic reproduction number, the threshold quantity that decides whether a rumor takes off. Using a Lyapunov function and the LaSalle invariance principle, they prove the rumor free state is globally stable under the right conditions. Simulations show that denser networks spread rumors faster. Making people aware helps rumors die out sooner, and diverting them toward exact information lessens the spread.
arxiv-2510-11172:
Regression models for spatial data often let each region have its own value, but neighboring regions usually deserve similar values. Yuko Kakikawa develops a model choice criterion for exactly this setting in a 2025 arXiv statistics paper. The work concerns spatially varying coefficient models fitted with a Bayesian generalized fused lasso, a prior that encourages adjacent regions to share values.

The standard criterion WAIC does not address how complex the class of priors should be here. Kakikawa adapts PIIC to this setting, deriving the estimator's asymptotic properties while keeping the prior's influence rather than assuming selection consistency. It is built as a bias-corrected estimate of predictive risk. In tests PIIC beat WAIC at reducing predictive risk, and on real data the two criteria gave very different answers.
arxiv-2510-11372:
Fine-tuning a language model on private or copyrighted text can teach it to recite that text verbatim, and the danger window opens earlier than most practitioners assume. Dean L. Slack and Noura Al Moubayed track memorization during fine-tuning in this 2025 arXiv paper. They trained Pythia, Llama3, and Mistral models, from 1.4 to 70 billion parameters, on common evaluation datasets and measured verbatim memorization throughout training.

Memorization rises dramatically in the first few epochs, often well before validation perplexity or task performance reaches its best point. A simple n-gram memorization score reliably moves before verbatim memorization appears, so using it as an early-stopping signal curbs memorization with minimal performance loss. The authors also add an n-gram-aware term to the training loss. That regularizer cut memorization by up to 40 percent across all model families tested, with smaller performance trade-offs than an existing mitigation strategy.
arxiv-2510-11672:
Yaroslav Kopylov and Vadim Leshkov work in homological algebra, the study of exact sequences and the structures that measure where exactness fails. Their 2025 arXiv paper examines commutative squares, which are small diagrams of objects and arrows, inside Grandis homological categories. These categories generalize the settings where homology is usually done. The authors focus on two invariants from Lambek that capture the defect of a square, built from kernels and images.

Kopylov and Leshkov prove that certain null sequences proposed by Nomura always exist in these categories. A null sequence is a chain whose consecutive arrows compose to zero. They also give sufficient conditions for those sequences to be exact, meaning the chains capture the homology precisely. Finally, they prove that left and right homology coincide in this setting. That coincidence removes an ambiguity that could otherwise force two separate theories.
arxiv-2510-12172:
Hung Pham and four colleagues steal the questions, not the data, from supposedly secure cloud stream processors. Streams run on untrusted clouds, so engines hide inside Intel SGX enclaves. Encrypting data is standard, but queries encode application logic worth stealing too. Their 2025 arXiv paper shows a malicious cloud provider can extract those queries by timing alone.

The attack works in two phases. Offline, the attacker profiles each stream operator's execution time on synthetic data, training a model that fingerprints operators. Online, the attacker isolates a victim query's operators, watches its timing, and identifies them with the model. Implemented against SecureStream on standard benchmarks, the attack recovered operators with success rates up to ninety-two percent. Defenses exist and need not be ruinously expensive, the authors note, but the lesson stands: an enclave that hides content while leaking duration hides less than its owners think.
arxiv-2510-12472:
Aggarwal and co-authors test exotic dark energy models against quasar and other cosmic observations, in a 2025 arXiv paper published in Annals of Physics. Their framework is f(Q) gravity, where gravity arises from non metricity rather than curvature. As the background fluid they use Chaplygin gas variants, fluids proposed to explain dark energy, alongside ordinary matter and radiation.

They constrain the models with three datasets: Hubble expansion measurements, baryon acoustic oscillation data, and quasistellar objects. For the quasar data they propose an analytic formula for distance errors, with no Monte Carlo simulations. Kinematic diagnostics, including the deceleration and jerk parameters and the Om diagnostic, measure departures from the standard model. The joint analysis places the universe's shift from decelerating to accelerating expansion at model dependent redshifts, each differing from the standard value. The results map how far these models stray from the standard picture.
arxiv-2510-12572:
Patra and a large team observe a star being torn apart by a black hole away from its galaxy's center, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. The event, AT 2024tvd, is the first optically chosen off nuclear tidal disruption event, where a wandering black hole shreds a passing star. Telescopes in space and on the ground captured its spectrum and images.

The host galaxy looks undisturbed, with smooth morphology. The team built the first near simultaneous energy distribution, from X-rays to infrared, for such an event. They split it into three components: the disruption's accretion flow, heated dust, and an unresolved nuclear star cluster. The accretion component implies a black hole of a few hundred thousand solar masses, feeding above its Eddington limit. The extra stellar light matches a massive star cluster or ultra compact dwarf. The authors favor a minor merger origin for the wandering black hole.
arxiv-2510-12672:
Belo, Soares, and Guimaraes suppress harmful outputs from language models by editing their internal representations at answer time, with no retraining, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Jailbreak prompts can trick models into bypassing safety guardrails. Their method, CALM, works on the latent representations of the model's last layer during inference.

CALM adapts concept whitening, a technique from computer vision, paired with orthogonal projection. It identifies latent directions associated with harmful concepts and removes those components from the representation while preserving the rest of the model's behavior. Experiments show CALM cuts harmful outputs and outperforms baseline methods on most metrics they tracked. The approach needs no additional training data and no fine tuning, and it adds only a small computational overhead at inference. The authors present it as a lightweight safety layer that can sit on top of an already deployed model.
arxiv-2510-12772:
Serrano de Haro and co-authors introduce TopROI in this 2025 arXiv paper, a method for dividing tissue images into regions of interest. Medical imaging now produces large point clouds, meaning sets of measured cell positions, but researchers usually cut them into plain square grids. Those grids ignore the tissue's own structure and can split meaningful features apart.

TopROI builds networks from cell neighborhoods and adds topology, the study of shapes and loops, to guide how points are grouped into communities. On synthetic clouds mimicking glands it kept the true structures better than grid and purely geometric methods. Applied to human colorectal cancer biopsies, it preserved crypt-like structures and revealed a gradual loss of organization from healthy tissue to carcinoma.
arxiv-2510-12972:
Zhong and colleagues test mobile apps by actually using them in this 2025 arXiv paper. Accessibility checkers help developers find barriers for users with disabilities, but most examine static screens or mechanically generated states, missing errors that only appear during real interaction. The authors call these functiona11ity errors, blending functionality with the accessibility shorthand a11y.

Their system, TaskAudit, generates interactive tasks from app screens, sends agents equipped with a screen reader proxy to perform them, and analyzes the interaction traces for accessibility errors. On real-world apps it found forty-eight such errors across fifty-four screens, while existing checkers found only between four and twenty. The analysis surfaced recurring patterns the older tools missed, including labels that mismatch what a control actually does, cluttered navigation, and inappropriate feedback after actions.
arxiv-2510-13072:
Wei and Xiao prove a concavity property for the first eigenfunction of the Laplacian in hyperbolic space in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. The first eigenfunction is the basic vibration mode of a domain, vanishing at its boundary. Since the 1970s it has been known that on convex Euclidean domains its logarithm is concave, meaning it bulges in a controlled way. Hyperbolic space, with its negative curvature, needs a replacement notion of convexity.

For horo-convex domains, domains convex with respect to horospheres, the natural spheres of hyperbolic geometry, the authors prove the first eigenfunction is super log-concave. It is a strengthened version of the classical property, provided the domain's diameter is not large. They also show the result is optimal: counterexamples exist both when the domain fails to be horo-convex and when its diameter grows too large.
arxiv-2510-13272:
Xu and co-authors reward faithful reasoning in retrieval-augmented generation in this 2025 arXiv paper. Reinforcement learning has begun training language models to search more effectively. Those methods chase final answer correctness. They may produce chains of thought that do not actually support the answer. The authors first build a framework to measure that unfaithfulness.

Their evaluation scores three links separately: whether reasoning faithfully uses retrieved information, whether the answer follows from the reasoning, and whether the reasoning matches the searches that were issued. A leading search agent showed large room for improvement on all three. Their training framework, VERITAS, folds fine-grained faithfulness rewards into the reinforcement learning process itself. Models trained with it improved reasoning faithfulness a lot while matching task performance across seven question answering benchmarks, showing correctness and faithfulness need not trade off.
arxiv-2510-13672:
Santos and Melo model ten years of dengue risk across Recife, Brazil, to guide public health planning. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses confirmed case data from 2015 to 2024 in a Bayesian hierarchical space-time model. Dengue clusters unevenly inside cities, shaped by climate and social conditions. Finer spatial detail and cleaner data matter for trustworthy risk maps.

Their model, fitted with the R-INLA tool, mixes census, social, and weather variables. Denser population and larger households raised dengue risk in their fit. Higher income and more drainage channels lowered it, by contrast. Rain from one month earlier also raised risk, while higher mean temperature lowered it. That heat effect hints at limits where the mosquito vector falters. Lasting high-risk clusters sat in the north and west zones, overlapping dense, vulnerable districts. The model also projects risk forward for early warning use.
arxiv-2510-13972:
George Webber and Andrew J. Reader propose a new way to judge reconstructions in inverse problems, the task of recovering a true signal from noisy measurements, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such problems drive medical imaging, geophysics, and signal processing. Standard methods score agreement point by point, which tempts algorithms to fit the noise itself rather than the underlying signal.

Their distributional consistency loss instead checks the whole data set at once: are the measurements statistically consistent with the noise distribution that the current estimate implies? The loss drops into existing methods as a direct replacement for terms like mean-squared error, trains the same way, and resists overfitting even without added assumptions about the signal. In image denoising it removed the need for early stopping while improving quality scores, and in medical reconstruction from noisy count data it reduced artifacts in heavily iterated reconstructions.
arxiv-2510-14072:
Hemjyoti Das and Christian Ott design a controller for a multirotor drone carrying a load slung beneath it on a cable, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such cable-suspended platforms are envisioned for construction sites, holding and transporting heavy objects like cranes do. But the swinging load and the drone form a coupled, underactuated system. That means there are fewer control inputs than motions to control.

Their approach uses partial feedback linearization, a technique that cancels selected nonlinear dynamics to make part of the system behave linearly. It deliberately exploits the coupling between drone and load rather than fighting it. Numerical stability analysis shows those coupled terms are crucial for stabilizing the complete system. They test robustness against wind disturbances, sensor noise, and modeling uncertainty, and the controller relies only on onboard sensors, suiting outdoor construction use. Extensive simulations and real experimental tests validate the approach.
arxiv-2510-14572:
Goloskokov and Xie study, in a 2025 arXiv paper, how often J/psi mesons are produced when a photon strikes a proton and nothing else is created. Such exclusive production is a clean probe of the gluons inside the proton. The key ingredients are generalized parton distributions, which describe how gluons share the proton's momentum, built here using the double distribution representation.

Within this factorization approach, their calculated cross sections match experimental data across a wide energy range. They also estimate spin asymmetries for the process, which future measurements could test. The calculations extend to ultraperipheral proton collisions, where the protons miss each other and interact through their photon fields. There the results agree well with LHCb data. They add predictions for the NICA collider's energy range and note the model can help pin down gluon distributions at future machines.
arxiv-2510-14872:
Amir, Hoter, and Koren run, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a large online experiment on how people behave in crowdfunding. In their game, each participant gets a private signal about a project's quality and decides whether to chip in, knowing funding needs enough others to join. Theory predicts two deviations from honest signaling: risk aversion, sitting out despite a good signal, and mutual insurance, joining despite a bad one, trusting others' signals to carry the project.

The results confirmed the core predictions. Compared with plain voting, crowdfunding made participants less likely to follow their private signals, with an odds ratio of 0.139 in the reported analysis, a highly significant effect. Raising signal accuracy from fifty-five to eighty-five percent reduced risk aversion but increased reliance on mutual insurance. One result defied theory: raising the funding threshold from half to four-fifths amplified risk aversion, which the authors suspect reflects cognitive limits.
arxiv-2510-15672:
The CMS experiment at CERN must flag unusual collisions in real time, without theory bias. Lino Gerlach, Elliott Kauffman, and Abhishikth Mallampalli evaluate new fast algorithms for this task in a 2025 arXiv paper. The CICADA system uses a convolutional autoencoder on calorimeter trigger data to spot anomalies. Its behavior is distilled into small student models that run on FPGAs within two hundred nanoseconds. The team tests student designs built on differentiable relaxations, trading slower training for faster inference.

On CMS open data under emulated FPGA conditions, the new models match quantized baselines closely. They do so with significantly lower resource usage on the chip. The savings leave room for richer input detail in future versions.
arxiv-2511-00072:
Pradeep M, Ritesh Pallod, and Satyen Abrol describe LookSync, a deployed large-scale visual product search system that matches AI-generated fashion looks to real products. Generative tools create virtual looks and avatars, and shoppers need the closest purchasable items. The pipeline has four parts: query generation, vectorization, candidate retrieval, and reranking against a large indexed product space.

Recommendation quality is judged with human assessments at internet scale. E-commerce readers get a production architecture, not a prototype. Matching generated style to sellable stock is where AI fashion imagery becomes revenue, so visual and semantic similarity both matter.
arxiv-2511-00572: Xiuling Gui, Jin Yang, Chunfeng Wang, Jing Hou, and Ji Shu study the long-term behavior of a nonlocal reaction-diffusion equation shaken by small random noise. They prove the noisy system has a random attractor, the random set that pulls solutions toward it over time. With additive or multiplicative noise, solutions converge to the matching deterministic equation as the noise shrinks, and the attractors vary upper semicontinuously in that limit. The noise used is a regular approximation to white noise with stated properties.
arxiv-2511-00672:
Jun Eshima, Luc Deike, and Howard Stone study the moment a smooth flow breaks into a shock, a sudden jump that hyperbolic equations produce across physics and engineering. The textbook case is the inviscid Burgers equation, where earlier work showed the dynamics near the newborn shock are self-similar and universal: the same shape appears whatever the starting conditions were.

The authors prove that generosity extends far beyond the textbook case. For general first-order strictly hyperbolic systems in one spatial dimension, shock formation is again self-similar and universal, with the same character as the Burgers case. They derive an analytical formula for the universal self-similar solution. Forecasters of breaking waves and traffic-like shocks gain a single local law to work with.
arxiv-2511-00972:
Alejandro Zamorano, Laura Morales, Denisse Pasten, and Victor Munoz revisit a classic model of solar flares: the Lu and Hamilton model. In it, each grid node is a magnetic flux tube that can suddenly release energy. Their change is structural: neighbors are no longer fixed by position on the grid.

Instead, connections follow a network that can rewire over time, mimicking magnetic reconnection. Rewiring lowers the power law exponent of the spread of released energy, and when rewiring dominates, the distribution turns exponential, decaying faster than the original model. The system then favors many small microflares and loses its scale free character. Using network rather than local neighbors also makes the dynamics nonlocal, with exponents like those in other nonlocal systems.
arxiv-2511-01172:
Ali Owfi and colleagues defend automatic modulation classification, the task of recognizing which radio modulation a received signal uses, against two threats at once. Deep learning leads on this task, but adversarial attacks can fool classifiers with crafted perturbations, and shifts in the signal environment can quietly degrade them.

Their unified framework works in two phases. Offline, meta learning trains the model on clean and attacked samples from one source domain, so the defense generalizes to attack combinations not seen before. Online, domain adaptation aligns the model's features with a new target domain without needing much labeled data there. The authors report significant gains in classification accuracy under the combined threats, addressing a real deployment problem for modern radio systems.
arxiv-2511-01272:
Sehui Jeong and colleagues knit origami. Soft robots made from compliant materials suit wearable devices, but keeping them both structurally sound and comfortable is hard. Their fabrication method translates origami patterns into knitted fabric designs, programming both stitch patterns and material choices.

Folds are encouraged in the wanted directions while unwanted buckling is suppressed, partly by weaving in heat fusible yarn that stiffens flat panels around compliant creases. Measurements of folding moments show stitch patterning improves folding directionality, and the fusible yarn reduces edge curl and out of plane deformation. The team reproduced complex tessellations including Miura-ori, Yoshimura, and Kresling patterns, and built a wearable knitted Kaleidocycle robot that can move.
arxiv-2511-01372:
Sagar Dutta and Vipul Arora retrieve similar audio events with deep hashing. Given an example sound, the goal is to find matching events fast, which hashing supports by turning each clip into a short binary code that can be compared at scale.

Their system, AudioNet, learns those codes under supervision, guided by a new loss function combining weighted contrastive and weighted pairwise terms with a hash code balancing term. A discrete gradient propagation trick lets gradients flow through the discrete codes during training, so standard optimizers can tune them directly. On multiple standard data sets the method sets new benchmarks for similar audio retrieval, and it keeps performing on imbalanced data, where rare event types often break retrieval systems.
arxiv-2511-01972:
Jesse Weder, Andrew Winter, and Christoph Mordasini try to settle how planet-forming disks die. Two mechanisms compete to move angular momentum and drain the disk: turbulent viscosity, and magnetic winds. Which dominates is unknown, and the authors look for a way to tell them apart using the irradiated environment of the Cygnus OB2 star-forming region.

They evolve synthetic disk populations with 1D models under both scenarios, including internal X-ray and external far-ultraviolet photoevaporation, in weak and strong radiation fields. Both scenarios can match the observed constraints. Telling detail emerges, though. Explaining disk lifetimes needs different transport parameters in the two regions. The same holds for the disk mass versus accretion rate relation. Weakly and strongly irradiated regions seem to demand different settings. They propose a test: compare stellar accretion rates with wind mass-loss rates. Those rates evolve differently under the two mechanisms.
arxiv-2511-02072:
Samuel Blitz and Rod Gover construct a new geometric quantity for surfaces sitting inside spaces whose angles matter more than their distances. Working in conformal geometry on even-dimensional manifolds, they use variational arguments to produce a symmetric, trace-free tensor attached to a hypersurface embedding. The tensor completes a known family called the conformal fundamental forms.

The object turns out to govern bigger questions. For the Poincaré-Einstein boundary problem, a certain Dirichlet-to-Neumann image is conformally invariant, and the authors show it is exactly the restriction of their new tensor. The proof yields further global invariants of the boundary. As a final application, compact manifolds that are Bach-flat with umbilic boundary are shown to admit a formal Poincaré-Einstein metric in their conformal class.
arxiv-2511-02372:
Oscar Combaluzier-Szteinsznaider, Daniel Glazer, Austin Joyce, Maria Rodriguez, and Luca Santoni compute how a black hole flexes when the tide squeezing it changes with time. Love numbers quantify an object's tidal response; for black holes the static response famously vanishes, but the dynamical response to a time-dependent gravitational field does not. Working with the Schwarzschild black hole inside a point-particle effective field theory, the authors extract those dynamical Love numbers.

The calculation matches a renormalised quantity in the effective theory against the classical field profile computed directly in general relativity, where the black hole's perturbation equations are solved in a low-frequency expansion. Alongside the known logarithmic running of the couplings, the team obtains their finite, scheme-dependent parts for the first time.
