The result sharpens a precision tool for reading gravitational-wave signals, since tidal response is one channel through which internal structure speaks.
arxiv-2511-02772:
James Hefford and Matt Wilson explore whether plain quantum theory could emerge from a stranger theory where cause and effect have no fixed order. Their 2025 paper works with quantum boxes, a higher-order framework with a non-signalling way of combining systems. A process called hyper-decoherence is meant to wash out the strangeness and leave standard quantum behavior.

The pair find such a process that meets the hyper-decoherence axioms and does yield standard quantum theory. It sidesteps a known no-go result by loosening two assumptions: limits on signalling to the past, and the uniqueness of purifications. They weigh two readings of the result. Either nature really does smooth an indefinite-causal theory into ours, or the axioms need a closer look, especially around purity.
arxiv-2511-02872:
Jiedong Jiang and ten colleagues built FATE, a benchmark that tests language models on formal algebra at research depth. Contest sets like the IMO miss the breadth and abstraction of modern math. FATE-H and FATE-X each hold one hundred problems in abstract and commutative algebra, spanning college exercises to questions past PhD qualifying exams. The 2025 paper says FATE-X is the first formal set to pass both marks.

The best model scored only 3 percent on FATE-H and zero on FATE-X, even with many tries allowed. A two-stage check showed the models' plain-language reasoning was notably better than their formal proofs, and the team classified the errors made in translation. One surprise: a specialized prover reflected less well than general models, hurting its first-stage accuracy.
arxiv-2511-02972:
Peiqiang Lin extends a classic lemma about logarithmic derivatives to a far more general geometric setting. Ahlfors' lemma is a workhorse of value distribution theory, the study of how holomorphic maps spread their values. Lin's 2025 paper carries it to holomorphic tangent curves of directed projective manifolds that meet closed subschemes, and names the results in an algebro-geometric form.

From the generalization flow several corollaries: transformed versions tied to a linear system, and Second Main Theorem type results for holomorphic curves. Second Main Theorems are the deep counting laws of the field, bounding how often a curve can hit chosen targets. Extending the lemma that feeds them widens the range of manifolds and targets those laws can handle.
arxiv-2511-03372:
Shenghao Li proposes LFC-DA, a pipeline that grows training data for logical reasoning under strict symbolic control. Hand labeling such data costs heavily, while free generation by language models yields dull, murky examples. The pipeline first turns logical text into formal expressions, then compiles a compact rule library.

A bounded search over states hunts for fresh valid formulas inside that library. Those formulas are then worded back into natural questions, keeping diversity with rigor. Training on the grown data lifted scores on two logic benchmarks, ReClor and LogiQA, by clear margins. The method shows how formal logic can steer generative tools rather than merely check them afterward.
arxiv-2511-03772:
Stergios Chatzikyriakidis and co-authors extend a Greek dialect corpus to ten varieties and more than six million words. GRDD+ grows the earlier set for Cretan, Cypriot, Pontic, and Northern Greek, and adds six more, from Griko in southern Italy to Tsakonian and formal Katharevusa. No Greek dialect resource of this breadth and size existed before.

Fine-tuning trials span three model families, including a Greek-focused model, and compare them with frontier commercial systems. Good dialect data lift smaller models notably on dialect tasks in the reported runs. Dialects carry identity and history that standard-language training erases, so a shared corpus helps both research and preservation. The set also gives a fair test bed for cross-dialect transfer.
arxiv-2511-03872:
Greg Markowsky and Clayton McDonald give purely complex-analytic proofs of two theorems Markowsky had earlier proved only by probability. One result is a general Phragmen-Lindelof principle linking finiteness of a Hardy norm for a conformal map to how fast an analytic function can grow inside a simply connected domain.

The pair prove that principle and discuss special cases. They also derive a series expansion for the Green's function of a disk, and show how it leads to an infinite product identity. The celebrated infinite product expansions for sine and cosine appear as special cases. The work shows analytic methods alone can carry results first found through probability.
arxiv-2511-04072:
Xinying Qian, Ying Zhang, Yu Zhao, Baohang Zhou, Xuhui Sui, and Xiaojie Yuan present Plan of Knowledge, a framework for answering time-sensitive questions over temporal knowledge graphs. Language models reason well in general but stumble on time constraints, hallucinate, and lack current facts, while older graph methods miss complex temporal meaning.

A planning module breaks a hard temporal question into a sequence of sub-objectives guided by predefined tools. In parallel, a temporal knowledge store with contrastive retrieval selects facts aligned in both meaning and time. Structured planning joined to careful retrieval aims to ground each reasoning step, reducing invention while handling the time logic such questions demand.
arxiv-2511-04872:
James Ndubuisi and two colleagues validate vision transformers for reading ear examination images. Even specialist ear doctors misdiagnose about twenty-seven percent of cases, the authors note. Better automated reading of otoscopy could cut that error rate.

Their data are real exam videos from a university hospital in Chile. Frames were filtered by sharpness and information measures, with blank frames removed. Swin transformer versions scored near perfect accuracy at first pass. The study then probes data leakage effects behind such scores. Careful leakage checks decide whether the headline numbers can be trusted in clinics.
arxiv-2511-04972:
Dylan Peek and co-authors tackle a data gap in teaching neural nets to read the shape traits of 3D forms. Classic tools that find holes and links in data are slow, so learned estimators could help, if labeled 3D data existed.

The team made a way to build labeled 3D sets with a set hole count, using a surface method that pushes points apart. They train a 3D network with attention to guess genus, the count of holes. Tests show that as forms warp more, scores fall, so warp matters as much as hole count.
arxiv-2511-05072:
Yu. A. Markov and co-authors derive a classical scattering matrix for how hard and soft excitations meet in a non-Abelian plasma, such as a quark-gluon plasma. Their route follows the Zakharov-Schulman method, in close step with quantum field theory tools.

The matrix is written as a broad series in the starting values of soft gluon waves and the color charge of a hard particle. They work out the first non-trivial term of that series. The result gives a firm base for tracking energy and charge exchange between fast particles and the soft field around them.
arxiv-2511-05172:
P. Schulte and co-authors report a proof-of-concept cryogenic heat pump that uses xenon as its working fluid. Future liquid xenon observatories, such as XLZD, need high-flow cleaning to strip out radon, and a sealed pump would ease upkeep and purity control.

The small unit runs a Clausius-Rankine cycle in reverse, with xenon changing phase to move heat. It stays fully sealed off from the radon system. Tests ran at two set pressures with a cold head, and check how the design fares. The work is a first step toward pumps built for rare-event physics.
arxiv-2511-05372:
Noah Linden and a co-author show cases where adaptive quantum phase estimation beats the non-adaptive form. Phase estimation is a core quantum tool. It can be run all at once with no feedback, at the cost of many more qubits, and for a fully unknown phase feedback gives no edge.

Their cases add a promise: the phase can take only set values. Under that promise, adaptive runs, which choose later steps from early results, are provably better. The result maps a crisp line where feedback helps in quantum sensing and algorithms.
arxiv-2511-05672:
Moisés Alves and co-authors show how to prove that light-based quantum devices make truly random numbers. Random output guards secure messages, but proving the numbers are random by quantum rules, not by a hidden flaw, is hard. Their plan trusts the setup only in part, through one clear claim about its size.

States are kept in a two-level space, while plain light-based tests do the checking. Even simple setups, the team shows, can break a size-based bound by enough to prove the output holds real entropy. The proof survives normal losses and frames that are slightly off line. The authors say workable quantum randomness is within reach without complex gear.
arxiv-2511-05972:
Guangyuan Liu and co-authors manage satellite-terrestrial wireless networks where devices also harvest power from the signal itself. These hybrid networks promise wide coverage with frugal energy use. Optimizing beams and power splits is hard: channels shift fast and tiers interfere, so learning agents trained the usual way need many samples and coordinate poorly.

Their framework gives each agent a world model, a compact predictor of how the environment behaves, so policies train largely in imagination. An uncertainty-aware gate calls for edge coordination only when interference or model error runs high. A decorrelation step at the edge then steers agents toward non-conflicting actions. In simulations the method converged far faster than baselines with much higher spectral efficiency.
arxiv-2511-06072:
Behrad Tajalli, Stefanos Koffas, and Stjepan Picek plant a backdoor in machine learning models trained on tabular data. Backdoor attacks make a model behave normally until a secret trigger flips its answer. Most past attacks used images; tables mix numbers with categories, which blocks the usual gradient tricks.

Their method, CatBack, converts category values into decimal numbers in a way that keeps the model's clean accuracy. One universal perturbation can then touch every feature at once. Across five data sets and four models, attack success reached up to total in both white-box and black-box settings, including a commercial cloud service. Four leading defenses and popular outlier detectors all failed to stop it, which the authors call a severe vulnerability.
arxiv-2511-06272:
Zijie Wang and colleagues apply generative diffusion models to lane centerline learning for self-driving cars. Centerline graphs guide path planning, but deterministic methods reason poorly about space and fail where lane markings are hidden. LaneDiffusion instead generates lane priors inside bird's-eye view data rather than drawing centerlines directly.

Two modules run the process: one injects lane priors into the features and one manages the diffusion that creates them. Centerlines in vector form and their links are then decoded from the enriched data. On the nuScenes and Argoverse2 datasets, LaneDiffusion beat existing methods across point-level and segment-level measures, setting new best results for centerline graph learning.
arxiv-2511-06472:
Adele Olof-Ors and Martin Smit argue that friendly, human-like artificial intelligence is a business tool rather than a neutral feature. Technologies that simulate emotional realism, from chatbots to virtual assistants, invite users to trust and open up. The authors connect that designed trust to surveillance capitalism, the system profiting from monitoring and steering behavior.

Drawing on Nicholas Carr's idea of an intellectual ethic, the paper claims such tools reshape how people think, not just what they think about. A new intellectual ethic carried by these systems serves the surveillance economy well. The authors close by discussing possible ways to push back against that arrangement.
arxiv-2511-06672:
Ben Harper and colleagues extend a hybrid quantum simulator from qubits to qutrits, systems with three levels instead of two. Simulating quantum circuits classically grows brutal fast, and mixing stabilizer methods with tensor networks recently bought big speedups for qubits. Whether the same trick pays for higher-level systems was untested.

Their generalized simulator, GCAMPS, carries the Clifford-augmented matrix product state approach over to qudit systems. Benchmarks on random Clifford circuits doped with extra gates show qutrit simulation gaining at least as much as qubit simulation did. In fact it gains more, because ordinary tensor network methods struggle harder with qutrits. Previously intractable many-body problems become reachable on classical machines.
arxiv-2511-06772:
An experiment by Zhen Su and eight co-authors reports a broad magnetic Feshbach resonance in an ultracold mixture of sodium-potassium molecules and potassium atoms. Both species were prepared in their lowest energy states. A Feshbach resonance is a magnetic-field effect that sharply changes how particles interact, and here it comes with an unusually large background scattering length.

The team measured the resonance through faster particle loss and through how quickly the two gases shared heat. Far from the resonance, the strong background interaction pushed the mixture into a fluid-like regime where atoms and molecules moved in lockstep at one shared frequency. The result opens a new route to studying strongly interacting gases whose particles have very different masses.
arxiv-2511-06972:
Jan Gavranovič and four co-authors improve how particle physics analyses estimate fake backgrounds, events that pass selection only because a particle was mis-reconstructed. A jet mistaken for a lepton, or a lepton from a secondary decay taken as prompt, can mimic a signal. The standard Fake Factor method reweights data using ratios of histograms in a few variables, which bins the estimate coarsely.

Their alternative trains neural networks on data to estimate density ratios in a higher-dimensional feature space. That yields a continuous, unbinned fake factor for each single event, more flexible and precise than the histogram version. A test analysis on LHC open data confirmed the method gives smoother, more stable estimates across phase space, with fewer binning artifacts and better extrapolation into signal regions.
arxiv-2511-07272:
William St-Arnaud, Margarida Carvalho, and Golnoosh Farnadi revisit the neural tangent kernel. The theory says infinitely wide networks trained by gradient descent behave like kernel machines stuck in a lazy regime where nothing internal changes. Two accepted conclusions say the theory fails at large width, because hidden activations supposedly freeze, and at large depth, because the kernel's prediction becomes data-independent and trivial. The authors challenge both.

Experimentally, while each single neuron's activation change vanishes, the aggregate norm of those changes does not, and a theorem confirms the last hidden layer's activations truly move. They further show that scaling depth and stopping time properly in wide ReLU networks yields well-behaved, non-trivial outputs on large data sets. The results reopen the question of what the kernel picture can explain about real networks.
arxiv-2511-07372:
Dake Bu and a team of co-authors ask why teaching language models in steps works so well. Curriculum post-training, which orders practice from easier to harder reasoning, often beats mixed practice. Until now the reasons and limits lacked a firm theory.

The authors model chain-of-thought generation as a branching reasoning tree. Curricula either lengthen the reasoning depth step by step or slowly remove hints. Under stated conditions, the step order cuts the needed training examples by an exponential factor. The framework also shows where gains should fade. Trainers get testable guidance instead of folklore about ordering practice problems.
arxiv-2511-07472:
Mehmet Can Yavuz rethinks the hidden space inside variational autoencoders, models that compress data into a small code. Standard versions force that code to follow a simple diagonal shape. The shortcut eases training but blocks linked uncertainty and often wastes dimensions.

The Multivariate Variational Autoencoder keeps a full covariance structure by combining per-sample scales with one shared coupling matrix. Correlated code factors become possible while the training objective stays in closed form. Sampling also stays simple. The goal is codes that are expressive, well shaped, and honestly calibrated. Better codes help generation, compression, and later analysis of what the model learned.
arxiv-2511-07672:
Ufuk Aydemir reviews a route to grand unification that starts from geometry rather than extra particles. Noncommutative geometry derives the Standard Model and gravity from one spectral action on an underlying algebra. Certain Pati-Salam models, which unify quarks and leptons, emerge from suitable algebras with unified couplings and few scalars.

Collider searches have found no clear new physics, so such models help aim future hunts. Aydemir surveys the phenomenological signatures these unified versions predict. Distinctive patterns could show up in proton decay, flavor, or collider channels. The review connects an abstract geometric program to tests experiments can actually run.
arxiv-2511-07772:
Shourya Batra, Pierce Tillman, and Samarth Gaggar stop language models from thinking private facts out loud. Personal assistants see sensitive user data, and even when final answers stay clean, the visible chain-of-thought can leak details. Guarding only the output leaves that reasoning trace exposed.

SALT steers internal activations during reasoning toward leakage-free thinking. The steering aims to preserve problem-solving power while suppressing private content in intermediate steps. Balancing privacy against utility is the central tension. As assistants gain memory and tool access, reasoning traces become a real attack surface, so defenses must move inside the model, not just filter its replies.
arxiv-2511-08172:
Georgios Pantazopoulos and Eda Ozyigit describe a lean training pipeline for interface agents that must locate screen elements from language. Visual grounding lets an agent find the button or field a user request refers to. Many current methods depend on huge, noisy synthetic data sets, which are expensive to build and train on.

The pipeline filters nearly five million synthetic examples down to twelve thousand clean, diverse cases by removing misaligned items and keeping hard ones. A three billion parameter vision language model is then trained three ways, including reinforcement learning. The compact models match or beat larger baselines on several interface benchmarks.
arxiv-2511-08372:
Bernd Kroger describes the current implementation of DYNARTmo, a dynamic articulatory model that generates ongoing movements of the human vocal tract for speech. Speech production links a linguistic plan to moving lips, tongue, and jaw, and finally to sound. A useful model must therefore represent both the abstract units of speech and the smooth physical motion that realizes them in time.

The model is neurobiologically inspired and builds motion from speech gestures organized in a gesture score. Kroger presents the inventory of ready gestures and explains how they are coordinated within the score. That score is then translated into ongoing articulator trajectories, which drive the DYNARTmo vocal tract model to produce the corresponding articulatory and acoustic output.
arxiv-2511-08672:
Longji Bing and thirty co-authors present AC-2168, a galaxy so buried in dust that the Webb telescope's main camera nearly misses it, while millimeter telescopes see it shining brightly. Found blindly in ALMA data in the COSMOS field, it sits at a redshift of six point six three, confirmed by carbon and carbon monoxide lines.

The galaxy forms stars at roughly two hundred forty solar masses per year and holds stellar mass near thirty-seven billion suns, with gas making up about half its total mass. Its dust is warm and packed into a compact core about a kiloparsec wide. The gas supply would drain in roughly one hundred seventy million years at the current pace. Such objects may be the ancestors of massive quiet galaxies seen later, and blind surveys matter because pointed ones overlook them.
arxiv-2511-08772:
Myeonghun Yu and three co-authors build a neural estimator for expected shortfall, the risk measure that averages losses beyond a bad threshold and complements the better-known value-at-risk. Unlike quantile regression, expected shortfall regression is still young, partly because standard training frameworks do not apply to it directly.

Their two-step method first estimates the conditional quantile with a deep feed-forward network, then treats it as a nuisance input for the shortfall estimate. Hierarchical structure in the underlying functions helps the networks dodge the curse of dimensionality. Because shortfall estimation breaks under heavy-tailed data, a tuned Huber loss is woven into training, making the estimator provably resistant to heavy tails and insensitive to first-stage errors. Simulations and an El Niño precipitation study support the claims.
arxiv-2511-08972:
Duc Anh Nguyen and four co-authors rethink how sparse mixture-of-experts models route tokens to experts. These models grow capacity cheaply by activating only a few experts per token. But keeping the load balanced usually takes extra loss terms or noisy trainable gates. Those complicate training and can misalign the objective.

Treating token-to-expert assignment as an optimal transport problem changes the picture. With balance constraints built into the transport itself, gating scores fall directly out of the transport map, and even minimal transport-based routing already improves the models with no auxiliary losses. The full method, Selective Sinkhorn Routing, keeps that efficiency while preserving flexible expert choice. Language modeling and image classification experiments show gains in training efficiency, accuracy, and robustness when inputs are corrupted.
arxiv-2511-09172:
Lucas Chesnel gives a lecture-style tour of how to make obstacles invisible inside waveguides, channels that carry waves in one endless direction. An obstacle usually scatters an incoming acoustic wave, producing reflection and transmission described by scattering numbers. Being invisible means tuning the setup so the obstacle leaves no trace.

Chesnel explains three methods for steering those numbers through shape, frequency, or material index. A continuation method uses shape derivatives to construct invisible defects step by step. Complex resonances near the real axis can hide obstacles, and a non-self-adjoint operator picks out frequencies that pass through completely. The methods draw on asymptotic analysis and spectral theory, with numeric tests that illustrate most results.
arxiv-2511-09472:
Volker Betz, Tobias Schmidt, and Mark Sellke study a Brownian particle that is pulled by its own past trajectory. The self-interaction is long-range, meaning distant parts of the path still influence the motion. Such systems model polymers and other objects whose history shapes their future movement.

The paper proves variance bounds describing how far the particle typically spreads. Those bounds are expressed through the spatial strength of the interaction and the rate at which its influence decays in time. Where the bounds fall below ordinary Brownian spreading, the motion is sub-diffusive, slower than a plain random walk. The results map out which combinations of interaction strength and decay produce those sub-diffusive regimes.
arxiv-2511-09572:
Tommaso Castellani and six co-authors build SynthTools, a pipeline that builds entire tool-use environments for training AI agents. Agents need many diverse, controllable environments to learn long-horizon tool use, but real application interfaces bottleneck their creation. Their pipeline is fully language-model-based, covering generation, simulation, validation, and task construction.

Top-down generation builds domain-grounded environments, and simulation checks that tools can be emulated well. Bottom-up task generation then produces solvable, checkable tasks with paths. The released data set holds nearly seventy-four thousand checked tools across 6,800 environments and one hundred fields, plus about eighty thousand checkable tasks. Qwen3 models trained on the paths gained across tool-use benchmarks, including some with real interfaces.
arxiv-2511-10072:
Shuxin Zhuang, Linjian Meng, Shuxin Li, Minming Li, and Youzhi Zhang tackle urban network security games, where defenders allocate scarce patrol resources across a city road network against an adversary. Finding a Nash equilibrium is hard because the action space is enormous and combinatorial. Standard oracle approaches need best responses each round, and computing them exactly is impractical at this scale.

Their approach, Tree-based Stochastic Optimization, maps the whole action space onto a tree that neural networks can represent. It then folds that representation into a loss shown equivalent to the unbiased loss used for equilibrium finding. A sample-and-prune step reduces the risk of settling into poor local optima. Tests showed the method beating baseline methods on these large security games.
arxiv-2511-10172:
Francesco Capolupo, writing alone, gives a strict math treatment of stand-in models for fuel sloshing in spacecraft. Slosh can wreck fine pointing in low gravity and can stress a craft under hard thrust at launch, re-entry, and landing. So control teams model the moving fuel as pendulums or as mass-spring-damper units bolted to the craft. Capolupo starts with one round pendulum on a stiff craft.

He works out the full nonlinear motion laws for that eight-degree-of-freedom system, then extends them to many pendulums for many slosh modes and many tanks. Straight-line versions of the laws follow, with a steady push along the craft's axis counted in either frame. Last, he proves the pendulum and mass-spring-damper models are the same model in two dressings, and checks both in time and frequency runs.
arxiv-2511-10272:
Shahaf S. Shperberg, Natalie Morad, Lior Siag, Ariel Felner, and Dor Atzmon extend bidirectional heuristic search to problems where a slightly suboptimal answer is acceptable within a stated bound. Bidirectional search runs from start and goal at once, and recent optimal algorithms such as BAE-star exploit consistent heuristics. Bounded-suboptimal variants promise large speedups, but designing them for the bidirectional setting is delicate.

Building on BAE-star, the authors introduce several variants tailored to bounded suboptimality. Experiments compare them with other bounded-suboptimal bidirectional algorithms and with the standard weighted A-star baseline. No single winner emerged: each algorithm excelled under distinct conditions. The paper maps those strengths and weaknesses so practitioners can pick the right variant for their problem's profile.
arxiv-2511-10672:
Marcelo Maciel Amaral builds an infinite family of one-dimensional quantum Hamiltonians from the combinatorics of the Fibonacci word. Each Hamiltonian in the hierarchy forbids a growing set of short patterns, the minimal forbidden factors of the word up to a Fibonacci length, and all of them are frustration-free.

The number of ground states grows with constants that shrink rung by rung. They start near the golden ratio and step down toward one, forming a staircase of entropy plateaus that ends at an aperiodic fixed point. The first nontrivial rung, the plastic chain, forbids two patterns and its ground-state counts obey a four-term recurrence governed by the plastic constant. Small cases run on a D-Wave quantum annealer matched the predictions, with harder rungs needing reverse annealing to succeed.
arxiv-2511-10872:
Shuyuan Zhang, Zihan Wang, Xiao-Wen Chang, and Doina Precup strengthen goal-conditioned hierarchical reinforcement learning, where an agent pursues goals through intermediate subgoals, by giving it a better memory of space. Graphs naturally represent task structure and can supply subgoals, but existing methods either hand-build the graphs or fail to pass graph knowledge to states the agent has not yet visited.

Their method, G4RL, trains a graph encoder-decoder on the state graph built during exploration. It can then evaluate unseen states and generate useful subgoal representations. High- and low-level intrinsic rewards drawn from the encoder-decoder guide learning. Bolted onto state-of-the-art hierarchical methods, the approach improved performance in both dense and sparse reward environments for a small extra computational cost. The tasks had mostly symmetric, reversible transitions.
arxiv-2511-10972:
Bo Fu, Kai-Zhi Bai, and their colleagues study how electric current flows in a thin material whose electrons act like lone Dirac fermions, particles with no partner of the other charge sign. Two flows matter: the straight flow along a field and the sideways Hall flow. Disorder, or random flaws in the material, can change both in linked ways.

The team finds a near half-ellipse link between the smallest straight flow and the Hall flow. Near the neutral point, disorder can push the material from insulator to metal. In the no-mass case, the paired values mark a special phase that matches recent lab results in magnetic materials.
arxiv-2511-11172:
Mubaraka Sani Ibrahim, Isah Charles Saidu, and Lehel Csato propose a group recommender that suggests items to a whole group from the group's joint tastes. Group tools often struggle because rating data are sparse and high-dimensional, with most users rating few items. Their method, Group Soft-Impute SVD, fills the sparse rating table by low-rank completion before making group calls.

Against matrix-based group baselines, the method won on recall for small groups and matched them at other sizes across book, movie, and synthetic data sets. It also recovered lower table ranks than the baselines. That shows the completion step handles sparse, wide data well.
arxiv-2511-11572:
William H. Press offers a compact summary of how large language models are built and what they cost, aimed at readers who want the essentials in one place. The standard design, a Transformer with query, key, and value self-attention, is laid out briefly and plainly.

Scaling laws connect computing power, measured in flops, and memory, split between parameters and training data. Rough 2025 cost estimates are given for models at several scales, so readers can see why frontier training runs are so expensive. DeepSeek is discussed as a possible special case. Nothing here is claimed as new; the value lies in gathering scattered facts into one short reference.
arxiv-2511-11672:
Zengyi Qin and twenty-seven co-authors present OSGym, infrastructure for running the many full operating system sandboxes that computer use agents need for training. Each agent needs a real graphical desktop, which is heavy, and varied software fails in varied ways, so the platform must absorb errors gracefully.

Three strategies carry the design: decentralized state management that confines failures to single replicas, hardware-aware placement that eases processor bottlenecks, and virtual machines with copy-on-write disks that share storage. Together they cut computing overhead while keeping environments realistic. Scalable, reliable sandboxes are a quiet bottleneck for agent research, and OSGym is built to remove it.
arxiv-2511-11772:
Chenyu Zhang and Xiaohang Luo present a system that grades student reflections and writes feedback. Five language model agents share the work. Their roles are evaluator, equity monitor, metacognitive coach, aggregator, and reviewer. Feedback strongly drives learning. Yet teachers in large or low-resource courses cannot reply to every reflection.

The agents score work against a shared rubric. They screen comments for biased or exclusionary language. They also add prompts that help students think about their own learning. The design is grounded in learning theory. Its aim is equity at scale: steady, bias-aware replies for every learner. Small, well-staffed classes should not be the only place feedback happens.
arxiv-2511-11972:
Sebastião dos Anjos Sousa-Júnior, Julián Faúndez, and Rubem Mondaini study spin-orbit coupling in a periodic Anderson model. That model is the standard lattice model of heavy-fermion materials. Mobile electrons hybridize with nearly localized ones there. Spin-flip hybridization rewrites the band structure in the non-interacting limit.

Flat bands and van Hove singularities appear. Dirac cones appear too, inside a single Kondo-Dirac semimetal phase. Strong interactions are explored with determinant quantum Monte Carlo. The run has no sign problem. A full ground-state phase diagram emerges. It reveals a second phase, an orbital-selective antiferromagnetic semimetal. Exotic semimetals born from Kondo physics are prime ground for new quantum materials.
arxiv-2511-12272:
Mihály Pituk gives a full spectral answer to a long-standing question in dynamical systems: when does a linear operator have the shadowing property? Shadowing means a slightly flawed orbit is always tracked closely by a true orbit. The study covers invertible bounded linear operators on a complex Hilbert space.

Pituk shows shadowing holds exactly when the operator's right spectrum stays disjoint from the unit circle in the complex plane. As a consequence, shadowing for the operator matches a uniform expansivity property of its adjoint. Earlier results covered only special classes, so a complete criterion for an arbitrary invertible operator closes a notable gap.
arxiv-2511-12472:
Mengying Wang and eight co-authors ask whether large language models can make serendipitous discoveries in knowledge graphs, using drug repurposing as the test case. Question answering over knowledge graphs usually rewards relevant but predictable answers. A drug found for a new disease, by contrast, must be surprising yet still valuable and grounded.

Their framework, SerenQA, defines the task formally and scores answers by relevance, novelty and surprise. A benchmark annotated by experts is drawn from a clinical knowledge graph. The evaluation splits into retrieval, subgraph reasoning and serendipity exploration. Experiments find leading models retrieve well but still struggle to surface genuinely surprising and useful discoveries.
arxiv-2511-12772:
Stephan Nef and Bruno Rodrigues present CareNet, a system that reads signs of depression from a home router instead of a phone or wearable. Phones and wearables demand permissions and constant cooperation from the user. CareNet instead works on network metadata at the home gateway, where all processing stays local. It converts daily traffic patterns into behavioral indicators matched to the symptom domains of the DSM-5, the standard diagnostic manual for mental health.

Its core method, FASL, blends header-level traffic metrics through fuzzy rules into daily likelihood scores for each symptom criterion. A time gate then smooths short bursts into persistent, interpretable indicators. On realistic multi-day traces, CareNet picked out patterns such as delayed sleep timing and unstable attention, without ever inspecting message content. The authors argue that router telemetry can support explainable, privacy-preserving mental-health sensing that families can reproduce and audit.
arxiv-2511-12872:
Taisuke Hosaka and Etsuo Segawa study a quantum walker moving on two graphs joined by a single weak bridge. The walk is a Grover walk, a quantum version of a random walk used in search algorithms. A parameter sets the strength of the bridge: at zero the two graphs are fully separate. The authors show that for a weak bridge, a pulsation occurs, meaning the walker swings rhythmically between the two graphs.

They derive a formula for the chance of finding the walker on either side when the bridge is weak. Surprisingly, the rhythm depends only on how many edges each graph has, not on their detailed shapes. The swing period grows as the bridge weakens, and when both graphs have the same number of edges, the walker transfers almost completely each swing. The result gives quantum walk designers a simple rule for coupled networks.
arxiv-2511-13072:
Antonio David Bastida Zamora, Ljubomir Budinski, Valtteri Lahtinen, and Pierre Sagaut present a quantum version of the lattice Boltzmann method, a workhorse for simulating fluid flow. Their algorithm uses Carleman linearization, a trick that rewrites nonlinear dynamics as linear dynamics in a larger space, which quantum computers can then evolve. Earlier encodings forced compromises in how particles collide at each site. The new encoding allows local collision rules, matching how the classical method works, while keeping a higher chance of reading out the right answer.

The authors analyze running the method for several time steps, with cost growing mildly with lattice size and channel count, and a constant number of qubits when dynamical circuits are used. The work appeared in Physical Review E. It is one step in a long program: making quantum simulation of fluids efficient enough to matter for engineering, where Boltzmann methods are already trusted.
arxiv-2511-13372:
M. Molero and 3 co-authors use galactic chemical evolution models to pin down where the rapid neutron-capture process makes heavy elements. Candidate sites such as neutron star mergers and special supernovae predict different rates, delays, and yields. Rather than fix one site, the team lets the data choose among flexible options.

They ran a large grid of models that vary yield, event rate, delay, and progenitor mass, then used Pareto fronts to match trends for several elements at once. Best fits favored short delays, lower-mass progenitors, and a modest europium yield per event. Heavy elements fit well, but lighter ones clashed, so at least two distinct components seem required.
arxiv-2511-13872:
Bukunmi G. Odunlami and Marcos Netto model power inverters that can switch between two control modes. Modern inverters either follow the grid or help form it, and switching between those roles mid-operation makes their behavior hard to track. The authors describe such devices as hybrid automata, with switch rules tied to voltage and frequency.

Reset rules keep phase, frequency, and droop settings consistent each time the mode flips. They then place the model inside an extended Kalman filter, a standard tool for estimating hidden states from noisy data. Tests show stable, well-behaved motion and better estimates near switching moments than smooth continuous models give.
arxiv-2511-14172:
Naveen Lamba, Sanju Tiwari, and Manas Gaur trace where hallucinations begin inside language models when symbolic triggers appear. Words like negations, numbers, exceptions, and named entities reliably trip models up, but earlier localization tools treated all tokens alike. Their framework uses symbolic linguistic knowledge to follow hallucination growth layer by layer.

Across five models tested on HaluEval and TruthfulQA, attention variance for these trigger elements spiked into instability in the very early layers, long before the wrong answer surfaced. Negation was among the strongest triggers. Knowing the failure starts early and symbolically gives model builders a concrete place to intervene.
arxiv-2511-14372:
Tao Wu, Zhao Guo, and Yan Li read the fingerprints that mass transfer leaves inside binary stars. When close companions trade mass, their interiors, rotation, and vibration patterns all change. Gravity modes, which probe the deep interior, show period spacings whose wiggles trace sharp features in the buoyancy frequency profile. The team explains those wiggles quantitatively for stars of a few solar masses.

Donor stars develop two chemical gradient zones, doubling the buoyancy peaks and adding extra periodic modulations to the gravity-mode spacings. Accretion reshapes the chemical profile too, shifting both the amplitudes and frequencies of the spacing variations. The patterns resemble those in compact pulsators, giving observers a seismic way to detect past mass transfer.
arxiv-2511-14672:
Amanda Burcroff, Kyungyong Lee, Lang Mou, Gregg Musiker, and Markus Reineke study rank-two cluster scattering diagrams, wall structures that encode how cluster variables change. They view the diagrams through spaces of quiver representations, which turn abstract algebra into geometry. A recent combinatorial tool called tight gradings gives a second handle on the same objects.

By joining the two views, the team proves and extends a set of conjectures by Elgin, Reading, and Stella about the coefficients on the walls. The grading view also yields a new proof that the diagram respects Weyl group symmetry. The work ties cluster theory more firmly to geometry and counting.
arxiv-2511-14772:
Zhuoyi Yang, Xu Guo, Tong Zhang, Huijuan Xu, and Boyang Li survey test-time scaling, the practice of giving a trained language model extra compute while it answers. Instead of sorting methods by surface tricks, they sort them by how a problem is split into smaller parts. Those parts may run in a line, side by side, or in a branching tree.

Under that lens, well-known methods such as chain-of-thought and tree-of-thought become versions of one shared idea. The survey gathers what is known about the strengths and weak points of each style. It closes with open questions and promising paths for making models reason better without retraining them.
arxiv-2511-14872:
T. S. A. N. Simões, F. Lombardi, and three co-authors connect two ways of testing whether brain tissue sits near a critical point. Recordings of neuronal avalanches, cascades of firing cells, often show scaling patterns that suggest the tissue balances between quiet and runaway activity. Separately, maximum entropy models built from the same data carry heat-like signatures of criticality.

The team records spontaneous activity in slices of rat cortex kept alive in the lab, then pushes the tissue toward quiet or excitable states with drugs. Each state is classed as below, at, or above criticality by avalanche behavior. Comparing the two lenses in the same tissue shows how their verdicts line up, a step toward trusting either one as a health marker.
arxiv-2511-15172:
Andrew Gracyk shows that a family of learning machines built on complex numbers carries a rich geometric structure. Variational autoencoders compress data into a latent space and rebuild it, and the real-number versions were recently found to carry Riemannian geometry. Gracyk adapts those arguments to autoencoders whose latent variables are complex.

The complex machines turn out to reveal Kahler structure, the special geometry that blends Riemannian, complex, and symplectic traits. Working on the decoder side, he derives the Fisher information metric for a complex Gaussian latent law and ties it to relative entropy through a potential function. A mixture-based proxy for the metric is also proposed. Geometry of this kind can guide better training and sampling.
arxiv-2511-15272:
Nilesh Vyas and Konstantin Baier design QADR, a protocol for anonymous data reporting that can survive quantum attack. Vast internet-of-things networks stream data for decades, and attackers can harvest encrypted traffic today and decrypt it later once quantum machines mature. Classical post-quantum schemes rest on assumptions that may not hold that long, while fully quantum schemes are too heavy for billions of devices.

QADR blends the two worlds in a hybrid security model aimed at future fully connected quantum networks. It targets quantum-resistant anonymity that still scales to huge device counts. The protocol is offered as both a working architecture and a theoretical benchmark for a problem that long-lived sensor networks cannot postpone.
arxiv-2511-15372:
Sam Adriaensen, Peter Sziklai, and Zsuzsa Weiner give a short proof of a result on minimal codes from subgeometries in projective space. A 2022 paper showed three subgeometries can union into a strong blocking set in a specific projective space. That construction proves certain linear minimal codes exist for every prime power. The codes have fully specified length and dimension parameters.

The new proof covers odd prime powers above nine. It uses the theory of small blocking sets in projective planes instead of heavier machinery. A shorter route clarifies why the construction works. Minimal codes matter for secret sharing and coding theory. Simplifications that widen understanding of existence proofs are valuable to finite geometers.
arxiv-2511-15672:
Marwan Ait Haddou, Mohamed Belfkir, and Salah Eddine El Harrauss propose a hybrid quantum machine learning framework for double Higgs searches at the Large Hadron Collider. Double Higgs production probes the Higgs self coupling, a key test of the standard model. Their model embeds event features into a quantum feature space with parameterized circuits. A classical neural network meta model keeps training stable.

The hybrid outperforms both a top gradient boosting model and a purely quantum model by about a factor of two in sensitivity. Expected limits on double Higgs production are reported under two background uncertainty scenarios. Constraints on self coupling and quartic couplings also improve. The study suggests hybrid designs can extract more from rare collider signals than either paradigm alone.
arxiv-2511-16172:
Eiji Kurozumi and Anton Skrobotov construct confidence sets for the dates when a bubble emerges, collapses, and recovers. Dating a bubble matters for policy and history, but a single estimated date hides doubt. Their method builds a confidence set for each date on its own. It does so by inverting tests for the location of a break date, turning test results into ranges of plausible dates.

They examine likelihood ratio style tests and a second family of break tests. Limiting distributions under the null case are derived, and consistency under alternatives is proven. Monte Carlo tests assess finite-sample behavior. Mixing the test types controls the empirical coverage rate well while keeping the sets at a sound length.
arxiv-2511-16672:
Omkar Thawakar and seven co-authors present EvoLMM, a way for a large multimodal model to improve its own reasoning with no labeled data and no external reward model. Two agents are instantiated from one backbone: a Proposer that invents diverse, image-grounded questions, and a Solver that answers them, with learning driven by internal consistency as a continuous self-reward.

The feedback loop rewards informative questions and cleaner reasoning structure at the same time. Built on Qwen2.5-VL, EvoLMM gained up to about three percent on multimodal math benchmarks including ChartQA, MathVista, and MathVision, using only raw training images. The authors offer it as a simple baseline for fully unsupervised self-improvement of multimodal models, with code and models released.
arxiv-2511-16772:
Jordi A. Montañà-López, Andreas Elben, Joonhee Choi, and Rahul Trivedi show that the noise of a many-body quantum simulator can be learned efficiently even when the noise has memory. That is the non-Markovian case expected to dominate as simulators scale. Efficient learning protocols existed for Hamiltonian and Markovian open-system models, but memory effects lacked one.

Their protocol targets geometrically local lattice models with quantum and classical non-Markovian noise, under a Gaussian assumption on the noise. It learns the noise with a sample count growing only logarithmically with system size. The recipe is simple to run: prepare product states, apply one layer of single-qubit Clifford gates, and measure product observables. The result extends the certification toolbox for quantum simulators into the regime where noise remembers its past.
arxiv-2511-16972:
Shuyang Yu, Jianan Liang, and Hui Hu present ToC, short for Tree-of-Claims, a system for improving patent claims with language models. Claim drafting is slow, costly, and uneven when done by hand, since each claim must stay novel while keeping its legal reach. Plain language models often lack the step-by-step search that careful claim editing needs.

ToC treats editing as a guided search. One agent proposes edits, a second agent plays the part of a patent examiner and critiques each draft for novelty and overlap with prior work, and a tree search steers the pair. A scoring rule balances novelty, kept scope, and clear sense. Tests on a patent benchmark are reported as favouring the search-based approach over plain model editing.
arxiv-2511-17072:
Nanami Nakamura, Yu Nakayama, and Ung Nguyen revisit a claimed law of two-dimensional physics. Along a renormalization group flow, which describes how a theory changes with scale, the number of charged degrees of freedom should only fall. This is the k-theorem, a charged cousin of the well-established c-theorem about total degrees of freedom. A clean proof of the k-theorem had been missing.

A recent proof of the c-theorem, built on sum rules and the positivity of averaged null energy, suggested a route. The authors follow it, taking care with partial contact terms that earlier attempts ignored. Ignoring those terms gives contradictions; handling them yields the correct sum rule and a complete proof. The result firms up a basic constraint on how quantum field theories can evolve.
arxiv-2511-17272:
Jonas Conneryd, Yassine Ghannane, and Shuo Pang prove limits on how well algorithmic hierarchies can relax constraint satisfaction problems. Such problems, and their promise variants, are attacked by hierarchies of increasingly strong approximation algorithms, and the question is how many levels a hard instance can force. The authors give a generic recipe: degree lower bounds for algebraic proof systems can be converted into level lower bounds for the hierarchies.

The conversion runs through pseudo-reduction operators, introduced by Alekhnovich and Razborov, which the authors show can fool the cohomological consistency algorithm at the heart of these hierarchies. As applications, they prove optimal level lower bounds for graph coloring promise problems across all parameters, and give a simpler proof of recent lower bounds for lax and null-constraining problems. The recipe unifies results that previously needed separate arguments.
arxiv-2511-17672:
Yinjie Zhao and three co-authors teach multimodal language models to doubt their eyes. As AI-generated imagery improves, models more and more accept synthetic pictures as real, and their reasoning on top of a deception inherits the error. The authors observe that models tend to over-trust visual inputs, and that injecting skepticism on purpose into the reasoning process sharply improves their ability to verify authenticity. Their framework, Inception, is built entirely from reasoning, with no special detector model.

Two agents iterate: an external skeptic challenges the visual evidence and an internal skeptic re-examines the model's own conclusions, each round strengthening the checking logic. The approach carries across generators and data distributions rather than memorizing one fake style. On the AEGIS benchmark it achieved state-of-the-art performance, improving by a large margin over the strongest existing language model baselines, the authors report.
arxiv-2511-17772:
Maria Bou-Sakr-El-Tayar, Jason Bramburger, and Matthew Colbrook show a simple trick that speeds up many data driven methods for dynamical systems: taper the ends of averages instead of treating all data equally. Plain long averages can converge painfully slowly, wasting good data.

Weighted averages can converge much faster, sometimes at a very fast rate, and they drop into existing tools with little change. The authors build weighted versions of five methods, from mode decomposition to weather related forecasting. Across fluid flows and climate data, weighting costs nothing, is easy to add, and often gives clearly better results.
arxiv-2511-18072:
Zhuo Yu and three co-authors estimate how often a proposed exotic particle state would be produced in decays of B mesons. The state is treated as a molecule like bound system of two mesons with a stated spin and parity. Such production rates guide experimental searches at particle colliders.

Using an effective Lagrangian approach with a meson loop mechanism, they find branching ratios in a small but accessible range for two decay channels. They also estimate how large a share the state would contribute in each. They propose a specific decay chain for searching for the state, which current experiments should be able to reach.
arxiv-2511-18172:
Juvenal Bassa and three co-authors build a simulation driven way to monitor data quality in particle collider experiments. In such experiments, detectors record huge volumes under harsh conditions, and bad data can ruin later physics analysis. Real data tie methods to one detector, so they simulate faults in a controlled setting instead.

Their network, MEDIC, learns normal detector behavior with a fast detector simulation, then flags anomalies and localizes the malfunctioning components behind them. In a simplified setup with large regions deliberately switched off, results are encouraging. The work lays groundwork for machine learning based monitoring in future detectors.
arxiv-2511-18272:
Richard J. Young tests a privacy fix for reading medical forms with vision and language models. Such tools can leak private health facts while they scan a bill or chart. The fix blurs parts of the image tokens, the units the model reads, in the hope that names and numbers stay hidden.

Young tries seven blur plans at distinct layers of a named scan model, on a set of fake bills with known ground truth. All plans cut leaks by the same share, a bit over two fifths. Long facts spread on the page, like names and street lines, vanish in full. Short codes, like record numbers and account numbers, still slip through. Blur alone, the work warns, cannot guard such forms.
arxiv-2511-18372:
Sofiane Bouarroudj, Quentin Ehret, Abdenacer Makhlouf, and Nurtas Shyntas extend a classic algebra lemma to a signed world. Superalgebras grade their parts by parity, and signs shift with swaps. Hochschild's lemma, a base fact for Lie algebras in prime characteristic, had no super form for a paired structure called Lie-Rinehart.

The team adapt a known proof to the super paired case and prove the new form. On that base they define restricted Lie-Rinehart superalgebras, where a prime power map is part of the data. They study how such objects act, build a semi direct product with a module, and give cases. A universal enveloping algebra caps the work, with the expected universal trait.
arxiv-2511-18572:
Mathias Hedegaard Kristensen, Paweł Piotr Cielecki, and Esben Skovsen sort materials by terahertz light with no reference scan. Terahertz reflection spectra carry a material's fingerprint, but a reference read is a chore in the field. The team ask if a few well chosen frequencies can do the job on raw, non referenced spectra.

Three pick strategies face off: a filter method, a shrinkage method built into the model, and a step wise search wrapper. Each feeds three sorter types. High accuracy comes from a small frequency subset, and raw spectra do at least as well as referenced ones. The step wise picks line up with true absorption bands of the materials. That match shows the sort rests on real physics, not noise.
arxiv-2511-19172:
Kehua Chen and ten co-authors present MetroGS, a framework for rebuilding large city scenes in three dimensions with Gaussian splatting, a fast rendering representation. Recent splatting methods have leapt forward on big scenes, yet doing so efficiently, stably, and with true geometric accuracy at once remains hard. MetroGS rests on a distributed two-dimensional splatting backbone that supports all its later modules as one unified base.

To fill sparse regions in complex streets, it densifies the starting points using structure-from-motion priors and a point map model, with a compensation scheme for thin coverage. A progressive optimisation then mixes monocular and multi-view geometric cues. The aim is city-scale reconstruction that surveyors and simulation builders can trust for measurement, not just for looks.
arxiv-2511-19272:
Felix Birkel presents Tiny-TSM, a time series foundation model built to be small, cheap to train, and still top-performing. Foundation models for forecasting are usually huge and industrially tuned, yet Tiny-TSM holds only a modest number of parameters and was trained on a single high-end graphics card in under a week. The economy comes from a new pipeline that generates and augments synthetic training data, rather than from architecture search or hyperparameter sweeps, which the author deliberately skips.

On a wide range of forecasting benchmarks the small model beats every rival foundation model the author evaluated on medium and long horizons. It stays competitive on short ones, at times matching far larger industrial systems. A causal input normalisation scheme adds to the package. The result challenges the assumption that forecasting quality needs scale.
arxiv-2511-19372:
Raimondo Pala brings the tools of instrumental variable analysis to panel vector autoregressions. The workhorse models that trace how several economic series push each other over time across many units, such as states or countries. Identifying true causal effects in such models is hard, and Pala adapts an identification strategy from a related literature that uses external instruments. Outside variables that shift one series without touching the others directly. He also introduces a form of local average treatment effect for when a continuous instrument acts on a binary treatment.

Simulations show that confidence sets built on a standard statistic recover impulse responses reliably. As an application, Pala instruments state military spending with each state's share of national spending and estimates the dynamic fiscal multiplier. He finds multipliers above one, with effects concentrated in the first year and persisting into the next.
arxiv-2511-19672:
Wuhuan Deng and Scott Nestler introduce new baseball metrics for plate discipline, a hitter's skill at judging which pitches to attack. A disciplined hitter swings at good pitches and lays off balls outside the zone, but most existing patience measures do not capture the taking side of that skill well. Their Discipline Score, and an adjusted version of it, judge a batter only on pitches that are balls. Comparing the batter's choices with what the league as a whole would be predicted to do in the same situation.

Scoring against the league's overall swinging probability makes the measure relative: a hitter gains credit for restraint that peers would not have shown. The metrics aim to separate true pitch judgement from mere passivity, giving analysts and teams a cleaner read on a skill that drives walks, pitch counts, and long at-bats.
arxiv-2511-19972:
Yun Xing and six co-authors propose Activation Replay, a training-free way to sharpen multimodal reasoning. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves reasoning in large multimodal models, but why it works is poorly understood. Using a logit lens view, the authors track how input activations shift after such training across several models.

They find that low-entropy activations shift unexpectedly while high-entropy ones move less, and controlled tests link this pattern to reasoning itself. Activation Replay works at test time on visual tokens, replaying low-entropy activations from the base model to steer its tuned counterpart. It improves reasoning in math, visual agent, and video tasks, widens answer coverage, and beats alternative replay choices in their comparisons.
arxiv-2511-20272:
Jiang, Xia, Xu, and colleagues test whether AI truly understands what it sees in videos. Their 2025 paper builds VKnowU, a benchmark for visual knowledge. Models recognize objects well yet miss basic world sense. Humans grasp intuitive physics and intentions at a glance. That middle layer bridges seeing and reasoning.

The benchmark holds 1,680 questions over 1,249 videos. Eight kinds of visual knowledge are covered. World-centric items probe physics-like understanding. Human-centric items probe intentions and feelings. Twenty-three leading multimodal models were evaluated. All still trail human performance noticeably. World-centric gaps were the widest of all. A training set, VKnowQA, attacks the deficit directly. Their model VideoKnow+ follows a see-think-answer routine. Reinforcement learning adds a visual knowledge reward. Scores rose by 3.7 points on VKnowU itself. Gains carried to MVBench, Video-MME, and MMVU too. Seeing is not understanding, the results insist.
arxiv-2511-20572:
Delbari, Alexandropoulos, Schober, Poor, and Jamali model wireless channels where bounced signals help instead of hurt. Their 2025 paper treats near-field MIMO, the antenna regime of future 6G systems. Close to huge antenna arrays, waves behave differently than far away. Walls and surfaces reflect paths that lack a direct line of sight. Past models treated reflectors as mere point scatterers.

The new model treats extended rough reflectors explicitly. Their surface roughness and size shape the channel's statistics. Exact integral evaluations validated the model's accuracy. Formula results show how reflectors feed into multi-user signal quality. Even though bounced paths are weaker than the direct path, they help. Simulations found conditions where they add multiplexing gain. More parallel streams become possible in multi-user setups. The framework extends to smart surfaces and near-field sensing. German and European grants supported the work.
arxiv-2511-20672:
Saad Mankarious and colleagues at George Washington University introduce in 2025 MindSET, a dataset for teaching computers to spot signs of mental illness in social media posts. Older benchmark sets had aged badly, with data hard to obtain and patchy cleaning. MindSET was built from Reddit posts by people who reported their own diagnoses, then filtered to English text with duplicates and explicit material removed.

The finished dataset holds over 13 million annotated posts spanning seven conditions, grouped into eight categories, and it more than doubles the size of earlier benchmarks. The team also ran a word-use analysis with the LIWC tool, which counts psychologically meaningful words, to compare language patterns across groups. As a proof of value, models trained on MindSET beat models trained on older benchmarks at detecting diagnoses. The gain reached 18 points of F1 score, a combined accuracy measure, on autism detection alone.
arxiv-2511-20972:
Jionghao Han and colleagues present in 2025 SingingSDS, a spoken dialogue system that answers users in song instead of speech. The system targets character roleplay and interactive entertainment, where a reply that is sung is more memorable and fun than one merely spoken. Its pipeline is modular: speech recognition transcribes the user, a language model writes an in-character reply fitted to a melody, and a singing voice synthesiser performs it.

Nearly every stage is swappable. The release combines 5 recognition models, 7 language models, singing models in Chinese-Japanese bilingual and Chinese-only versions, and 5 melody control settings. That makes 350 possible configurations, trading latency, quality, and musical style. Melody sources range from existing songs to generated tunes, and personas follow a standard character format adapted for lyrical dialogue. SingingSDS ships as a plug-and-play web demo with open-source code, built on the ESPnet ecosystem for easy extension.
arxiv-2511-21572:
Liming Yang, Junyu Luo, Xuanzhe Liu, Yiling Lou, and Zhenpeng Chen build AI agent teams that respect a budget, in 2025. Multi-agent systems, where language models collaborate as autonomous agents, solve hard tasks but burn money as they scale, and popular frameworks leave the cost-performance trade-off to chance. Their system, BAMAS, treats construction itself as an optimization problem with an explicit spending cap.

BAMAS works in three steps. Integer linear programming first picks the set of language models that best balances skill against price under the budget. Offline reinforcement learning then chooses the collaboration topology, who talks to whom, and the system is instantiated with those agents and links. On three representative tasks, BAMAS matched leading agent-construction methods while cutting cost by up to 86 percent, inside its predefined budgets. The result reframes multi-agent design as engineering under constraint.
arxiv-2511-21672:
Pavel Andreev unifies the small-scale origins of a chiral magnetic interaction and traces their wider consequences, in 2025. The Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction, a handed exchange that twists neighboring spins, is governed by one constant. That constant collects several distinct contributions with different analytic forms, and mixing them carelessly muddles predictions for spin dynamics.

Andreev reviews three contributions and combines them in a general Keffer form of the constant, then suggests going further. The effects surface in the Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert equation as novel spin torque terms, in added energy density terms, and in force densities in the momentum balance equations, with polarization dynamics treated as well. Ligand ion shifts relative to magnetic ion pairs, in both ferro- and antiferromagnetic materials, feed each term. Andreev also proposes a Keffer-like form for the exchange integral of the symmetric Heisenberg Hamiltonian, exposing a real ligand role there too.
arxiv-2511-21872:
Padovese and colleagues test whether AI-generated training data can help detect Southern Resident killer whale calls in underwater recordings. These endangered whales are monitored with hydrophones in the Salish Sea, but labelled call examples are scarce and costly. The team compared traditional tricks, like shifting calls in time, with three deep generative methods that synthesize new calls: variational autoencoders, GANs, and diffusion models.

All the generative approaches beat the plain baseline at classification. Diffusion-based augmentation did best among them, reaching a recall of 0.87, meaning it found 87 percent of real calls, with an overall F1 score of 0.75 in the reported results. A hybrid strategy mixing generated calls with traditional augmentation performed best overall, at an F1 score of 0.81 in the same evaluation. They call generative augmentation worthwhile when annotation is scarce and missed calls are costly.
arxiv-2511-22072:
Li and Wang, computer scientists, forecast electric vehicle charging demand with a framework called HyperCast. Grid operators need accurate short-term forecasts to schedule generation and let vehicles join electricity markets. Graph neural networks, the usual tool, only model pairwise station relationships, missing the group-wise patterns of urban charging, where whole neighborhoods surge together. HyperCast instead uses hypergraphs, whose edges can link many stations at once, to capture those collective dynamics directly.

Two hypergraph views, one from geographic proximity and one from demand behavior, are fused with inputs at multiple timescales separating recent trends from weekly rhythms, using specialized hyper-spatiotemporal blocks and cross-attention. Across four public datasets HyperCast significantly outperforms a wide range of state-of-the-art baselines. The authors read this as evidence that explicitly modeling collective charging behavior, rather than station pairs, is what sharpens these forecasts for grid operation.
arxiv-2511-22372:
Pacuit and Yang revisit a famous result about agreement. Aumann showed in 1976 that two agents who start from the same prior beliefs cannot have common knowledge that they disagree about an event's probability. Once their updated opinions are fully shared, they must match. Later work by Monderer, Samet, and Neeman weakened this to near-agreement: if agents commonly believe, to a high degree p, in each other's updated opinions, those opinions must be close.

Pacuit and Yang replace probabilities with plausibility measures, a general ranking of plausibility that need not use ordinary numbers. They prove a generalised agreement theorem here: common p-belief in each other's plausibility judgements still forces them to be close. Their counterexamples separate the conditions involved, showing that four natural multiplication rules do not deliver one common-prior property. The result clarifies which features of belief agreement really depends on.
arxiv-2511-22572:
Kurpiewski and colleagues build a verification framework for the safety of suborbital rocket flight. Their case study is SpaceForest's Perun rocket, flown to create microgravity for scientific experiments. The team models flight as a probabilistic multi-agent system. Telemetry feeds the model: velocity, pitch, attitude, and GPS data. Weather enters as randomness, modelled explicitly rather than ignored. Safety requirements are written in Probabilistic Alternating-Time Temporal Logic, a formalism about what groups of agents can guarantee.

The specifications flag states where the rocket risks landing in prohibited or hazardous zones. Those flags enable real-time monitoring and responses, such as emergency engine shutdown. The team compared three model variants: deterministic, probabilistic with perfect information, and probabilistic with imperfect information. Deterministic models verified safety at all precisions. Probabilistic models exposed limits at higher confidence thresholds. Verification cost also grew steeply with precision, so thresholds must be chosen carefully.
arxiv-2511-22672:
Szabo offers a panoramic introduction to noncommutative geometry as a model of quantum spacetime. The expanded lecture notes, from a mini-course at a 2025 Marseille conference, explain how classical geometry can be rebuilt algebraically, replacing spaces with operator algebras. The machinery extends to noncommutative spaces where coordinates fail to commute, as quantum spacetime should behave at the Planck scale. Key tools include C-star-algebras, K-theory, spectral geometry, quantum groups, and deformation quantization.

The lectures answer two questions, what noncommutative geometry is and what noncommutative physics is, mostly through worked examples. Applications range across string theory, quantum field theory, and a spectral-geometric derivation of the Standard Model's structure, plus condensed matter systems. Szabo stresses the framework's reach within pure mathematics too, from foliations and index theory to the Riemann hypothesis. The notes induct newcomers while offering insights even experienced readers may find new.
arxiv-2511-22772:
Bentz and Cloët connect two of nuclear physics' most consequential numbers to three-nucleon forces. The symmetry energy's slope and the incompressibility's skewness govern neutron skins, neutron star radii and maximum masses, and heavy-ion flow. Yet both are third derivatives of the energy density and hard to pin down. Using Landau's Fermi liquid theory, they derive exact, model-independent relations expressing these slope parameters through three-particle interaction parameters.

Feeding empirical information in, they conclude the isoscalar three-body parameter must be positive and larger than unity, its isovector counterpart negative and smaller in magnitude. Their leading-order Faddeev-series estimate makes it positive but smaller than unity, hinting higher-order three-body cluster terms contribute importantly to the skewness. In the second part, Bethe-Brueckner-Goldstone methods show three-particle cluster diagrams, and even medium-modified four-body terms, emerging naturally inside Fermi liquid theory.
arxiv-2511-22872:
Li and colleagues close a privacy hole in federated recommenders: the user embeddings themselves. Federated recommenders keep raw data on devices, but learned embeddings still encode sensitive attributes like gender or age, exposed to attribute inference attacks. Attribute unlearning aims to scrub that information; at user level, the practical setting, adversarial training is the most feasible tool, yet it suffers instability from heterogeneous user data and leaks through gradients.

FedAU2 answers both. An adaptive adversarial training strategy adjusts training dynamics in response to local optimisation behaviour, taming instability from non-identical user data. A dual-stochastic variational autoencoder perturbs the adversarial model, blocking the gradient channel for leaks. Across three real-world datasets, FedAU2 beat baselines on both unlearning effectiveness and recommendation quality, metrics that usually trade off. It matters for regulatory compliance too, since privacy law increasingly demands personal influence on models be removable.
arxiv-2511-22972:
Li and colleagues speed up large language models, which generate text one token at a time and so answer slowly. A known trick is speculative decoding, where a small draft model proposes words and the big model checks them in parallel. But the standard check accepts only exact matches, throwing away many draft words that mean the same thing.

Their method, FLy, loosens that check without any training: an entropy gate first asks whether the spot allows several plausible words. Then a short window watches whether the big model carries on smoothly, which signals the draft wording was fine. FLy kept at least 99 percent of the target model's accuracy while running 2.81 times faster on a 70-billion-parameter model and 5.07 times faster on the 405-billion version. And it beat a leading trained rival by a wide margin on unfamiliar data.
arxiv-2511-23072:
Mahmudlu and colleagues improve expected goals, the football metric that estimates the chance a shot becomes a goal from its context, by letting each player finish differently. Standard models treat every shooter as the same finisher. So the team built a hierarchical Bayesian model that learns player-specific effects while borrowing strength from expert ratings taken from the Football Manager 2017 game database.

Fit on 9,970 shots from StatsBomb's 2015-16 data, the model cut uncertainty for players with few shots and agreed well with standard predictions. It flagged hidden ability in Immobile and Belotti before their later improvement confirmed it. Its what-if swaps are the payoff: Sansone is predicted to add 2.2 expected goals from Berardi's chances. Replacing Vardy with Giroud at Leicester would cost about 7 expected goals. Yet the reverse swap at Arsenal would cost only about 1, showing how much tactical fit matters.
arxiv-2511-23172:
Chen and colleagues speed up text-driven 3D editing, where a user changes a 3D object or scene by typing an instruction. Existing methods edit one rendered view at a time with a 2D image model and average the edits back into the 3D asset over hundreds or thousands of iterations. This is slow and blurs textures because the views never agreed with each other.

Their ViP3DE instead borrows the temporal consistency of pretrained video generators. It conditions one on a single edited view to produce all the other edited views in one forward pass, ready for direct 3D updating. Two additions make the views land at the required camera poses and agree geometrically: motion-preserved noise blending and geometry-aware denoising. On a curated set of 100 assets, the method beat prior approaches in both quality and speed. Large shape changes remain out of reach.
arxiv-2511-23472:
Matsushita and colleagues extend quantum separation logic. A Hoare-style verification method that reasons locally about quantum programs by treating separation as disentanglement between qubits. They identify two new further forms of locality unique to the quantum domain and build RapunSL around them themselves. With new logical connectives for linear combination and mixing joining the usual separation connective in the system's core rules for program verification.

The linear combination connective delivers basis-locality, soundly reducing reasoning about superposition states to reasoning about the pure states inside them. While the mixing connective delivers outcome-locality for mixed states produced by measurement. Together the three locality principles dramatically improve the scalability of formal deductive reasoning. Which the authors demonstrate on a series of genuinely challenging case studies in their evaluation where earlier quantum separation logic would bog down badly in full detail.
arxiv-2512-00472:
Lattices are the discrete skeletons inside continuous symmetry groups, and classifying them reveals a group's arithmetic character. Béchir Dali and Moncef Riahi describe and classify splittable lattices in a metabelian solvable Lie group in 2025. The group is a semidirect product of two abelian vector groups.

The action between the two factors is given by a continuous representation built from exponentials of the parameters. Splittable lattices are those compatible with that product structure. Classifications like this serve geometry and number theory, where knowing a group's discrete subgroups is a first step toward understanding its quotient spaces. Semidirect products are the standard way to combine two groups with an action between them.
arxiv-2512-00572:
Yoga improves health when poses are done correctly, and injures when they are not. Mohammed Mohiuddin and co-authors integrate skeleton-based representations for robust yoga pose classification in 2025, using deep learning models. Automated classification reduces reliance on expert practitioners.

Skeleton representations track body joints rather than raw pixels, which makes classification robust to backgrounds, clothing, and lighting. A reliable classifier can power apps that correct a practitioner's form at home. The approach reflects a wider pattern in health technology: pose estimation turning ordinary cameras into movement coaches. Skeleton input also protects privacy, since faces and rooms never enter the model. Robustness is the stated goal, across viewpoints and body types.
arxiv-2512-00672:
Yaswanth Chittepu, Raghavendra Addanki, Tung Mai, Anup Rao, and Branislav Kveton present ML-Tool-Bench in a 2025 paper. The bench is a test ground for machine learning agents that must do a full data science job on their own. Such agents chain many steps together, from first look at data to final model.

Along the way, an agent must clean data, build features, pick a model, and tune its settings. Each choice affects the next, so planning and revision matter. A shared bench lets researchers compare agents on the same tasks and tools. That makes progress in autonomous data science easier to measure and harder to fake.
arxiv-2512-01272:
Shun Xu works on modules for vertex algebras with a twist. A vertex algebra is a math frame for fields on a string. An automorphism can twist how its modules act. Zhu's theory links those modules to simpler algebras.
