Xu builds a two-sided module that links Zhu-type algebras at two levels. The build works for a twist of any finite order. It fills a gap in the twisted form of Zhu's correspondence. Such links let scholars move hard tasks about twisted modules to simpler algebra tasks that are easier to solve.
arxiv-2512-01372:
Wei Yang and co-authors improve how apps suggest goods using images and text. A good suggestion blends what users did with what items look and read like. Noise in one mode can spoil the blend. Meanings can also clash across modes.

Weak fusion of the modes leads to poor guesses on new users. The team uses spectral reasoning, which works in the frequency domain. Their method adapts to each mode's traits as it fuses them. It also steadies how signals spread over the user-item graph. Steadier fusion should give picks that hold up better in real shops.
arxiv-2512-01572:
Letian Yi and co-authors rebuild full physical fields from very sparse measures. Few sensors must stand in for a whole field of flow, heat, or stress. That reverse task is ill-posed, with many fair answers. Hierarchy in probability models offers a path.

Their frame, Cas-Sensing, stacks an autoencoder with a diffusion cascade. Latent layers hold doubt step by step. Marginal sums resolve that doubt at inference. Fields rebuilt from sparse data could cut sensor costs in weather, oceans, and factory monitoring. Sparse sensor layouts can be random, which suits drifters, balloons, and ad hoc field kits where planned grids cannot be placed.
arxiv-2512-01672:
Zhongyuan Wu and co-authors build one anomaly detector for many data types with language models. Modern IT systems emit time series, logs, and tables at once. Each type once needed its own detector. Fast change in those systems makes upkeep hard.

Their ICAD-LLM uses in-context learning to adapt to each type. Few examples in the prompt set the task. One model then covers diverse streams. A single adaptive detector could cut the cost of guarding large, mixed IT systems against faults and attacks. Logs, metrics, and tables differ wildly in shape, so one learner for all three is a strong test of in-context skill itself.
arxiv-2512-02072:
Quantum chromodynamics, the theory of quarks and gluons, is dense, mathematical knowledge that language models ingest during training. Patrick Connor's 2025 study asks what modern open-source models, including Llama, Qwen, and Gemma, actually know about it when their insides are examined.

By reverse engineering the models' internal representations, Connor uncovers idiosyncratic patterns in how basic QCD concepts are embedded in their parameters. The embedding is uneven, reflecting the quirks of training data rather than a textbook's order. Probing a specialist science this way shows both the promise and the patchiness of using language models as physics knowledge stores.
arxiv-2512-02172:
3D Gaussian Splatting renders new views of a scene quickly and beautifully, but users often want sharper output than the training photos provide. Pranav Asthana and three co-authors present SplatSuRe in 2025, which applies super-resolution selectively to lift render quality without breaking consistency between views.

The naive fix, enhancing each input image on its own, introduces contradictions between viewpoints that blur the final render. SplatSuRe chooses where enhancement helps, keeping the multi-view geometry coherent. Higher-resolution scene rendering matters for virtual production, games, and digital twins, where the source footage is rarely as sharp as the display demands.
arxiv-2512-02472:
Wenhao Yu and colleagues at Tencent AI Lab and Washington University ask whether language models can teach themselves. Models that learn from their own practice runs could keep improving with little human help. In practice, though, unguided self training often stalls fast, or even gets worse over time.

Their 2025 study adds guidance to that loop while keeping human input small. The aim is steady gains rather than drift, with models taking in and refining what they learn. Work of this kind speaks to a long held hope for AI that improves on its own, safely and well. The work shows why a guide still helps when a model trains on its own past work.
arxiv-2512-02672:
Subhaditya Bhattacharya, Niloy Mondal, and Arunansu Sil link three cosmic puzzles inside one extended particle framework. Neutrinos have tiny masses, the universe holds more matter than antimatter, and dark matter fills space unseen. Their setup extends the type I seesaw with a scalar mediator and a dark scalar field.

Right handed neutrinos join the cast, tying mass generation to leptogenesis, the process that may have created the matter surplus. The same framework hosts WIMP dark matter, particles that interact weakly. It also predicts gravitational waves, so future detectors could test the whole story at once. One frame that ties three big gaps at once is rare, and that is what makes the test plan so neat.
arxiv-2512-02772:
Weihang Su and seven co-authors join two fields that both fight false statements from language models. Hallucination detection judges a model's own output from the model side. Fact verification checks a written claim against outside evidence, from the text side.

Working apart, each field misses tools the other has built. The authors argue for unification toward a shared framework for trustworthiness. Combined methods could catch errors that pure self checks or pure database checks miss. That need grows as models write more news, code, and advice each day. Two fields that check the same lie in two ways can lend each other tools, tests, and hard won norms for what counts as proof.
arxiv-2512-02972:
Guowen Zhang and three co-authors fuse camera and LiDAR data for 3D object detection, with LiDAR in charge. Merging both sensors in a bird's eye view has proven effective for finding cars and pedestrians. The two sensors differ sharply in geometric accuracy, though, so naive merging can hurt results.

BEVDilation is a LiDAR centric framework that prioritizes LiDAR geometry during fusion. Camera detail adds in where it helps, without blurring the precise depth structure. Careful fusion matters for self driving stacks, where a shifted box can mean a missed obstacle. Depth first, looks next is a rank rule that road gear can run in real time with the chips it has on board.
arxiv-2512-03172:
Crossing kernels link different views of the same theory. Julien Roussillon and Ioannis Tsiares report new results for Virasoro kernels in this 2025 work. These kernels matter in two-dimensional conformal field theories and three-dimensional topological theories.

The authors cover all rational values of a key parameter. That range matches all rational central charge values in a wide domain. They establish two main results for modular and fusion kernels. Exact kernels help compute in quantum groups and in models of critical systems, where many other methods fail. Rational values are dense in the parameter line, so results there reach many models.
arxiv-2512-03872:
Smart surfaces that bounce wireless signals toward users usually steer those signals by retuning the surface itself. Matteo Nerini and Bruno Clerckx compare that approach with a different one in a 2025 information theory preprint. Their alternative keeps the surface fixed and instead moves the signal, adjusting its frequency while the surface's properties stay put.

The comparison covers dual-polarised surfaces whose reflection can be a simple diagonal matrix or a richer beyond-diagonal one. In every pairing, movable signals on a fixed surface beat a reconfigurable surface, gaining at least fourfold. When the transmitter and receiver use different polarisations, the beyond-diagonal fixed surface pulls further ahead. The result reframes a design question for future wireless systems. Engineers may get more from shifting the signal than from endlessly reconfiguring the mirror it hits.
arxiv-2512-04072:
Reasoning models that think in long chains use recognisable moves: checking an answer, backtracking, trying another method. Zayne Sprague and colleagues ask how a model can learn moves it does not already show, in a 2025 preprint. Their answer, SkillFactory, prepares the model during supervised fine-tuning, before reinforcement learning begins, using training data built from the model's own samples.

The trick is rearrangement: outputs the base model already produces are restructured into traces displaying the target skills, even if imperfectly. These silver traces prime the model so reinforcement learning has something to sharpen. Afterwards, SkillFactory-initialised models generalised better to harder task variants, despite lower starting performance. The skills were verifiably used, and the models resisted regression on out-of-domain tasks better than plain baselines. The authors argue that inductive biases planted before reinforcement learning make the resulting skills more robust.
arxiv-2512-04172:
Arhum Ansari, Sachin Jain, and Dhruva K S study how particles interact in a curved space that physicists use as a model of quantum gravity. The space is the four-dimensional anti-de Sitter world, and the team works on its boundary, where a matching flat theory lives. Their 2025 arXiv paper looks at four-point functions, which encode how four particles scatter in real time.

When the middle two particles move on spacelike paths, the team shows each exchange splits cleanly into a product of three-point functions. The same result can be shifted to a round, Euclidean form without hard nested integrals. That shortcut skips the bulk integrals that the standard diagram method needs. The authors then restate key parts in twistor space, a language built from light rays. They give a neat closed form for one test case, opening a path to simpler gravity math.
arxiv-2512-04272:
Space plasmas rarely settle into tidy Maxwellian velocity distributions; their particles follow kappa distributions, with heavier high-energy tails. Seiji Zenitani addresses a practical simulation need in a 2025 plasma physics preprint: how to generate such a distribution inside a particle-in-cell simulation, cheaply and simply.

His answer is a rejection-sampling procedure that uses a Pareto distribution as the envelope. The method needs only uniform random numbers, nothing more exotic. Its acceptance efficiency runs around three quarters to four fifths, so few sampled particles are wasted. For kinetic modelling of space plasma processes, that makes loading a kappa distribution a routine step rather than a numerical chore.
arxiv-2512-04772:
Mauro Martini, Marco Ambrosio, Judith Vilella-Cantos, and co-authors release TEMPO-VINE, a large dataset for testing robot navigation among vineyard rows. Precision farming leans on autonomous machines, yet most navigation research trains on simulations or one-off field trials. Real vineyards shift with seasons, growth, and weather, and no shared benchmark captured that change. Their 2025 arXiv paper fills the gap with repeated visits to working vineyards.

Robots recorded the same rows across many times, carrying fused sensors for vision, depth, and motion. The data targets sensor fusion, simultaneous localization and mapping, and place recognition under real farm conditions. A system that maps a row in spring must still know its place when vines leaf out in summer. Such a public, multi-season record lets labs grade navigation fairly and harden farm robots before growers trust them alone.
arxiv-2512-04872:
Carlos Rafael Nogueira da Silva, Maria Cecilia Luna Alvarado, and Fernando Darío Almeida García offer two tractable stand-ins for the lognormal distribution, a workhorse model that resists exact math. The lognormal rules signal fading in wireless links and appears across biology, finance, and engineering. Its key metrics usually have no closed form, forcing slow numerical work. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds surrogate models from products of Nakagami variables and their inverses.

The surrogates are asymptotically exact where it counts. They yield closed-form expressions for the characteristic function, bit error rate, and channel capacity. Even the density and distribution functions come out in usable form. Engineers can then size wireless systems with formulas instead of heavy simulation. The same trick may serve other fields where the lognormal's stubbornness blocks clean analysis.
arxiv-2512-04972:
Peng Liu, Zhonghao Tu, Jianping Yuan, and Ang Li examine the giant glitch of the pulsar PSR J1718-3718, a sudden jump in spin that the star went through in 2007. Pulsars are dense dead stars that rotate with clock-like steadiness, so a glitch points to violent changes deep inside. The team asks what the star's slow recovery afterward reveals about its inner layers and the forces that brake its spin.

They fit the timing record with a model in which tiny whirlpools in the star's superfluid interior creep inward and outward, while the braking torque from outside also changes with time. The fit matches the data and suggests the glitch began with a crack in the crust that set the whirlpools moving and shifted the star's shape. The work shows that even sparse timing data can pin down events inside a neutron star.
arxiv-2512-05072: Jordan Cotler, Prateksh Dhivakar, and Kristan Jensen ask what holography allows for flat-space quantum gravity. Holography says gravity in a region can be fully described by a theory on its boundary. For flat space the proposed boundary theory is Carrollian, named for the physics of extremely slow motion. The authors translate the scattering data of flat-space gravity coupled to matter into that boundary language. They show that interactions in the bulk force the boundary theory to be non-local, constraining any such dual.
arxiv-2512-05172:
Wentao Wang, Chunyang Liu, Kehua Sheng, Bo Zhang, and Yan Wang introduce Semore, a framework that gives reinforcement-learning agents a richer view. Agents that learn from raw images struggle because their backbones capture limited meaning. Prior work used language models to steer the policy itself; this team attacks the representation, using a vision-language model to enrich what the agent perceives before it decides.

Semore's two-path backbone reads video frames and pulls out two kinds of features at once: semantic ones, about what things are, and motion ones, about how they move. The vision-language model's commonsense knowledge and a pretrained image-text aligner guide that extraction. Separate supervision lets the two feature types develop while interacting freely. In experiments the agents learn efficiently and adapt better than leading alternatives, suggesting feature-level guidance from pretrained models is a strong lever for control.
arxiv-2512-05272:
Ahmet Berke Gokmen, Ajad Chhatkuli, Luc Van Gool, and Danda Pani Paudel teach a system to rebuild moving, multi-object scenes in three dimensions plus time — without ever showing it one. Scenes mix still and moving objects, and capturing a four-dimensional example is impractical, so earlier methods handled one object at a time and leaned on category-specific shape models. That left inconsistent scenes and narrow coverage.

Their method, COM4D, splits the learning problem in two. From multi-object scenes it learns how objects compose; from videos of moving objects it learns dynamics — training spatial and temporal attention pathways on two-dimensional video. At test time, an attention-mixing mechanism alternates between the two kinds of reasoning and assembles persistent four-dimensional scenes from a video. Despite never seeing data, COM4D sets state-of-the-art results on both four-dimensional and composed three-dimensional reconstruction.
arxiv-2512-05772:
Mariami Gamsakhurdia, Matthias Baaz, and Anela Lolic settle a decidability question in fuzzy logic. Gödel logics are many valued systems where truth comes in degrees. The Bernays-Schönfinkel class is a family of logical sentences, named for a 1928 proof, whose decidability is famous in ordinary logic. The question is whether such sentences stay decidable when truth is graded.

The answer is yes, on both of the paper's tests. For validity, the key is that Skolemization, a standard rewriting that removes existential claims, still works for prenex Gödel logics. For the companion notion of 1-satisfiability, the team uses structural features of prenex formulas. Both properties turn out decidable in every Gödel logic, and they persist across all infinite valued ones. A class tame for machines in the two valued world stays tame when truth is graded.
arxiv-2512-05972:
Lizhe Hong's study grows graphene inside a computer, atom by atom, and fixes two flaws that plagued earlier simulations. Graphene, a single sheet of carbon, is often grown on copper, and molecular dynamics with the LAMMPS package can mimic the process. Carbon atoms, freed from methane, rain onto a copper crystal face and link into flakes. Hong compared growth at three temperatures, checking flake quality and deposition rate.

Earlier work had quiet problems. Earlier setups let the system's pressure climb until the simulation crashed, cutting off everything after. And potential function choices were only partly understood. Correcting both produced a stable system whose pressure stays sane to the end. A potential function selection table is included. Others can build on results only when failure modes are named and repaired.
arxiv-2512-06072:
Ecaterina Leonova and seven co-authors hunt for the reason some infant galaxies shine through the fog of the early universe while others stay hidden. In the epoch of reionization, the first galaxies were clearing the cosmic fog. Which galaxies show Lyman-alpha light is a clue to the clearing. Using JWST FRESCO data, the team mapped emitter neighborhoods, and recovered eight new ones from archival Keck spectroscopy, fourteen in total.

The obvious theory fails. Bright emitters were expected in overdense, pre-ionized bubbles. They do not: their environments are no denser than average, and overdensity measures for emitters and non-emitters match. Emitters show slightly brisker recent star formation; little else distinguishes them. Visibility, then, is not mainly about address. Escape routes through a galaxy's own gas may decide instead. The clearing's map is written in more than clustering.
arxiv-2512-06372:
Alexander Tarasenkov and five co authors report a month of watching a small binary star system flare up. The system is a dwarf nova of the WZ Sge type, where a white dwarf pulls gas from a tiny companion star until the stolen gas erupts in a bright outburst. This flare was huge, and its light curve broke the usual pattern for its class.

Early in the decline the team found rapid light wiggles, called early superhumps, ticking at a steady short period. After a flat stretch of about eleven days, a second kind of wiggle showed up, later than in most such stars. That delay is a rare trait for this class. From the wiggle timing the authors weigh both stars, judge the companion to be very light, and place the system at a fair distance. The odd timing gives theorists a fresh case for how these eruptions unfold.
arxiv-2512-06472:
Javier Bracho and Luis Montejano study a family of shapes in complex projective space, driven by a question about complex ellipsoids. They first pin down what makes an ellipsoid special in complex terms. It is a compact set that every complex line meets in a set way: at one point, or cutting out the image of a full disk. That property sets up the broader study.

They turn to compact sets in complex projective space. Any complex line that meets such a set does so in one of three ways. It can touch at a single point, run along the rim of a complex disk, or lie along the whole line. Within that family they focus on sets cut out by quadratic equations over the real numbers. The work maps how such sets behave as shapes.
arxiv-2512-07072:
Bin Wu, Xu Zhu, Wenwen Zhou, and Zewen Wang ask how reliably one can recover the hidden start of a vibrating system from scraps of measurement. When both the system and its equations are discretized and noisy. Their model is a one-dimensional stochastic hyperbolic equation, fully discretized, with three unknowns at once: the initial displacement, the initial velocity, and the random source driving it. The data are spare: spatial derivative readings at the left end, plus the solution and its time derivative at the final moment.

The key tool is a new Carleman estimate, a weighted energy inequality tailored to this discrete stochastic setting. Built on it, the authors prove Lipschitz stability: errors in the recovered unknowns are controlled proportionally by errors in the data. One extra term appears on the bound's far side, priced by the mesh size, an honest tax imposed by discretization itself.
arxiv-2512-07372:
Asma Ababafi and co-authors give the contact binary EZ Oct its first full portrait. Contact binaries are pairs of stars so close they share one envelope, and this one's eclipses are total, making it a clean laboratory. The team combines their own multiband observations from an observatory in Argentina with the continuous stare of the TESS space telescope. Then models the light curves with a standard binary code explored by Markov chain sampling.

The orbit is widening steadily: the period grows along a smooth quadratic trend, the signature of mass flowing from the lighter star to the heavier at a slow, measured rate. A cold starspot had to be added before the model fit the light.
arxiv-2512-07472:
Siyu Xu, Zijian Wang, Yunke Wang, Chenghao Xia, Tao Huang, and Chang Xu wrote this 2025 robotics paper. Vision-language-action models steer robots by linking what they see and hear to motion. When a scene changes, such models often repeat memorized paths instead of adapting.

The authors call that failure the memory trap. It grows from designs that lack reasoning about three-dimensional space. Their fix, Affordance Field Intervention, plugs in a map of where action is physically possible. The system senses a memory trap through the robot's own body signals. It then pulls the robot back to a recent spot with high affordance. New waypoints grow out of the affordance map and anchor the model's actions. A scorer picks the path with the best total affordance score. Tests on real robots under shifted conditions show clear gains in success. A manipulation benchmark shows the same pattern of improvement.
arxiv-2512-07572:
Benjamin Diamond wrote this 2025 mathematics paper in algebraic geometry. It studies Fano schemes, which collect all the flat spaces of a fixed size inside a given shape. The shape itself is cut out by several equations inside projective space.

Diamond asks how the topology of such a Fano scheme compares with a simpler host space. That host is the Grassmannian, the space of all flat spaces of the same size. He proves the two share the same integral cohomology across a certain range of degrees. The range depends only on the basic sizes in the setup, not on the equations' details. Earlier work by Debarre and Manivel had settled the same question with rational numbers. Moving to whole numbers is stricter and answers a question posed by Benoist and Voisin. His proof adapts techniques that Tu first built for a different purpose.
arxiv-2512-07872:
Ishaan Kunwar, Henry Cantor, Tyler Rizzo, and Ayaan Qayyum wrote this 2025 engineering paper on locating sound. Beam localization asks where an audio source sits, using a small microphone array. Sampling limits cap the precision of that estimate in ordinary systems.

Their system, LocaGen, learns to beat the sampling grid itself. Machine learning models train on realistic synthetic data from a simulation. Three microphones supply the raw timing cues for each estimate. The models sharpen both direction-of-arrival and the precise source position. Quantization error from coarse sampling is the specific enemy here. The full system runs on a low-powered embedded device. Resource use rises only slightly while accuracy climbs steeply. Direction error falls by roughly two-thirds in their demonstration. Even a modest rate suffices. Cheap arrays in smart devices could locate speakers far better this way.
arxiv-2512-07972:
Natsuko Yamaguchi, Kareem El-Badry, and three co-authors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper. Some main-sequence stars orbit white dwarfs in wide, well-measured pairs. 

When the white dwarf's parent star was a giant, it shed material. The companion could accrete that wind and keep its chemical signature. Slow neutron capture in giant stars forges the telltale elements, barium among them. The team measured abundances for a large, uniform sample of companions. Gaia supplied the orbits for all of these white dwarf pairs. Dozens of barium dwarfs turned up, most of them newly found. That roughly doubles the known population in such binaries. Their enrichment varies widely from star to star in the sample. The pattern tracks component masses and metallicity, not orbital separation. The number of thermal pulses the giant endured explains much of the spread. They form a clean lab for mass transfer physics.
arxiv-2512-08172:
Kyle Yates, Antsa Pierrottet, Abdullah Al Mamun, and colleagues, researchers in cryptography and computing, posted a security study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is an attack on a variant of the learning with errors problem that skips modular reduction, known as the integer version. The attack matters because popular post quantum signature schemes, such as CRYSTALS Dilithium, rely on this problem and use rejection sampling.

An earlier least squares attack from a 2018 conference targeted the problem directly. This team tests how well that attack works on small instances drawn from real signature schemes, building their test cases from signatures alone rather than side channel leaks. They add new simulation techniques for handling huge sample counts efficiently. Their experiments support the claimed security of these signature schemes. The authors also discuss what the results mean for real uses, including intelligent transportation systems that will need trustworthy digital signatures.
arxiv-2512-08272:
You Hung Hsu, a mathematician in representation theory, posted a short note on arXiv in December 2025. The note concerns a family of algebras called zero affine quantum groups, in the version introduced by Arkhipov and Mazin. Hsu shows that the positive part of this quantum group can be realized in a completely different language. That language is Hall algebras: the K theoretic Hall algebra built from the type A Dynkin quiver.

Hall algebras build new structure from how quiver representations fit together, and the K theoretic version uses a richer counting scheme. Hsu then constructs a categorical action of that positive part, which induces semiorthogonal decompositions on the matching weight categories. His main example is the derived category of coherent sheaves on partial flag varieties. The note links quantum groups, Hall algebras, and category theory in one concrete picture.
arxiv-2512-08672:
P H F Arruda and S D Campos study low mass neutron stars with a simple model for matter inside them. Their equation of state joins a polytropic crust to a core of modified van der Waals type, in separate pieces. The model stays easy to solve while still allowing pressure to depend on density in a nonlinear way.

The authors enforce rules for physical consistency and for signals not exceeding light speed. They find the densities where the shape of the pressure curve changes, which marks transition like behavior. Solving the standard equations for star structure gives mass and radius sequences with fairly low masses. The chemical potential also shows the expected signs of a phase change well above the matching density. The work offers a controlled test bed for low mass star models.
arxiv-2512-08772:
Hamsini Ramanathan and coauthors use a generative protein model to design new terpene synthases, enzymes that build the core structures of many natural products. Terpenes include important drugs, such as the anticancer drug Taxol. Designing such enzymes from scratch by directed evolution is costly and slow, so a learned design method could speed discovery.

Their model, TpsGPT, fine tunes a protein language model on a large curated set of synthase sequences taken from a public database. From tens of thousands of generated candidates, the team applies many checks on classification, structure confidence, diversity, and domain content. Seven candidates pass all filters. Lab tests confirm enzyme activity in at least two of them, even though they are distant from known natural enzymes. The result shows that focused training plus strict filtering can yield working new enzymes.
arxiv-2512-08872:
Ianniccari and coauthors derive an equation for the long term stats of waves that interact with each other in flat space and act in a turbulent way.

The waves are tracked through their multipoles, the parts that describe how the field spreads by angle. Injecting many gravitons with large multipoles drives the system, at large times, toward an inverse cascade in multipole space. That drift to larger scales is the main long term effect the equation predicts. The authors present the equation as a tool for the stats of such wave systems at late times, where direct tracking of each wave is not a practical option.
arxiv-2512-08972:
Hamed Bouzari Nezhad constructs a metric affine version of degenerate higher order scalar tensor theories of gravity. Such theories add a scalar field with higher derivative terms, while degeneracy conditions prevent unwanted extra degrees of freedom. In the metric affine setting, the connection is independent and enters through curvature and second derivatives of the scalar.

Starting from a completed quadratic action, the author solves the connection equation by fully decomposing the distortion tensor. That gives a closed form effective metric theory. Imposing the standard degeneracy conditions then selects a specific branch that is fixed by two free functions in the action. Analysis of the tensor sector adds one more demand: gravitational waves must travel at light speed. That demand narrows the theory to a one function family. The work gives a detailed, self contained map of this sector and shows what wave observations imply for its form.
arxiv-2512-09072:
Mohid Farhan proposes relic density topology as a tool to tell apart three dark matter models: an inert doublet model and two supersymmetric models. All three can host a heavy particle that could account for dark matter. A unified numerical scan over the heavy mass regime compares their profiles on equal footing.

The inert doublet model shows a broad, stable region that yields the observed relic density, driven by efficient gauge couplings. The supersymmetric models usually overproduce dark matter and reach the observed value only through narrow, finely tuned resonance channels. A fine tuning measure shows the inert doublet space is far more natural. Thermal history measures confirm all viable regions fit cosmological observations, yet the models differ in their decoupling stories. Distinct signatures are identified for each model. Finding a heavy dark matter particle without sharp resonance features would favor the scalar doublet picture over minimal supersymmetry.
arxiv-2512-09272:
Wei Teng and co-authors investigate an anomaly in how atomic nuclei release energy. When a nucleus steps down through its excited states, the strength of one gamma-ray transition compared with another is usually above a standard value. Recent experiments found several neutron-deficient nuclei where that ratio, called B4/2, drops below one instead.

The team models these cases with the proton-neutron interacting boson model, which treats protons and neutrons as separate collective systems, using a standard consistent-Q Hamiltonian. Their calculations reproduce the suppressed ratio and link it to triaxial shapes, nuclei stretched unevenly along three axes, together with strong mixing between energy bands. The results explain the odd behavior seen in tungsten, osmium, and platinum isotopes. The authors present this as new insight into the B(E2) anomaly, a standing puzzle about transition strengths in these nuclei.
arxiv-2512-09372:
Jingxuan Yang and colleagues present IRTest, a framework for stress-testing decision-making agents for control systems. Testing is hard because the agent's inner design may be unknown, its states may be hidden, and the space of scenarios is enormous. Testers often rely on surrogate models of the agent, but a mismatch between surrogate and reality limits what the tests can prove.

IRTest adapts its surrogate while testing runs. It starts from a model trained offline, then closes the gap to the agent in two ways. It uses online neural fine-tuning when data are plentiful, and a light importance-sampling correction when data are scarce. An optimization strategy with a bias-corrected scoring rule steers scenario generation between exploring ground and exploiting weak spots. Across tasks of varying complexity, IRTest improved failure discovery, robustness, and generalization between systems, which the authors offer as a route to resilience testing.
arxiv-2512-09572:
Anish Sambamurthy and Ashesh Chattopadhyay diagnose a failure mode of diffusion forecasting for turbulent flows and propose fixes. Diffusion models offer a probabilistic way to emulate turbulence, but turbulent flows have power-law spectra coupling fine scales to large ones. The authors show diffusion models cause spectral collapse: the high-wavenumber features are swamped by noise earlier than large features, biasing the model against fine structure.

They reinterpret the noise schedule as a spectral regularizer and introduce power-law schedules that preserve fine-scale structure longer. Their Lazy Diffusion method distills generation into a single step guided by the learned score geometry, avoiding the reverse trajectories where fine scales degrade. Tested on high-Reynolds-number two-dimensional Kolmogorov turbulence and on ocean data for the Gulf of Mexico, the methods restored scaling, stabilized rollouts, and kept forecasts probabilistic. The authors argue Gaussian scheduling is mismatched to power-law physics.
arxiv-2512-09672:
Mehedi Hasan Rumi introduces the Pattern-Based Stabilizer Tripwire, a hybrid quantum-classical key distribution protocol that works with any stabilizer-based quantum error-correcting code. Quantum key distribution promises security from physics, but schemes discard many transmission slots in sifting. This design aims to sift well in operation while turning any spying attempt into a glaring failure.

Logical data is embedded in the commutation links of physical Pauli operators. The qubit layout is hidden by a group of permutations known only to the parties. An interceptor who cannot align with that frame blinds the receiver's decoder with a mismatched syndrome, forcing an uncorrectable error rate of fifty percent and converting anomalies into a sure tripwire. Public messages, built from commuting syndromes, act as an information-theoretic blinding mask through a conditional XOR scheme. Combined with a time-split channel and privacy amplification, the adversary's information collapses to zero.
arxiv-2512-09772:
James Luther and Donald Brown measure the cultural alignment of language models, asking whose values their answers resemble. They use Hofstede's VSM13 survey instrument to score six models: two DeepSeek versions and four OpenAI models including GPT-4 and GPT-5. Two levers are tested for steering alignment. One is the language of the prompt, English or Simplified Chinese. The other is cultural prompting, a system instruction asking the model to answer as someone from a country.

DeepSeek's models and GPT-5 aligned with the United States and never achieved soft alignment with China, despite cultural prompts and Chinese prompting. GPT-4 aligned closer to China when prompted in English, but cultural prompting shifted it toward the United States. GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 responded to both levers and reached alignments with both countries. The authors frame the results as evidence that cultural defaults in these models are sticky and unevenly steerable.
arxiv-2512-10072:
Megan Delamer leads a team solving the mystery of radio emission from the F star HD 220242. Low frequency, circularly polarized radio signals can hint at star planet interaction or exoplanet emission. In a large LOFAR survey, nineteen M dwarfs showed such emission, but HD 220242 was the only F star. The team gathered radial velocity measurements with the Habitable-zone Planet Finder, adding archival velocities and proper motion accelerations from the Hipparcos and Gaia missions.

Together, the data reveal a stellar companion orbiting about every seventeen years, with roughly three fifths the Sun's mass. Spectral energy distribution fitting and the absence of ultraviolet excess rule out a white dwarf. The companion is an ordinary M dwarf. F stars lack the coronal properties to produce the observed coherent emission, while M dwarfs produce it readily. The radio signal therefore most plausibly comes from the companion, not from any planet.
arxiv-2512-10172:
Nicholas Clark, Ryan Bai, and Tanu Mitra build Offscript, a tool that checks whether language models actually follow the custom instructions users give them. People increasingly personalize chatbots and search systems through behavioral prompts: cite sources this way, answer in that tone. Nothing verifies that the instructions are obeyed. Offscript audits automatically, flagging likely instruction following failures in conversation. In a pilot study, the authors sourced real custom instructions from Reddit and ran the auditor over the resulting chats.

The auditor flagged potential deviations in the large majority of conversations. Human review then confirmed about a quarter of the flagged cases as material violations, real failures rather than technicalities. That two step pattern is the point: automated auditing can triage at scale, and humans can verify a manageable subset. The authors conclude automated auditing is a viable way to evaluate compliance with behavioral instructions for information seeking.
arxiv-2512-10772:
Kevin Glocker and co-authors ask whether growing a model first is the cheapest way to teach it a new language. Models adapted to medium- and low-resource languages still lag, and plain continued pretraining on target-language text is data-hungry. Their study compares strategies at matched computing cost, testing whether upscaling an English base model before adaptation beats the standard route.

Once the larger models saw enough target-language data, they matched or beat smaller models that had been continually pretrained on far more of it, a clear data-efficiency win. Scaling also protected the base model's English skill, cutting the catastrophic forgetting that adaptation usually causes. The authors then merged separately adapted, upscaled models into modular multilingual systems. Merging still trails joint multilingual training, but upscaled merges beat small ones, and the wide spread between merging methods suggests room for language-aware improvements.
arxiv-2512-11072:
Valery Asiryan studies a classic number theory problem about matching sums of fifth powers, restricted by a linear condition on the numbers involved. Two pairs of whole numbers are sought whose fifth powers add to the same total, with the pair sums differing by a fixed amount. That extra condition lets Asiryan bring the geometry of curves to bear.

After proving the difference must be a multiple of thirty, he shows the problem defines a family of genus one curves. Studying their Jacobian partners, he finds each carries a special rational point of order two, but never the full set of such points. A computer assisted argument using a genus two curve rules out extra torsion in special cases. For every allowed difference, the relevant group of rational points turns out to have rank exactly one, with an explicit point of infinite order constructed.
arxiv-2512-11172:
N. Mohammad and colleagues calculate the rates of several fusion reactions driven by helium-3 nuclei, reactions that matter for how stars and the early universe built heavier elements. At the low energies found in stars, fusion happens by quantum tunnelling through an energy barrier, and predicting its probability needs a good model of the nuclear forces involved.

They study three reactions involving helium-3 striking itself, lithium, and boron targets. Their tunnelling model uses a potential derived microscopically from nucleon interactions, with densities folded together and adjusted for density dependence, improving on earlier work. From it they compute the astrophysical S factor and fusion cross section that astronomers use. The calculated results agree fairly well with experimental values reported in the literature, supporting the refined potential for low energy reaction studies.
arxiv-2512-11272:
Do Hai Son and a large team detect cyberattacks on blockchain systems by turning transaction data into pictures and letting a vision model read them. Blockchains now serve finance, health, and energy, yet attackers exploit transactions and smart contracts to steal assets or corrupt the system. Text based detectors miss patterns that become visible in image form.

Their pipeline first uses language processing techniques to convert key transaction features into image representations. A vision transformer, a model known for capturing complex patterns and relationships, then analyses those images for attack signatures. Tests on benchmark datasets beat existing leading methods on both accuracy and robustness across many attack types. The authors present the hybrid design as a broadly effective shield for blockchain transactions and contracts.
arxiv-2512-11572:
Agnes P C van Hoof and a large team report telescope views of a distant cosmic flash named EP240801a. The Einstein Probe and Fermi satellite caught it as a fast X-ray flash at redshift 1.67. The Webb and Hubble space telescopes then studied the faint galaxy and fading light at that spot.

The light matches a broad lined Type Ic supernova, named SN 2024aihh. At about 23 days it shone near magnitude minus 19, much like the famed 1998bw blast. It sits about 6 kiloparsecs from its galaxy core, in a dim zone whose stars average 1.4 billion years old. It is the most distant blast of its kind yet confirmed by spectra.
arxiv-2512-11872:
Mingwang Xu and a large team present WAM-Diff, a driving system that plans with masked diffusion instead of word by word style generation. Self driving stacks fuse camera input and language commands into motion plans. Masked diffusion, which fills a masked sequence in flexible order, had barely been tried for trajectories.

WAM-Diff adds three parts: a masked diffusion planner with free decoding order, a sparse mixture of experts brain trained on motion and driving questions, and online reinforcement learning at the sequence level. It scored 91.0 PDMS on NAVSIM-v1 and 89.7 EPDMS on NAVSIM-v2, top tier marks. The results make masked diffusion a real rival for driving policy design.
arxiv-2512-12472:
Thomas A Trainor reanalyzes hadron spectra from lead lead and proton proton collisions at 2.76 TeV in a 2025 paper. He uses a two component model with soft and hard parts to study jet suppression, the apparent loss of high energy jets in heavy ion collisions. Standard work leans on the Glauber model for collision geometry and on spectrum ratios for suppression claims.

Trainor sets geometry from mean transverse momentum data instead, and questions the factorization assumption behind ratio methods. His results point to exclusivity and time dilation for participant partons as key effects missing from standard models. Patterns once read as jet suppression from quark gluon plasma match fixed target data, he argues, with no clear plasma signal.
arxiv-2512-13372:
Sara Pena-Gutierrez and co-authors present emergent learning, a way to turn a disordered optical medium into a photonic computing device. Light passing through a multiply scattering material produces a complex output pattern. They show that pattern is governed by an optical-synaptic matrix with the same form as a Hebbian memory matrix.

By shaping the input, they engineer that matrix to store a chosen memory pattern, an attractor. The device then compares new patterns with the stored one by light intensity alone, with no digital layer in between. Its storage capacity is astronomically large in their estimate. Training happens mostly in the optical domain, cutting computing cost.
arxiv-2512-13572:
Zeki Hayran and John B. Pendry build a theory of space-time refraction for structured light waves. Refraction is the bending of a wave at a boundary. Here both the wave packet and the boundary move in space and time, and either can have an apparent speed above that of light.

By finding what stays fixed at a translating boundary, they derive refraction laws for baseband, X-wave, and sideband packets. The laws hold for any boundary speed and connect to static and pure time cases. They reveal a push-broom regime that squeezes many speeds into a narrow band, and a fission regime where one X-wave splits into two branches. Uses may include time gating and optical buffering.
arxiv-2512-13672:
Kunhee Kim and co-authors improve textual inversion, a way to personalize text-to-image models with a learned token. The method is cheap but often fails on complex prompts. They trace that failure to norm inflation: learned tokens drift to odd magnitudes that weaken prompt conditioning.

Their fix, Directional Textual Inversion, holds the token magnitude at a normal scale and learns only its direction. They argue meaning in CLIP token space sits mostly in direction, not size. Learning runs on a unit sphere with a von Mises-Fisher prior. Across tasks, their method improved text fidelity while keeping subject likeness. It also allows smooth blending between learned concepts, which standard textual inversion lacks.
arxiv-2512-13872:
Kamil Ciosek and co-authors tackle how to measure the calibration error of a binary classifier from finite data. Calibration asks whether a model's stated probabilities match real outcome rates. Estimating that error well matters for trusting a classifier, but finite samples make the estimate itself uncertain.

They give an upper bound for any classifier whose calibration function has bounded variation. They also give a method to modify any classifier so its calibration error can be bounded efficiently, with little loss of performance and no restrictive premises. All results are non-asymptotic and distribution-free. The paper closes with practical advice on measuring calibration error, and its procedures run on real data sets with modest overhead.
arxiv-2512-14272:
Brian Buckley, Adrian O Hagan, and Marie Galligan present VBphenoR in a 2025 paper. The R package groups patients from electronic health records into phenotypes, meaning sets of traits that mark a condition, using a variational Bayes latent class method with closed form updates.

First, a Gaussian mixture model finds the latent class for each patient by coordinate ascent variational inference. Then a variational Bayes logistic regression gives the chance that a patient has the phenotype of interest. It also measures biomarker shifts versus a healthy group and tests how well clinical and medication codes predict the class. The latent class from the first step informs the second, linking the two stages.
arxiv-2512-15072:
Jin-Tian Zhang and four coauthors design a quantum battery that stores its energy in the light field of a coherent Ising machine. Quantum batteries promise to hold and deliver energy using quantum effects, but decoherence, the decay of quantum order, ruins most designs, and few platforms are practical. An Ising machine's signal field offers a mature optical home for one.

The team splits the battery's extractable work, its ergotropy, into coherent and incoherent parts. The coherent part fades at roughly half the rate of the incoherent part, so it resists decoherence far better. Both the coherent work and the average charging power peak at nearly the same moment, which tells the user exactly when to switch off the pump. Coupled to a two level load, the battery then discharges efficiently. The design can be built on existing optical hardware.
arxiv-2512-15172:
Linus Head leads fifteen authors using the Juno probe to read Jupiter's far northern lights for signs of plasma bursts. Bright, sharp features in the UV aurora are thought to mark times when plasma is flung inward in the space around the planet. Two rival ideas compete to explain them: scattering in the magnetodisc, and fast waves high above the poles.

The team found the features with an automatic search, then matched Juno-UVS images with data from Juno's other tools. Scattering seems to explain most of the rain of electrons tied to these burst marks. The marks also split into two types: dawn storm and non dawn storm, and the team shows the second type does occur. Arc like features in the outer glow look much like chains of burst marks stretched into arcs as electrons drift at speeds set by their energy.
arxiv-2512-15572:
Timo Grasser and co authors show that spin dynamic mean field theory can simulate spin diffusion in static solids from first principles in a 2025 paper. Nuclear spin ensembles interact through long range dipolar coupling, so many spins move together and exact calculation is impossible. The mean field approach needs only those couplings as input.

The method works when each spin interacts with many others. The team applies it to spectral spin diffusion in static samples and to zero quantum line shapes, which had lacked an efficient accurate simulation. Benchmarks on two test substances match published experimental data closely. The authors recommend the method for large scale spin diffusion studies in magnetic resonance.
arxiv-2512-15672:
Jing Ming and co authors report the deepest search yet for continuous gravitational waves from three young neutron stars in a 2025 paper. The targets sit at the centers of the supernova remnants Cassiopeia A, Vela Jr, and the remnant named G347 point 3 dash 0 point 5. Volunteers in the Einstein@Home project supplied the computing power.

Starting from O3a data, the team followed up about 45 million candidates in stages, using independent O3b and O4a data at the end. They set the tightest limits yet on wave amplitude, equatorial ellipticity, r mode saturation, and, for the first time, crustal anisotropy. One candidate from that remnant survived every follow up. Newer data exist but are not yet public.
arxiv-2512-15972:
Ayoub Kasmi, El Houssine Azroul, and Mohammed Shimi wrote this pure mathematics paper, which appeared on arXiv in 2025. They define a new kind of function space that blends fractional calculus with Musielak spaces. Such spaces describe functions whose growth rules can change from point to point, which suits problems with memory and long-range effects.

The authors prove basic facts about the new space, such as how it sits inside other known spaces. They then use a tool called the mountain pass theorem to show that a related nonlinear fractional equation has a nontrivial solution. The work gives analysts a fresh setting for nonlocal boundary value problems, where conditions at the edge of a region shape what happens inside.
arxiv-2512-16072:
Nan Gao, Pu Zhang, and Shijie Zhu answer a structural question in research shared on arXiv in 2025. An algebra is called left weakly Gorenstein when every module that almost passes the Gorenstein-projective test truly passes it. Such algebras form a well-behaved class, and the authors check whether two common constructions stay inside it.

Using monomorphism categories, they prove a tensor product algebra keeps the property exactly when one factor has finite global dimension and the other factor has the property. For Morita algebras, block matrices built from two algebras and connecting modules, the property holds exactly when both diagonal blocks have it. A neat consequence: the upper triangular matrix algebra over a ring is left weakly Gorenstein precisely when the ring itself is.
arxiv-2512-16272:
Ora Nova Fandina and six co-authors study AI graders at work in a paper shared on arXiv in 2025. Companies now use language models as judges to grade generated code at scale. In one production setting, modernizing legacy systems by generating COBOL code, the authors found even deployed judges miss domain-critical errors in consistent blind spots.

Working with experts, they built a taxonomy of those blind spots and a lightweight analytic checker that flags more than 30 domain-specific issues. Feeding the checker's findings into the judge's prompt as hints made it revisit what it missed. On 100 test programs with four production judges, judges alone caught only about 45 to 63 percent of errors. The checker alone lacked explanations, but judge plus hints reached up to 74 percent coverage with richer reasoning. The team released the data set and prompts.
arxiv-2512-16372:
Yu-Sen Zhou and three co-authors test the stability of exotic black hole signals in their 2025 arXiv paper, accepted by Physical Review D. Total transmission modes are waves that cross a black hole spacetime with no reflection at all. Carefully shaped incoming waves can excite them and cancel reflections entirely, an effect called virtual absorption.

Using pseudospectrum methods, which measure how much a spectrum wobbles under small disturbances, the team studied these modes around Tangherlini black holes in various dimensions. Most modes proved spectrally unstable, and higher overtones were more fragile. One purely imaginary mode stood out as far stabler in higher dimensions, with a much smaller condition number. Genuinely complex mode families appear only in eight or more dimensions. Four-dimensional results hint at instability, though norm choices limit firm conclusions.
arxiv-2512-16472:
Omar Namnakani and three co-authors study hands-full phone use in a 2025 arXiv paper. People often operate handheld devices while carrying things, walking, or otherwise encumbered. Gaze input could help, but nobody had measured how encumbrance affects it.

In a study with 24 participants, the team compared gaze with dwell time, gaze plus touch, and one- or two-handed touch, each with and without visual feedback where relevant. Touch was generally faster, but gaze, especially with feedback, performed consistently whether participants were encumbered or not. Preferences flipped with circumstance: people favored gaze while encumbered and touch when free-handed. The findings guide designers choosing input methods for mobile interfaces that must handle situational impairments gracefully.
arxiv-2512-16572:
Giulia Codenotti, Roberto Riccardi, and Lorenzo Venturello work on the symmetric edge polytope of a simple graph. For each graph, this shape is built by taking the convex hull of points tied to the graph edges, and the authors ask how few edges such a shape can have.

They prove a sharp lower bound for the edge count, stated with basic graph data such as numbers of vertices and edges. They also pin down exactly which graphs reach the bound. A second thread links the shape to its h-star values, a counting tool, and tests how that tool changes when an edge is removed from the graph.
arxiv-2512-16672:
Anis Maddi and coauthors show how to steer sound scattering extremes with quasi-bound states in the continuum, called qBICs. Their setup is a non-Hermitian acoustic system, meaning it has tuned losses that act as an extra design knob.

By tuning losses in a two-port cavity through Friedrich-Wintgen interference, they reach critical coupling and get narrowband perfect absorption, taking in sound fully at one tone, with a quality factor of 140. Joining two unlike resonators brings an exceptional point, where two modes merge and vanish, giving one-way absorption. The work ties qBICs to scattering extremes and points to acoustic gear with sharp tones and tuned loss.
arxiv-2512-16872:
Shayan Hundrieser and coauthors prove a universal representation property for spiking neural networks, which pass information as discrete spikes over time, much like real neurons. Such networks promise energy-thrifty computing, but their exact power was not fully charted.

Viewing the networks as spike-train processors, the team shows they can represent a natural class of spike-train functions. The results are quantitative and constructive, with near-best counts of weights and neurons needed. Networks shine on functions with few inputs, low time complexity, or built from such parts in layers. A use case on spike train classification shows how the theory guides design of neuromorphic systems.
arxiv-2512-16972:
Samuel Koovely introduces the Ascona model, a queueing-based way to build continuous-time temporal networks, where links switch on and off over time. Such models test tools that hunt for communities, scale patterns, change points, and cycles in network data.

In the Markovian version, link start times follow a Poisson process and link spans are exponentially spread. Koovely derives traits of the link streams and uses them to make synthetic networks with set smoothness and event patterns. Joining the time mechanism to block-structured endpoint rules gives a continuous-time cousin of stochastic block models. Extensions reach discrete time and instant-contact limits.
arxiv-2512-17072:
Thiago Ferreira and a large team characterize 32 exoplanetary systems around thick disc stars, the old, chemically distinct population of the Milky Way. Planet making there should be inefficient, with thin solid supplies, short disc lives, and harsh radiation, yet the planets found look odd.

Adding archival reassessments brings the thick disc planet tally to 66. A notable share are giants on more eccentric orbits than thin disc kin, a challenge to standard disc models, though small samples and detection bias urge caution. Two finds, TOI-1927 b and TOI-2643 b, are the first puffy low-density giants known around thick disc stars, odd in old metal-poor settings where planets should shrink.
arxiv-2512-17272:
Evgeny Korotyaev continues a study of the vector nonlinear Schrödinger equation when its waves repeat in a fixed period. Physicists use that equation for pulses that travel without changing shape, here with three linked components. The math rests on a helper operator whose allowed energies form bands along the whole number line, split by narrow gaps.

Korotyaev maps the curved surface that organizes those bands and finds where its branch points sit, showing they turn real at high energy. He then derives trace formulas, exact sums that recover conserved quantities such as the total energy from the band data. Last, he bounds that energy using only the lengths of the gaps. Tools like these let researchers read a wave's fate from its spectrum.
arxiv-2512-17472:
Thomas Sanchez and eight co-authors release Fetpype, an open pipeline that carries a fetal brain scan from raw MRI to finished measurements. Scanning a brain before birth is hard: the fetus moves, the signal is faint, and cleaning the images takes many linked steps, from motion repair to sharpening and tissue mapping. Each step had its own tool, and gluing them together differed from lab to lab.

Fetpype wraps the whole chain in one standard, modular workflow. A lab feeds in raw scans and gets volume and surface measures out, with every step recorded the same way for every study. Shared plumbing like this makes results easier to repeat and compare, a real need in a field guiding care before birth.
arxiv-2512-17772:
Charles Elbar, Alejandro Fernández-Jiménez, and Filippo Santambrogio study the Keller-Segel system, a model of cells that drift toward a scent they release themselves. At a key exponent, spreading and clumping act at the same strength, so solutions may either smooth out or pile up. Classic tools for heat flow do not apply directly.

The team builds versions of two famous heat estimates for this system, using a stand in for pressure. The bounds give smooth global solutions when the starting mass is small, with density capped by a set rate. They also pin down the exact mass that marks the edge between calm and clumping, equal to 8 pi in two dimensions.
arxiv-2512-18172:
Jayani P. Gamage and coauthors present cardinalR, an R package that fabricates high dimensional data with known structure. Simulated data with ground truth built in is a standard way to test and improve the algorithms used in dimension reduction and in supervised and unsupervised learning.

The package generates many kinds of structure from math functions and statistical distributions: variables tied together in linear or nonlinear ways, grouped clusters, and planted anomalies. Ready made example datasets ship with it as well. The authors aim the tool at researchers who want to see how an analytical method behaves and where it breaks, with a special focus on nonlinear dimension reduction. The package adds to the shared stock of benchmark data for judging algorithms.
arxiv-2512-18372:
Mrinmoy Basak's PhD thesis, posted to arXiv in December 2025, reworks a tool for quantum theories that span many energy scales at once. Flow equations, known as the Similarity Renormalization Group, gradually separate high-energy from low-energy behavior. Basak rebuilds that method on a Daubechies wavelet basis, which sorts physics by resolution the way an image sorts detail by zoom.

He applies the wavelet flow to a two-dimensional scalar field theory and shows it block-diagonalizes the Hamiltonian by resolution, with cleaner truncation than earlier studies. In a model of two coupled scalar fields, the flow suppresses links between low- and high-resolution parts. That gives a clear route to effective Hamiltonians that capture low-energy physics without tracking every fine detail. The thesis shows wavelets can organize multiscale quantum problems.
arxiv-2512-18572:
Riki Shimizu, Xilin Jiang, and Nima Mesgarani work on target speaker extraction: pulling one chosen voice out of a recording where several people talk at once, guided by a reference clip. Diffusion and flow-matching models do this well but need many sampling steps, which is too slow for live use. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, squeezes the process into a single step.

MeanFlow-TSE trains with mean-flow objectives, defining a flow between the background mixture and the target voice that is steered by the mixing ratio. On the Libri2Mix corpus it beats existing diffusion and flow-matching extractors on separation quality and perceptual scores, using just one inference pass. The code is public. One-step extraction makes real-time hearing aids, calls, and voice assistants more practical.
arxiv-2512-18672:
Ugo Moschella builds a new form for quantum fields in anti-de Sitter spacetime in this 2025 paper. Two-point functions, the basic correlation tools of field theory, are usually tied to a choice of coordinates. Moschella builds them in a fully covariant, coordinate-free way, as sums of plane waves. His plane waves are holomorphic. They are defined globally on the universal covering of AdS, using chiral cones in the complex null cone.

Imposing AdS invariance, locality, positive definiteness, and a spectral condition yields integral formulas that reproduce the standard maximally analytic solutions in Legendre functions. In Poincaré coordinates the functions split into a Källén-Lehmann sum of flat space correlators weighted by Bessel functions. This clarifies how Euclidean and Lorentzian AdS field theory connect, and lets Euclidean Feynman diagrams rotate to Lorentzian ones on a single patch.
arxiv-2512-18872:
Gábor Gévay, György Kiss, and Tomaž Pisanski settle a case of double discovery in geometry. In 1990 Grünbaum and Rigby presented a striking point-line pattern, the GR(21_4) configuration. Ferenc Kárteszi had in fact published an equivalent figure in 1964 and a general theorem in 1986 generating a whole family, K(n;l,m). Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, explores the Kárteszi family and the overlap.

They show the Grünbaum-Rigby configuration is exactly K(7;2,3) in Kárteszi's notation. They also prove necessary and sufficient conditions on the parameters n, l, and m. Those conditions decide when such a configuration can be drawn as a real geometric figure, with n-fold rotational symmetry and no extra incidences beyond the intended ones. The work gives credit its due and gives configuration hunters a complete rulebook for this family.
arxiv-2512-19272:
Maria Mannone, Paulo Vitor Itaborai, Omar Costa Hamido, and Miriam Goldack turn epileptic seizure signals into sound, then try to fake the sound with quantum models. Sonification maps brain recordings to polyphonic audio, where patterns can be heard rather than only seen. The team first sonified real seizure channels from cortical recordings.

Two quantum computing approaches then simulated a similar episode, and those outputs were sonified too. Side-by-side listening exposes where the models match real seizures and where they drift. The authors frame the loop as a fresh test bench: sound plus quantum simulation, aimed at sharper models and, one day, better seizure prediction.
arxiv-2512-19472:
Lorenzo Capelli, Leandro de Souza Rosa, Gianluca Setti, and Mauro Mangia build one trust score that flags three kinds of trouble in neural networks. Regulators now demand transparency from high-stakes models, yet add-on confidence tools usually need retraining or tackle only one failure mode at a time. Their method, MACS, works after the fact on frozen models.

Intermediate activations are turned into classification maps, one per layer, and a score is distilled from them. The same score serves confidence estimation, out-of-distribution detection, and adversarial attack detection. Unifying the three, the authors argue, makes deployed models easier to audit without touching their weights.
arxiv-2512-19872:
Mihail Kolountzakis, Ruxi Shi, and Sha Wu study when a measure living on a handful of line segments can support a Fourier basis. A measure is spectral when the exponentials at some frequency set form an orthogonal basis for its square-integrable functions, and the question is what those frequency sets, the spectra, can look like. For arc-length measure on two segments in the plane, the answer is rigid.

Any spectrum of such a measure must lie along a line, and when the two segments are not parallel, only line spectra occur at all, so every spectrum is one-dimensional. Three segments break the pattern: the authors construct spectral measures on three or more segments whose spectra sit on no line. A general bound caps how many orthogonal frequencies fit inside a ball, growing at most linearly with radius.
arxiv-2512-19972:
Pengchao Han, Xi Huang, Yi Fang, and Guojun Han review how knowledge distillation behaves when the students teach each other. Collaborative learning lets distributed agents train together without surrendering private data, and distillation, transferring knowledge between models, is its central courier. What memory and knowledge each agent holds, and how they interact during transfer, had not been systematically mapped.

The review defines and categorizes memory and knowledge inside the distillation process, then examines distributed, hierarchical, and decentralized collaboration patterns. Task heterogeneity gets extended treatment, spanning federated learning, multi-agent domain adaptation, multimodal and continual federated variants, multi-task learning, and graph knowledge embedding, alongside model, data, and resource heterogeneity and privacy concerns. Existing work is sorted by how it handles memory and knowledge, and open challenges close the survey.
arxiv-2512-20272:
Yuanjian Xu, Yuan Shuai, Jianing Hao, and Guang Zhang train generative models for stochastic differential equations, which describe systems evolving randomly over time. Adversarial training can learn the path shapes they produce. The weak point is the discriminator, which must judge whole paths while staying fast and stable to train.

Their approach, HGAN-SDEs, builds that judge from neural Hermite functions, a structured basis suited to path data. That choice lowers runtime cost and steadies training compared with controlled differential equation discriminators. The authors prove a universal approximation property and analyze convergence. On synthetic and real-world systems, the method delivers better sample quality and learning speed than earlier approaches.
arxiv-2512-20772:
Daniel Cortild, Meggie Marschner, and Mathias Staudigl tackle layered equilibrium problems in optimization. A variational inequality, a broad way to state balance conditions, must here be solved only over points that already satisfy another equilibrium. Such stacked problems appear when choosing among equilibria or optimizing under balance constraints.

Their method blends two smoothing tricks, Tikhonov regularization and proximal penalization, into a two-loop algorithm. They prove it converges and give speed estimates using gap functions, which measure how far a candidate sits from a true solution. The scheme fits many structured splitting methods already in use. Numerical tests on several examples confirm the theory.
arxiv-2512-20872:
Jakir Hossain and four co-authors release Better Call Graphs, a dataset for spotting Android malware by structure. A function call graph maps which functions in an app call which others, exposing behavior that surface signatures miss. Older datasets were stale, small, or stuffed with near-duplicates from repackaged apps.

BCG collects large, unique call graphs from recent Android packages, both harmless and malicious, across many families and types. Graph-level features accompany every sample, and the dataset is public. Baseline classifier experiments show models trained or tested on older sets can overfit badly. Fresh, varied graphs give researchers a fairer test of graph-based malware detection.
arxiv-2512-21272:
Kingshuk Adhikary, K. M. Athira, and M. Rohith find two practical dials for detecting quantum synchronization. Synchronization, a self-sustained oscillator locking phase with an external drive, is hard to certify in the quantum regime, where noise blurs coherence and full state reconstruction is costly. Their testbed is the driven quantum van der Pol oscillator, the canonical quantum limit-cycle system. Two experimentally friendly measures do the work: a nonclassical area read from homodyne tomograms, and the second-order photon correlation at zero delay.

Analytical formulas for the steady state and its tomogram, valid at any drive strength, show both measures lighting up across the synchronized region. The tomogram itself displays phase locking, and the synchronization domain, the Arnold tongue in drive-strength and detuning space, can be mapped using just these two numbers. Lab teams gain a scalable testing kit that skips Wigner-function reconstruction while still witnessing nonclassicality.
arxiv-2512-22672:
Achraf Hsain and Fouad Mohammed Abbou run the first experiment in generating fluid flow data with quantum machine learning. Quantum generative models had been tried on fluid statistics, but never on compressed latent representations of full flow simulations. The authors simulate fluid vorticity fields with a GPU-accelerated Lattice Boltzmann code, then squeeze those fields into a seven-dimensional discrete latent space with a vector-quantized autoencoder.

Two quantum generators, a Quantum Circuit Born Machine and a Quantum Generative Adversarial Network, are compared against a classic LSTM baseline at modeling that latent distribution. Under their conditions, both quantum models produced samples landing closer to the true distribution, with the Born machine scoring best. The team releases the full pipeline and frames the study as groundwork for this intersection.
arxiv-2512-23072:
Bernard Parent and Felipe Rodriguez Fuentes extend a model for how electrons heat up in nonequilibrium plasmas, behind hypersonic flight heating and plasma-assisted combustion. Predicting electron temperature matters because it controls ionization and chemistry. The authors' earlier model forced electron and vibrational temperatures to agree at equilibrium, as thermodynamics demands. But it only allowed molecules to change vibrational level one quantum at a time, limiting it to cooler regimes.

The generalized model adds multi-quantum overtone jumps, where a molecule trades several quanta in one collision. The authors show that ignoring those hot-band transitions creates a systematic heating error passing forty percent once the vibrational temperature exceeds its threshold value, blocking thermal relaxation. Their fix writes the heating as a sum over jump channels, each scaled by a thermodynamic factor. The energy transfer then vanishes exactly at equilibrium, while the model extends to high-energy regimes.
arxiv-2512-23172:
Francesca Gladiali, Massimo Grossi, Peng Luo, and Shusen Yan analyze the critical points of the Kirchhoff-Routh function. A tool from fluid mechanics that predicts where point vortices sit in equilibrium inside a bounded region. The function combines each vortex's interaction with the boundary, through the Robin function, with the mutual interaction given by the Green function. It also governs concentration phenomena in nonlinear elliptic problems.

For regions with a small hole, the authors determine not only how many critical points exist and roughly where they lie, but also that those points are nondegenerate. The hole's position turns out to play a decisive role in the count. Building on the analysis, they prove the existence of multiple two-peak solutions for related elliptic problems, in a paper running to seventy-seven pages.
arxiv-2512-23572:
Daiki Shiono, Shumpei Miyawaki, Ryota Tanaka, and Jun Suzuki measure what fine-tuning does to the instruction-following ability of large vision-language models. These models join a language model to vision components, but after visual instruction tuning they often stop obeying task instructions that the original language model handled easily. The decline had been noticed anecdotally; this study quantifies it.

The authors built training data sets that differ in whether the required output format is stated explicitly. Models tuned on commonly used data indeed lost instruction-following ability. Models whose training instructions spelled out the output format kept noticeably more of that ability. The practical lesson is that including format-specifying examples during visual instruction tuning can prevent much of the decline.
arxiv-2512-23872:
Emily McMillon and Kathryn Haymaker construct the first algebraic examples of hierarchical quasi-cyclic codes, error-correcting codes with layered structure. Their raw material is the classic Reed-Solomon code family, combined through a superimposed code construction published by Kautz and Singleton in 1964. Hierarchy lets different parts of a message enjoy different levels of protection, and quasi-cyclic structure keeps encoding hardware simple.

Both the number of hierarchy levels and the index of their codes turn out to be fixed by the underlying field size. The same holds for wider classes of polynomial evaluation codes. The authors give explicit parameters plus bounds on rank and distance; starting from two-dimensional Reed-Solomon codes yields Tanner graphs of girth six. Some small examples match the best known minimum distance for binary codes while adding the hierarchical structure. Unlike the simulation-heavy literature on related codes, their bounds are proved algebraically.
arxiv-2512-24072:
Ahmad Jafar Arifi and Kei Suzuki study what happens to quarkonia, bound states of heavy quarks such as charmonium, inside a changing magnetic field. In a steady field, the energy levels of these particles show avoided crossings, places where two states mix rather than pass through each other. Sweeping the field turns those crossings into dynamic events.

Borrowing the Landau-Zener framework, the authors build a multi-channel model from the static spectrum and run it under several field histories: steady ramps, single decaying pulses, and double pulses. They track how the population of each state evolves across a wide range of sweep speeds. Non-adiabatic jumps at crossings and interference between successive passages strongly reshape the final populations. The findings speak to the real-time behavior of magnetized hadrons and give guidance for future lattice simulations of these systems.
arxiv-2512-24172:
Yu-Tang Chang, Pin-Wei Chen, and Shih-Fang Chen report on hyperspectral image segmentation. Each image carries a huge volume of spectral data. Datasets can overflow ordinary hardware. Models pretrained on satellite imagery transfer poorly to close-range jobs. Crop disease monitoring is one such job. Signatures and scales differ there in basic ways.

Their framework learns global grouping from small patches. The patches overlap to enforce consistency. No pretraining is needed. Memory use stays constant during training. Training takes under half an hour on consumer hardware. On a leaf disease dataset, background separated cleanly from tissue. Disease spots were detected without labels. The authors are candid about a weakness. Training is unstable. Good representations form fast, then degrade as clusters over-merge. Principled loss balancing is the missing piece.
arxiv-2512-24272:
Jiawei Zhang and four colleagues speed up robot motion planning under constraints. Manipulation tasks often confine the robot's valid poses to a thin manifold. Latent-space methods approximate that manifold and plan fast. Approximation errors cause trouble, though. Collision conflicts are hard to spot inside the latent space. Validity checks and replanning eat the time saved.

Their fix learns distance directly in latent space. A neural network predicts the smallest distance to obstacles. Its input is the latent vector itself. The learned gradient then points the way away from obstacles. A local path optimization uses that gradient. It is woven into the validity-checking process. Replanning time drops as a result. Comparisons with leading algorithms cover several scenarios. The method posted the fastest planning speed among them.
arxiv-2512-24372:
Chuntian Cao and Hans-Georg Steinrück write a perspective on measuring electrochemical systems. Batteries and kindred devices matter for a fossil-free energy future. Standard electrochemical measurements are accurate and precise. Many reactions run at once inside a cell, though. The measurements alone cannot say which reaction took how much charge. That missing split blocks real understanding.

The authors name a remedy X-ray Coulomb Counting. X-ray methods quantify, on an absolute scale, where the charge goes. Each reaction's share becomes measurable during the experiment. Detailed interpretation of the electrical data follows. Materials and process development can then proceed rationally. Recent lithium-ion battery studies supply the examples. In them, the method produced foundational insight into working cells. The perspective argues the concept deserves wider use.
arxiv-2512-24472:
