Chon-Fai Kam introduces three-axis spin squeezed states. Spin squeezing cuts noise below the standard quantum limit in atomic ensembles. That enables quantum-enhanced measurement. Classic schemes twist the collective spin about one or two axes. Kam extends the paradigm to three axes. The setting is the anisotropic Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model.

Direction-dependent couplings interpolate between uniaxial and biaxial regimes. The model reads as an asymmetric quantum rotor. Semiclassical dynamics, Majorana representations, and Husimi-Q distributions map the states. Known scalings are recovered at the extremes. One-axis twisting and Heisenberg-limited two-axis twisting both appear. The three-axis family adds tunability between them. Entanglement generation strengthens in low-spin systems. Tuning the anisotropy also drives phase transitions. Ground-state and excited-state transitions appear, one tied to level clustering.
arxiv-2512-25072:
Haozhi Qi, Yen-Jen Wang, Toru Lin, and others present a system for joint humanoid manipulation built on modular teleoperation and a learning method called Choice Policy. Humanoids promise work in human spaces, but coordinating head, hands, and legs as one body is hard. Their teleoperation surface splits control into natural modules: hand-eye coordination, grasp basics, arm tracking, and locomotion.

Modular design makes collecting high-quality demonstrations lean, and the learning framework scales from those demonstrations. Robotics readers get a practical path to whole-body skills. Choice Policy is introduced as the imitation method that turns modular demonstrations into joint robot behavior.
arxiv-2601-06672:
Adir Rahamim and co-authors ask why some models merge well in 2026. Model merging combines several fine-tuned models into one multitask model. It promises multitask ability without retraining from scratch, they note.

Yet factors deciding merging success or failure remain poorly understood. They investigate why specific models merge better than others systematically. To do so, they propose a concrete, measurable definition of mergeability. A measurable definition turns folklore into testable claims about models. Practitioners merging checkpoints get guidance on which pairs should work. The study matters as merged models proliferate in open model ecosystems. Readers learn mergeability is a property to measure, not guess. Their definition gives future merging methods a target to optimize.
arxiv-2601-06772:
Xiao-Yu Cao and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with experimental coherent One-Way quantum key distribution with simplicity and practical security. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Coherent one-way quantum key distribution (COW-QKD) has been widely investigated, and even been deployed in real-world quantum network.

However, the proposal of the zero-error attack has critically undermined its security guarantees. And existing experimental implementations have not yet established security against coherent attacks. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07172:
Research by Mehran Moghadam and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with TranSC. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. The hardware-friendly implementation of transcendental functions remains a longstanding challenge in design automation.

These functions, which cannot be expressed as finite combinations of algebraic operations, pose significant complexity in digital circuit design. The work introduces a new approach, TranSC , that use stochastic computing (SC) for lightweight yet accurate implementation of transcendental functions. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07372:
Research by Xin Cheng and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with conditional memory via scalable lookup. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. While Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) scales capacity via conditional computation, Transformers lack a native primitive for knowledge lookup, forcing them to inefficiently simulate retrieval through computation.

To address this, the authors introduce conditional memory as a complementary sparsity axis, instantiated via Engram. A module that modernizes classic N N -gram embedding for 𝒪 O lookup. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07872:
E. Wes Bethel, Roel Van Beeumen, and Talita Perciano survey where quantum computing meets visualization. Quantum computing has grown fast, with robust programming environments, accessible simulators, and cloud hardware. Interest in practical quantum methods keeps rising. Visualization research faces new questions in this landscape. Their 2026 preprint lays out challenges and opportunities at the intersection.

Quantum data cannot be viewed directly like ordinary data. Scholars need ways to inspect states, circuits, and results without destroying them. Visualization also helps teach and debug quantum algorithms. The authors map open problems for the visualization community. They also point to chances for quantum tools to aid visualization itself. The paper serves both communities at once. It frames a research agenda rather than reporting a single experiment.
arxiv-2601-08172: Farhad Mirkarimi presents a gradient-based Bayesian optimization framework built on variational mutual information. The 2026 arXiv paper addresses costly black-box functions known only through noisy evaluations. Bayesian optimization is the standard tool for such expensive searches. Neural network surrogates have grown popular as scalable stand-ins for Gaussian processes. Yet older frameworks still pay heavily for posterior sampling and acquisition optimization. VBO-MI aims to make both steps fully gradient-based. Faster surrogate handling could widen Bayesian optimization to larger, noisier engineering and science problems.
arxiv-2601-08272: V. A. Bogachev and co-authors compute phase gradient correlations for light crossing turbulent media. Their 2026 arXiv paper works in the weak scintillation regime. Special attention goes to the off-diagonal part of the phase gradient correlation function. That component does not depend on the outer scale of the turbulence. Simulation results agree well with analytical expressions from earlier work. The study helps optics researchers predict how turbulence distorts wavefronts in imaging and free-space communication links.
arxiv-2601-08372: Hiroki Sakamoto and Kazuhiro Sato develop data-driven model reduction for discrete-time linear systems. Their 2026 arXiv paper solves a time-limited H2 optimal reduction problem over a finite horizon. Only impulse response data are used, with no full system model required. The authors also show the algorithm converges to a stationary point under stated assumptions. Smaller reduced models let engineers simulate and control large systems faster. Data-driven routes matter when first-principles models are missing or too costly to build.
arxiv-2601-08472: Benedikt Droste and three co-authors present sui-1, a model for grounded, verifiable long-form summarization. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that language models often produce plausible but unfaithful summaries. Users cannot easily check such summaries against the source text. That weakness is critical in compliance-sensitive fields like government and legal analysis. Sui-1 is a 24-billion-parameter model that adds inline citations to abstractive summaries. Each claim can be traced to its source sentence, which makes audits and corrections far easier.
arxiv-2601-08572: Suman Mandal and five co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on how the shape of a setup steers the spin of light in a crystal. The crystal guides waves and is of the kind called plasmonic. The team asks how the polarization of light, the lean of its waves, shifts with the setup. They vary the angle at which light comes in, and the angle around the beam. They run finite element models in COMSOL. They read the results with Jones-Mueller tools, to gauge how the optical traits shift.
arxiv-2601-08772:
Ruiqi Zhang, Fuchuan Wei, and Zhaohui Wei ask how to use flawed quantum tools for real work. Such tools make errors, and most plans try to wash those errors out. The clean result is then read from the noisy runs. As tools grow, that wash step gets costly and may eat the gain of the tool.

The team looks for ways to let noise help, or at least hurt less. They add noise aware steps to the way a class sim runs on a host PC. A class sim is a plain code run that acts like a quantum run. A reader gets a fresh angle. Noise need not be a pure foe if the method is built to live with it.
arxiv-2601-08972:
Yiluo Wei and Gareth Tyson study what takes place when a VTuber starts fresh in a new guise. A VTuber is a screen face moved and voiced by a hid human. Firms oft own the face, while the human bears the stress of two lives: their own, and the face. A fresh start, called reincarnation by fans, can free or harm that human.

The pair track what shifts for the human, for fans, and for the firm when a face is left and a new one starts. Old fans may hunt for the link. The firm may lose a star it built. A reader in media work gets a close look at a new kind of fame, and its costs.
arxiv-2601-09072:
Jean Feng and eight co-authors give a way for doctors and data staff to build care risk tools as a team, with AI help. Such tools guess which sick folk may worsen, so staff can act fast. Good ones need fine picks: who counts, what facts count, how groups are cut. Those picks take long back and forth talks in most labs.

Their frame puts a human and an AI in a joint design loop. The AI drafts, checks, and flags weak picks. The team keeps the last call on each pick. A reader in care data gets a work plan that keeps skill in the loop. It may cut build time with out loss of care in the fine points.
arxiv-2601-09372:
Pedro Antonino and Namrata Jain work on checking zero-knowledge programs for errors before they run. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents NAVe, a tool for formally verifying programs written in Noir. Zero-knowledge proofs let one side show that a claim holds without revealing the private input behind it.

Behind each proof sits a complex arithmetic circuit, a set of polynomial equations over a finite field. A small flaw in that circuit can break the proof's promise. NAVe aims to verify that the circuit matches the intended relation between public and private values. Such checks matter as zero-knowledge systems move into money and identity uses.
arxiv-2601-09472: Dietrich Burde studies sums built from the partition function, which counts the ways to write a whole number as a sum of smaller ones. His 2026 arXiv paper defines a weighted binomial sum over partition values and seeks estimates for it. The sum mixes binomial coefficients with partition numbers at smaller indices. Partition numbers grow fast and unevenly, so clean bounds are hard to get. Estimates of this kind support counting arguments across combinatorics and number theory.
arxiv-2601-09572:
Tianli Tao and four co-authors tackle holes in brain scan histories. Their 2026 arXiv paper completes missing longitudinal brain MRI data with a deformation-based method. Brain scans over a lifetime are key to studying development and disease, but people drop out, leaving gaps.

The method warps known scans with a learned deformation model, enhanced by a diffusion model using Kolmogorov-Arnold networks. Filling gaps faithfully matters more than filling them smoothly: warped anatomy must stay true to the person. Trustworthy completion would let long studies keep participants whose visits were missed. It also supports cleaner measures of how brains change with age.
arxiv-2601-09672:
Lucas Caron and four co-authors create large cat states of light in free space. Their 2026 arXiv paper reports squeezed coherent-state superpositions on optical pulses. Such non-Gaussian states are a key requirement for universal continuous-variable quantum information processing.

The team reached a superposition amplitude of 2.47. To their knowledge, that exceeds all values reported before. Bigger cat states are more useful for real tasks but also far more fragile. Making them on free-space pulses suits setups that send light across a bench. It also suits links that carry light across a wider network.
arxiv-2601-10272:
Yuxuan Lou, Kai Yang, and Yang You build a model that takes in both speech and text. Most mixed models use the same weights for all inputs. But speech and text code facts in unlike ways. One set of weights may serve both poor.

The team made MoST, with a mix of expert nets at its core. Each input is routed to experts fit for its type. Speech goes to speech experts, text to text experts. The route is named modality aware. It lets one model hold both skills in one frame. The aim is smooth work across speech and text.
arxiv-2601-10572:
Fang Zhou, Yuyang Huang, Miao Yu, Sixiang Ma, Tongping Liu, and Yang Wang track down lag spikes that apps can not see. A spike can come from the kernel or the chip. Those layers sit below the app. Their events leave no mark in app logs. Yet they can stall a run for a real span.

The team built VarMRI, a tool chain to watch those layers. It logs kernel and chip events over long spans. It then links spikes to the events that drove them. Long term watch is key, since spikes can be rare. The work is a field report on what the chain found.
arxiv-2601-10672:
Carlo Cafaro and James Schneeloch ask how well a qubit can be steered when the magnetic field around it changes with time. In the best quantum evolutions, motion follows paths of least length within an ideal time frame. Other good paths waste no energy and reach full speed efficiency. The authors weigh these traits for one-qubit systems.

They track efficiency, curvature, and complexity of the evolutions. A path can be short yet bent, or fast yet costly in control effort. Sorting these trade-offs helps engineers design control pulses for real qubits. The work adds to the geometry of quantum control, where fields that vary in time are the norm, not the exception.
arxiv-2601-10772:
Mirco A. Mannucci and Corey Thuro extend resource-bounded type theory to Martin-Löf type theory. Type theory is the logic base of proof assistants and some programming languages. Resource bounds attach a cost to each program, so types can promise not just correctness but also price. Dependent types, where types depend on values, raise the stakes.

Their calculus gives size-indexed cost bounds for programs over inductive families. Function types carry bounds that depend on the argument itself. Pair types add costs in a clean additive way. Such a system could certify that a verified program also runs within a set budget, a need in safe and embedded software.
arxiv-2601-10872:
Simon Fontaine and co-authors build a statistical model for microbiome studies that follow subjects over time. Differential abundance analysis hunts for microbes whose levels link to health states. Most current methods fit cross-sectional data, a single snapshot. Many real studies are longitudinal, with repeated samples that show microbial dynamics.

The authors propose a locally sparse varying coefficient mixed model for such data. Local sparsity lets effects switch on only where and when they matter. Varying coefficients let a microbe's link to health drift over time. The model is aimed at oral and gut studies like the Michigan team's periodontics data. It gives researchers a finer tool for microbes that change with us.
arxiv-2601-11272:
Yiwei Bao, Andrea Addazi, and Shuai Zha study flavor change in supernovae. Their 2026 preprint looks at fast flavor conversions of neutrinos. Neutrinos can swap flavor as they fly through dense matter. In a supernova, neutrino-neutrino refraction can drive fast swaps.

Such swaps can even out all flavors in a rush. That shift could change how the star blows up. The team points to matter clumps as a brake on swaps. The clumps have red spectra, with power piled at large scales. Such clumps arise in layered zones of the dying star. They speed up decoherence, which then holds the fast swaps down.
arxiv-2601-11372:
Eva Deltl joins fairness and low cost in one allocation problem. Her 2026 preprint defines the minCost-EFx allocation task. Fair sharing often ignores what a sharing plan costs. Cost cutting, in turn, often ignores what is fair.

Costs here can be transport, storage, or the like. The fairness bar is EFx, envy-free up to any item. It means no agent envies another once one item is dropped. The goal is an EFx split with the least cost of all. Deltl studies how hard that joint task is to solve. It is NP-hard even with just two agents in the split. That result sets a clear limit on exact solvers.
arxiv-2601-11572:
Timo Aukusti Laine views LLM embedding spaces through Hamiltonian dynamics. The 2026 preprint uses linear algebra and physics analogies. Embeddings place words and texts as points in space. Those points seem to form distinct, discrete states.

That discreteness hints at semantic states in the space. Laine applies the Hamiltonian formalism from mechanics to them. The analogy borrows from quantum mechanical systems as well. Semantic relationships become paths and energies in this view. Discrete states may act like levels in a physical system. The frame is exploratory, a math lens on model internals. It could yield new ways to read what embeddings encode.
arxiv-2601-11672:
Deepak Babu Piskala traces a Unix idea into modern agentic AI. The 2026 preprint runs from files to files-are-all-you-need. Unix's creed from the 1970s was everything is a file. That design philosophy collapsed diverse resources into uniform interfaces.

Piskala follows the idea through the DevOps movement. It then lands in present-day autonomous agent systems. The same principle solves like problems at new scales. Uniform interfaces let tools compose without custom glue. Agents that treat resources as files gain simple, sturdy tools. The essay links old operating system wisdom to AI design. It argues the file remains a powerful abstraction.
arxiv-2601-11772:
Yimu Pan, Hongda Mao, Qingshuang Chen, and Yelin Kim present a way to build a 3D scene from just one view. Past fast methods work well from many views for a scene, or from one view for a lone object. One view of a whole scene is much less clear, since depth is lost.

Their method, called studentSplat in the work, uses 3D Gaussian splatting. That is a way to store a scene as many soft 3D blobs. The name hints at a student model that learns the task. A good one-view method would help apps that have just a single photo to work from.
arxiv-2601-11872:
Nguyen Tien Phat, Ngo Vu Minh, Linh Van Ngo, Nguyen Thi Ngoc Diep, and Thien Huu Nguyen build topic models that work across tongues. A topic model finds themes in large text sets. For many tongues at once, themes should line up by sense, not just by tongue.

Most past models learn themes in split spaces, one per tongue. They then align themes with word lists, which can miss deep sense links. Their model, named GloCTM in the work, learns in one shared context space. A shared space could give cleaner theme matches for news and research sets.
arxiv-2601-12272:
Shahrzad Esmat, Mahdi Banisharif, and Ali Jannesari prune neural networks under a strict compute budget, guided by a language model. Pruning helps fit models on small devices. Most past tools cut parameter counts, not true compute cost.

That leaves latency hard to predict where multiply-accumulate budgets are strict. Their frame, AgenticPruner, uses a model to search prune plans in a loop. Each loop learns from the last result. A direct MAC budget gives deploy teams a firm target.  Direct cost caps suit phones and small edge boxes.  The loop learns a prune plan, not just a fixed prune rate.
arxiv-2601-12372:
Anna Fino, Gueo Grantcharov, and Alberto Pipitone Federico work in complex geometry. They build a changed form of the twistor space of a Kahler scalar flat surface. They then study the shape and metric traits of this new space. Twistor spaces are a bridge between geometry and complex analysis, so a new form draws close study.

The team build complete balanced metrics on their new space. They also prove a negative result of note. When the base surface is a compact simple hyperkahler manifold, the new space cannot be Kahler. Results of this kind help map out where key structures can and cannot exist. The paper sits in the fields of differential geometry and complex variables.
arxiv-2601-12472:
M. N. Mazziotta and a large team report work on a detector for a future collider experiment. The experiment is ALICE 3, proposed for later runs of the Large Hadron Collider. One of its jobs is to tell charged particles apart at high energy. A Ring Imaging Cherenkov detector is a classic tool for that job.

The team develop a novel version based on SiPM sensors. Their design aims to be compact and fast at once. Cherenkov light forms rings whose size reveals a particle speed. The team also study whether the same device can time particles from their light. A compact, fast design would ease the tight space and rate limits at the collider.
arxiv-2601-12772:
Madhav Dhiman and Rohan Pandey probe the Collatz problem with two adic arithmetic. The Collatz problem asks whether repeated halving and tripling rules always reach one. Approaches based on Presburger arithmetic try to characterize Collatz cycles in a decidable logic. The team investigate structural limits of that strategy.

They show the Collatz cycle equation has a unique solution in the two adic integers. They term this object a ghost cycle. Ghost cycles are genuine periodic orbits of the two adic Collatz map. They satisfy all local parity constraints, yet they are not ordinary integer cycles. Their existence blocks clean Presburger characterizations of true cycles.
arxiv-2601-12972:
G. Bertinelli, W.-H. Zhou, and P. Tanga trace rotation in asteroid families over billions of years. An asteroid family is a swarm of fragments from one broken parent body. Its long term evolution is governed by orbital and rotational change together. Thermal forces and collisions drive that slow drift.

The YORP effect, a thermal torque, spins small asteroids up or down over time. The team aim to observationally trace rotational evolution in main belt families. Comparing spin states across a family can date and reconstruct its history. Their context and aims frame a survey style study of family members. The work serves planetary science and asteroid hazard knowledge alike.
arxiv-2601-13272:
Aaron Pim and Tristan Pryer cut the cost of doubt scores for neural nets. One stock way to score doubt is Monte Carlo dropout. The net is run many times with random parts switched off. The spread of the runs marks the doubt. That cost grows fast with each pass.

Their frame stacks runs by grade. Low grade runs are cheap and coarse. High grade runs are dear and fine. By mix of grades, in a multi level Monte Carlo plan, the same doubt score can be had for less cost. The dropout masks are treated as the chance source to be stacked. For teams that must ship doubt scores live, the cut in cost is the point.
arxiv-2601-13572:
Xiangchi Yuan and co-authors merge behaviour skills in reward taught agent models with no loss of each skill. Reward learn is core to post teach, most of all for agents that need set sense skills. Merge of models can join many such agents, each taught for one task, into one generalist.

Old merge tools were made for supervised fine tune. On reward taught agents they waste task skills. The team's merge is built for that case. It aims to keep each task's behaviour while the weights join. For agent teams, a merge that holds skills beats a re teach of one big agent from scratch.
arxiv-2601-13672: Guanlong Bao, Liu Tian, and Hasi Wulan study the size of the Hilbert matrix operator on Bergman spaces. Bergman spaces are sets of functions studied in complex analysis. Karapetrović put forth a guess for the exact norm of this operator. The guess gives a value built from pi and a sine term, for a set range of the key parameters.
arxiv-2601-14172:
Víctor Yeste and Paolo Rosso detect human values in single sentences at scale in 2026. They study the nineteen human values in the refined Schwartz continuum. Their corpus holds about seventy-four thousand English sentences from news and political manifestos. The corpus is the ValueEval'24 set, annotated for value presence.

Each sentence yields a binary moral-presence label and a nineteen-way multi-label task. Severe class imbalance makes the task hard, since rare values appear seldom. Transformer ensembles tackle the detection in their work. Sentence-level value maps could track moral themes in public debate.
arxiv-2601-14572:
R. Lazauskas, R. Ya. Kezerashvili, and I. Filikhin study exotic light nuclei in this 2026 paper. Their work is motivated by recent HAL QCD simulations of the phi-N interaction. That interaction was simulated in two spin channels, and one channel was modified by the results. The team asks whether phi mesons can bind with light nuclei.

They develop a first-principles few-body framework for the question. It embeds the simulated potentials into configuration-space Faddeev-Yakubovsky equations, the standard exact method for few-body systems. Their title lists the candidate nuclei they test, built from phi mesons with hydrogen and helium. Readers get a rigorous check on whether such exotic nuclei can exist.
arxiv-2601-14772:
Adrian Braun and six co-authors study the Hall coefficient in NiTi in this 2026 paper. NiTi is a shape-memory alloy used in medical and engineering devices. The team presents a mean-field charge density wave theory for it. Their starting point is a density functional theory bandstructure, a computed map of the material's electronic states. From that base, they calculate the Hall coefficient as a function of temperature.

They compare the result with recent experimental results. They also analyze contributions to the Hall coefficient from different parts of the Fermi surface. They find the coefficient is dominated by certain hot spots. Readers get a theory of how charge density waves steer electrical response in a workhorse alloy.
arxiv-2601-14872:
Hirofumi Ota and Masaaki Imaizumi study a data mix-up that plagues linear regression. In their 2026 arXiv paper, the rows of data have been shuffled by an unknown rule. Each response is paired with the wrong inputs, and no one knows the pairing.

The shuffle itself is part of how the data was made. Yet it is hard to study, since the count of possible shuffles grows at a factorial rate. The authors build finite-sample inference for this sparse case. That means firm claims that hold for the data size at hand.
arxiv-2601-15172:
Ilia Kuznetsov, Rohan Nayak, Alla Rozovskaya, and Iryna Gurevych ask whether peer review is truly getting worse. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the system at the heart of modern science. Submissions keep rising and communities keep growing, and many fear review quality is in decline.

But is that fear true? Review quality is hard to measure in the first place. Review customs also change over time, which makes fair comparison tricky. The authors analyze reviews across venues and across years. They test the decline story against what the records actually show.
arxiv-2601-15272:
Ronald Orozco López adds new functions to the Lucas calculus, a variant of calculus built on Lucas sequences. His 2026 arXiv paper sets out a Lucas-Pantograph type exponential function. The pantograph twist scales the input in a way drawn from delay equations.

He then defines matching trigonometric functions. For them he proves the classic set of identities: parity rules, sum and difference formulas, and Pythagorean identities. Double-angle formulas and some special values join the list. Hyperbolic versions of these new functions are set out in the same careful, parallel style throughout.
arxiv-2601-15472:
Jana Franceska Funke and seven co-authors present a new way to track effort in exercise in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their system is called XEM 2, short for exercise exertion muscle-work monitor. It uses a camera to measure muscle work during stationary exercise. The method rests on the Hill-type muscle model, a classic model of how muscles produce force.

The team aims to fix weak spots in older ways of tracking effort. Calorie counts can be imprecise when movements are not uniform. Scales based on self-perception say little about strain in each body part. XEM 2 instead shows muscle work directly, part by part. That gives users and trainers a clearer view of where the effort lands.
arxiv-2601-15572:
Jieyun Bai and a large team launch a benchmark for ultrasound segmentation in a 2026 arXiv paper. The task is to outline cervical structures in transvaginal ultrasound scans. Good outlines help assess the risk of spontaneous preterm birth. Supervised learning needs labeled scans for this task. Such labels are scarce, which caps model performance.

Their answer is the Fetal Ultrasound Grand Challenge, or FUGC. They call it the first benchmark for semi-supervised learning in cervical segmentation. It was hosted at ISBI 2025. Semi-supervised methods learn from a few labeled scans plus many unlabeled ones. A shared benchmark lets teams compare methods fairly. Better segmentation from fewer labels would help clinics that cannot annotate at scale.
arxiv-2601-15672:
Jia Zhang, Sheng-Bang Qian, Li-Ying Zhu, and Xu-Zhi Li revisit a stellar puzzle in a 2026 arXiv paper. Contact binaries are pairs of stars that touch and share an envelope. In W-type systems, something odd happens. The less massive star shows a higher surface temperature than its heavier partner. That reverses the A-type pattern, where the more massive star is hotter. The puzzle has challenged astrophysicists for over half a century.

The title promises a reason for the W-type pattern. The record cites data facilities including Gaia and LAMOST. Modern survey data give fresh leverage on an old question. Explaining the temperature reversal would firm up models of how contact pairs evolve. These systems are common, so the answer shapes a broad swath of stellar astrophysics.
arxiv-2601-15872:
Three authors listed as Jaekwon, Natalia, and Taketo generate music from dance in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their model is PF-D2M, a pose-free diffusion model. Dance-to-music generation aims to match music to movement. Existing methods rely on body motion features from a single dancer. Datasets for the task are also limited. Those limits restrict real-world use. Scenes with several dancers, or non-human dancers, fall outside them.

A pose-free approach skips explicit pose extraction. The model works from the video more directly. Diffusion generation then produces music aligned with the dance. Universal generation is the title's ambition: one model for many dance scenes. Creators who cut dance video could use such tools for instant, fitting soundtracks.
arxiv-2601-16172:
Zac Burton tests if plain hints help top proof models find Lean proofs. His 2026 preprint deals with neural proof tools. Top tools like DeepSeek Prover join language models with trial based learning. They score well through long and rich training. Burton asks if such trained tools still gain from plain form hints at use time.

He gives each tool a fixed prompt with form cues. He then checks proof scores with and sans the hint. Gains would show that cheap hints still count at the top. No gains would show training has soaked up that help. The test is light, cheap and easy to rerun.
arxiv-2601-16372:
Hyunuk Shin and four coauthors hone group finds on signed webs with a learn step. Their 2026 preprint deals with webs that hold both good and bad ties. Group finds on such webs map how ties shape group form. Past finds oft give groups that clash from run to run. They can also miss the push and pull of bad ties.

The team adds a refine step plus a paired learn step. Refine cleans first groups, while paired learn sharpens tie sense. Clean groups help read trust and strife in real webs. Such webs span social, trade and cell fields. The work aims for firm, true group maps.
arxiv-2601-16572:
Haida Li and Xiangdong Zhang study how light bends round a black hole in a new gravity. Their 2026 preprint uses the revised Deser Woodard frame. That frame adds far reach terms to known gravity maths. The hole is round and still in the sums used. Bend of light is a key test that splits gravity frames.

The team sums bend in both weak and strong field zones. Each zone gives marks that set this frame off from kin. Marks could be checked in views of real black holes. A frame that fails bend tests must then be cut. The work gives bend marks for that check.
arxiv-2601-17172:
Tunazzina Islam audits slant in chatbot texts made for set crowds. Chatbots can now write apt pitches for each crowd at scale. That skill raises fair-use fears in new ways. Her 2026 preprint gives the first set check of such acts. Three top models face the same check frame. They are GPT-4o, Llama-3.3, and Mistral-Large 2.

Each model writes texts set for set crowd traits. Shifts in tone and pitch by crowd then show. Some shifts may cross from apt to unfair. Clear audits help set rules for such tools. They also warn firms that use them blind.
arxiv-2601-17772:
Youngkyoung Bae, Hajime Shimao, Seungwoong Ha, Luna Yang, and David Wolpert ask if hidden patterns drive how societies change. Their 2026 preprint starts from the flood of digitized records of social and cultural life. Older methods tend to freeze that life into snapshots or average effects. Real history moves in a flow, and chance plays a part at each step.

The team instead infers Langevin dynamics from the data. Langevin models split change into a steady drift and a random push. That split fits a past that is both shaped and uncertain. If shared patterns show up in the drift terms, they may point to deep rules of social change. The work gives historians and modelers a new lens on old records.
arxiv-2601-18272:
Yuta Tanabe, Kentaro Yaji, and Kuniharu Ushijima design bodies that move because the flow pushes them. Their 2026 preprint proposes a topology optimization method for such passive movers. Sails and turbines are the classic cases: the body does not drive the flow; the flow drives the body. Most past frames treat the active case, where motion is imposed. The authors build an unsteady, time-dependent formulation for the passive case, where forces from the fluid set the motion.

Topology optimization lets an algorithm sculpt the body's shape for a goal. Passive movers harvest energy or hold station without motors. Designing them well serves wind power, sailing, and ocean devices. The method fills a clear gap in design tools.
arxiv-2601-18372:
Christos Petrou and four colleagues work on a core task for virtual reality: guessing where a user will look next. A good guess cuts the lag that comes from slow sensors. It also makes sharp, focused rendering possible. The system can spend its power on the spot the eye is about to reach.

Head sets do not always track the eyes. Some lack the needed parts, and some users do not want that kind of watch kept on them. The team thus builds its guess from two other cues. One cue is what the scene shows at each point. The other is how the head moves as the user turns and tilts. Blending sight and motion may let a head set feel fast and smooth with no eye sensor at all.
arxiv-2601-18572:
Franziska Weeber and three colleagues study how cues about a user change what a language model says to them. A persona is a set of facts about a user, such as age or home land, fed to the model to make its replies fit. Past work fed the model one cue at a time, like a name or a plain tag. That thin feed may not match how cues come in real life.

In real use, cues stack: a name, a tongue, a style of speech, and more. The team test if the stack gives the same tilt as each cue on its own. It may not: cues can clash or boost each other. A clash could mean past bias grades rest on thin ground. The work calls for care in how persona tests are built and read.
arxiv-2601-18672:
Spyros Rigas and three colleagues give a class of smart nets a way to bend their own grid as they learn. The nets are built on a famed claim that any smooth rule can be built from plain one-way curves. Each curve sits on a grid, and the grid can shift in training to fit the task. Past shifts set the grid by how thick the data is at each spot.

That rule of thumb can miss spots where the rule it-self bends in a hard way. The team set the grid by the shape of the task and by signs from training it-self. A grid that bends where the task bends should learn with less waste. Such nets are prized for their clear form, so gains here could serve labs that need both skill and a form they can read.
arxiv-2601-18872:
Ladina Hausmann and Renato Renner argue that a quantum state holds more than a list of chances. A state can be written as the set of outcome chances for a chosen group of measures. Such lists show up across physics, from field theory to broad chance based frames.

The pair press on what such a list leaves out. If two states give the same chances for the chosen measures, are they the same state? Their title gives the stance: no, the state is more than its chance lists. The paper probes what extra facts a full state carries past any one set of measures.
arxiv-2601-20072:
Atik Faysal and colleagues train vision transformers when labelled images are scarce. Vision transformers are powerful but data-hungry. Many real collections have abundant unlabelled images and few labelled ones. The authors propose a semi-supervised masked autoencoder framework for exactly that regime.

Their method, SSMAE, jointly optimises two tasks. Masked image reconstruction learns from all images, labelled or not. Classification learns from the labelled few, aided by pseudo-labels chosen dynamically for the rest. Dynamic selection aims to use only trustworthy guessed labels. Strong performance with little labelling would widen where transformers can be deployed, from medicine to ecology. The work balances self-supervision against label noise. Tags are the scarce thing, not shots. Most frames come with no tag at all. The method learns from both kinds. The scarce tags still guide the whole net. The rest is learned from raw shots with no tags.
arxiv-2601-20172:
James Amarel and seven colleagues study how neural models of physics equations pick up symmetries of the system they mimic. Their models emulate solutions of partial differential equations, the equations behind fluid flow, heat, and many other processes. The team asks whether a model truly learns a symmetry, such as a rotation, or only fits the data it saw.

They build a diagnostic based on influence functions, which trace how a training update at one state affects states linked by symmetry. The test measures how updates spread along the orbit of a symmetry group. It offers a way to check robust generalization, and to spot models that will fail on shifted but symmetric cases.
arxiv-2601-20472:
Madina Zhakipova, Arman Tursunov, Saken Toktarbay, and Martin Kološ study how black holes interact with large-scale magnetic fields that arrive tilted. Magnetic fields power the relativistic jets of black holes. The field near the horizon usually is traced to the accretion flow, the gas spiraling in.

But other fields can reach the horizon too: from a companion neutron star in a binary, or from galactic fields around a supermassive black hole. When such a field is inclined, it may change how much magnetic flux threads the horizon. That flux sets the jet's power, so the tilt of an outside field could shape the most energetic outflows known.
arxiv-2601-20972:
Vipin Chandra Dubey, Subhajit Saha, and Abdulla Al Mamon test a single-fluid story for cosmic expansion. Their 2026 paper models the universe with one dark fluid. Its equation of state blends a logarithmic term with a power law term. Both terms involve the Lambert W function, a classic special function. This particular form was proposed earlier in the literature. The authors put it against fresh survey data.

The test data are DESI baryon acoustic oscillation measurements. These give the expansion history with high precision. A single dark fluid must match that history to survive. The model unifies what is often split into dark matter and dark energy. The paper checks whether that economy costs accuracy. Results of this kind help decide if the dark sector needs two parts or one.
arxiv-2601-21172:
Bo Yuan and four co-authors uncover a quantum spin Hall effect carried by magnons, not electrons. Their 2026 paper studies bilayer altermagnets. Altermagnetism has drawn considerable interest in recent years. Its spintronic phenomena, though, have been largely confined to electronic systems. The authors extend the story to magnons, the wave-like excitations of a magnet's order. They find a magnonic quantum spin Hall effect with chiral magnon transport.

Their strategy is universal and symmetry-based. It realizes topological altermagnets with a nonzero spin Chern number. Protected helical edge states carry the magnon currents. Edge channels resist scattering, which suits low-loss spin devices. Bilayer systems offer knobs to tune the effect. The work opens altermagnet spintronics to a new carrier. It may guide materials design for magnon-based logic.
arxiv-2601-21572:
Jinhao Li and seven co-authors stabilize the training of spiking neural networks for control tasks. These networks promise very low energy use, since their units fire only in brief spikes. Training them for long, high-dimensional control jobs is hard because gradients cannot pass through spikes.

Population methods that skip gradients give noisy estimates instead. Noisy steps can be too bold and wreck a good policy. The authors adapt the trust region, the safe step size, to the signal strength at hand. Calmer, better-sized steps should let spiking controllers learn hard tasks without blowing up.
arxiv-2601-21772:
Carmen Pita-Romero and four co-authors tackle a hard control problem: keeping many drones in a shared shape while the shape itself changes. Formations of unmanned aerial vehicles must hold complex structures and still follow complex paths. Their 2026 preprint presents an algorithm for this flocking behavior.

The method rests on an idea the authors call the Virtual Centroid, a moving reference point that helps define the structure of the flock. Around that point, each craft can take its place without a central planner directing every move. If it works as described, the approach could make drone swarms easier to shape, resize, and steer during shows, surveys, and rescue work.
arxiv-2601-22072:
Daniel Bath and Mircea Mustaţă study singularities of spaces defined by determinants. Start with a smooth space and a matrix of regular functions on it. The vanishing of its largest minors cuts out a subscheme, a determinantal space, whose singular points are where geometry gets rough.

The authors relate the singularities of that pair to an incidence correspondence in a larger space built with a projective factor. They work with log canonical thresholds, numbers that measure how mild or severe a singularity is. Their 2026 preprint adds to the toolkit of birational geometry, where such thresholds govern deep classification questions about the shapes of algebraic varieties.
arxiv-2601-22972:
Bhaswati Mookerjea and three co-authors report the first detailed look at a long filament in the outer Galaxy. The filament, called G183, feeds a massive young star known as IRAS 5480+2545. Using a large radio telescope in Spain, they traced the molecular gas at two wavelengths.

The maps show how gas is arranged along the filament and around the young star. Filaments act as supply lines that channel gas into forming stars. Learning how they feed massive stars helps explain how the biggest stars in the Galaxy are born. Multi-tracer observations let the team cross-check the gas picture, since different molecules trace different densities and temperatures.
arxiv-2601-23072:
Santanu Subhash Rathod, Pietro Liò, and Xiao Zhang improve flow matching for dynamical systems. Flow matching is a scalable way to learn continuous generative flows. Standard versions link states with straight-line paths, which may not match how a real system evolves.

Their SplineFlow uses B-spline interpolants, flexible curve pieces, for the conditional paths instead. Curved paths suit higher-order dynamics and irregularly sampled observations better. Better system models help forecast everything from cells to climate variables. Irregular sampled observations are a stated strength of the design, matching real sensors that rarely report on a tidy grid.
arxiv-2603-01472:
Light that can ionize hydrogen sometimes leaks out of young galaxies, and how it escapes is still unclear. Fang-Ting Yuan, Zhen-Ya Zheng, Chunyan Jiang, and Shuairu Zhu study nearby star-forming galaxies in this 2026 work. They focus on twenty known strong leakers and sort them by what infrared data show.

One group lacks infrared glow and fits the classic picture of a fully ionized, low-mass galaxy. The other group glows in infrared light, weighs more, and yet still leaks a fair share of its light. For that group, the authors say light likely slips through thin channels in a dense, clumpy gas. Both paths seem to occur across cosmic time, so dusty, heavier galaxies may also have helped ionize the early universe.
arxiv-2603-01872:
Wenchao Wu, Min Qiu, Yansha Deng, and Jinhong Yuan protect the image regions that matter most when sending pictures over weak wireless links. Their 2026 work serves tasks like remote diagnosis, where classification must hold up despite tight bandwidth and noisy channels. Most joint coding schemes guard all regions alike, as if each pixel mattered equally.

Their framework ranks regions by how much each one drives the classification call. Importance comes from Shapley values, a fairness-based score borrowed from explainable AI methods. High-ranked regions then get finer compression and stronger error protection than the rest. A new coding efficiency metric judges how well bits and protection serve the final task. The design goal is guaranteed classification under constraint, not merely a prettier received image.
arxiv-2603-01972:
Megan Harris, Mohammad Naderi, Ehsanoddin Ghorbanichemazkati, and colleagues propose one shared frame for tangled societal problems. Their 2026 work lists climate change, urbanization, and water management as cases that cross many fields. Disciplinary silos fragment insight, and clashing ontologies block fields from even sharing terms.

Their system-of-systems convergence paradigm rests on a meta-cognition map with five domains. The domains join real-world observations, systems thinking, visual modeling, mathematics, and computing in one loop. A standard systems modeling language gives the frame a neutral, shared notation. The Chesapeake Bay watershed, spanning land use, water, economy, and policy, demonstrates the approach. Agile system-of-systems modeling there shows strategies for large, multi-dimensional decisions that no single field can carry alone.
arxiv-2603-02172:
Srikumar Sastry, Dan Cher, Brian Wei, and colleagues build a satellite image maker in this 2026 paper. Their model, GeoDiT, turns text into satellite views. Older tools need full pixel maps to guide them, which take long to draw and say little. GeoDiT instead takes single points, each paired with a short text note.

A point marks where a feature should sit, and its note says what that feature is. A new attention step weighs those points so they steer the image well. The team also tests which image and location codes train best. In their trials, GeoDiT beat leading remote sensing image makers. Point control is quicker to give and richer in meaning than map control.
arxiv-2603-02372:
Max Baak and Hella Snoek revisit the Drake equation in this 2026 paper. The equation estimates how many communicative alien civilizations fill our galaxy. A famous argument says our own existence teaches nothing about life elsewhere. Selection effects, it claims, make Earth an uninformative data point.

A recent challenge argues that the famous argument mishandles its probability logic. Judged correctly, the selection effect vanishes and Earth's life does carry information. Following that line, Baak and Snoek count humanity as one real data point. They derive a pessimistic floor for civilization counts in the observable universe and the galaxy. The floor rules out models that predict far fewer civilizations, they note. Humanity's existence, on this view, is evidence after all.
arxiv-2603-02472:
Hiroto Odaka, Barbara Lopez-Doriga, and Kunihiko Taira compare flows over a wing hit by extreme gusts in this 2026 paper. Gusts can swing a wing's lift violently in a short burst. The team studies massively separated flow over a square wing. Two regimes are compared: smooth laminar flow and turbulent flow at far higher speed scales.

Large swirling cores drive the big lift swings in both regimes. Those cores look strikingly alike across the two cases. A strong gust-driven vorticity flux at the wing surface forms them in each. Fine-scale swirls appear quickly in the turbulent case, but the large pattern persists. Splitting the turbulent flow by scale recovers the laminar shapes. Simple laminar models may thus teach real lessons about extreme turbulent aerodynamics.
arxiv-2603-02872:
Jialiang Zhang, Junlong Tong, Junyan Lin, and colleagues make video models think while the video still plays. Most such systems wait for the full clip before they start to reason. That wait adds delay, and their focus drifts as the clip grows long.

Three changes make streaming work. A mask blocks peeking at frames that have not yet arrived. A new position scheme sorts out clashes between image order and text order. A split memory cache lets new frames arrive while the answer is still being written. On a video test, scores rose a bit. The wait for the first word fell from over ten seconds to nearly zero. Timing errors dropped by more than half.
arxiv-2603-03172:
Carolin Heinzler, Kasra Malihi, and Amartya Sanyal prove that deleting data from a model needs less noise than privacy rules suggest. Certified unlearning must make a model statistically indistinguishable from one retrained without the deleted data. Existing methods borrow differential privacy machinery and add noise sized for the worst change over any neighboring dataset.

The key observation is that unlearning never promises to protect the data that stays. A new measure, retain sensitivity, fixes the retained set and only varies what gets deleted, which is exactly what unlearning must hide. Noise calibrated to that smaller quantity keeps the same certificates. Tests on spanning trees, principal components, and standard learning confirm the savings, and two popular algorithms get sharper analyses through the same lens.
arxiv-2603-03572:
Abdelmalek Boumali studies a relativistic oscillator under a relativity with two speed limits. Doubly special relativity adds an invariant energy or length scale beside the speed of light. His 2026 paper takes the general Dirac oscillator and rebuilds it under that deformed kinematics. The oscillator swaps the usual linear coupling for an arbitrary interaction function. The paper also reviews its factorization into partner Schrödinger-like problems.

Certain complex interactions make the system pseudo-Hermitian or parity-time symmetric yet keep real energies, and the paper clarifies the inner products that make that consistent. Two deformation recipes then diverge. One bends the energy map through an energy-dependent mass, asymmetrically between branches. The other deforms momentum and imposes a hard admissibility ceiling on states. A complexified Morse interaction illustrates both, including how deformation truncates bound states, and how the massless limit separates the two recipes.
arxiv-2603-03872:
Xizhong Yang and others propose DistriVoting, a method for choosing the best answer among several candidates generated by large reasoning models. Test-time scaling raises accuracy by sampling many responses, but picking the right one is the hard part. Internal confidence scores partly track correctness and correlate with accuracy in distribution, yet earlier methods never used that distributional information to guide selection.

DistriVoting first splits the mixed confidence distribution into positive and negative components with a Gaussian mixture model, then applies a rejection filter based on samples from each to reduce their overlap. A companion technique, SelfStepConf, uses step-level confidence to adjust the inference process itself and widen the separation. Across many models and five benchmarks, the method beats prior state-of-the-art approaches, showing that distributional priors make confidence-based voting markedly more reliable.
arxiv-2604-20772:
Adam Shaw's thesis studies general relativity through chiral formulations, which split the geometry of spacetime into self-dual and anti-self-dual parts. In Plebanski's formulation the basic variables are triples of two-forms rather than a metric, and a pure connection view goes further still. These viewpoints expose extra structure in Einstein's equations and suggest new tools.

The thesis builds the ideas in stages, starting with fibre bundle geometry, then the linearized equations and their gauge choices in the chiral setting. Later parts reach the nonlinear regime, the complex geometry behind black hole spacetimes, and numerical relativity schemes built from the chiral forms. It is a broad exploration of one reformulation of Einstein's theory.
arxiv-2605-00372:
Xiaohui Liu and 29 co-authors study the polarization angles of repeating fast radio bursts, millisecond flashes of radio energy from deep space. Within one burst the angle usually stays nearly constant, yet it jumps from burst to burst while its overall statistics stay stable across observing sessions. The measured angles cluster in a bell-shaped spread.

The authors argue the bursts likely come from a localized region inside a neutron star's magnetosphere. A search for any repeating rhythm in the angle sequence, across timescales from milliseconds to months, found nothing credible. They extend the classic rotating vector model with a magnetosphere that evolves dynamically, its effective magnetic axis wandering randomly within a confined region. Projection effects in that picture reproduce the angle spread and the missing rhythm, and the same story may cover bursts that never repeat.
arxiv-2605-00772:
Pravy Prerana and Sascha Wald ask how much entanglement a quantum walk can create on an irregular network. Quantum walks move a particle through a network in a way that can support transport and algorithms. The usual entanglement measure splits coin and position, so it fails on complex graphs. The authors instead give each node two roles, as both source and target.

That split defines a new source-target measure suited to general networks. Network connectivity sets an upper bound on the entanglement, and graph matchings turn out to govern how it grows. Tests on random graphs show a surprise: better connectivity can lower the entanglement that is actually reachable, which limits quantum correlations.
arxiv-2605-00972:
Nihanth W. Cherukuru and six co-authors present a visual analytics workbench for exploring weather and climate data through embeddings. Earth system datasets are now large and high-dimensional, and embedding neighbors can be searched quickly. But neighbors are not automatically meaningful: they may reflect real weather structure or artifacts of preprocessing, geography, or model bias. Scientists need tools to inspect latent organization and trace results back to physical evidence.

The open-source system links embedding experiments to shared source data, metadata, spatial context, and model settings. Users can query by image or local patch, filter by several constraints, and inspect analogs in familiar meteorological views. A tropical cyclone case on ERA5 data demonstrates the loop, and the backend scales to tens of millions of embeddings.
arxiv-2605-01172:
Elon Litman and Gabe Guo present a new theory for why deep neural networks can learn from training data and still do well on new data. Their account centers on the neural tangent kernel, a tool that tracks how a network changes as it trains.

In their picture, the kernel splits the output space into a signal part and a vast noise part. Real signal is learned fast, while odd details of single examples are stored slowly in the noise part, where tests cannot see them. The theory ties together known puzzles such as benign overfitting, double descent, and grokking. It also yields a risk score from one training run alone, with no held-out data, and a tweak to the Adam optimizer that speeds up grokking and cuts memorization.
arxiv-2605-01272:
Rajesh Sureddi, Shreshth Saini, Avinab Saha, and Alan C. Bovik present GameScope, a large benchmark dataset for assessing gaming video quality. Game streaming has grown rapidly on platforms using different codecs, so quality models must work consistently across codecs. Existing subjective datasets are few and limited. GameScope is described as the largest gaming quality dataset to date, covering user-generated and professional content with extensive visual diversity.

The dataset spans the three most widely used codecs and contains thousands of video samples, each rated by dozens of viewers on overall quality. Coarse-grained quality attributes are also collected to clarify perceptual factors. Leading assessment methods are benchmarked, including a vision-language model that outperforms all the others. The dataset is publicly released.
arxiv-2605-02072:
James Wang and Surbhi Goel improve conformal prediction when test data shift away from training data. Conformal methods give prediction sets with coverage guarantees, but those guarantees rest on training and test data being exchangeable. Weighted conformal prediction handles shifts, yet it can under-cover badly when the density ratio is unbounded or must be learned.

Their method, clipped least-squares importance fitting, estimates that ratio with lower variance. Used inside weighted conformal prediction, it gives bounded expected undercoverage. The shortfall can then be fixed by aiming at a slightly higher coverage target, and the needed inflation can itself be estimated. The authors show how to compute that correction from the data.
arxiv-2605-02272:
Omar Alnaseri and colleagues review quantum satellite links, a path to secure global networks. The review centres on the blocks that still stop large-scale use. Those blocks include loss in air, beam pointing, payload limits, timing sync, scale, and links to ground networks.

A short overview of core concepts and key tools sets the scene. Milestones such as the Micius mission show what has been done. The authors then survey new work on protocols and hybrid space-ground designs. They also cover ways to cut turbulence effects and use AI to optimise links. Future paths include a quantum internet, daylight use, satellite repeaters, and quantum computing in space.
arxiv-2605-02372:
Judith Sáinz-Pardo Díaz and Álvaro López García present a full privacy-preserving workflow for federated learning on sensitive tabular data. Federated learning trains models on decentralised data without centralising it, a response to privacy law and AI growth. Yet data integrity and privacy risks remain inside the federation itself.

Their workflow joins anonymisation with differential privacy techniques. They give a formal definition of client drift and ways to detect it, aimed at mitigating poisoning attacks. They also detail how to assign personalised privacy budgets for global differential privacy to each client, based on a re-identification risk metric. The methodology is presented and tested on an openly available data set in the paper.
arxiv-2605-02472:
Stanisław Sójka and Witold Kowalczyk address a hard use case for language models: legal clauses that turn on exact logic. Large reasoning models can explain such clauses, the authors note, but they still make errors and cost a lot to run at scale. Their answer is to translate each legal text once, then judge cases with fixed rules.

The translation target is a typed graph form they call DACL, which a program can run step by step with a visual trace. Against strong model baselines run at the time of each case, the graph-based agent was far more consistent. It also cut compute costs by more than ninety percent in high-volume work, while keeping an audit trail suited to legal review.
arxiv-2605-02672:
Panagiotis Tzirakis and eight co-authors introduce a workshop and challenge on modeling feelings and social dynamics in two-person conversations. Most benchmarks treat each speaker alone. Real dialogue, though, is coupled: partners influence each other, coordinate timing, and build or lose rapport over a whole interaction. The challenge is built to capture those joint processes.

Three linked tasks share one dataset: predicting the direction of influence between partners, predicting turn-taking, including who speaks next and when, and predicting how rapport evolves. The data hold hundreds of dyadic conversations, with hundreds of hours of audio and video in five languages, recorded under natural conditions. Fixed data splits, standard metrics, and released baselines support multimodal modeling and fair comparison across teams.
arxiv-2605-02972:
Amir Erez builds reduced models of biological dynamics from a single binary operator that can generate all standard elementary functions. Modelers often need responses that rise, overshoot, then settle, as in recruitment effects and adaptive transients. The standard saturating response curve is monotone, so it cannot show overshoot alone; two opposed blocks are needed, doubling the parameter count for that part of a model.

Using the operator as a grammar for reduced differential equations, Erez obtains a single activation-suppression module that captures overshoot directly. Three validations follow. On protein relocalization data, the grammar finds a compact surrogate matching known biology. On recruitment data, an exhaustive search picks the same form across all traces. A fifty-state simulated network is compressed by a cascade acting as a fixed time basis.
arxiv-2605-03072:
Wissem Ahmed Zaid and Alain Hertz test how design choices shape tactical wireless networks built under real limits. Optimization is common for such networks, but how much each parameter matters for the final layout and performance has been poorly mapped.

Using tabu search to build layouts, they vary hub rules, antenna beam width, and terms in the goal function across network sizes, then check which changes matter with standard statistical tests. Some choices reshape the layout itself, while others only shift performance scores. Scale-linked shifts and threshold effects give practical tuning guidance for mission use.
arxiv-2605-03372:
Vít Růžička and fifteen co-authors present a fully automatic system for detecting trace gas plumes in imaging spectrometer data. Future instruments will flood analysts with far more data than human review can handle, so plume hunting must scale without people in the loop.

Blending machine learning shape analysis with physics-based spectral fitting, the system runs on EMIT data in two modes: a daily digest flagging the largest events, and a retrospective sweep for missed plumes. It found that at least a quarter of large plumes had been overlooked by human review. Detection also extends to ammonia, nitrogen dioxide, and carbon monoxide.
arxiv-2605-03472:
Tianze Han, Beining Xu, Hanbo Zhang, and Yongming Lu audit a hidden failure in mental-health chat models. Some replies sound empathetic while quietly backing harmful thinking. AI evaluators often reward surface warmth and fluency. They miss backing of catastrophizing, avoidance, or hopeless forecasts.

Their clean matched benchmark pairs hundreds of contexts with controlled response windows. It is audited against leakage. A structured audit scores the direction of clinical-state change across meaning, affect, and distortion, rather than free-form judgment. It beat the strongest baseline on risk detection, arguing that safety checks need explicit clinical state models.
arxiv-2605-03572:
Daniel Pereira, Vana Pezelj, Florian Prawits, and Hannes Hübel report an experiment that attacks a real continuous-variable quantum key distribution system. Such systems promise secure sharing of secret keys, but real devices have flaws an eavesdropper can exploit. Their attack uses coherent light to blind the receiver's detector.

Blinding stops the receiver from estimating the channel properly, which hides the noise left by the eavesdropper's wider attack. The team shows that excess noise above two and a half shot-noise units can be hidden reliably, proving the attack works in practice. They also suggest ways to strengthen it and countermeasures that could block it.
arxiv-2605-04272:
Timothé Lemistre studies the volume of maximal representations, a way of mapping a surface's fundamental group into a specific Lie group that arises in higher Teichmueller theory. Volume gives a single number that summarises such a representation, and its possible range was not fully understood for this target group.

Lemistre proves the volume stays bounded above by one constant, no matter how large the genus of the surface grows. On the special Gothen components of the representation space, he also proves the volume stays above a strictly positive constant. Together the two bounds confine the volume to a controlled band in those settings.
arxiv-2605-04572:

They find benign training pushes parameters cumulatively toward directions aligned with dangerous behaviour, progressively weakening safety. Building on that, they score each training sample by how much its induced update projects onto the danger direction versus the safety direction. Those continuous risk scores let practitioners flag risky samples in advance, turning a vague fragility into something measurable per example.
