A three-man committee would draw up the reparations bill, under this Soviet proposal of February 7, 1945. The Allied Reparation Committee would hold one representative each from the Soviet Union, Britain, and the United States. Each man could call in as many experts as he wished. The committee's task was fixed by the Crimean Conference itself.

It would work out a detailed plan for exacting reparations under the principles the conference adopted. When other Allied powers might join, and in what form, the three governments would decide later. The paper turns a slogan — Germany must pay — into a machine with seats, staff, and orders.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d472:
De Gaulle was to receive two telegrams from the three heads of government, under Stettinius's instructions to Ambassador Caffery in Paris. The messages were to be delivered with British and Soviet colleagues as soon as possible after 8:30 p.m. Paris time on Monday, February 12. The first pointed de Gaulle to the communiqué and its Declaration on Liberated Europe.

Its last paragraph, the telegram notes, hopes the French government may be associated with the action suggested. Had circumstances permitted, the three leaders would have welcomed discussion with de Gaulle of the declaration's terms. The terms, it adds, matter less than the joint obligation to act. The wire manages an excluded ally with care.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d72:
Acting Secretary of State Stettinius drew up this list on 15 November 1944 under the heading “Matters To Discuss With the President.” It is a working checklist for building the new world security body. The paper appears in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations of the United States.

The world body items lead the list. On Council voting, Stettinius backs a formula of seven votes, including the permanent members. A party to a dispute would not vote on peaceful settlement. Other items cover first membership and a headquarters district on Swiss and French soil near Geneva. Study of trusteeships, drafting the court statute, and ending the League of Nations round out the page.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d172:
Ambassador Kirk reported Field Marshal Alexander's worries about American troop cuts in a telegram from Caserta on June 28, 1945. The message is document 172 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Alexander, the Allied supreme commander in the Mediterranean, had spoken frankly at dinner the night before.

Alexander was disappointed by word that only 2,500 American troops would remain in Italy by the end of 1945, apart from a division near Trieste. He asked whether Washington might keep large forces in Europe until the war's major problems were fully settled. Churchill, he said, had asked him for estimates of the forces Italy would need. He would take up that case with Truman, with great vigor. The case was for leaving strong American forces in Italy and elsewhere in Europe.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d272:
The British Embassy shared London's orders for Austria in an extract dated July 10, 1945. The extract is document 272 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It comes from the political directive sent to General McCreery, the British commander in chief in Austria.

British policy remains the restoration of a free and independent Austrian state, the directive says. Austrians should carry the burden of administration themselves as early as possible, under Allied control. One of McCreery's first tasks is to secure an early move from the Renner government. He must secure it with his Soviet, American, and French colleagues. The move would lead to a fully representative Austrian government that all four powers can recognize. Renner's government may have served a purpose when only part of Austria was free, London holds, but one drawn from so narrow a base cannot continue.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d372:
A British aide-mémoire, dated July 9, 1945, complains of American haste over property removals from Germany. On June 27 Pauley had shared with Sir Walter Monckton his instructions to his Frankfurt man and to the American zone commander. They covered the withdrawal from Germany of art objects, other property, and supplies, and Pauley suggested the British send like orders to Montgomery.

London says it would have welcomed a chance to comment before action was taken. The subject, it argues, most needs a policy common to all four zones. That fits the wider aim of treating Germany as one economic unit. The note is polite, but the rebuke is plain.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d472:
A draft interim settlement for Italy is summarized in Kirk's cable from Rome of July 15, 1945. Answering the Department's circular telegram of July 3 on immediate revision of the Italian armistice terms, Kirk submits a draft agreement. Signed by the Supreme Allied Commander, Mediterranean, it would serve as a modus vivendi in place of the instrument of surrender.

Its first section abrogates the earlier instruments: the armistice of September 3 and the surrender of September 29, 1943, and the later terms restoring Italian territory. The provisions that follow would then govern relations between the parties. A second section, on allied aid to Italy, dissolves the Allied Commission, save for its land, navy, and air subcommissions.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d572:
Field Marshal Alexander, the Allied commander in the Mediterranean, wrote to the Combined Chiefs of Staff on June 25, 1945. His secret message, sent in paraphrase, is document 572 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. He asks the chiefs to back his reading of the Belgrade agreement.

Alexander says a split arose over paragraph 3, on the keeping of civil rule in Venezia Giulia. He cites radio broadcasts, Yugoslav attitudes, and statements by local Slovene groups. On the ground, he reports, Italian offices still work in part, but Yugoslav committees set up in the occupation now hold the real power. The Yugoslavs claim the Allies must adopt that committee system whole. Alexander quotes the deal's words, which let him use only such local rule as he finds working well.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d672:
Paris ambassador Caffery relayed a British note on the stalled Tangier talks on July 9, 1945. The secret wire is document 672 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. The British Embassy in Paris had delivered the note to the French foreign ministry that afternoon.

The note says the Soviet request to join the Paris talks has created a new situation. It involves Russian participation in Tangier's administration, not mere attendance. London will likely need some time before it can state definite views. In the meanwhile, it suggests Moscow be told that no meetings will be held in Paris until the Soviet request is decided. France is asked for its views on that proposed reply. A similar message, Caffery notes, was going to Washington through the British Embassy there.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d72:
Churchill sent a pointed reminder to President Truman on June 16, 1945, about the President's travel plans. Telegram number 93 is document 72 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Press reports said Truman might stop in Paris and see General de Gaulle before going on to the Berlin conference.

Churchill notes that President Roosevelt had promised him several times that he would not visit France before visiting Britain. He is sure Truman will keep that in mind in any decision he takes. The short message shows Churchill guarding Britain's pride of place with the new president, even as the two men planned their first meeting. Personal protocol, it makes clear, still counted alongside grand strategy.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1072:
Ambassador Lincoln MacVeagh cabled Washington from Athens on July 19, 1945, to rebut Moscow's picture of Greece. There is no comparison, he writes, between Greece and the Soviet puppet regimes of the Balkans. Talk of anarchy and monarchist-fascist terror is, in his word, a fantastic distortion.

Despite rightist excesses after last winter's leftist rising, he argues, ordinary Greeks enjoy more personal freedom than anyone else in the Balkans. Leaders of the December rising walk free and speak out. Newspapers of every view, the Communist one included, sell openly in Athens. Greece holds 17,351 prisoners out of seven million people, most for common crimes. Nor can Greece threaten its neighbors: its northern border is held by only 7,000 guardsmen.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1172:
Kennan in Moscow wrote to Caffery, the American ambassador in France, on 28 July 1945. The note joined two of America's key posts in Europe, Moscow and Paris, while the Potsdam talks ran their course. Kennan shared his reading of the Soviets with a fellow envoy who faced them from the West.

Envoys compared notes across the continent as a matter of craft. What Paris heard from French leaders and what Moscow saw in Soviet conduct made one picture when joined. This message is that joining at work. It shows the foreign service thinking as a network, not as lone posts.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1272:
On 23 July 1945 the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. Behind every choice at Potsdam stood staff work of this kind. The chiefs' papers gave the team the services' judgment in a form that could be quoted, traded, and filed.

This note dates from the second week's start, when the bargaining over Germany's terms was at its hardest. The military view mattered there: occupation forces would live with whatever was signed. The memorandum is the chiefs speaking to that duty. It is one more sheet in the thick file the American staff built at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1372:
A working paper of the United States delegation, dated 25 July 1945, survives as document 1372. Working papers were drafts in progress, written by staff for the men who would speak at the table. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Drafts show thought before it hardens into policy. In a working paper, readers can see options weighed and phrases tried out, the raw state of a position. Such papers rarely flatter their writers, which is part of their worth. Set beside the signed texts at the volume's end, this draft helps measure the talks. It shows how much the American line moved, and where it never budged.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-72:
Department of State minutes record the sixth session of the foreign ministers, July 23, 1945, at 11:30 a.m. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Molotov sat in the chair and opened by listing the day's questions.

Seven items were named for discussion. Reparations from Germany and Italy came first, then economic principles for Germany. The Council of Foreign Ministers report, trusteeships, and the directive to the Allied commanders in Germany followed. A paper on cooperation in solving urgent European economic problems was sixth, and Iran a possible seventh. Eden pointed out that Iran stood on the Big Three agenda, and Molotov agreed to pass it over. Tangier was added by consent in its place. Molotov also proposed settling the texts of the invitations to China and France before the ministers drafted the Big Three agenda.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d772:
Document 772 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 17, 1945. It belongs to the conference's opening day. Staff brought drafts with them to Germany, ready for the first sessions. This paper was kept in the delegation files and printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Opening-day working papers show preparation meeting reality. Teams had planned for months; now the plans met rival plans. Readers can compare this early draft with the texts that emerged two weeks later. The document honors the planners whose unseen work shaped the summit's first hours. Their paper trail starts the volume's story.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d872: Foreign Minister Molotov submitted this Soviet proposal at Potsdam on July 23, 1945. It is the first Soviet draft of Article 19 of the Economic Principles. The clause says that after reparations, Germans must be left enough to live without outside help. It also provides means to pay for imports approved by the Control Council. If funds fell short, all deliveries would be cut in proportion.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d972:
The Drafting Committee on reparations from Germany reported to the conference on August 1, 1945. Its message is that no agreement was reached on a protocol. An attached draft text failed on a single dispute: what the Soviet Union had promised about German wealth abroad.

American and British members held that Moscow, in return for its equipment percentages, had agreed to drop claims to external assets, captured gold, and western company securities. The Soviet member denied any such decision existed. The report says the draft would suit the western members if the Soviets confirmed that understanding. The Soviet member objected to how the question had been raised.
gao-gaoreports-b-296972: Standard Communications took its November 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297172: FN Manufacturing doubled its December 2005 protest — two case numbers, one arms-manufacturing fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-298172: Knowledge Connections took its April 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298572: Buckley & Kaldenbach took its October 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-299072: Hydroid LLC took its January 2007 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Underwater-tech deals get the same surface-level fairness.
gao-gaoreports-b-304272: GAO's circular letter on prepackaged news stories went out in February 2005, and this ruling sets the propaganda guidance. The letter draws the line for federal PR. The news had to be real. The line was drawn. The guidance was issued.
gao-gaoreports-b-310372: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Pemco Aeroplex, Inc. Decided December 27, 2007, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-272: A thin GAO record from 2005 — docket gao-05-272 — survives mostly as a title. The metadata offers little more than the identifier. The entry marks its place in the catalog. The record was thin. The entry marks its place in the catalog.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-372: Prescription drug import bans needed a strategy in 2005, and GAO's report says a strategic framework would promote accountability. The findings demand the plan. The report warns that the smuggled pills should not reach medicine cabinets. The framework had to be built.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-672: Radiological sources in Iraq needed evaluating in 2005, and GAO's report says the Pentagon should assess its recovery effort and apply lessons. The findings demand the review. The report warns that the loose hot material should not be lost. The effort had to be evaluated.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-872: Iraq's taps and toilets needed better scorecards in 2005, and GAO's report says the U.S. effort had to be measured well. The findings demand the metrics. The report warns that the thirsty deserved honest accounting. The thirsty deserved honest accounting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-272: The 2010 Census address lists needed fixing in 2006, and GAO's report says the bureau had to act promptly on mapping challenges. The findings demand the speed. The report warns that the headcount could not miss the houses. The actions had to be prompt.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-372: Hospital drug prices varied widely in 2006, and GAO's report says the survey showed price variation and data lessons. The findings do the counting. The report warns that the pill prices deserved sunlight. The variation had to be faced. The pill prices deserved sunlight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-472: VA hospital partnerships offered lessons in 2006, and GAO's report says the Denver and Charleston experiences could guide future medical alliances. The findings extract the wisdom. The report warns that the veterans' care partnerships needed learning. The lessons had to be applied.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-672: The internet's disaster recovery plan needed building in 2006, and GAO's report says DHS faced challenges in developing the joint plan. The findings map the obstacles. The report warns that the net's backbone needed a backup plan. The plan had to be developed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-72: Competitive sourcing's health cost comparison had minimal impact in 2006, and GAO's report says DOD needed uniform implementation procedures. The findings demand the consistency. The report warns that the outsourcing contests needed fair rules. The procedures had to be uniform. The outsourcing contests needed fair rules.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-872: The nation's oil stash was valuable but tricky in 2006, and GAO's report says the reserve's oil could bring significant benefits, though many factors should guide its future. The findings balance the promise and the caution. The report warns that the underground treasure needed wise handling. The reserve had to be managed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1072: The Pentagon's business side needed a single throat to choke — GAO's 2007 report says only a chief management officer could bring focus. Reform energy kept scattering across the brass. The findings argue for one empowered leader to drag the world's largest bureaucracy into shape.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1172: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report on climate-change research data: agencies had data-sharing policies but could do more to make federally funded research data available. Taxpayer-paid science was not always reaching other scientists or the public. GAO's findings press agencies to open up the data behind climate research so findings can be checked, reused, and built upon.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-272: Enrolling the poorest in drug plans stayed hard in 2007 — GAO's report details the hurdles facing the dual-eligible at every step. The findings map the enrollment maze from start to finish. The report asks why the neediest faced the steepest paperwork of all.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-572: Retiree drug coverage was holding on in 2007 — GAO's report says most sponsors kept offering prescription benefits and picked the federal subsidy option. The findings map the employer choices in detail. The report captures the moment before the retiree-health tide turned for good.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-772: Washington's road money was loosening up in 2007 — GAO's report finds flexible funding let states and towns chase their own transport priorities. The findings praise the multi-use dollars while watching for drift. The report frames flexibility as trust: let locals pave where the potholes are.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-372: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on entitlement Reform Process: Other Countries' Experiences Provide Useful Insights for the United States. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-672: The Government Accountability Office dug into maritime Security: National Strategy and Supporting Plans Were Generally Well-Developed and Are Being Implemented in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-72: This 2007 GAO report finds the Energy Department dragging its feet on rounding up bomb-grade material — plutonium and hot uranium strewn across its sites. Years after pledging to lock it down, GAO said, little had moved. The report presses the department to hurry on one of the gravest housekeeping jobs on earth.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-972: The Government Accountability Office dug into DOD Business Systems Modernization: Key Navy Programs' Compliance with DOD's Federated Business Enterprise Architecture Needs to Be Adequately Demonstrated in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
govdocs-archive_org-ZeteticTheVol1No1Jul:
The Zetetic was a journal of the flat-earth movement, and this file holds its very first issue: volume 1, number 1, dated July 1872, edited by Chas. Brough. Zetetic astronomy taught that the earth is a flat plane and that direct experience, not authority, settles such questions.

As a first issue, the journal sets out the movement's claims and its method, which demanded that readers accept only what could be tested for themselves. The flat-earth cause in Victorian Britain ran through periodicals like this one, passed among committed believers. The issue survives as the debut of the movement's own press.
hernandez-martin-fierro-1872:
Jose Hernandez published Martin Fierro in 1872, a long poem in Spanish about a gaucho on the Argentine pampas. Fierro is a singer and horseman who is forced into army service on the frontier. He deserts, loses his home and family, and becomes an outlaw. A second part, published later, follows his return.

Fierro tells his story in song, in the voice of the payada tradition. He speaks of hard work, unfair laws, and loyalty among friends. The poem became the national epic of Argentina. It is still read as a defense of the gaucho way of life against a changing state.
hodge-systematic-theology-vol1-1872:
Charles Hodge taught at Princeton Seminary for more than fifty years and made it the stronghold of Calvinist teaching in America. His Systematic Theology, Volume 1, came out in 1872. It opens his great system with first principles, the doctrine of God, and the doctrine of man.

Hodge says theology gathers its facts from the Bible the way a student of nature gathers facts from the world. This volume treats how we can know God, his nature and perfections, the Trinity, creation, and the fall of man. Students at Princeton learned their faith from Hodge, and his clear definitions shaped Presbyterian teaching in America for years.
ibn-al-athir-kamel-rhc-1872:
Ibn al-Athir chronicled the Crusades from the Muslim side in his Kamil, excerpted here in the French Recueil of 1872. The great Mosul historian's al-Kamil fi'l-ta'rikh, his Complete History, covers the Frankish wars from 1098 to 1231 in this extract. Tome I of the Historiens orientaux gave French readers the eastern voice on events the West usually tells alone.

Sieges, truces, and the rise of Saladin pass in annal form, year by year. Ibn al-Athir judges the Franks shrewdly and his own princes harshly when they divided. The extract remains a first source for the Crusades, precious for its outside view.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-luboml-10172:
Luboml, a town in the government of Volhynia, Russia, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky. Jews lived there as early as the sixteenth century, facing open hostility from Christian neighbors. In 1897 the town counted 4,600 people, of whom 3,300 were Jews.

Fearing attack or fire, the community ruled in 1557 that no member should buy property inside the town, and it reaffirmed that rule in 1576. Outside town, Jews held eight parcels of land and leased mills and three lakes, paying in money and goods worth about 400 gold ducats. The article closes with figures on Jewish artisans, day laborers, and schoolchildren. It offers a close, number-filled snapshot of a small town where Jews formed most of the population yet lived under tight limits.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magnus-heinrich:
Heinrich Gustav Magnus, a German chemist and physicist, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in Berlin on May 2, 1802, he graduated from its university in 1827. He then studied under Berzelius at Stockholm and under Gay-Lussac in Paris. He began teaching at Berlin in 1831 and became a full professor in 1845. He died there in 1870.

The article catalogs a wide field of discovery. At Stockholm he found the green salt that still bears his name. He discovered several acids and studied how blood absorbs oxygen and carbonic acid. His work on the expansion of gases appeared in 1841, close beside Regnault's. Later experiments on heat passing through gases set off a long dispute with Tyndall. He also built up the university's physical cabinet. The entry honors a researcher who ranged across chemistry and physics alike.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mannheimer-sigm:
Sigmund Mannheimer, an American educator, receives an entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Kemel, Hesse-Nassau, on May 16, 1835, he trained at the teachers' seminary at Ems. He taught in Jewish schools at Schierstein and Hegenheim. In 1861 he entered the University of Paris, taking his degree in 1863.

The article follows his Atlantic crossing and his books. He became professor of German at Paris in 1864, then emigrated to America in 1865. Baltimore, New York, St. Louis, and Rochester followed in turn. In 1884 Hebrew Union College at Cincinnati made him professor of exegesis and Aramaic, and its librarian. His Hebrew Reader and Grammar reached a fourth edition by 1903. He also translated works defending the Talmud and attacking anti-Semitism. The entry records a schoolmaster who carried European Jewish learning into American classrooms.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mat-moses-ben-a:
Moses ben Abraham Mat, a Galician rabbi, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Solomon Schechter and Bernhard Friedberg. Born at Przemysl about 1550, he studied Talmud under his uncle R. Zebi and under Solomon Luria. He became rabbi of Beldza, where pupils gathered around him, and after a quieter interval at Vladimir he served as rabbi of Przemysl and then, from 1597, of Luboml. He died at Opatow in 1606 as head of its community.

Three books carry his name. "Taryag Mizwot," printed at Cracow in 1581, sets the 613 commandments in verse. "Matteh Mosheh" treats the practical ritual laws, and "Ho'il Mosheh," published at Prague after his death, is a plain, homely commentary on the Pentateuch that sometimes explains Rashi. Some of his legal answers survive inside the responsa collections of his contemporaries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendes-mendez-m:
Moses Mendes, an English poet and dramatist of the Drury Lane world, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and Edgar Mels. Grandson of Fernando Mendes, the queen's physician, and son of a Mitcham stockbroker, he took his degree at St. Mary Hall, Oxford, made a fortune in stockbroking himself, bought an estate at Old Buckenham in Norfolk, and settled down to literature. He died there on February 4, 1758.

His successes were early: the ballad-opera "The Double Disappointment" in 1746, and "The Chaplet," with music by Boyce, a great hit in 1749 thanks partly to Mrs. Clive. Later pieces, "Robin Hood" and "The Shepherd's Lottery," failed, and his Spenserian poems and the satirical "Battiad" mark him, the entry says frankly, as a dilettante. His sons dropped the name Mendes and took Head by royal warrant.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mezei-moritz-10:
Moritz Mezei was a Hungarian jurist born at Satoralja-Ujhely on January 17, 1836. He spent his life fighting for Jewish emancipation in Hungary. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer tell his story in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. As a law student in Budapest, he joined the movement to restore the Hungarian constitution. In 1861 he founded the National Judaeo-Hungarian Society.

His nationalist journalism brought a court-martial, and only a royal amnesty saved him. He lost his editorship. But by the king's leave he began practicing law in 1864, though the bar was still closed to Jews. He served as secretary of the 1868 congress on Jewish communal affairs. He led the campaign that won legal recognition for Judaism in 1892. He entered parliament in 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-milius-paulus-c:
Paulus Milius, also called da Gin or Grynus, was a Hebrew bibliographer, publisher, and teacher born at Rödlsee in Germany early in the sixteenth century. Moses Beer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He copied Hebrew manuscripts for a living, traveling to the libraries of Paris, Louvain, and Rome, and at Rome he embraced Christianity.

At Augsburg in 1544 he printed a Judaeo-German Pentateuch whose translation, the article says, was still in use in Poland in 1901. He became professor of Hebrew at Ingolstadt in 1547, then wrote an anti-Jewish pamphlet a year later. His 1562 Judaeo-German Samuel hid an awkward fact: it copied, uncredited, a version published at Augsburg in 1543 by Ḥayyim Schwarz.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mirels-zebi-hir:
Ẓebi Hirsch ben Aaron Mirels was a German Talmudist who served as rabbi of Schwerin in the middle of the eighteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and S. J. Levinson wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He was educated first in London, then at several yeshivot, and held a pulpit at Wreschen in Poland before Schwerin.

His one book, Mispar Ẓeba'am, printed at Berlin in 1787, is a pilpulistic treatise on the Talmud — the sharp, argumentative style of study then in fashion. It falls into two parts, named Pinnot Ẓeba'aw and Ereẓ Ẓebi. The entry's bibliography runs through Fuenn, Walden, Steinschneider, and Fürst, the standard guides to rabbinic biography of the period.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monzon-10972:
Monzon, a town near Lerida in the old kingdom of Aragon, had a considerable Jewish community. The community was deep in the money-lending business. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling write about it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its richest Jew in 1260, Solomon de Daroca, farmed the taxes. He lent the court large sums, taking the taxes of two Jewries as security. He also leased the salt-works of Arcos.

Privilege marked the town. When Aragon's Jews were taxed for James II's Sicilian war, Monzon's Jews won exemption by special agreement. In the persecution of 1349 they shut themselves inside the Jewry. They fasted and prayed until the danger passed. The chronicles add a darker tale of a Passover massacre sparked by a street quarrel. It is told here from the records Jacobs collected.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-danie:
Moses ben Daniel of Rohatyn was a Galician author of the late seventeenth century. Herman Rosenthal and Max Schloessinger wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Though named for Rohatyn, he lived at Zolkiev, as his own preface states. His one known work deals with how the Talmud argues.

The Sugyot ha-Talmud, printed at Zolkiev in 1693, is a method book for Talmud study and its commentaries. Its forty sections treat the special terms the Talmud uses in argument, and it rests on the teaching of his own masters. Approved by the scholars of his day, it was later translated into Latin. The translation appeared at Hanover in 1714, inside an edition of the Halikot Olam.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moss-mary-11172:
Mary Moss was an American author born at Chestnut Hill, Philadelphia, on September 24, 1864. Cyrus Adler wrote her short Jewish Encyclopedia entry. From 1902 she published fiction and essays in the magazines at a steady pace. Her Jewish novel Julian Meldola ran in Lippincott's Magazine in March 1903.

Moss also wrote sketches on the Yiddish theater for the Philadelphia press. Her other novels include A Sequence in Hearts and Fruit Out of Season, the latter printed in 1902. Her short stories and essays appeared in the Atlantic Monthly, McClure's, The Bookman, Ainslee's, and Scribner's. The entry catches a working magazine writer at the start of her career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-wolf-ben:
Wolf ben Abraham Nathan was a German Bible scholar. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Dessau on July 8, 1751. He died there on Sept. 6, 1784. His short life still stirred a public storm.

His study of Job, Pesher Dabar, came out in 1777. Mendelssohn and Wessely praised its clear, lucid style. In 1782 he published a reader on Jewish religion for the young. It set out the rabbis' differing views side by side. Its preface attacked faults he saw in Jewish life. Angry readers forced him to rewrite that preface and apologize.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumann-moses-s:
Moses Samuel Neumann was a Hungarian Hebrew poet. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Ban in 1769. His father was a poor cantor who died young. Hardship marked the poet's life from childhood on.

He studied at Boskowitz under Rabbi Samuel Kolin. At Prague, Baruch Jeiteles shaped his mind for good. He tutored and traded in town after town. Presburg, Kittsee, and Vienna all knew him as teacher. He settled at last in Budapest in 1822. His mastery of Hebrew was complete and famed. His drama Bat Yiftah appeared at Vienna in 1805. Grammars, poems, and a letter-writer flowed from his pen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-og-11672:
Og was an Amorite king of Bashan, in the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch, E. Schreiber, Wilhelm Bacher, and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He ruled from Ashtaroth, his chief town. Moses and Israel beat him in war at Edrei. Sixty walled towns of Argob fell with him.

Og was one of the last of the Rephaim, a race of giants. His iron bed is told of in the book of Deuteronomy. It was nine cubits long and four cubits broad. Rabbis told wild tales of how he lived so long. One tale says the Flood rose just to his ankles. One says he sat on a rung by Noah's ark. He was fed each day through a hole in its side.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palitschinetzki:
Joseph Hirsh Palitschinetzki was a scholar of the Bible. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in the year 1805. He died at Berdychev on February 27, 1886. He taught Bible at the rabbis' school at Jitomir.

Joseph taught at that school till the school was shut. He was a keen pupil of books all his life long. His chief work was Kera Mikra, out in 1874. It treats the Hebrew tongue and themes of the Bible. His short pieces in the journals show the same breadth. They show wide knowledge of Hebrew books and speech. His work is named in the chief lists of his age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pecherski-feodo:
Feodosi Pecherski was a Russian saint of the eleventh century. He led the great monastery at Kiev from 1057 to 1074. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His life is told in the early Russian chronicles.

At night Feodosi visited learned Jews to argue about faith. He scolded them and hoped to die a martyr in debate. His letters to the grand duke show a large Jewish community in Kiev. He still taught that Jews must not be denied Christian charity. That mix of zeal and fairness marks the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pethor-12072:
Pethor was the home city of Balaam the seer. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Numbers places the city by the river. Deuteronomy puts it in Aram Naharaim, or Mesopotamia. Balak sent messengers there to hire Balaam.

The city stood north and east of Palestine. Scholars link it with the Hittite town Pitru. Shalmaneser the Second took Pitru in the ninth century BCE. His own inscription tells of crossing the Euphrates. He took the town on the far bank of the Sagur.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinner-ephraim-:
Ephraim Moses Pinner dreamed of translating the whole Talmud. Isidore Singer and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Pinne about 1800. He died at Berlin in 1880, the dream unfinished.

His specimen volume appeared at Berlin in 1831. Nicholas of Russia let him dedicate the work to him. Twenty-eight folio volumes were planned for the set. Only the tractate Berakot ever appeared, in 1842. Kings and princes subscribed to that single volume. His Odessa manuscript catalog of 1845 fared no better. It spread Firkovich's finds, most of them fake.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabai-of-rob-12: Rabai of Rob, also written Rabai, was the youngest teacher of the first set of saboraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He followed Simona as head of the school at Pumbedita. He died in the year 550. Sherira says of him that he was a gaon. That word, Sherira means head of a school in such a case. It does not mean that Rabai was the first gaon. Jose, last of the amoraim, is called gaon in the same sense.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raphael-henry-l:
Henry Lewis Raphael was an English financier born in London in 1832. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He died at Newmarket on May 11, 1899. He was senior partner in R. Raphael and Sons.

The article says his voice carried weight on the Stock Exchange. He gave evidence to royal commissions and Parliament groups. One was the Gold and Silver Commission of 1888. Raphael also gave widely to charity, Jewish and beyond. He gave twenty thousand pounds to Guy's Hospital. That gift named a ward for his late wife. The entry closes with a note on his son Herbert.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-remak-moses-ben:
Moses ben Jacob Cordovero, called Remak, was a rabbi of Safed and cabalist. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in 1522. He died on June 25, 1570.

The article says he studied rabbinical literature under Joseph Caro. At age twenty his brother in law taught him Cabala. He soon became a known authority in that field. He kept to thoughtful, metaphysical Cabala, the writers say. He avoided the wonder working kind then spreading at Safed. His main work, Pardes Rimmonim, explains the sefirot and emanation. It also treats divine names and the alphabet. His view of God strikingly matches Spinoza's later view. The entry presents a deep thinker with lasting reach.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-right-of-way-12:
Right of way is the legal right to pass over another's land. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Law separates private way from public way. Hebrew law adds a broader right for the king's highway.

The article also counts the way to the grave as broader. Sales of part land may or may not grant passage. A right of way from necessity is generally recognized. Landlocked owners must have access and exit, it holds. The Mishnah gives the case of a cistern inside another's house. Its owner may enter at usual hours only. He may not bring beasts inside to water them. Each owner must make his own key. The entry works through access rules case by case.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-leon-:
Leon Rosenthal was a Russian financier and philanthropist born in Wilna on November 16, 1817. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He rose in the Günzburg family's service to become a leading St. Petersburg banker.

Through a busy life Rosenthal stayed devoted to Hebrew letters and learning. He aided many authors and students of the Haskalah movement. In 1863 he founded the Society for the Promotion of Knowledge among Russia's Jews. He served as its treasurer and guiding spirit until his death. His gifts, public and private, were described as very great.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sabora-plural-s:
Sabora, plural Saboraim, titles the scholars who led Babylonia's academies after the Amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, working alone. Their age opens where the Talmud's own teachers close.

Sherira Gaon's letter dates their start from Rabina's death, in 499. Rabina, head of Sura's academy, counts as the last of the Amoraim. Then followed the Saboraim, most of whom died within a few years. The entry names the last of them at each great academy. They were Gizai at Sura and Simuna at Pumbedita, by that account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ha-nagid:
Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel ha-Nagid. Born at Cordova in 993, he died at Granada in 1055. He was a Spanish statesman, grammarian, poet, and Talmudist. Civil war drove him from Cordova in 1013. He settled at Malaga and kept a small shop there.

His fine Arabic handwriting changed his life. The vizier of Granada hired him as a private secretary. In time Samuel became vizier himself under King Ḥabus. He ran the state's diplomacy and its wars. As nagid, or chief, of Granada's Jews, he also acted as their rabbi. He spent large sums on books for poor students. His Mebo ha-Talmud, an introduction to the Talmud, still survives. So does part of his book of maxims, Ben Mishle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sandalfon-13172:
Wilhelm Bacher and Ludwig Blau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Sandalfon. He is an angel in Jewish mystical lore. His name is a Greek formation meaning co-brother. He is pictured not as God's brother, but as the brother of Meṭaṭron. Sandalfon ranks among the oldest figures of Merkabah mysticism, the lore of God's throne-chariot.

An early teaching calls the wheel-like ofan of Ezekiel by Sandalfon's name. He stands on earth while his head reaches the heavenly creatures. He towers over his fellow angels by a journey of five hundred years. He binds crowns for his Creator. Later mysticism kept him near God in the seventh hall. There he carries the prayers of men before God. He also guards mankind and the shofar blasts of New Year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schiller-armand:
Isidore Singer and Edouard André wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Armand Schiller. He was a French journalist. Schiller was born at Saint-Mandé, near Paris, on August 7, 1857. He studied at the Lycée Condorcet. He took his law degree from the faculty of Paris. He then entered his father's printing house.

Schiller also wrote for various papers, chiefly the legal journal L'Audience. In 1879 he became general secretary of the board of Le Temps. That was one of Paris's leading evening papers. He founded Le Petit Temps, a stream of hourly extras after Le Temps appeared. He teaches at the Ecole du Journalisme as well. In 1897 he was elected syndic of the French republican journalists' body. He received the Legion of Honor in 1892.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbethai-ben-:
Shabbethai ben Isaac, called Sofer and Medakdek, was a Talmudist and grammarian born at Lublin. Crawford Howell Toy and Isaac Broydé wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He lived at Przemysl in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Among his pupils was the Talmudist and cabalist Hayyim Bochner.

His writings join law and language study. One responsum deals with writing the sacred name of God. Other works annotate Kimhi's grammar and the prayer book's grammar. He left studies on the basics of Hebrew and on why grammar must be learned. The entry shows a scholar who treated correct language as part of correct faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silveyra-silvei:
Abraham Gomes Silveyra, also Diego, was a poet and preacher of the Portuguese Jewish diaspora. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He lived long in various French and Dutch towns. Finally he settled at Amsterdam in the Netherlands.

Silveyra joined the Academy of Poets founded by Manuel de Belmonte. That academy dated from the year 1676 at Amsterdam. His printed Sermones gather six homilies on Bible texts. A funeral oration for Rachel de Pinto stands among them. Other works of his survive only in manuscript today. One offers playful dialogues between a Jew, Turk, Reformed, and Catholic. Another set treats the Messiah, translated from French sources. The entry preserves a wandering preacher's scattered works in two languages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-singer-isidor-1:
Isidor Singer was an Austrian economist born in Budapest on January 16, 1857. Isidore Singer and Emil Jelinek wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He moved to Vienna with his parents in 1861. He studied mathematics, astronomy, and law. In 1881 he took his law degree at Vienna.

Singer gave his full time to political economy instead of law. He traveled to study workers in northeastern Bohemia. His findings appeared in a book published at Leipsic in 1885. He later visited the United States for three years. On his return he founded the weekly Die Zeit with Heinrich Kanner. That paper became a daily in 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-jud:
Solomon ben Judah of Lunel was a Provençal philosopher born in 1411. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His Provençal name was Solomon Vives. At only thirteen years of age he wrote a major work. His master, Frat Maimon, directed that early effort.

The work was a commentary on Judah ha-Levi's Cuzari. It survives in manuscript under the title Heshek Shelomoh. In it the boy shows wide knowledge of philosophy. He knew the philosophical literature of his time in depth. A quotation suggests he wrote another commentary as well. That one dealt with the Ruah Hen, a philosophic introduction.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spitz-moritz-13:
Moritz Spitz was an American rabbi born at Csaba, Hungary, in 1848. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born there on October 14 of that year. He was educated at the University of Prague. Rabbi Judah Teweles of Prague gave him his rabbinical diploma.

From 1870 he served Congregation B'nai Sholom in Chicago. From 1871 to 1878 he served Emanu-El in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Since 1878 he has been rabbi of B'nai El in St Louis. He wrote for the American Israelite under the name Ben Abi. He formerly edited the Jewish Tribune in St Louis. By 1905 he edited the Jewish Voice of that city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-straus-14072:
Straus is an American family that came from Otterberg in the Palatinate. Cyrus Adler and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Its earliest known member, Lazarus, lived in the 1700s. A descendant sat in Napoleon's Assembly of Jewish Notables in 1806. The family took the name Straus in 1808.

Lazarus Straus emigrated to the United States in 1854. He settled first in Talbotton, Georgia, then moved to New York. In 1865 he founded a pottery and glassware business there. His sons joined him in the firm in 1872. The article then profiles his eldest son Isidor. Isidor helped organize L. Straus and Son in New York. Later sections follow other family members and firms. The entry traces one migrant family's American rise.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-szanto-abauj-sz:
Szanto is a Hungarian town on the slopes of Tokay. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Its Jewish community ranks among Hungary's oldest. Two cemeteries mark that long presence. The newer burial ground has served since 1780.

A 1790 document covers the town's burial society. It already counted ninety-six members that year. A 1787 pledge promised to build a school. Rabbi Jeremiah was the first rabbi known by name. Later rabbis included Eleazar Löw, who died in 1837. Leopold Lipschitz led the line into the new century. Paul Jungreisz has held the post since 1896. Jews number 1,500 among 5,000 townspeople. The entry gives a small town's full communal record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tawwah-abraham-:
Abraham ibn Tawwah was an Algerian Talmudist of the 1500s. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He lived and worked at Algiers. His mother descended from the famed Duran family. Through her he traced his line to Nahmanides.

Tawwah was a contemporary of two Duran rabbis at Algiers. One Duran's son Zemah studied under him. Thirty-five of his responsa were printed inside a Duran collection. That collection is called Hut ha-Meshullash in Hebrew. Other answers survive as quotations in later books. Judah Ayyash prints parts titled Nofek in his works. Solomon Zeror quotes a section named Sappir. Tawwah likely split his responsa into twelve parts. Each part bore the name of a breastplate stone. The entry shows responsa scattered yet traceable.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-thorns-and-this:
Palestine's thorns and thistles, plant by plant, are cataloged in this article. Isidore Singer and Immanuel Löw wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia, published in 1906. The desert flora there is unusually rich in prickly growth. Star-thistle, globe-thistle, milk-thistle, and many kin appear.

Farmers cursed these plants and burned fields to clear them. Prophets warned the people with plagues of briers and thistles. Scripture likens a tyrant to a useless bramble. Genesis says the cursed earth would yield thorns and thistles. The article matches Bible and Talmud plant names to Latin species. Box-thorn, blackberry, hawthorn, and jujube all get identified. Botany and Bible study meet on every line.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ulm-14572:
Ulm, a city of Württemberg, first shows a Jewish settlement on a 1243 tombstone. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A legend puts Jews there before the Christian era. The tombstone honors Huknah, daughter of R. Solomon ha-Levi. A 1274 council record calls the community a loan society.

That record let Jews dispose of unredeemed pledges freely. Emperors pawned Ulm's Jewish taxes to various nobles. The Jews even collected taxes from smaller towns nearby. Complaints from those towns brought a reprimand in 1348. Imperial prefects then took Ulm's Jews under protection. Protection money funded the city's new fortifications in part. Well-poisoning charges soon brought mob persecution anyway.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-verein-fur-judi:
Verein für Jüdische Geschichte und Literatur names societies across Germany. Gotthard Deutsch wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Such societies spread Jewish history and literature to a wide public. They arose in many German cities from about 1890. Rising anti Semitism had stirred Jewish interest in the past.

Gustav Karpeles founded a Berlin society in January 1892. In 1893 he united the groups into one national union. The union supplied speakers and printed pamphlets. Since 1898 it has published a yearly volume on Jewish history and literature. By 1905 about 200 societies counted some 15,000 members. Similar groups formed in America, England, and France.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-walton-bryan-14:
Bryan Walton was an English churchman who edited a polyglot Bible. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Yorkshire in 1600. He died in London on November 29, 1661. He studied at Cambridge and became a London clergyman.

At Oxford, Walton planned a Bible in many languages. It would beat the Paris edition on quality and price. Subscriptions funded the six volume work. It appeared between 1654 and 1657. Single books carry up to eight versions each. Castell's seven language lexicon served as its supplement. Charles II made Walton Bishop of Chester in 1660. His Polyglot stayed the standard for centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wessely-naphtal:
Naphtali Hirz Wessely was a German Hebraist and reformer of education. Isidore Singer and N. Slouschz wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Hamburg in 1725. He died there on February 28, 1805. His family fled Podolia after the 1648 massacres. They rose to wealth at Amsterdam and Wesel.

Wessely spent his childhood at Copenhagen. He studied rabbinics under Jonathan Eybeschütz. He also learned modern languages with care. As a banker's agent he visited Amsterdam. There he published a study of Hebrew roots in 1765. The work lacked method but showed wide learning. His later writings urged modern schooling for Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolf-abraham-na:
Abraham Nathan Wolf (1751-1784) was a German scholar who sought a new path for Jewish schools. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born and raised at Dessau, he won the praise of Moses Mendelssohn. His free views on faith set him apart from most scholars then.

Wolf tried to join old Jewish training with new European culture. Strict scholars fought him for that stand. Even his friends called him the backslider in jest. In 1777 he brought out a full study of the Book of Job. Mendelssohn praised its deep Talmud learning in print. Wolf also wrote a plain guide to the Jewish faith. That book has been lost for fifty years, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolfenbuttel-13:
Wolfenbuttel is a German town famed for the Samson School for Jewish boys. Isidore Singer and Lesser Knoller wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The school grew from a gift left by Herz Samson of Brunswick. His brother Philip opened a Talmud school in the town in 1786.

Gifts from the kin of the founders swelled the funds. In 1805 two funds merged as the Samson Free School. Boys learned German, French, sums, maps, and fine hand work there. Paying boarders soon joined the free boys. Talmud study was dropped in time. In 1843 the school became a grammar school with three grades. After 1871 it grew step by step into a high school.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zipser-maier-15:
Maier Zipser was a Hungarian rabbi praised as one of the most scholarly of his day. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Balassa-Gyarmath on August 14, 1815, he died at Rechnitz on December 10, 1869. He studied in several yeshivot and gained secular learning largely by his own effort.

Chosen rabbi at Stuhlweissenburg in 1844, Zipser clashed with Orthodox members over a divorce he had granted. He defended himself in a printed legal opinion in 1853. About 1850 he spent time in England, where he defended Judaism in print against a speech in Parliament. From 1858 he served as rabbi of Rechnitz, writing sermons and many pieces for the Jewish press.
josselyn-new-englands-rarities-1672:
John Josselyn, an English traveler who lived for years in Maine, published New-England's Rarities Discovered in 1672. It is the first English natural history of New England. Josselyn listed what he had seen and heard during two long stays in the colony.

Birds, beasts, fishes, and serpents all enter his catalogue, plant by plant and creature by creature. Some entries are sharp field notes, and others are wonders repeated from settlers' talk. English readers in 1672 met American wildlife here for the first time in print. The book is part field guide and part wonder book, and both parts reward attention.
l-alchimie-1872: L'Alchimie presents a text by Erasmus in a new French translation by Victor Develay. Librairie des Bibliophiles published it in Paris in 1872. The printing was limited, on fine paper stocks. Only five hundred copies were printed on laid paper, plus ten on China paper. Such care marks the book as an item for collectors. Its subject is alchemy, the old art of changing metals. Readers of French can see how a classic author treated that curious subject.
lavater-of-ghostes-and-spirites-english-:
Lavater's book on ghosts reached England in 1572 as Of Ghostes and Spirites, Walking by Night. The translator signed only as R. H. Tudor readers took to it at once, and it became Elizabethan England's favorite manual of apparitions, reprinted for a wide market.

The English text asks what ghosts are, why they appear, and how hearers should judge strange noises. Lavater answers as a Reformed pastor, wary of Catholic purgatory but firm on spirits. His cases range from haunted houses to churchyard walkers. Sturdy English prose carries the Zurich doctrine home. The book shaped how England talked about ghosts for the next hundred years.
legge-chinese-classics-vol-5-part-1-1872:
James Legge published Volume 5, Part 1 of The Chinese Classics in 1872. The text is the Ch'un Ts'ew, the Spring and Autumn Annals, a terse chronicle of the state of Lu. Tradition ascribed the Annals to Confucius himself, and Chinese scholars read deep moral judgments into its spare words.

Part 1 gives the Chinese text with Legge's translation and notes, the first English version of the Annals. Entries record births, deaths, battles, and eclipses in a few dry words each. Legge's prolegomena, his long opening study, explained the text, its commentaries, and its history. The dryness is the point: readers see the seed from which centuries of commentary grew.
legge-chinese-classics-vol-5-part-2-1872:
Volume 5, Part 2 of Legge's Chinese Classics appeared in 1872, completing his Spring and Autumn Annals. James Legge, the Scottish scholar of China, paired the Annals with the Tso Chuan, the great commentary that turns the dry chronicle into narrative. Part 1 had introduced the Annals themselves.

The Tso Chuan tells the stories behind the Annals' bare entries: speeches, battles, plots, and the fall of states. Legge translated the commentary with notes drawn from Chinese scholars. With this part, English readers could read both the record and its classic explanation together. The volume completed Legge's five-volume Chinese Classics, the foundation of Chinese studies in English for a century.
maxwell-theory-of-heat-1872:
James Clerk Maxwell wrote his Theory of Heat in 1872 as a plain textbook for students. Maxwell was already famous for his work on electricity and light. Here he turns to a humbler topic: what heat is, and how it moves.

The book explains temperature, conduction, and the way gases behave when warmed or squeezed. Maxwell shows how tiny moving particles can explain the pressure and heat of a gas. His famous thought experiment about a sorting 'demon' also appears here, and it still sparks debate about order and chance. Teachers used it for years as a first guide to the subject.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume thirteen of Saint-Simon's memoirs opens at chapter ninety seven. Saint-Simon goes back to the rest of the year 1719. The Marquise de Charlus, rich and old, dies in this part.

She looked, he says, like an old clothes woman in her dress. At a supper at the Princesse de Conti's, her high head dress caught fire. The Archbishop of Rheims snatched it off and threw it down. She threw a boiled egg in his face, not knowing why he had acted. Laughter shook the whole room at the egg and the flames. Court farce breaks the grave tone of the memoirs here.
middle-english-bestiary-morris-1872:
The Middle English Bestiary is a verse book of beasts made around 1250 by an unknown English poet. Richard Morris edited it in 1872 for the Early English Text Society. It renders the old Latin bestiary tradition in the common tongue, for English readers and hearers.

Lion, fox, whale, and other beasts appear with their natures and morals. The famous chapter on the siren, half woman and half bird or fish, warns against sweet-voiced danger. Each creature becomes a small sermon in verse. The poem shows animal lore leaving the cloister for a wider world. Morris's edition remains the standard way to read it.
neue-alchymistische-bibliothek-fur-den-n:
Friedrich Josef Wilhelm Schröder gathered this German library of alchemy for the nature student of his century. The record dates it 1772, while the sampled title page shows 1773. Its contents list works by Edmund Dickinson and Theodor Mundan on the gold art and the quintessence of the philosophers.

Other pieces treat Elias the artist and the making of metals by art. A later gathering prints Gabriel Clauder on the universal stone, and Claude Germain on secret philosophy. Old German tracts on the birth of metals follow. The editor's own preface admits he long hesitated to print works written so plainly.
new-illustrated-self-instructor-in-phren:
O. S. and L. N. Fowler, who called themselves practical phrenologists, made this self instructor in phrenology and physiology. The record dates this copy 1872, and its title page boasts a fiftieth thousand printing. W. Tweedie in London published it for L. N. Fowler of New York. Over one hundred engravings fill the book.

Two mottoes state its creed: self knowledge is the essence of all knowledge. Your character, the second says, matches your organization, meaning your body's build. A chart and character reading come with the lessons. Phrenology held that bumps and shape of the head show the mind. Readers could test themselves at home with this guide.
nixon-smoking-gun-transcript-1972:
On June 23, 1972, six days after the Watergate break-in, President Richard Nixon met his chief of staff, H. R. Haldeman, in the Oval Office. Their taped talk produced the record later known as the smoking gun. The transcript became public in August 1974, after the Supreme Court ordered the White House to release the tapes.

In the conversation, Nixon approves a plan to have the CIA tell the FBI to back away from its Watergate inquiry, using national security as the excuse. The words proved the president had joined the cover-up from its first week. His support in Congress collapsed within days of the release, and Nixon resigned before the House could vote on impeachment.
nostradamus-true-prophecies-garencieres-:
Theophilus de Garencieres, a French doctor who lived in London, turned Nostradamus into English in 1672. His was the first full English text of the famed French seer. The book also holds a long preface on the seer's life and times. That life tale was read as fact in England for a long span of years.

The verses run in their set order, with notes to help the reader through hard lines. Garencieres kept the dark tone of the French while he made the words plain English. His text fixed Nostradamus in the English mind as a true prophet for years to come.
openalex-w1924088672:
Leanne Robinson, Ivo Mueller, and co-authors ran this trial. It appeared in PLoS Medicine in October 2015. Two malaria species hide dormant forms in the liver. Those hidden forms, called hypnozoites, cause later relapses. Their share of disease burden was unknown before.

The team studied children in Papua New Guinea. A randomized, placebo-controlled trial tested clearing strategies. A mathematical model helped interpret the trial results. Direct measures aimed to size the hidden reservoir. Cutting relapses could speed malaria elimination in endemic lands. The study guides programs that target dormant parasites.
openalex-w2004402272:
Huiyu Wang, Ignacy Misztal, Ignacio Aguilar and colleagues compared gene mapping methods in broiler chickens. Their paper appeared in Frontiers in Genetics in 2014. The trait was body weight at six weeks. Such mapping helps breeders find genes that shape growth.

The team applied several methods to the same real chicken data. Two methods used records from relatives that had no gene data. Other methods used single gene markers or a Bayesian model. They compared the regions each method found. They also checked shared findings, explained variation and computing speed. They noted traps that can mislead readers of results. The work helps animal breeders choose sound mapping tools.
openalex-w2140370872:
Vitaliano Cama, Caryn Bern, Jacqueline Roberts, and colleagues published this study in Emerging Infectious Diseases in 2008. They followed young children in Peru to see whether illness from Cryptosporidium, a gut parasite, depends on which species or subtype infects them. The parasite causes diarrhea and spreads through contaminated water and food.

A four-year birth cohort of more than five hundred children yielded over one hundred fifty infection episodes. One species, C. hominis, was linked to diarrhea plus nausea, vomiting, and general sickness. It also shed more parasites for longer. Other species were linked to diarrhea alone. Certain subtype families of C. hominis carried the heavier symptom pattern.
openalex-w2166915172:
G. Aad and colleagues in the ATLAS Collaboration published this study in Physical Review Letters in 2013. They measured long-range correlations between particle pairs in proton-lead collisions at the Large Hadron Collider. A ridge pattern, pairs linked across a wide angular span, had appeared in busy proton collisions, raising questions about its cause.

ATLAS used data from a short 2012 proton-lead run, scanning pairs across a broad span of directions. The team found associated long-range correlations on both the near side and the away side of the collision. Seeing the pattern in this larger system sharpens the puzzle. Proposed causes include multi-parton interactions, dense gluon states, and collective expansion of the produced matter.
openalex-w2344991172:
Ricardo Huamán published this review in Economía in 2009, assessing the book The Economics of Microfinance by Beatriz Armendáriz and Jonathan Morduch. Microfinance, small loans and services for poor producers shut out of formal banking, had become a policy priority. Yet officials, aid workers, and academics largely talked past each other, the reviewer notes.

The book, he explains, aims to bridge those camps using economic analysis. Its ten chapters run from conceptual foundations through group lending, its reach and limits, to efficiency and management. Early chapters rethink banking through market failure and lopsided information, asking why credit markets deserve intervention at all. Huamán presents the volume as a shared reference for practitioners and scholars alike.
openalex-w2534848372:
Geoff M. Gurr, Anne C. Johnson, and Gavin James Ash, with colleagues, reviewed coconut lethal yellowing diseases in Frontiers in Plant Science in 2016. These diseases are caused by phytoplasmas, tiny bacteria-like organisms that live inside plants and insects. They kill palms of huge economic and social value. Outbreaks have destroyed millions of coconut and other palms in several regions.

The review gathers research on detection, insect carriers, and control methods for these diseases. It covers better rapid tests, genome sequencing, and how pathogen, insect, and palm interact. A disease called Bogia coconut syndrome reached Oceania for the first time, in Papua New Guinea. Another outbreak in Mozambique threatens over three million people's livelihoods. The authors also update the naming of the phytoplasmas involved, which changes often. Their survey aims to support faster, better-grounded management of palm diseases.
openalex-w2547269372:
Hazem Mohamed Kalaji, Gert Schansker, and Marián Brestič lead a very large author team on this review in Photosynthesis Research. Published online in 2016, it continues an earlier question-and-answer paper on chlorophyll fluorescence. That faint glow from green leaves lets scientists study photosynthesis without harming the plant. The sequel takes up further topics the first paper left aside.

In question-and-answer form, the authors explain how to read fluorescence signals correctly. Topics include correcting standard values for light from photosystem I, and probing the donor side of photosystem II. They cover energy partitioning, delayed fluorescence, and the meaning of low-temperature emission bands. Practical worries appear too, like sampling tree canopies and using fluorescence in breeding studies. The review serves as a reference for anyone measuring photosynthesis through leaf fluorescence.
openalex-w2553241472:
Michelle M. Haby, Evelina Chapman, and Rachel Clark, with colleagues, wrote this 2016 rapid review in Health Research Policy and Systems. It asks how rapid reviews of research evidence should be done. Health policymakers often need evidence fast, and slow systematic reviews miss decision deadlines. Rapid reviews promise timely answers, but their methods vary wildly.

The team searched eleven databases and two websites for studies of rapid review methods. Five systematic reviews and one randomized trial qualified for inclusion. None of the reviews was strong enough to support firm conclusions, they warn. The field has no agreed definition of a rapid review and no standard method. Many shortcuts are used to save time, with unclear effects on quality. The authors present their findings cautiously, as a map of what is known and unknown.
openalex-w2911976672:
Alberto Paniz-Mondolfi, Adriana Tami, María Eugenia Grillet, and colleagues wrote this 2019 perspective piece in Emerging Infectious Diseases. They describe how Venezuela's economic collapse and failing health system brought back diseases that vaccines once held in check. Measles, diphtheria, and malaria are spreading again inside the country.

The authors link the return of these diseases to deep poverty, drug shortages, broken disease tracking, and weakened vaccine programs. They also note that mass migration out of Venezuela risks carrying infections into Colombia, Ecuador, and Brazil. They call for urgent action inside Venezuela and at its borders, and they offer clear steps for responding to the crisis.
openalex-w4289638372:
Heidi Kreibich, Anne Van Loon, Kai Schröter, and colleagues examined how places cope with floods and droughts worse than any seen before. Their study appeared in Nature in 2022. Global vulnerability to such events has fallen over past decades as risk management improved. Yet impacts stay severe, and climate change is projected to make extremes more frequent and stronger.

The team compared pairs of events, an earlier disaster and a later, harsher one, in the same region. Managing the unprecedented second event usually proved hard. In two success stories, though, damage fell despite the greater hazard. Better governance and heavy investment in joined-up management explained the difference. The lesson is hopeful but rare, which is why the authors call it alarming.
openalex-w4410198872:
Hitoshi Iida and Hirotaka Watada review pancreatic beta-cell dysfunction and diabetes. Their review appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2025. Diabetes is defined by high blood sugar. It arises when insulin action is absent or too weak.

Beta cells in the pancreas make insulin and release it as blood sugar rises. When these cells fail, the body cannot keep glucose in range. The authors note that beta-cell dysfunction sits at the core of many forms of diabetes. Damage then spreads to eyes, kidneys, nerves, and blood vessels. With hundreds of millions affected worldwide, protecting beta cells is central to preventing complications and easing the disease's burden.
openalex-w4412377772:
Hideyuki Miyahara, Hyu Yoneki, Tsuyoshi Mizohata, and Vwani Roychowdhury apply a clustering algorithm to the Vicsek model of flocking. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2025. The model treats agents that align with nearby neighbours. It famously shows a sharp change into collective motion.

Simulations visibly form clusters of agents. Yet describing those cluster phases precisely has been hard. The authors use DBSCAN, a standard density-based clustering method, on simulation data. That gives an objective way to detect and classify the clusters. A firm cluster measure helps compare flocking phases across conditions. The approach can transfer to real swarms, from bacterial colonies to animal herds.
openalex-w7128094572:
Hisaya Akiba explains how the immune system recognises a vast range of antigens. His review appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2026. The system must attack countless pathogens while sparing the body's own tissues. Two molecule families make that discrimination possible.

MHC proteins sit on cell surfaces and display short protein fragments. In humans they are called HLA molecules. Class I molecules show fragments from inside the cell to killer T cells. T-cell receptors then read those displayed fragments. Their diversity lets T cells match almost any invader. Akiba reviews how diversity in both families arises. The principles underlie vaccines, transplants, and modern immunotherapy.
openalex-w7204260272:
Maria Cryslanne Santana Freitas led a Portuguese-language study, published in Brazil in 2026, on defending the rights of women who suffered obstetric violence. The term covers physical, verbal, and psychological abuse during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period, which the authors treat as a violation of fundamental rights. Drawing on literature, court cases, and testimony from affected women, the study examines the social, psychological, and legal effects of that defense.

Defending these rights, the authors find, raises awareness, improves legal protection, and helps reduce cases of obstetric violence. Schooling and community support strengthen women's ability to claim their rights. The study frames obstetric violence as a human rights problem and offers guidance for health professionals, public managers, and society.
openalex-w7204627872:
Rebeca Araujo Pimentel and Carlos Magno de Marce Rodrigues Barros released a Portuguese-language review in Brazil in 2026 on caffeine and Parkinson's disease. Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors that sit in brain regions controlling movement, including the basal ganglia. As Parkinson's grows more common, authors hunt for modifiable risk factors and neuroprotective strategies, and caffeine is a leading candidate. The review, run from late 2025 into early 2026, gathered medical and experimental studies.

A consistent inverse association appeared between caffeine consumption and Parkinson's risk, often stronger at higher intake, mainly in cohort work, and experiments suggest antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and mitochondria-related effects. But randomized trials are mixed and do not firmly prove slower progression or better long-term motor results. Long medical studies are still needed, the authors conclude.
openalex-w7206150172:
Ana Sara Gomes de Souza and Yuri Anderson Pereira Jurubeba take up a hard question in Brazilian criminal law: can evidence gathered illegally ever be used when it helps the accused? Brazil's constitution generally bars such evidence, and the criminal procedure code repeats the ban. Their 2026 article weighs that rule against the right to a full defense, the presumption of innocence, and the idea of proportionality.

Reading legal scholarship and Supreme Federal Court rulings, the authors push back on broad readings of the case law. The court, they argue, has not given a general license for defense use of illegal evidence; it decides case by case. They would allow it only in rare cases, when the proof is directly needed, cannot be replaced, is genuine, and can be challenged in court, and never to widen the charges.
openalex-w7207663672:
Thamilly Silva Lopes leads a team asking whether children can learn to save lives. Their 2026 integrative review gathers studies from the last five years on teaching first aid and basic life support, including clearing a blocked airway, to school-age children. Searching a Latin American health database, the team applied set criteria and kept nine studies for close reading.

Teaching programs worked: children gained knowledge, built practical skills, and grew more confident about acting in an emergency. The studies also linked training to changed behavior and fewer accidents. Two gaps stand out, though: first aid is still rarely built into school curricula in a systematic way, and few education professionals are trained to teach it. The authors present childhood first-aid education as a health strategy with lasting effects.
openalex-w7208821772:
Renan Costa Valle Scarano, in a lone study, tracks how low mood turned into a named ill. The line runs from old views of black bile to the big low-mood name in the DSM books of our day. His past-and-crit read sets the DSM's takes side by side, age by age. He asks what the name's spread means. That spread, he holds, is bound with the turn of plain woe into an ill for drugs and care.

Low mood, the study closes, is not a firm kind, but a fought-for one. Scarano notes that work must still split two things that rise as one: the craft's growth in spot the ill, and a true growth in the mind's pain. He also marks what flows when one name sits at the core of the mind trade: it shapes care, marts, and how folk read their hearts.
openalex-w7213403572:
Constantino Ossi Chicote and Simão André Camajinga Muxinda argue for urgent use of digital technology in secondary maths classes. Their 2026 article is a qualitative review of national and international research. Maths teaching, they note, has long relied on transmission methods and has high failure rates.

When teachers are well trained and lessons are planned with care, technology can raise motivation and autonomy. It can also help pupils grasp abstract ideas that are hard to show on a board. Barriers include digital exclusion, weak infrastructure, and too little ongoing teacher training. The authors call for public policies that widen access and build teachers' classroom technology skills.
openalex-w7213664672:
Igor Câmara and Luana Priscila Wünsch argue that academic research develops the teacher-researcher who fights school violence. Their 2026 article uses a narrative literature review joined to dialectical method. It is a qualitative study that claims no absolute truths, aiming instead to prompt further research.

Research is inseparable from teaching work, the authors contend. A teacher who researches gains didactic and scientific autonomy. That autonomy becomes a tool against violence, which appears at every level of schooling. Constant practice and rethinking of research drive the teacher's intellectual growth. Support from Amazonian universities and research funders is acknowledged, placing the argument in a regional effort to train researchers.
openalex-w7213938572:
Maurício Pinto de Oliveira, as named in the sample, leads a study of maps as instruments of power. Their 2026 qualitative, bibliographic article uses Portuguese-language books and papers from university journal portals and Google Scholar. It pairs the history of cartography with the rise of tactile maps.

States have long used maps to fix territory and show political and economic control, the authors argue. Maps also shape how people picture space itself. Tactile maps mark a turn toward inclusion for people with visual disability. The same tool that once served domination can now serve access, they conclude. That double role anchors a critical, inclusive reading of cartography.
openalex-w7213987372:
Ana Vitória Damasceno Amorim leads a team on autism and basic schooling in Brazil. Their 2026 library article analyses ten papers from 2013 to 2026 found in Google Scholar and SciELO. Inclusive teaching practice, school resources, and teacher challenges are the three concerns.
