Effective strategies include curriculum adaptation, flexible methods, playful activities, and visual and technological resources. Universal design for learning grounds several approaches. Barriers include too little continuing training, scarce resources, and missing specialist support. Real inclusion depends on joining practice, training, and institutional backing, the authors conclude. Collaborative work among school, family, and multiprofessional teams completes that condition. Teachers are left neither alone nor blamed in this account.
openalex-w7214010372:
Bruna Mabilly Dias leads a literature review on biomarkers for drug-related jaw bone death. That grave complication is tied mainly to bone-protecting drugs such as bisphosphonates and denosumab, and to some anti-vessel agents. Exposed jaw bone, without prior jaw radiotherapy, defines the condition.

Diagnosis still rests on drug history, clinical examination, and imaging, the review notes. Candidate markers cover bone turnover, bone formation, inflammation, vessel growth, proteins, genes, and microRNAs. Results across studies are mixed, they find. No single marker yet predicts or confirms the disease reliably on its own. Biomarkers remain complementary tools while the search for a dependable test continues.
openalex-w7214617272:
Thays Gomes Ferreira, Sophia Bertoldi Vasconcelos, and Elias José Oliveira built a computer prototype, described in 2026, to support nursing assessment and diagnosis in Brazil. The tool rests on the theory of basic human needs, a framework that organizes nursing care around what patients fundamentally require. It was developed with invented data only, without patients or outside users.

Inside, the prototype organizes dozens of clinical findings into blocks, links them through association rules to a starter catalog of nursing diagnoses, and presents diagnostic suggestions. The nurse stays in charge, confirming, adjusting, or rejecting each suggestion. Internal review checked the content's organization and the rules' coherence. The authors are clear about limits: the tool is an initial base that still needs content validation, usability testing, and a security audit before any real care use.
openalex-w7215090872:
Nataniele da Silva Ricardo and Edilson Nobuyoshi Kaneshima reported, in a 2026 study, the building of a clinical protocol for an emergency care unit in a small town in southern Brazil. Working in four stages, they assessed the service's situation, drafted the protocol, had it validated by a panel of specialist judges, and trained the whole care team to put it to use.

The first stage exposed overcrowding, high demand, an absence of clinical protocols, and too little training. The finished protocol scored strongly on content validity and internal consistency, and team training raised team knowledge a lot. Uniform conduct and an orderly care flow are the gains they promise, the authors conclude, while future studies must still measure the protocol's effect on real care measures. The work shows how a small service can make triage and treatment decisions formal instead of making them up shift by shift.
openalex-w7220918972:
Melkiades Palmeira Ferreira and four co-authors reviewed studies from 2018 to 2025 on harmful oral habits and anterior open bite. That condition leaves a gap between the front teeth when the mouth closes. Their 2026 article asks how these habits shape the problem in children with mixed dentition, and when early functional treatment helps.

Across thirteen selected studies, thumb sucking, pacifier use, mouth breathing, and related habits were tied to open bite, with effects growing by duration, frequency, and intensity. Treatment during mixed dentition can still guide growing jaws and teeth. The authors close by urging care planned child by child, based on cause and clinical picture, rather than one fixed routine.
owen-debatable-land-1872:
Robert Dale Owen walks the edge twixt worlds once more in The Debatable Land, his book of 1872. His first book on the theme had made his name in 1860. Here he goes past tales to claims: what the dead are, how they speak, and what their words mean for how we live and what we hold dear.

Fresh cases and long thought fill the tome. Owen writes as a man of state, not a cult chief. His calm won fans who shunned wild tracts. The book was the most cited work of its kind from his land.
plos-pbio-0000072:
David F. Savage, Pascal F. Egea, Yaneth Robles-Colmenares, and their group solved a protein structure for PLOS Biology in 2003. Their subject is aquaporin Z, a channel in the bacterium E. coli. Aquaporins are pores that let water cross cell membranes fast, while keeping other things out.

Using X-ray methods, the team mapped the channel down to 2.5 angstroms, fine enough to see its shape in detail. The map shows how the pore stays narrow and lined so water passes in single file but ions do not. That design lesson reaches beyond one bacterium. Human aquaporins play roles in the kidney, the eye, and the brain, and their faults cause real disease.
plos-pone-0000072:
Staffan Bensch, Henrik Andrén, Bengt Hansson, and a large team studied a small wolf population in PLOS ONE in 2006. Scandinavian wolves descend from very few founders, so they are highly inbred. Inbreeding usually harms health and breeding, yet this population kept growing.

The team found that wolves choosing mates less related to themselves, keeping offspring more heterozygous, did better. That sorting gives the population some relief from its narrow gene pool. For wildlife managers, the lesson is hopeful but narrow: behavior can soften inbreeding, not erase it. Bringing in new wolves from outside remains the surer cure, and the data help judge when that step is needed.
plos-pone-0000172:
Wook Kim, Tag-Keun Yoo, Sung-Joo Kim, and colleagues published this population genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It tests whether Y-chromosome haplogroups, the family lines traced through fathers, are linked to prostate cancer risk in Korean men. The title gives the result: they found a lack of association.

Negative findings like this one keep the record honest. Many gene-disease links reported in small studies fade when checked in a defined population. The authors genotyped Korean men and compared haplogroup rates between cases and controls. Their null result narrows the search for the genetic roots of prostate cancer in this population.
plos-pone-0000272:
M. Thomas P. Gilbert, Wendy Moore, Linea Melchior, and colleagues published this museum methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Museums hold huge numbers of dry-preserved beetles and other insects whose DNA could serve genetic research, but extracting it used to require damaging the specimen. The authors present a method to extract DNA from dry museum beetles without visible external damage.

Keeping the specimen intact preserves its value for future study. The authors show their method recovers usable DNA while leaving the beetle's outside unchanged. The technique opens museum drawers, some over a century old, to genetic analysis of species that may now be rare or extinct.
plos-pone-0000372:
Mireille Plamondon and colleagues reported on hepatitis C virus infection in Guinea-Bissau in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Hepatitis C spreads mainly through blood, and it often goes unnoticed for years while it harms the liver. The authors examined which strain of the virus circulates in this West African country and how it may be spreading.

The study centers on genotype 2 and raises the possibility that sexual spread plays a role, amplified by exposures involving blood. Knowing how a virus moves through a population shapes screening and prevention plans. The paper adds West African evidence to a disease map drawn mostly from other regions.
plos-pone-0000472:
Bruno Lamontagne and Sherif Abou Elela studied how a cellular cutting enzyme chooses its targets, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme is eukaryotic RNase III, which cleaves RNA, the cell's message-carrying molecule. The team showed that short RNA guides direct its cleavage, pointing the enzyme to specific spots.

Guided cutting is the principle behind RNA interference, the gene-silencing system that became a major research tool and drug strategy. Showing that short guides steer this enzyme clarifies how cells use small RNAs to control bigger ones. That mechanism underlies both natural gene regulation and engineered attempts to switch off disease genes.
plos-pone-0000572:
Pier Paolo D'Avino and colleagues traced how a key division kinase reaches its post. That post matters at the final step of cell division. Their account appeared in PLOS ONE in 2007. Polo kinase must arrive at the spindle midzone, the bridge between separating chromosome sets, during cytokinesis. The team showed that recruitment of polo kinase there requires the Feo/Klp3A complex, a pair of motor and linker proteins.

Division fails in specific ways when a player misses its cue. Establishing that one complex recruits another orders the cast of cytokinesis into a chain of command. The work was done in fly cells, whose division machinery mirrors our own closely enough to guide human cell biology.
plos-pone-0000672:
Justin G. Boyles and Jonathan J. Storm linked picky eating to extinction risk in bats, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Earlier studies had tied bat extinction risk to two things: smaller geographic range raised it, and habitat specialization raised it too. The authors tested a related hypothesis about diet. Insect-eating bats vary from generalists eating many prey types to specialists eating few.

Their title states the relationship: dietary breadth tracks extinction risk, with narrow eaters in more danger. A specialist starves when its one food source fails, while a generalist can switch. The result gives conservation planners a simple trait to flag at-risk species before populations crash.
plos-pone-0000772:
Coy D. Heldermon, Anne K. Hennig, Kevin K. Ohlemiller and colleagues charted how a storage disease unfolds in mice, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Sanfilippo syndrome type B, also called MPS IIIB, is caused by deficiency of a lysosomal enzyme named Naglu. Children with the disease develop disturbances of sleep, activity, coordination, vision, hearing, and mental functioning, worsening over time.

A mouse model lets researchers watch that progression in sensory, motor, and behavioral deficits in order. Knowing the sequence and timing of decline is essential for testing therapies: a treatment must be given before the damage it hopes to prevent. This natural history in mice sets the benchmarks.
plos-pone-0000872:
Dov Dori and Mordechai Choder argued that clear conceptual models can lead to real findings in systems biology, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Biology now produces facts far faster than any one person can hold in mind. Many modeling tools, they note, struggle to show both structure and behavior at the same time.

To make their case, the authors work through the life cycle of messenger RNA, the copy of a gene that cells use to build proteins. They show how a careful model of that cycle can point to things worth testing in the lab. The article is part method paper, part plea for better shared language.
plos-pone-0000972:
Matthew Hartman, Kristopher Josephson, Chi-Wang Lin and colleagues widened the set of building blocks the ribosome can use, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Ribosomes build proteins from a fixed menu of amino acids. Feeding them unnatural ones could yield huge libraries of modified peptides, rich hunting grounds for new drugs.

The limit is how picky the translation system is about what it accepts. The team present an expanded set of amino acid analogs the ribosome will translate into peptides. Each accepted analog multiplies the shapes a library can take. The work is chemistry groundwork: broaden the menu first, then screen what the new peptides can do.
plos-pone-0001072:
Dan Cojoc, Francesco Difato, Enrico Ferrari and colleagues measured the force exerted by growing cell protrusions, in PLOS ONE in 2007. As neurons differentiate, thin spikes called filopodia and sheets called lamellipodia explore the surroundings. They search for the path the axon should take to its final target.

Their motion had been characterized, but the force they exert was barely known. Force is what lets a growth tip push, pull and test surfaces. The team measured that force and asked which cytoskeletal parts produce it. The cell's skeleton is its muscle and scaffolding in one. Numbers like these turn pictures of growth into mechanics.
plos-pone-0001172:
Finding the variable spots in a genome, called polymorphisms, is easy in humans but hard and costly in species where variation is scarce. Nathalie van Orsouw and colleagues present a method for that problem in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They call it CRoPS, for Complexity Reduction of Polymorphic Sequences.

The approach simplifies complex genomes before sequencing, so large-scale polymorphism discovery becomes practical even in low-variation species. Single nucleotide polymorphisms have revolutionized human medical research, and similar tools could open up breeding and conservation work in plants and animals. The paper describes the method and its intended use.
plos-pone-0001272:
Human bone marrow holds mesenchymal stem cells, which can renew themselves and turn into bone, cartilage, fat, and muscle cells. Atsushi Nagai and colleagues derived a stable human mesenchymal stem cell line from fetal marrow, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. A stable line gives researchers the same cells to work with across many experiments.

The authors report the multilineage potential of the line, testing which tissue types it can still produce. Stem cell lines can drift or lose potency over time, so demonstrating retained potential matters. Such lines are tools for studying development and for regenerative medicine research.
plos-pone-0001372:
Martina Buck and Mario Chojkier wrote a 2007 PLOS ONE study on liver scarring, called fibrosis. When the liver is hurt, star shaped cells wake up and lay down scar tissue. Too much scar tissue can wreck the organ over time. The pair asked which inside cell signals drive this scarring step by step.

The authors show that one signal chain is key for scars to grow. When a certain protein in the star cells is switched on, scarring moves ahead. Long term use of a liver drug also comes into the tests. The work names a clear target for drugs that might slow or stop liver scars.
plos-pone-0001472:
Jie Yang and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a hormone in pikas, small mammals of cold high lands. Pikas do not sleep through winter, so they must cope with harsh cold. Stress from the world can speed change in stress reply proteins. The team traced the hormone leptin across the pika family.

They found marks of strong natural choice on leptin in these cold land pikas. The changes fit a need to burn fuel and hold heat in thin air. Such cases show evolution at work on a known gene. They also hint at how mammals adapt when they settle in extreme homes.
plos-pone-0001572:
Edgar Turner and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on research gaps in oil palm farming. Palm oil groves are often blamed as a top threat to tropical wild life. They sit in some of the richest wild zones on Earth. The team searched the science base for oil palm papers since 1970 and sorted them by topic.

They found wild life checks form a thin share of that work. Most papers chase yield and pests, not species loss. That gap means policy rests on a weak proof base. The study urges a shift in funds toward field checks of real grove impacts.
plos-pone-0001672:
Maria I. Davidich and Stefan Bornholdt built a computer model of the fission yeast cell cycle in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Their model is a Boolean network. Each control protein is treated as simply on or off, and the rules come only from the known wiring of who acts on whom. No numbers were tuned to force the right answer.

When run, the model faithfully reproduced the known order of activity in the real cell cycle of Schizosaccharomyces pombe. The full text gives the network, the rules, and the simulated sequence step by step. That a stripped-down on-off model can replay the cycle suggests the order is built into the wiring itself. That is a useful lesson for modeling other cell circuits.
plos-pone-0001772:
M. Estee Torok and co-authors described HIV-linked tuberculous meningitis in Vietnamese adults in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Tuberculous meningitis, TB infection of the membranes around the brain, is among the deadliest forms of TB, and HIV makes it worse. The study followed patients forward from admission.

Fifty-eight patients were admitted to the study hospital. The team recorded clinical and microbe features, outcomes, and which starting factors predicted death. The full text gives the patient data and the risk factors. Such lists help doctors in busy hospitals spot the patients who need the closest care first.
plos-pone-0001872:
Eric Peters and colleagues asked a plain drug question in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Do genes that break down drugs shape how well a common drug for low mood works? The drug was citalopram, and the data came from the large STAR*D group of patients treated for depression. The genes in view code for the enzymes that clear the drug from the body.

Using a two-stage case and control design, the team split the group in two. They tested whether gene forms tracked with who got better, or who had side effects. As the title states, they found no such link. The null result still helps, since it tells doctors that these genes, at least, do not guide dose choice.
plos-pone-0001972:
Frederique Sauvat and co-authors tested frozen ovary grafts in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Better cancer care now saves more children, but treatment can cost them puberty and fertility. For girls too young for other options, freezing one ovary is the sole path. A few births had already followed grafts of such tissue in women.

The team froze immature mouse ovaries, grafted them back, and watched for puberty and fertility. As the title states, the grafts restored both, and the chemical marks that guide gene use in the young were not altered. That safety point matters for girls who bank tissue before treatment.
plos-pone-0002072:
Anan Yaghmur and co-authors filmed a fat film reshaping itself in real time, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Mixes of two membrane lipids can sit as stacked sheets, called the L alpha phase. Past work showed that adding calcium ions drives vesicles of these lipids toward cubic phases, at rest over long times.

The team joined rapid mixing with time-resolved X-ray scattering at a synchrotron, to catch the shift from sheets toward the H2 phase as calcium hits. Watching the change step by step shows how membranes fuse and bend, a basic step in cell life and in drug carrier design.
plos-pone-0002172:
Luc Djogbénou, Fabrice Chandre, Arnaud Berthomieu, and co-authors tracked a pesticide-resistance gene in West African mosquitoes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The malaria mosquito Anopheles gambiae comes in two molecular forms, called M and S, that are on their way to becoming separate species. Cross-breeding between forms matters because it can move useful traits, such as resistance, from one form to the other.

The team found signs that a resistance change in the ace-1 gene, and a doubling of that gene, had crossed between forms. Such gene flow can speed the spread of insecticide resistance, a serious threat to mosquito control programs that rely on treated nets and sprays.
plos-pone-0002272:
Jae-Hyung Lee, Gloria Culver, Susan Carpenter, and co-authors compared a regulatory RNA element in two lentiviruses, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Lentiviruses such as HIV-1 and equine infectious anemia virus carry an RNA element called the RRE. The viral protein Rev binds it, a step the virus needs to copy itself.

The team analyzed the EIAV version of the element and found a conserved RNA motif within it. That motif is required for tight binding of Rev in both viruses, despite their distance as relatives. A shared grip point across lentiviruses is useful basic knowledge for anyone designing drugs that block viral replication.
plos-pone-0002372:
Research by May and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Tobias May, Lee Eccleston, Sabrina Herrmann, and others. Its subject is bimodal and Hysteretic Expression in Mammalian Cells from a Synthetic Gene Circuit. In order to establish cells and organisms with predictable properties, synthetic biology makes use of controllable, synthetic genetic devices.

These devices are used to replace or to interfere with natural pathways. What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002472:
Poinsignon and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Anne Poinsignon, Sylvie Cornelie, Montserrat Mestres-Simon, and others. Its subject is novel Peptide Marker Corresponding to Salivary Protein gSG6 Potentially Identifies Exposure to Anopheles Bites. In order to improve malaria control, and under the aegis of WHO recommendations.

Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002572:
Led by Roh, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Meejeon Roh, Omar E. Franco, Simon W. Hayward, and others. Its subject is a Role for Polyploidy in the Tumorigenicity of Pim-1-Expressing Human Prostate and Mammary Epithelial Cells. Polyploidy is a prominent feature of many human cancers.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002672:
Work by Ying Yu and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was an integrated epigenetic and genetic analysis of DNA methyltransferase genes ( DNMT s) in tumor resistant and susceptible chicken lines. Authorship is credited in the record to Ying Yu and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Both epigenetic alterations and genetic variations play essential roles in tumorigenesis. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002772:
Work by Koichi Fujimoto and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008, dealing with network evolution of body plans. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Koichi Fujimoto, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. One of the major goals in evolutionary developmental biology is to understand the relationship between gene regulatory networks and the diverse morphologies and their. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002872:
Camilla H. Andreasen, Mette S. Mogensen, Knut Borch-Johnsen and colleagues tested two claimed obesity gene links in a 2008 PLOS ONE study of 18,014 Danes. Earlier genome-wide scans had tied common variants in the genes INSIG2 and PFKP to obesity. Later checks gave mixed answers, so the link was still in doubt.

The Danish data were used to try to confirm, or fail to confirm, those same links in one large group. The title reports non-replication, meaning the earlier links did not hold up here. The study is a useful caution on how gene findings need repeat testing before they can be trusted.
plos-pone-0002972:
R. Maithreye, Ram Sarkar, Veena Parnaik and co-authors modeled delay effects in self-repressing gene circuits in 2008. Every chain of reactions in a cell takes time, from gene expression to daily rhythms. That delay is generic, meaning it shows up in almost all intracellular processes.

In circuits where a gene represses itself, delay can briefly boost expression and create unevenness between cells. The PLOS ONE paper models that transient rise and heterogeneity mathematically. Systems biologists get a clearer sense of when timing alone, without any change in parts, alters cell behavior. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003072:
Carolina Perdigoto, Louis Gervais, Erin Overstreet and co-authors studied unequal protein placement in fly sensory cells in 2008. Unequal division of cell fate determinants is a conserved way to generate diversity in development. In Drosophila, each sensory organ precursor divides into an anterior pIIb and a posterior pIIa cell.

Overexpressing Partner of Numb induced asymmetric distribution of the kinase Skittles in those dividing cells, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, the detail shows how polarity proteins position the enzymes that mark daughter cell fate, a basic step in building sense organs. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003172:
Gayane P. Manukyan, Karine A. Ghazaryan, Zhanna A. Ktsoyan and colleagues study immune responses to gut microbes in familial Mediterranean fever in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. This autoinflammatory condition brings acute, self-limiting bouts of fever and serositis. It also brings chronic low-grade inflammation even in remission. The team studied what the condition does to levels of these antibodies in the body.

The title reports elevated systemic antibodies toward the normal commensal gut microbiota in this condition. Readers see the gut's usual microbes drawn into a disease passed through families. The finding raises questions about the gut barrier. It also asks how the immune system learns to leave these microbes alone, well past the fever attacks.
plos-pone-0003272:
Laura Savolainen, Liana Pusa, Hwa-Jung Kim and colleagues run a pilot tuberculosis test study in Finland in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In recent years, T cell based interferon gamma release assays had been developed for immunodiagnosis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. At present these assays cannot tell disease and latency apart. So the search went on for better antigens and test tools.

The pilot study tests diagnostic potential of the recombinant HBHA protein in a vaccinated group in Finland. Readers see a candidate marker tested where BCG vaccination is common. A test that separates active disease from latent infection would change TB care greatly.
plos-pone-0003372:
Stuart J. McDougall and co-authors tackled a lab measurement problem in this 2008 paper. They worked with isoflurane, a gas used to put patients and animals to sleep. The gas fades fast in open lab dishes, so the true dose is hard to know. The team paired dose checks with recordings from nerve connections.

Their method measured the real gas level in the dish at the same time as nerve signals. That pairing let them match each dose to its true effect on synapses. Honest dose data matters because sleep drugs are judged by dose and response curves. The approach gives other labs a cleaner way to test gases like this one.
plos-pone-0003472:
Kenneth C. Catania studied a Florida folk trade in this 2008 paper. Families near Apalachicola National Forest earn money gathering large earthworms for bait. They drive a wooden stake into the soil and vibrate it. The giant worms then crawl to the surface on their own.

Catania argued the trick mimics a digging mole, the worms' predator. Worms flee upward to escape what they take for a hunter. People have used the method for generations without knowing why it works. The paper ties folk practice to a neat piece of animal behavior.
plos-pone-0003572:
Christopher D. Wiley and co-authors studied gene imprinting in hybrid deer mice in this 2008 paper. Imprinting silences one parent's copy of certain genes. Crosses between two Peromyscus species disturb growth and development. One cross direction gave growth-retarded but healthy offspring.

In hybrids, imprinting was lost in tissue- and cluster-specific patterns. Which parent a copy came from mattered differently by tissue. The patchwork shows imprinting is regulated locally. No single genome-wide rule explains the losses. Deer mice are a common wild model for how genes and parents shape growth. The two species can still breed, which makes the contrast sharper.
plos-pone-0003672:
Michelle M. Riehle, Jiannong Xu, Brian P. Lazzaro, and colleagues published this malaria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Earlier mapping had found a stretch of the Anopheles gambiae mosquito genome that sways infection outcomes. The team hunted the genes inside that region using the rodent malaria parasite.

They identified APL1, a family of varied proteins built from leucine-rich repeats. APL1 proved required for protection driven by the Rel1 pathway against Plasmodium berghei. The finding names mosquito immune genes that help decide whether a bite can pass malaria on to a person.
plos-pone-0003772:
Cristina Mazzaccara, Giuseppe Labruna, Gennaro Cito, and colleagues published this reference study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The mouse is the most used animal model for human disease. Yet reference values for blood tests were scanty for the strains labs use most. The team set out to fill that gap.

They measured the main biochemical and blood cell parameters in three strains: C57BL/6J, 129SV/EV, and C3H/HeJ. Values are given by age, so normal change over a mouse's life is not mistaken for disease. The tables give researchers baselines for spotting real effects in experiments.
plos-pone-0003872:
Magdalini Polymenidou, Rita Moos, Mike Scott, and co-authors described a set of lab tools for prion research in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article centers on the prion protein and its harmful folded form. That folded form builds up in prion disease and drives damage to the brain. Studying it requires antibodies that bind to known spots on the protein.

The team built a set of monoclonal antibodies called the POM series. Each antibody binds a different spot, and the spots do not overlap. Together they cover the prion protein in a planned way. Other labs can use the set to detect the protein and probe how it changes.
plos-pone-0003972:
William E. Banks, Francesco d'Errico, A. Townsend Peterson, and co-authors modeled Neanderthal extinction in 2008. Debate has long split between climate change and competition as the cause. Modern humans spread as Neanderthals vanished from Europe. The authors brought a new method to the old question.

Their PLOS ONE article joins archaeological and dating data with climate models. The results support extinction by competitive exclusion by modern humans. In that view, two groups cannot long share one niche. The study weighs evidence toward rivalry rather than weather alone. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004072:
Robert Reiner, Natalie Krasnov-Yoeli, Yana Dehtiar, and co-authors studied a chromatin-bound enzyme complex in 2008. Human RNase P was first known for trimming transfer RNA. It is built from an RNA called H1 plus at least ten proteins. Newer findings tied it to transcription of small RNA genes.

Their PLOS ONE article examines RNase P attached to chromatin. That form is required for efficient transcription by RNA polymerase I. One complex thus serves both RNA processing and gene transcription. The dual role reshapes how this classic enzyme is understood. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004172:
Jung Boo and colleagues published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Presenilin is a protein involved in many cell events in health and disease. Earlier reports found that cells lacking presenilin grow too fast and resist the normal process of cell death.

The team asked how presenilin loss affects one specific death route: damage from reactive oxygen species, the harmful molecules called ROS. They report that phosphorylated beta-catenin, a signalling protein, builds up in the deficient cells and makes ROS-driven death stronger. The finding complicates the picture of presenilin loss as simply protective, and it matters for diseases where presenilin fails, including Alzheimer's.
plos-pone-0004272:
Emilie Sapin and colleagues published this sleep neuroanatomy study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Paradoxical sleep, also called REM sleep, brings a busy cortex, rapid eye movements, and limp muscles. Fifty years after its discovery, the neuronal network that generates it was still only partly identified.

The team had proposed that GABAergic neurons, cells using the inhibitory signal GABA, hold the key. Here they localise the brainstem GABAergic neurons that control paradoxical sleep. Pinpointing the switch for the dreaming state brings a half-century-old map closer to completion. The brainstem is the stalk that links the brain and the spinal cord.
plos-pone-0004372:
Ulf Meyer-Hoffert, Zhihong Wu, and Jens-Michael Schröder published this skin study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Kallikrein-related peptidases are serine proteases involved in desquamation, the shedding of skin. Their activity is tightly controlled by epidermal protease inhibitors such as LEKTI, and defects in the LEKTI gene cause severe skin disease.

The team report finding lympho-epithelial Kazal-type inhibitor 2 in human skin. They report that it is a specific inhibitor of kallikrein-related peptidase 5. Naming a dedicated brake for one skin protease refines the picture of how skin renews itself without digesting itself. Skin sheds its outer layer every day, so the brakes matter constantly.
plos-pone-0004472:
Marmoset monkeys keep group traditions going, but maybe just from personal habit, suggest Mario Pesendorfer, Tina Gunhold, Nicola Schiel, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. In humans, copying the group speeds the spread of behavior and keeps customs alive. Few field studies had tested whether social conformity, rather than habit, keeps animal traditions in place.

The team ran a field experiment with marmosets that had learned a way to get food. They then watched whether monkeys followed the group's method or their own first-learned one. The evidence pointed to individual habit, not social conformity, as the glue. That is a sharp distinction for animal culture research: a tradition can look social while resting on private routine alone.
plos-pone-0004572:
Thinner silicone films for lab-on-a-chip devices can be made with a gentler solvent, show John Koschwanez, Robert Carlson, and Deirdre Meldrum in PLOS ONE in 2009. The material is PDMS, a clear silicone rubber. Thin PDMS films are often used as flexible membranes in microfluidic devices, tiny plumbing systems for biology.

To spin a thin film, PDMS is diluted, usually with hexane. Hexane can swell the PDMS base underneath, spoiling the device. The authors test long spin times and tert-butyl alcohol as a solvent that dissolves uncured PDMS without that swelling. Methods notes like this rarely make headlines, but device makers rely on them: a better solvent means cleaner membranes and fewer ruined chips.
plos-pone-0004672:
Agata Kranjc and colleagues mixed theory and lab tests to study bestrophins for PLOS ONE in 2009. Bestrophins are a newer found family of channels that let chloride ions pass through cell walls. No clear shape was known for them at the time. Some members switch on when calcium rises inside the cell.

The team focused on a short, acid rich stretch near one end of the protein. They asked how calcium acts on that stretch to open or tune the channel. Clear rules for that control would help explain how these channels work in the eye and other tissues. The work gives later studies a testable model.
plos-pone-0004772:
Miguel Sanz and colleagues found a dual route for making Sindbis virus proteins in infected and uninfected cells, in PLOS ONE in 2009. When the virus infects hamster cells, host protein making shuts down hard. Yet making of viral structural proteins from a shorter viral message goes on for hours under the same conditions.

The team sought the mechanism that lets the viral message escape the shutdown. They found the message uses one route in infected cells and another in clean cells. Knowing the trick may reveal drug targets. It also clarifies how viruses hijack cell machinery. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are.
plos-pone-0004872:
Aneta Koseska, Alexey Zaikin, and Jürgen Kurths studied timing cellular decision making under noise via cell cell communication, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many cellular processes require decision steps acting reliably despite substantial noise. Multistable genetic switches underlying decisions are dominated by fluctuations that can induce spurious transitions. Yet coupled cells communicating with neighbors can time collective decisions robustly in theoretical models explored.

Communication averages out single cell noise effectively. Tissues decide more reliably than single cells. Principles apply to growth and synthetic biology. Noise becomes manageable through coupling. Further tests can show how widely the pattern holds beyond the cases studied here. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is.
plos-pone-0004972:
Pet dogs develop cancers much like human cancers. A new program set out to use that fact. Melissa Paoloni and colleagues launched it in PLOS ONE in 2009. The program is the Comparative Oncology Trials Consortium. It runs preclinical trials in dogs with natural tumors. The National Cancer Institute directs and sponsors the effort.

The consortium's first trial targeted tumor blood vessels. The drug aimed the signal TNF-alpha at the cancer vasculature. Testing in dogs promises more lifelike results than mouse models. It also helps the dogs themselves. The paper reports the launch of this infrastructure. It lays out how canine trials feed into human drug development.
plos-pone-0005072:
Fruit fly larvae must reach the right size before metamorphosis. What starts that clock was incompletely understood. Magdalena Walkiewicz and Michael Stern tested insulin signaling in PLOS ONE in 2009. Insulin pathways report growth and nutrition. Metamorphosis itself is triggered by the hormone ecdysone. The prothoracic gland makes that hormone.

Increasing insulin and growth factor signaling advanced the onset of metamorphosis. The growth signal doubles as a starting gun. Body-size sensing feeds directly into developmental timing. The work links nutrition to a major life transition. Similar logic may govern puberty timing in other animals. The fly offers a clean system for testing how size and timing talk to each other.
plos-pone-0005172:
Some cancer cells survive drug treatment by pumping the drugs back out. Two pump proteins, ABCC1 and ABCG2, play a large part in that multidrug resistance. Zheng and colleagues tested in PLOS ONE in 2009 whether the cancer drug vandetanib could block those pumps.

Vandetanib is taken by mouth and blocks several growth signal proteins in cancer cells. The study found it also stops the transport work of ABCC1 and ABCG2, as the title states. If pumps are jammed, standard drugs can stay inside cancer cells longer. The result points to a second use for a drug already in cancer care.
plos-pone-0005272:
In some couples, one partner has HIV and the other does not. A large trial asked whether treating herpes in the infected partner could cut HIV transmission. Lingappa and colleagues described the couples enrolled in that Partners Study in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Participants had both HIV-1 and HSV-2, the herpes virus, and took daily acyclovir or a placebo. Profiling the enrolled couples shows who the trial results will apply to. It is the groundwork paper for a phase III test of herpes suppression as an HIV prevention tool. How these pairs live, earn, and care for their health shapes the spread of both viruses. So a full profile of the pairs is key to reading the main trial with care.
plos-pone-0005372:
Written language follows statistical laws, of which Zipf's law about word frequency is the most famous. Serrano and colleagues modeled the broader statistical properties of written text in PLOS ONE in 2009, beyond that single law.

Universal regularities in text can reveal how brains process information and how societies organize shared knowledge. Their models aim to capture several such patterns at once. The work treats language as a complex system whose numbers can be explained, not just described. If text has deep laws, then search tools, code that sums up long works. And tests that spot fake text can all be built on those laws and work better than rules of thumb.
plos-pone-0005472:
Mari Nelis and colleagues mapped the genetic make-up of Europeans in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. They used a method that sums up many small gene differences at once. Their data covered more than three thousand people from across Europe, each checked at a huge number of DNA sites.

Clear patterns emerged, with people from the north-east of Europe standing out in useful ways. The map shows how closely groups are related and how genes vary with place. Such maps help medical studies avoid false links caused by mixing groups with different roots.
plos-pone-0005572:
Lo-Kong Chan and co-authors studied a tumour-blocking protein in liver cancer in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The protein DLC1 helps control cell shape and movement. It is often missing or reduced in liver cancer and in several other cancers.

The team found a new place on DLC1 where a partner protein, tensin2, binds. They showed that this binding is needed for DLC1 to suppress tumours. Knowing the exact contact point helps explain how the protein works and what goes wrong when it is lost in cancer. Liver cancer has few good treatments, so each firm detail of its blocking proteins draws real interest.
plos-pone-0005672:
Mookkan Prabakaran and colleagues combined lab-made antibodies to fight bird flu in mice, in work published in 2009. H5N1 flu can kill, and recent strains resist the standard antiviral drugs. A single antibody can protect, but the virus may change shape and slip past it.

The team paired chimeric monoclonal antibodies, which are built to home in on the virus. Together, the pair protected mice from a lethal dose of H5N1. The mix also blocked the rise of escape mutants that dodge one antibody alone. Paired antibodies may offer a stronger plan if H5N1 ever spreads widely in people.
plos-pone-0005772:
Mercedes Montero-Balaguer and co-authors showed in 2009 that zebrafish embryos need the full dose of a vessel glue protein to build sound blood vessels. VE-cadherin holds the cells of vessel walls together at their seams. Mice without it die early from failed vessel growth.

In fish, partial loss still allowed vessels to form, but their links and remodeling went wrong. That finer view shows the protein's job continues past first assembly. Stable connections need its full presence. The work helps explain vessel leaks and malformations, and why this glue is a focus in vascular medicine.
plos-pone-0005872:
Johan Holmkvist and co-authors tested in 2009 whether a diabetes-linked gene variant changes how the pancreas answers a glucose drink. Variants in KCNQ1, a potassium channel gene, had just been tied to type 2 diabetes risk. Whether they blunt insulin release was the obvious next question.

Carriers of the minor variant at one marker released less insulin after an oral glucose load. That functional clue links the statistical association to a real defect in insulin secretion. It helps explain how a channel best known from the heart and ear affects blood sugar. Such links guide which carriers might benefit from early checks.
plos-pone-0005972:
Reading one person's whole genome was a brand new feat in 2009. Maria Costantini and Giorgio Bernardi worked with the genome of Craig Venter, one of the first people to have his DNA fully read. Their PLOS ONE paper maps three kinds of small differences across his chromosomes: insertions, deletions and single-letter changes called SNPs.

A map of one man's variants shows how much any two genomes differ in fine detail. Such maps help in the hunt for genes behind disease and in reading how genomes are rearranged. The work stands as an early brick in personal genomics, the field that now reads a patient's own DNA to guide their care.
plos-pone-0006072:
A pig germ that crosses into people has been changing fast. Matthew Holden, Heidi Hauser, Mandy Sanders and colleagues read its genome history in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies Streptococcus suis, a zoonotic pathogen that infects pigs and can cause grave illness in people. Cases appear most often in Europe and North America, and a recent major outbreak struck China.

The genome shows rapid evolution of both virulence and drug resistance. Fast change in a germ that already kills is a warning worth heeding early. Tracking which genes move and which resistances spread helps health teams in farming regions judge the risk and shape controls before the next outbreak grows.
plos-pone-0006172:
Diamond-Blackfan anemia is a rare illness in which the body fails to make enough red blood cells. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Alvaro Martinez Barrio and colleagues re-read the gene region called RPS19, which is linked to the disease. The same region has also been tied to a shorter childhood form of low red cell counts.

Changes in the RPS19 code had already been found in about one in four patients with the main illness, but not in the childhood form. The team sequenced the region in detail to map its variants more fully. Careful maps like this help doctors test families and sort look-alike blood disorders. They also guide the search for other genes behind the disease.
plos-pone-0006272:
Giant tortoises survive only in the Galapagos, with two shell shapes across the islands. Ylenia Chiari and colleagues studied a newly discovered, endangered tortoise taxon in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Tortoise naming began with shell characters, then genetics clarified many boundaries.

Body measurements paralleled the genetic divisions in the new taxon, the title reports. Shape and DNA telling the same story strengthens the case for protecting the group separately. Endangered island animals need correct units for conservation law to work. The study adds both evidence types for this tortoise. Such care helps doctors give sound advice to the families of these rare birds.
plos-pone-0006372:
The smallest eukaryotes in seawater are hard to count by microscope, but their genes betray them. Linda Amaral-Zettler and colleagues present a method for protistan diversity using massively parallel sequencing in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They target the V9 hypervariable regions of small-subunit ribosomal RNA genes.

Similar sequencing of bacterial communities was already common using the V6 region. Extending the approach to protists opens the hidden diversity of single-celled eukaryotes. Environmental samples can now be censused far more completely. The method became a standard tool for ocean surveys.
plos-pone-0006472:
Jane Natividad, Xianxi Huang, Emma Slack, and colleagues studied gut microbes and gluten sensitivity in mice for PLOS ONE in 2009. In a leaky gut, antigens from normal gut bacteria can cross the intestinal barrier in excess. In a host with the wrong genetic makeup, that may distort immune responses to those antigens. The team explored how the host reacts to intestinal microbial antigens in gluten-sensitive mice.

Their work bears on celiac disease and other gut immune disorders. It asks how much the barrier, the microbes, and the genes each contribute. Mouse models let researchers vary one factor at a time. The results help frame how food, microbes, and immunity interact.
plos-pone-0006572:
Michiel Houben, Peter Nikkels, Grada van Bleek, and colleagues studied inflammation and labor onset in PLOS ONE in 2009. Different factors contribute to the onset of labor at term. In animal models, onset of labor is characterized by an inflammatory response. The role of intrauterine inflammation in human term labor was their question.

They ran a cross-sectional study of the association between intrauterine inflammation and spontaneous vaginal delivery at term. If inflammation accompanies normal labor, it may be part of the trigger rather than a problem. The distinction matters for managing both early and overdue labor. Human data here complement animal work.
plos-pone-0006672:
Juliet Addo, Liam Smeeth, and David A. Leon studied high blood pressure in Ghana for PLOS ONE in 2009. Their focus was damage to organs caused by hypertension. Detection, treatment, and control of the condition are often low in sub-Saharan Africa. That gap raises the risk that organs are harmed before anyone notices.

The researchers ran a cross-sectional study of urban civil servants aged twenty-five and older. More than a thousand workers from seven central government sites took part. They checked participants for signs of target organ damage. The results map how much silent harm hypertension causes in this group. They also show why earlier detection and steadier treatment are needed in the region.
plos-pone-0006772:
Seiichi Mori and colleagues used gene patterns to hunt for drugs matched to cancer types in PLOS ONE in 2009. Human cancers are complex and highly varied. Few treatments can match that complexity. The authors describe an approach built on genomic signatures. A signature is a pattern of gene activity marking a state.

Their method links signatures to drugs that fit specific phenotypes. A phenotype is the observable character of a tumor. Matching drugs to phenotypes expands discovery opportunities. It may find new uses for existing compounds. The approach offers a systematic shortcut through cancer's variety, pairing each tumor pattern with candidate treatments.
plos-pone-0006872:
Kazunori Namiki and colleagues exposed human prostate cells to a microbe over a long period in PLOS ONE in 2009. Infection and inflammation are suspected of starting some cancers. Prostate cancer is among them. Roughly a fifth of worldwide cancers are attributed to infection. Mycoplasma is a genus of tiny bacteria often found in people.

Persistent exposure to mycoplasma induced malignant transformation of the prostate cells. Transformed cells gained cancer-like behavior in the laboratory. That outcome supports a direct role for chronic infection in prostate cancer. It moves the suspicion beyond statistical association. The model offers a way to study each step from infection to malignancy.
plos-pone-0006972:
Richard van der Wath, Anne Wilson, Elisa Laurenti, and colleagues modelled stem cell behavior in PLOS ONE in 2009. Blood stem cells in bone marrow do two very different jobs. They supply all blood cells day by day for life. They also repair the system after heavy cell loss. How one pool does both was an open question.

The team built detailed models of label-retaining cell data. Cells were tagged with a marker called bromodeoxyuridine, then tracked over time. The models separated dormant stem cells from active ones. Their rates help explain how a quiet reserve can guard the blood system for decades.
plos-pone-0007072:
Jiangning Song, Hao Tan, Khalid Mahmood, and colleagues built a protein prediction tool in PLOS ONE in 2009. Residue depth measures how buried each building block of a protein is. It adds information beyond the usual surface area measure. Depth links to protein stability and to where working sites hide.

Their tool, Prodepth, predicts depth from the protein's sequence alone. It uses a learning method called support vector regression. Sequence-only prediction matters when no crystal structure exists. For most proteins that is the normal case, so fast estimates from sequence help guide experiments.
plos-pone-0007172:
Hyoung-gon Lee, Qun Chen, Julie A. Wolfram, and colleagues wrote a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on heart muscle disease. Their subject is the protein Myc, which rises in enlarged hearts. They ask what Myc actually does once heart cells start to grow too large and fail.

The team built a transgenic mouse model to switch Myc activity on in the heart. They track heart cells that re-enter the cell cycle, plus defects in mitochondria, the cell parts that make energy. Their work links those changes to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and heart failure.
plos-pone-0007272:
Sam Harris, Jonas T. Kaplan, Ashley Curiel, and colleagues scanned brains during belief judgments in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Religious faith is a major feature of human life. Yet little was known about how religious belief relates to ordinary belief inside the brain, or how believers judge factual claims.

The authors compare religious and nonreligious belief while people evaluate statements. They ask whether believers and nonbelievers differ in that evaluation. Their imaging work places faith alongside everyday truth judgments. Neuroscientists and psychologists can use the comparison to study belief as a brain process.
plos-pone-0007372:
Jing Wen, Hua Zhang, Ge Li, and colleagues studied a polarity protein in mouse ovaries in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. PAR proteins mainly appear in the cytoplasm and control cell polarity. The authors show one of them, PAR6, behaves differently in egg cells that form primordial follicles, the resting egg reserves of the ovary.

PAR6 was localized in the nuclei of those selected oocytes. Most germ cells die, and only some are chosen to form follicles. The authors propose PAR6 as a potential marker for the selected cells. Such a marker helps study ovarian reserve formation.
plos-pone-0007472:
Shiming Zhang and Glenn Gerhard published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on artemisinin, the malaria drug drawn from the sweet wormwood plant. Artemisinin and its relatives also kill cancer cells selectively. Heme, the iron-carrying molecule known from blood, had been tied to the drug's antimalarial power. The source and exact role of that heme stayed controversial.

The authors show that heme mediates the drug's ability to kill cells. Because of that, heme becomes a general target for slowing cell proliferation. The same mechanism may explain both the antimalarial and the anticancer effects. A single iron-based switch thus links two very different uses of one drug. The result gives drug developers a clearer handle on how artemisinin works.
plos-pone-0007572:
Lin Wang and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the repair cells the bone marrow keeps in reserve. Endothelial progenitor cells can leave the marrow and help rebuild blood vessels. They hold promise for tissue regeneration. How they are summoned and controlled in the body had been unclear. The team focused on Notch signaling, acting through a transcription factor called RBP-J, in mice.

RBP-J proved to modulate the progenitor cells' release and function. It works by dynamically adjusting CXCR4, a receptor that guides where the cells travel. Turning that receptor up or down changes how the cells mobilize. A understood summoning signal is something medicine can imitate. Boosting repair cell release on demand could aid healing after heart attacks and wounds. The study names the chain of control behind it.
plos-pone-0007672:
Nichola Fletcher and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It asks how female fish choose mates. In the species they studied, a female breeds only once in her life. Her choice of male therefore shapes her whole chance of success.

The team found that females use smell to pick males with more mating experience. Those seasoned males are the ones most likely to give good care to the young. For readers, the work shows how a scent can carry news about a male's past. Females read that news before they commit.
plos-pone-0007772:
Hamid Haghighi and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It identifies a T cell target in an H5 bird flu virus, in chickens. H5N1 viruses have caused severe illness and death in people. Wild birds carry the virus, but chickens may pass it to humans.

The target sits on the virus's hemagglutinin protein. Unusually, the same epitope serves two T cell functions, making it dual-specific. A shared target like this could help design poultry vaccines. Protecting chickens better would cut the virus at a key bridge to people. The finding supports flu control that starts on the farm.
plos-pone-0007872:
Marcy Beildeck and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It shows how vitamin D helps control a cancer-linked gene. The vitamin D receptor pathway helps prevent several cancers. One of its routes crosses the Wnt pathway, which can drive tumors when overactive.

When the receptor binds vitamin D, it inhibits the Wnt chain at a factor called TCF-4. The authors mapped control of TCF-4 expression in the mouse mammary gland. They also used colorectal cancer cell lines. The results tighten the case that vitamin D signaling restrains a core cancer pathway.
plos-pone-0007972:
Steven Smith and colleagues audited a blood test used in tuberculosis research for PLOS ONE in 2009. The test, ELISpot, counts immune cells that react to TB germs. Labs run it in many small variants, and results from one lab often clash with another's.

The team varied the recipe step by step to find what sways the result most. A few factors stood out as the main sources of the clash. Naming them gives labs a shared recipe to follow, so studies in different places can be fairly compared, a basic need for vaccine trials.
plos-pone-0008072:
Suki Lee and colleagues compared how human immune cells answer two flu viruses in PLOS ONE in 2009. Seasonal H1N1 flu sickens many but kills few. Avian H5N1 flu kills a large share of those it infects, often by driving the immune system into a storm.

Macrophages, the immune cells first on the scene, answered the two viruses in sharply unlike ways across whole gene networks. The bird flu sparked a far fiercer and wider alarm. Mapping that gap shows where a drug might calm the storm without leaving the body defenseless.
plos-pone-0008172:
Nilesh Dharajiya and colleagues found a counter-attack inside allergic lung inflammation in mice for PLOS ONE in 2009. Allergic asthma is classed as a Th2 disease, after the helper cells that drive it. Yet the inflammation fades on its own, which suggests a brake is built in.

Allergen challenge also woke a Th1 response, the rival program, including a family of GTPase proteins driven by interferon gamma. Those proteins form part of the brake. Knowing the brake's parts may let doctors strengthen it, easing asthma without shutting down defense wholesale.
plos-pone-0008272:
Darragh Duffy and colleagues tested tuberculosis vaccine memory in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Tuberculosis kills and sickens people worldwide at high rates. A new vaccine to replace BCG is a long-standing goal. Several tuberculosis antigens have been made into subunit vaccines for trials. The team studied CD4 T cells specific for a fused antigen, Ag85B-TB10.4.

Immunological memory moved with those cells in their experiments. Persisting antigen enhanced the protection the cells gave. That finding matters for how subunit vaccines should be dosed. Lasting antigen may keep protective memory stronger for longer.
plos-pone-0008372:
Cesira de Chiara and colleagues studied a disease protein's partnerships in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Ataxin-1 belongs to the polyglutamine-expanded protein family. Its expansion causes spinocerebellar ataxia type 1, a degenerative movement disorder. Disease requires the expansion, entry into the nucleus, and phosphorylation at one site, S776. The team combined bioinformatics with experiments to map its interactions.

Phosphorylation of S776 and binding of 14-3-3 proteins modulate ataxin-1's links to splicing factors. Splicing factors assemble the cell's RNA messages. Altered interactions could explain how the disease harms neurons. That points to targets for intervention.
plos-pone-0008472:
Ana Helena Pereira and co-authors test a gene in mouse hearts in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. A family of factors called MEF2 promotes heart enlargement and failure. One member is MEF2C. Its own role in disease was not clear. Heart enlargement, or hypertrophy, can be triggered by extra load on the heart. The team silence MEF2C in mice and then add that load.

Silencing MEF2C lessens the enlargement that load would cause. The effect runs through a growth path called mTOR and S6K. That path controls protein making in cells. The work names MEF2C as a driver worth targeting in heart disease.
plos-pone-0008572:
Karin Elfving and co-authors study ticks on migrating birds in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Migratory birds are known long-distance vectors for many microorganisms. They carry ticks across continents as they travel. The team investigate whether rickettsial agents spread this way in Europe. Rickettsia cause spotted fever diseases in humans. They gathered ticks from over thirteen thousand migratory passerine birds in Sweden. They characterize tick infestation and test the ticks.

They find spotted fever Rickettsia agents in ticks carried by the birds. Birds thus disseminate these pathogens across Europe. Surveillance of migrating birds could warn of disease spread. The study links bird migration routes to human health risk.
plos-pone-0008672:
Frans Walther and co-authors study a lung surfactant protein in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Surfactant protein B, or SP-B, plays functional roles in lung surfactant. Surfactant keeps air sacs open and eases breathing. SP-B belongs to the saposin protein superfamily and has seventy-nine residues. Its N- and C-terminal domains were predicted to fold as charged helices. The team test analogs, synthetic versions, of SP-B. They focus on the N-terminal insertion sequence.

They find that sequence has critical structural and functional roles. Without it, analogs fail to mimic natural surfactant activity. Synthetic surfactants for premature infants depend on such analogs. The result guides design of better artificial surfactants.
plos-pone-0008772:
W. Hamish Wallace and Thomas Kelsey charted the egg supply of the human ovary across life. Their modeling study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Girls are born with all the resting follicles they will ever have. That reserve drains steadily with age. The drain ends at menopause, around age fifty. A precise curve from conception to menopause had not been drawn.

The authors fitted data from many ovaries into one model. Their curve shows the reserve peaking before birth, then falling. The shape changes pace at key ages. Doctors can use the curve to judge fertility and the effects of treatments like chemotherapy.
plos-pone-0008872:
Pilar Gonzalez-Cabo, Sheila Ros, and Francesc Palau rescued cells missing a key mitochondrial protein by supplying a vitamin-derived compound. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Friedreich ataxia destroys nerve and heart cells through lost frataxin. Frataxin works inside mitochondria, the cell's power plants. It interacts with parts of the energy transport chain. Flavin adenine dinucleotide, built from vitamin B2, carries electrons in that chain.

Supplying the flavin compound restored the defective cells' phenotype. Energy handling improved toward normal levels. A cheap, vitamin-based rescue invites further testing in animal models. The rare disease field welcomes any lead this concrete.
plos-pone-0008972:
Yi-Hung Carol Tan and co-authors checked how often a braking gene is faulty in lung cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Non-small cell lung cancer is a mixed group with many gene faults. The gene CBL helps tag worn-out growth signals for disposal. Two known cancer genes, MET and EGFR, send growth signals in these tumours.

The team catalogued changes in CBL across lung cancer samples. They compared those changes with the state of MET and EGFR in the same tumours. CBL turned out to be altered quite often, not a rare side event. Faulty disposal of growth signals may team up with the signals themselves to drive cancer.
plos-pone-0009072:
Yanlan Yu and co-authors rebuilt a rabbit antibody so it could treat human tumours in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rabbit antibodies bind targets with prized precision and strength. Those traits suit lab tests, but rabbit proteins were unused as human medicines. The target was VEGF, a signal tumours use to grow blood vessels.

Humanising the antibody kept its grip while making it body-friendly. In mice carrying human tumours, it blocked new vessel growth. Tumour growth slowed as its blood supply was choked. The study opens rabbit antibodies as a source of future cancer drugs.
plos-pone-0009172:
Eric Tang and Cun-Yu Wang placed a relay protein inside the cell's virus alarm chain, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When viruses invade a cell, sensors spot the foreign RNA inside it. Two sensors, RIG-I and MDA-5, each watch for different kinds of viral RNA. Both send their signal through a hub protein called MAVS to raise interferon defences.

The team showed that TRAF5 works downstream of MAVS in this chain. Without that relay in place, the antiviral response lost much of its strength. Each link in the chain is a possible lever for future drugs. Mapping the wiring explains how cells raise the alarm so fast.
plos-pone-0009272:
Hao Zhang and co-authors published this immunology computing study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Predicting which peptide pieces bind MHC class II molecules matters for vaccine design. Data-driven predictors need large binding datasets for each MHC type. Structure-based methods promise to skip that need by modeling the physical contact directly.

The authors tested how far such from-scratch predictions can be trusted. They found real limitations in the structure-based approach for class II molecules. Knowing where a method fails is as useful as knowing where it works. Their analysis tells immunologists when predictions need lab data behind them and when they stand alone.
plos-pone-0009372:
Hung-Teh Kao and co-authors published this exploratory study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Autism involves unusually high rates of genome damage, like rearranged chromosomes and new copy-number changes. Cancer, too, is a disease of rearranged genomes. That resemblance raised a simple question for the authors.

They compared rates of cancer and autism across populations in an ecological analysis. A correlation between the two could hint at shared genetic roots. The authors present the work as exploratory, a first look rather than a verdict. Even a tentative link would guide deeper studies of the genome instability behind both conditions.
plos-pone-0009472:
Christofer Juhlin and co-authors looked at gene silencing in parathyroid tumors in PLOS ONE in 2010. These growths most often lie behind overactive parathyroid glands. Their genetic causes are only partly known. Genes can also be switched off by chemical tags, without any change to the DNA code. The team checked two tumor suppressor genes, APC and RASSF1A, for such tags.

Both genes were often switched off by heavy tagging in these tumors. That pattern suggests silencing helps the tumors grow. It adds a layer beyond DNA mutations to the story of this disease. Drugs that remove such tags are already used in some cancers, so the finding may point to care options.
plos-pone-0009572:
Katharina Galmbacher and colleagues used bacteria against breast tumors in mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. In a common mouse model of breast cancer, macrophages fill the tumors. Instead of fighting the cancer, these immune cells help it grow. The team used Shigella bacteria, which can kill macrophages. They gave the bacteria to tumor bearing mice and watched the tumors.

As the tumor's macrophages were depleted, the tumors shrank. That result shows how much the cancer leaned on its immune helpers. Using a pathogen as a weapon is a bold approach, and it worked here. The study opens a new line of attack on cancers that hide behind immune cells.
plos-pone-0009672:
Andrew Parnell and co-authors improved a diet tracing method in PLOS ONE in 2010. Stable isotopes in an animal's tissues record what it has eaten. Scientists use those records to split a diet among its sources. Real data are messy, though, with wide variation between samples. Standard methods can strain or fail under such noise. The team set out a statistical approach that copes with heavy variation.

Their guidance helps ecologists draw reliable diets from messy field data. Bayesian methods in the approach handle uncertainty honestly rather than hiding it. Diets underpin food web science, so sturdier estimates matter widely. The paper is a practical repair kit for a common field method.
plos-pone-0009772:
Jenny Frånberg and co-authors published a brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study compares an enzyme called gamma-secretase in embryonic and adult rat brains. The enzyme cuts the protein that yields the amyloid blamed in Alzheimer's disease, and it cuts many other proteins as well.

Embryonic brain membranes made the most cut products of all five test proteins. In adult brain, only two of the five cuts could be detected, at like levels in young and old rats. The starter pieces for most proteins had also fallen sharply. The authors conclude that this cutting work fades as the brain matures.
plos-pone-0009872:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, slowly kills the nerve cells that move muscles. Laura Cox and colleagues searched for gene mutations behind a lower motor neuron form of the disease. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The gene is CHMP2B, which helps cells sort and discard worn-out proteins. Mutations in it turned up in patients whose disease mainly hits lower motor neurons. Those are the neurons running from the spinal cord to the muscles. Each new ALS gene sharpens diagnosis and hints at how neurons fail. ALS is also called Lou Gehrig's disease.
plos-pone-0009972:
Tree rings and other records let scientists rebuild Europe's past growing season weather. Joel Guiot and Christophe Corona extended that record across fourteen centuries. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fourteen hundred years reaches back before the medieval warm period.

Growing season temperatures shape harvests and ecosystems year by year. The authors compared the rebuilt record with climate forcings, the pushes that drive climate change. Forcings include volcanic eruptions, solar shifts, and greenhouse gases. Matching wiggles to causes shows what drove Europe's climate before thermometers. Winters and springs leave marks in wood and ice alike.
plos-pone-0010072:
Richard L Kravitz and co-authors audit peer review at a medical journal in a 2010 PLOS ONE article. Peer review, outside experts judging submitted papers, is used everywhere but seldom measured. The authors used records from the Journal of General Internal Medicine from two thousand and four to two thousand and eight.

Over two thousand manuscripts drew nearly six thousand reviews. Reviewers agreed on reject versus accept or revise barely above chance. Yet editors leaned hard on their calls: rejection was near certain when all reviewers agreed to reject, and rare when all agreed against it. The authors urge work to make reviews more reliable, and to warn editors of their limits.
plos-pone-0010172:
The authors were Mohammad Khan, Liesl De Sevilla, Virendra Mahesh, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study examined brain wiring for fertility hormones in rats. GnRH neurons release the hormone that drives reproduction. Glutamate excites those neurons, while GABA mostly calms them, and both signals reach them through synaptic contacts.

The team counted those contacts across the female cycle and with aging. On proestrus, the fertile peak, excitatory contacts rose and inhibitory ones fell. Aging changed that pattern, a shift that may help explain declining fertility in older females. The study used female rats at different ages.
plos-pone-0010272:
Ilona U Rafalska-Metcalf leads a 2010 PLOS ONE study watching single living cells switch a gene on. Gene activation was thought to follow an ordered series of steps, with packed DNA slowly opening first. The timing of those steps in single mammal cells had not been fully tracked.

Using a visible gene site, the team filmed helper proteins arriving with a strong activator. All arrived fast, together with the gene's RNA product, and the packed DNA opened quickly. A weaker activator switched on fewer cells. Blocking RNA making blunted the DNA opening even though helpers still arrived. Transcription itself, the authors conclude, drives large-scale opening.
plos-pone-0010372:
Shilpa Aggarwal, Birgit Bradel-Tretheway, Toru Takimoto and others measured copying errors by the flu virus enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2010. Influenza A copies its genome sloppily, and those errors fuel its fast change. Many assumed the copying enzyme itself was the error source. The team set out to test that enzyme's accuracy directly. Careful chemical tests can count how often it inserts a wrong building block.

Knowing the true error rate matters for predicting how flu evolves. It also affects ideas for drugs that push error rates past a breaking point. If the enzyme is more careful than assumed, other steps must explain the sloppiness. Either way, the measurement sharpens a basic fact about a major virus. Flu's talent for change starts with this enzyme.
plos-pone-0010472:
Clément Bellemer and colleagues used yeast genetics to show how ribosome building depends on RNA modification in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ribosomes are the cell's protein factories, assembled in many steps. One small ribosomal protein, Rps15p, was known to help export young ribosome parts from the nucleus. The team searched for gene partners that become lethal when combined with Rps15p faults. That synthetic lethal screen exposes hidden teamwork.

Partners clustered in the machinery that chemically modifies ribosomal RNA. Without those modifications, Rps15p's job in building ribosomes faltered. The finding ties two steps of factory building together. Yeast ribosomes mirror our own in most basics. Lessons here carry into human cell biology and diseases of ribosome production.
plos-pone-0010572:
Jinze Xu and colleagues published a rat feeding study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The team tested a nutrient blend built around Q-ter, a form of coenzyme Q10. They asked whether the mix could protect the energy-making parts of cells as animals age.

Rats given the blend performed better on tests of physical ability. Their mitochondria, the tiny structures that make energy inside cells, also worked more normally. Levels of harmful oxidative damage were lower as well. The results suggest that well-chosen antioxidant blends may help slow some cell changes tied to aging, though human tests would still be needed.
plos-pone-0010672:
Min Yang and colleagues studied toxin and antitoxin pairs inside the TB germ, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many bacteria carry such pairs: a toxin that halts growth and an antitoxin that keeps it in check. Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the germ behind tuberculosis, carries three pairs of the RelBE type.

The team tested how the three pairs interact and control each other. The pairs were not isolated; each could sway the others. Cross-control makes the system act like a web, not three lone switches. These pairs may help the germ wait out stress and drugs. Mapping them could point to new ways to wake or kill dormant cells.
plos-pone-0010772:
Gunjan Arora and colleagues characterized an unstudied kinase in the TB germ, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mycobacterium tuberculosis fine-tunes its behavior by tagging proteins with phosphate groups. The tagging enzymes, called kinases, form a family of eleven. One member, PknJ, had no known target when the study began.

The team purified PknJ and tested its chemistry in the lab. It tagged a metabolic enzyme, pyruvate kinase A, as a new substrate. That links a signal enzyme directly to the germ's energy economy. Each mapped link in this germ is a possible drug foothold, since human cells run their tagging with different parts.
plos-pone-0010872:
Matt Ramer, Mario Cruz Cabrera, Nima Alan and co-authors published this cell discovery paper in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neurons are famous for their outer shapes, axons and dendrites, while their inner compartments were thought to be fairly standard. Using layered staining and powerful microscopes, the team found something very different inside rat sympathetic neurons.

Scattered singly through a distinct subset of these neurons sits a huge inner body, several micrometers wide, most often shaped like a doughnut. The authors named it the loukoumasome, after a ring-shaped pastry. Near the nucleus it forms rings, while out in axons it stretches into twists or rods. It binds an antibody against a neuron-specific skeleton protein. Ramer and colleagues show that even well-studied nerve cells can hide large structures, raising fresh questions about what such a body does.
plos-pone-0010972:
Tao Huang, Xiao-He Shi, Ping Wang and co-authors published this protein prediction study in PLOS ONE in 2010. How long a protein lasts before the cell breaks it down, its metabolic stability, shapes many of its functions, but measuring stability in the lab is slow and costly. The authors built a computer method to predict it from a protein's other traits.

Their model combines sequence traits, physical and chemical traits, the cell part where the protein lives, its partners, and the protein groups it joins. A selection procedure kept only the most informative features while dropping redundant ones. Huang and team aim to give biologists a quick stability estimate for any protein. Such predictions can flag which proteins are worth expensive experiments and hint at how diseases arise from mistimed protein destruction.
plos-pone-0011072:
Susan Pereira Ribeiro, Daniela Santoro Rosa, Simone Gonçalves Fonseca and co-authors published this HIV vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most HIV vaccine designs chase killer CD8 responses, but evidence increasingly credits helper CD4 T cells with controlling the virus. The authors built a DNA vaccine from eighteen carefully chosen HIV fragments, conserved across strains and recognizable by many immune system variants.

The fragments came from an algorithm and from regions that infected patients frequently recognize. Tested in mice engineered to carry several common human immune presentation molecules, the vaccine induced broad T cell responses across those different genetic backgrounds. Ribeiro and colleagues show one vaccine can speak to many immune systems at once, a requirement for any HIV vaccine meant for a genetically diverse, worldwide population.
plos-pone-0011172:
Kawaguchi, Hirakawa, Miyauchi and colleagues compared two anesthetics in rats for PLOS ONE in 2010. Doctors use both propofol and isoflurane to keep patients asleep during surgery. The team used a scanning method on rat brain tissue and pattern analysis to tell the two drug states apart.

Brain extracts from rats under each drug carried distinct chemical signatures. Those signatures show the drugs do not act on the brain in identical ways.
