Clear differences may help guide drug choice for different patients and operations. The method also offers a way to study new anesthetics before they reach people.
plos-pone-0011272:
Liu, Li and Du exposed breast cancer cells to old industrial chemicals in PLOS ONE in 2010. PCBs were banned decades ago but persist in the environment and in body fat. The team asked whether these chemicals change how breast cancer cells behave, beyond any role in starting cancer.

Exposure made the cancer cells more able to spread, by switching on a protein that drives cell movement. That environmental link strengthens the case for strict PCB limits. It also warns that pollutants can worsen existing cancers, not only trigger new ones. Public health protection gains a mechanistic reason, not just statistical worry.
plos-pone-0011372:
Hannah Sheppard Brennand and colleagues tested in 2010 how warmer, more acidic seas affect young sea urchins. The species they studied lives on reefs where larvae must grow and build a small skeleton before settling. Ocean warming and acidification are arriving together, so the team raised larvae under combined future conditions rather than testing each stress alone.

Larvae under the combined stress grew and built their skeletons less well, with development thrown off course. The harm matters beyond one species, since urchins graze algae and help keep reefs in balance. Reef managers reading the study get a clear warning: the two stresses together can undercut the next generation of a key grazer. Protecting reefs will need to account for both heat and acidity at once.
plos-pone-0011472:
Mathieu Marella and co-authors reported in 2010 a gene therapy success in rats blinded by mitochondrial failure. Mitochondrial optic neuropathy starves the optic nerve of energy and destroys sight, and no good treatment existed. The team borrowed a gene from yeast, NDI1, which makes a spare energy enzyme that can bypass the broken step in the power chain.

Delivering the yeast gene to rats with the disease eased their vision loss, rescuing function that would otherwise be gone. A gene from a simple fungus patching a mammalian power failure is a bold proof of concept. It will not reach patients quickly, since safety and delivery in human eyes are hard problems. But it proves the bypass idea works in a living animal, giving gene therapy for mitochondrial blindness a real starting point.
plos-pone-0011572:
Annie Yang and co-authors mapped in 2010 where two guardians of the genome sit on DNA inside living cells. The proteins p63 and p73 are cousins of p53, the famous tumor suppressor, and they guide development and guard against cancer. Whether the cousins divide the genome between them or share it was unknown, so the team mapped their binding sites genome-wide.

The two proteins proved to co-occupy many target sites and to hold similar DNA-binding profiles in vivo. Siblings sharing duties can cover for one another, which may explain why losing one is sometimes survivable and sometimes catastrophic, depending on whether the other is present in that tissue. For cancer biology, shared binding means drug effects on one cousin must be read alongside the other. The map also gives development researchers the target lists they need to explain the cousins' roles in skin, limb, and nerve formation.
plos-pone-0011672:
Beatrix Steer and co-authors studied how a herpesvirus slips past immune defences to start infection, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Gammaherpesviruses carry a protein that mimics the host's own regulators of complement, a blood system that marks invaders for destruction. That mimic blocks complement attack at an early step.

The team found the viral protein does more than shield the virus. It also switches on a host growth signal, Akt, which helps infection get established. Turning a defence blocker into an ignition key shows viral cunning in detail and suggests new points where infection might be interrupted.
plos-pone-0011772:
Daniela Trisciuoglio and co-authors traced a survival chain in oxygen-starved melanoma cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIF-1 is a critical mediator of the response to low oxygen, and high levels of its alpha subunit are linked to tumour vessel growth, spread and treatment resistance. How the subunit stays stable in tumours needed clarifying.

The team showed the protein Bcl-2 regulates that stabilisation in hypoxic melanoma cells through the chaperone HSP90. The support chain helps tumours endure suffocating conditions deep inside a mass. Interrupting it could make melanoma more vulnerable to therapy.
plos-pone-0011872:
John Morgan and co-authors reported in 2010 that a major malaria mosquito in Uganda is resisting the main insecticides used against it. Anopheles funestus is a key malaria carrier across Africa, yet its resistance status is poorly known because the species is hard to raise from field catches. The team assessed a population from Tororo district.

Their tests found resistance to pyrethroids, the chemical class used on bed nets and in indoor spraying. Those tools are the backbone of malaria control, so resistance in a major carrier threatens real gains against the disease. A clear local record tells control programs where nets alone may no longer be enough.
plos-pone-0011972:
Jing Xie and co-workers examined in 2010 whether ABO blood group predicts who develops skin cancer. Earlier studies had linked blood group to the risk of several cancers, but no large prospective study had tested skin cancer. The team drew on two large United States cohorts followed over time.

Comparing incidence across blood groups in such numbers can detect modest risk differences that small studies miss. A blood group link would not change anyone's type, but it could refine who is watched most closely for skin changes. It would also hint that the same surface molecules distinguishing blood types play roles in tumor biology.
plos-pone-0012072:
Eva Göb and co-workers described in 2010 the protein bridges that shape the head of a mammalian sperm cell. LINC complexes span the nuclear envelope, linking the nucleus to the cell's skeleton through SUN and KASH proteins. They anchor and move nuclei in many cell types, and sperm head formation is one of the most extreme shaping jobs in the body.

The team found two novel LINC complexes taking different polarized positions during sperm head formation. Opposite placement suggests a division of labor in pulling the sperm head into its streamlined form. Faults in such machinery are a candidate cause for some male infertility cases with misshapen sperm.
plos-pone-0012172:
Matthew Schaller, Hannah Logue, Sumanta Mukherjee, and co-authors studied a signal that steers helper T cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Notch pathway, a cell-to-cell signaling system, is needed to hold a certain allergy-leaning T cell type in place. Its several signal proteins, though, do different jobs during T cell activation, and the team isolated the role of one called Delta-like 4.

They found this signal controls how much those T cells multiply, working through a growth-regulating protein inside the cell. Allergy and asthma ride on exactly this T cell type, so its growth controls are valuable knowledge. Fine-grained maps of immune signals help design treatments that tune one response without shutting down the whole system.
plos-pone-0012272:
Desirée Salazar, Nobuko Uchida, Frank Hamers, and co-authors transplanted human neural stem cells into injured mice in PLOS ONE in 2010. A crushed spinal cord costs movement through lost nerve cells, damaged wiring, and stripped insulation on surviving fibers. Well over a million Americans live with the chronic form of this injury, long past the window where most trials aim.

Their model treated animals in that early chronic phase, the stage most patients actually occupy, and the grafted cells matured and helped the mice move better. Success at a realistic stage matters more than success at an easy one. It strengthens the case for cell therapy trials aimed at the patients who need them most.
plos-pone-0012372:
Iain Buxton, Cherie Singer and Jennifer Tichenor studied stretch-sensing potassium channels in the human womb in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. During pregnancy the womb must stay relaxed while it stretches, then contract strongly in labor. The authors tested whether two channels, TREK-1 and TRAAK, which open when stretched, help keep the womb calm until the right time.

They measured the channels' genes and proteins in womb tissue from pregnant and laboring women. The channels were present and their levels changed with pregnancy stage, fitting a role in relaxation. If these channels help time labor, drugs that tune them might one day prevent early birth or help stalled labor, though that use is still far off.
plos-pone-0012472:
Marcus Hamilton and Briggs Buchanan used archaeology to test how modern humans spread across northeastern Eurasia and into the Americas, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The late Ice Age expansion set the deep ancestry of peoples across two continents. Knowing when and how fast groups moved constrains every story about the first Americans.

The authors found support for a three-stage expansion: growth in a homeland, spread across Siberia, then entry into the Americas. A staged model matches dated sites better than a single wave. It gives geneticists and archaeologists a shared timeline against which to test new finds and ancient DNA.
plos-pone-0012572:
Eduardo Fernández-Duque, Horacio de la Iglesia and Hans Erkert followed owl monkeys in the wild, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Owl monkeys are the only truly nocturnal monkeys, yet their night activity puzzled researchers, since dark, moonless nights seem safest from predators. The team recorded activity against moonlight in the monkeys' natural environment.

The monkeys needed moonlight to be active at night, moving and feeding far more on bright nights. Vision, not predator avoidance, sets their schedule. The finding ties a primate's daily rhythm to lunar cycles, with lessons for zoo care and for predicting how light pollution may disturb wild populations.
plos-pone-0012672:
Lewis, Glasgow, Glandon and co-authors studied how gene therapy viruses enter dopamine neurons in the brain. Gene therapy is a hopeful route for Parkinson's disease, since it can deliver help to exact cells. Their 2010 paper used adenoviral vectors, viruses rebuilt as delivery trucks, aimed at the neurons lost in the disease.

They found that entry depends on how much of a docking protein, called CAR, those neurons carry. That insight tells engineers how to retune the trucks for the right cells. Precise delivery is the main hurdle for brain gene therapy.
plos-pone-0012772:
Seimon, Kim, Blumenthal and co-authors found protein-folding stress inside the immune cells of tuberculosis granulomas. A granuloma is the wall of immune cells the body builds around TB bacteria it cannot kill. Their 2010 study examined macrophages, the eating cells inside those walls, in human and mouse tissue.

The cells showed strong activation of the unfolded protein response, the alarm for misfolded proteins. That stress may shape whether macrophages live, die, or let bacteria persist. It marks a new front in understanding why TB can linger for decades.  Both human tissue and mouse models showed the pattern.
plos-pone-0333572:
Shekoufeh Forouzan and colleagues dug soil profiles in Fars Province, southwest Iran, to trace how deep microplastics sink. Seventy six layers from twenty seven profiles across farm and wild land reached over a metre down. Nearly four hundred plastic pieces were recovered, mostly fibres, with chemical fingerprints taken for a subset.

Plastics appeared in almost every layer, including the deepest, with no tidy sorting by size or type with depth. Fibre dominance and few local sources point to air fallout as a major input, moved down by water flow, dry cracking, and soil animals. Soil plastic is not a surface film; it is a whole profile burden with long persistence.
plos-pone-0338072:
Hu and colleagues, in a 2026 study, test a fungus that kills insects as a greener weapon against two greenhouse pests, whiteflies and aphids. Chemical sprays breed resistance and leave residues, so growers want living alternatives. The team fished four fungal strains from the environment using mealworms as bait and identified them all as one Metarhizium species.

Young whiteflies and aphids were dosed with the spores at several strengths. Deaths rose with dose for both pests, and the four strains ranked differently against each pest, so no strain was best at everything. One strain, labeled SG-A, led against both insects at the highest dose by the eighth day. The authors present the screen as a first filter: these fungi can infect both pests under lab conditions. The strongest strains now merit greenhouse trials, where humidity and leaf cover will test them harder.
plos-pone-0340372:
Letting nursing students run a health careers event, instead of just attending one, might deepen their loyalty to the profession. Shilai Yang and colleagues present a trial plan, in PLOS One in 2026, testing that idea at a medical vocational college in China.

About one hundred ten students will be split into three groups that take turns leading the event, in a stepped pattern where every group eventually leads. Commitment to nursing is the main measure; confidence in study and burnout are also tracked. Because students cross from watching to leading, the design can separate the effect of leading from simply taking part. No results are reported yet.
plos-pone-0342572:
John Brand and his team asked if bleak news can push folk toward food and drink. Forty-two young adults came to the lab twice, a week apart. Each time they watched news clips for a quarter of an hour. Ads for food, drink, and plain goods ran in the gaps. Eye gear tracked where each gaze fell. Mood forms came at the start and the end.

Bleak news did sour mood. It also stretched the gaze on food and drink goods. The first glance shifted less, and that shift was not firm. The team thinks the sour mood may carry part of the gaze shift, though the proof fell just short. They link hard news to snack and drink urges.
plos-pone-0342672:
Salil Ghosh leads a team of six building mathematics for a two weapon attack on cervical cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The cancer is driven by persistent infection with high risk papillomavirus. Oncolytic viruses offer a strike: they infect and burst cancer cells while waking the immune system. The team's equations track infected surface cells, cancer cells, virus infected cancer cells, free virus, and the killer immune cells that answer it, alone and combined with chemotherapy.

They proved the model's good behavior and found the threshold conditions deciding whether the therapeutic virus persists or dies out. A global sensitivity analysis then ranked which biological and treatment parameters truly steer the outcome, separating levers from noise. Finally, optimal control methods sketched how the two therapies should be scheduled over time. The paper is a planning instrument: it tells trial designers which knobs deserve attention before a patient is treated.
plos-pone-0342872:
Amaha Haile Abebe and Rose Mmusi-Phetoe audited how fifty public health centers in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, refer women with risky deliveries to hospitals. They reviewed a year of registers. They also interviewed the midwives and managers involved. Their 2026 mixed-methods study scored each center against eight standards for a working referral system.

Only a quarter of centers met every standard. Ambulances were scarce. Formal agreements with hospitals were often missing. Hospitals rarely reported back on referred cases. Nearly a third of deliveries were referred onward. Rates ran far higher at centers lacking surgical capacity. Midwives described risk-averse referring, driven by fear of blame and by doubts about their own monitoring tools. The authors prescribe clearer accountability, feedback loops, and updated labor guidance.
plos-pone-0343472:
Arul Selvam P and Tamije Selvy P worked on making large language models understandable, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. Trust in AI depends on understanding it, yet big language models are famously inscrutable. The pair proposed hybrid explainable AI approaches that aim to bridge trust and performance when interpreting these models.

Their hybrid explanations try to keep a model's power while making its behavior legible to the people who rely on it. Legibility matters most where model outputs guide health, legal, or financial choices. Pure accuracy with no explanation struggles to win adoption in such fields. The paper contributes designs that other teams can test, adding to a fast-growing effort to open the black box without breaking what makes the models useful.
plos-pone-0343872:
Parisa Mobasheri, Ali Aranizadeh, and Behrooz Vahidi combined three jobs that battery managers usually handle separately: reading charge level, predicting remaining life, and judging reliability. Heat and driving patterns make all three harder for lithium-ion batteries in cars and solar storage. Their 2026 study tested two pouch cells across temperatures and standard driving cycles, building one linked framework from the measurements.

Charge estimates stayed within a small error band, and the aging model captured how heat speeds wear. A survival analysis also showed that two seemingly identical cells can age at wildly different rates, one lasting about five times longer than the other. By joining estimation, aging, and reliability in one pipeline, the work aims to give battery systems more honest forecasts under real conditions.
plos-pone-0344172:
Zeynab Falihzadeh and Laleh Roomiani studied a sugar-rich extract from a red seaweed, Gracilaria corticata, to see whether it can harm colon cancer cells while acting as an antioxidant. They first tuned the extraction, using sound waves to pull the compounds out, then described the extract's makeup, which proved to be mostly carbohydrate with some sulfate and a trace of protein.

In lab dishes the extract mopped up harmful free radicals more strongly as the dose rose. It also slowed colon cancer cells far more than normal cells, pushing the cancer cells into programmed death by raising internal stress signals. The work is early and dish-based only, but it marks the seaweed extract as a candidate worth testing further against this cancer.
plos-pone-0345072:
Yan Li and coauthors published a study in PLOS ONE asking whether a poem's emotional sound can reach listeners who do not understand its words. The first experiment measured joyful and sad Mandarin recitations: joy rides higher, louder, and faster, while sadness is lower, softer, slower, and less pure in tone. The second experiment played native Mandarin speakers and Japanese listeners with no Mandarin recordings where sound and meaning agreed, conflicted, or stayed neutral.

When sound matched sense, both groups judged the emotion most strongly. When they conflicted, the Japanese listeners, locked out of the words entirely, were steered powerfully by the sound alone. Native listeners combined both channels, yet strong prosody still weakened and sometimes overrode what the words said. Musical delivery, they conclude, is not decoration on poetry but a carrier of feeling in its own right, robust enough to cross a language barrier.
plos-pone-0345872:
Prakhar Agrawal and co-workers map spots on dengue virus proteins where a chemical tag can be added or removed. Cells use this tagging, called phosphorylation, to pass signals, and viruses can hijack it to grow inside human cells. Their 2026 paper uses computer analysis to find likely tag spots on the proteins of all four dengue types and the enzymes that place them.

Many of the tag spots are shared with related viruses, which hints they matter for survival. The spots also sit where dengue proteins meet human proteins, antibodies, and each other. That makes the map a starting point for drugs that block tagging and slow the virus. The authors offer the full list as a resource for other labs.
plos-pone-0346672:
Yasin Jafari Rahim Abad, Kiyana Saadati, and Fatemeh Ghaffari adapt a scale that measures nurses' skill at caring ethically for use in Iran. Nurses face hard moral choices daily, and Iranian practice is shaped by local culture and faith. Their 2026 study translates the twenty-two-item scale under world health guidance and tests it on close to seven hundred nurses in teaching hospitals.

The scale kept its four-part structure in the new setting and explained over half the differences between nurses. Checks confirmed the parts fit together soundly, scores were consistent, and men and women read the items the same way. Hospitals and nursing schools in Iran now have a trusted yardstick for a skill that shapes patient trust.
plos-pone-0347672:
Muhammad Saleem, Muhammad Hamid, and Saadia Malik built a diabetes system that does two jobs: predict who likely has the disease and then give personal lifestyle guidance. Most prediction tools stop at the diagnosis. Their system pairs a deep learning model that reads patterns in health data with a rule-based engine that turns the result into advice.

The prediction model was trained on a merged dataset cleaned with care to avoid leaking answers into training. It beat seven standard machine learning models and other deep learning designs under ten-fold cross-checking. For patients, the guidance half is the point: a risk score alone changes nothing, while tailored steps for food and activity might.
plos-pone-0347772:
Jonas Tögel and Christof Kuhbandner ask why some people kept wearing face masks after rules requiring them ended. Their 2026 study treats mask wearing during the COVID-19 pandemic as a case of outside rules becoming personal habits. They surveyed more than four hundred adults after mandates were lifted and asked about fear of the virus, mask beliefs, and reasons for wearing one.

Fear stood out as the strongest factor. People who feared the illness more were far more likely to keep wearing a mask by choice. That link held even for people who doubted masks worked or disliked their side effects. Fear also tied to taking the rule in as a personal value, though not to fully free, self-driven habit.
plos-pone-0347872:
Joung Ha Park and colleagues used South Korea's national health data to test whether catching COVID-19 raises the risk of later autoimmune disease. Reports had hinted that the virus can turn the immune system against the body. Their 2026 study compared thousands of patients' diagnosis patterns before and after infection in the pandemic's early phase, using each person as their own control.

New diagnoses rose after COVID-19 for several conditions, including Behçet's disease, ankylosing spondylitis, Crohn's disease, psoriasis, type one diabetes, and Graves' disease. The pattern held even for people whose COVID-19 was not severe. The authors advise doctors to watch for autoimmune symptoms in patients recovering from the infection.
plos-pone-0348072:
Shi Qiao and Panpan Xu published this 2026 study of police emergency dispatch across regions. Their system first grades how severe an emergency is and what each site needs, then plans vehicle routes through the transport network and solves the plan with an improved swarm search algorithm.

The improved solver iterated much faster than standard versions. In test dispatches, every demand point received most of what it needed, and some supplies, like vegetables and tents, reached full coverage. Qiao presents the model as a feasible way to move rescue materials quickly across jurisdictions.
plos-pone-0348272:
Hongbing Wang and colleagues built a reliability model for gears whose tooth tips have been shaved, a common tweak that softens the shock as teeth engage. They combined models of tooth contact and root bending with the standard theory that pits load stress against material strength, assuming both vary in bell-shaped fashion. From that they computed the chance a gear set survives its duty.

Tip relief did reduce meshing shock and raise overall reliability. But stretching the shaved length or height too far ate into strength, lowering reliability at the moments teeth enter and leave contact, and heavier loads dragged reliability down regardless. The authors advise designers to treat the shave dimensions and the working load as a matched set, tuned together rather than maximised separately.
plos-pone-0348372:
Martha Thomas and a large team set out a plan for testing whether a tailored activity programme can help frail people who live with several long-term conditions at once. Their programme, called PERSONAL-AGILITY, shapes a full day of movement, sitting, and sleep around each person, with help from carers and simple technology. The plan comes from Leicester hospitals in England.

Rather than chase a cure, the planned trial asks a smaller question first: can such a study even be run well? Fifty volunteers will be split between the programme and usual care for about six months, and the team will track recruitment, dropouts, and quality of life. Results will decide whether a larger trial is worth doing. No results are reported yet.
plos-pone-0348572:
Telemedicine powered by large medical models must keep patient data safe while answering fast. Zhenfeng Weng and colleagues designed a defense system that changes its tactics as attacks evolve, rather than relying on fixed rules, in this 2026 PLOS One engineering study.

A learning agent makes the security decisions. Supporting parts include a secret-sharing scheme guarding the model itself, training that anticipates attacks, privacy noise on the data, blockchain-style verification among servers, and a hardware chip speeding the work. The combined system targets leaks of model settings, weak privacy, and single points of failure. Tests on a real hardware platform checked whether speed survives the added armor.
plos-pone-0348672:
Anthroposophic medicine, a system blending mainstream care with spiritual ideas, is popular in Austria. Nikolas Reisecker and colleagues surveyed Austrian adults in this 2026 PLOS One study to learn who uses such care and who sees it as truly scientific.

About four hundred thirty people answered, and their replies were weighted to match recent voting patterns. Women and people over fifty used these therapies more often. Seeing the approach as scientific went with older age, higher income, and rural living. Stronger authoritarian attitudes and low tolerance for uncertainty also lined up with trust in it. The team hopes the patterns guide wider research on why people choose such care.
plos-pone-0348772:
Lawrence Barros and colleagues give the first detailed ultrasound account of ovarian cycles in the plains zebra, following four mares day by day. Breeding programs for zebras are hampered by basic unknowns, because wild equids are hard to handle and monitor. The team tracked follicles on the ovaries and changes in the womb lining through natural cycles and through hormone-induced cycles.

Natural cycles proved long, with roughly thirty-eight days between ovulations, and daily growth of the egg-bearing follicles was slow. Knowing the normal rhythm and size patterns lets veterinarians time breeding and assisted reproduction properly. The findings also offer a comparison point for rarer, endangered zebra species whose populations need more help.
plos-pone-0348872:
Chunxiang Guo and colleagues tested whether adding woven fiber mesh inside concrete floor slabs makes them stronger and less prone to cracking. They built five one-way slabs, some with carbon mesh and some with glass mesh at two different weights, then bent each one until it failed. Computer models of the same slabs were checked against the real tests.

Every mesh slab cracked later and carried more load than the plain slab, with many small fine cracks instead of a few wide ones. The heaviest carbon mesh performed best, more than doubling the load at first cracking. Carbon beat glass at equal weight, and the models matched the tests closely, giving engineers a checked tool for designing stronger slabs.
plos-pone-0348972:
Puwitch Charoenchue and colleagues tested a short, dye-free MRI scan for finding colorectal cancer that has spread to the liver. The standard scan uses contrast dye, which costs time and money and excludes some patients. Their abbreviated version uses three basic sequences only. Eighty-seven patients' scans were read independently by a senior radiologist and a trainee, with the full contrast scan as the referee.

Both readers performed strongly, catching more than nine in ten spreads while keeping false alarms low, and their overall accuracy was statistically indistinguishable. Agreement between the readers was substantial. The authors propose the short scan as a dependable option when dye is unsafe or impractical, noting that the trainee matched the expert, which bodes well for wider adoption.
plos-pone-0349072:
Kumakech and colleagues, in a 2026 survey, ask young women in northern Uganda living with HIV two linked questions. Do they want children, and do they use the family planning services offered inside their HIV clinics? Little was known about either in this semi-rural region, though both shape safer conception and prevention of HIV passing to babies.

About four hundred women attending HIV treatment clinics took part. Nearly nine in ten said they wanted children, a strikingly high share. Married women wanted children more than single women, as did women whose past pregnancies were planned. Yet among women who wanted children, only about three in ten had used the combined HIV and family planning services, far below the share among women without fertility desires. The authors say clinics must close that gap, so women who hope for children get contraception, safer conception advice, and support in one place.
plos-pone-0349172:
Md Rabiul Auwul used computational biology to find fingerprints of mastitis, the udder infection that drains dairy farms through lost milk and sick cows. The toll includes a hidden form with no visible symptoms. Comparing gene activity between healthy and infected tissue and mapping how the proteins interact. The analysis distilled three key genes shared across both obvious and silent disease, plus the pathways they travel in.

Machine learning checks supported the trio as diagnostic candidates, and the shared genes pointed to existing drugs that might be repurposed against the disease. The highlighted biology centres on cell growth control and tissue processes. Auwul frames the work as groundwork for precision veterinary medicine: tests that catch the silent form early, and treatments aimed at the infection's molecular machinery rather than its symptoms alone.
plos-pone-0349372:
Jianping Sun and colleagues built an optimization model for rushing emergency supplies by rail after disasters, when both demand and travel times are uncertain. Their framework treats demand as a fuzzy random quantity and times as ranges rather than fixed numbers, then searches for plans that balance response time against cost. A swarm algorithm variant solves the model, repairing impossible plans by nudging them toward workable ones.

In a case study the improved algorithm beat rival methods at finding the frontier of best trade-offs between speed and cost. Railway emergencies cannot wait for perfect information, so a planner that prices uncertainty honestly and still decides fast has direct operational value. The approach extends to other relief logistics where several kinds of uncertainty collide.
plos-pone-0349572:
Desalegn Shiferaw and co-authors analysed deaths of children under five in a southwest Ethiopian surveillance area from 2005 to 2019 in work published in 2026. Knowing what kills young children, and whether it is changing, guides where health money should go.

The surveillance system followed a defined population for fifteen years, with verbal autopsy interviews used to assign causes for the last seven. Trends in overall deaths and in cause shares were tracked over time. Long local records like these catch shifts that national snapshots miss, such as which infections are retreating and which causes now dominate.
plos-pone-0349672:
Takafumi Ohshima and co-authors checked whether keyhole spine surgery through a small scope can be done safely under local anesthesia alone, even in frail patients. Staying awake lets surgeons hear nerve feedback in real time, but the anesthetic dose must stay within safe limits tied to body weight. Their 2026 review covered one hundred eight patients who had single-level surgery this way at their center.

Every operation finished under local anesthesia with patients talking throughout, and no case of serious anesthetic poisoning, lasting nerve injury, or post-surgery delirium appeared. Frail patients had a stricter dose cap, and nearly all stayed inside it. Doses overall did not differ between frail and non-frail groups. The authors judge the approach feasible across frailty levels, while noting their backward-looking design calls for some caution.
plos-pone-0349772:
Predicting which children in intensive care will die helps teams act early, but most patients survive, so the rare deaths are hard for algorithms to learn. Wenqian Chen and colleagues tackled that imbalance with blood test data from more than eight thousand young patients, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Twenty-two first-day blood measures were used, with missing values filled by repeated estimation. Splitting the data into more balanced subgroups, and a stacked combination of models, both lifted accuracy above single models. Artificially boosting the rare cases during training helped every method. The authors say subgroup training is a practical trick for skewed medical data.
plos-pone-0349872:
Zhen Yang, Ming Liu, and Longyi Cai compared what visitors say about two famous rice terrace landscapes in China. The Hani Terraces in Yunnan and the Longji Terraces in Guangxi are both World Heritage sites, carved into hillsides over many generations. Their 2026 study drew on more than four thousand visitor reviews posted on a major Chinese travel platform.

Word counts and network maps of the reviews showed clear differences between the sites. Longji drew more reviews and more talk about leisure services, while Hani visitors wrote more about culture and heritage. Complaints at both places centered on transport and site management, with weather a bigger problem at Hani. The findings give local managers concrete clues for improving visits while protecting the terraces.
plos-pone-0349972:
Hammad and colleagues designed a scoreboard for fairness in local pharmacies in Pakistan in a 2026 study. Town and village pharmacies differ widely in staffing, stock, and service quality, yet no shared yardstick existed. Interviews with pharmacy staff first mapped the gaps, then experts refined a set of measures by group agreement.

The measures were built into a visual dashboard using common business software. Reviewers judged the content sound for tracking fairness across sites. A shared scoreboard lets health officials see which districts lack pharmacists or key medicines, instead of relying on scattered reports. Fairness data are a first step toward closing rural service gaps.
plos-pone-0350272:
Wen Sun, Sihan Yu, and Zhengye Jiang tackled a safety hazard of rooftop solar and local generators: islanding, where a disconnected patch of grid stays live and endangers repair crews. Standard detectors develop blind spots when many generators connect at once. Their 2026 study proposes converting voltage and current signals into time-frequency pictures, then training a convolutional neural network to tell islanding from normal connection.

Simulations built on an international smart-grid standard produced the training signals. On a held-out test set the detector scored near ninety-nine point nine percent accuracy, and repeated cross-checks missed only a small share of events. The authors say the method sharply shrinks the blind zone that plagues older hybrid detectors in complex multi-generator systems.
plos-pone-0350372:
Delphine Poquet and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies the ECAIL trial, which targeted socially disadvantaged families. The authors examine reach and engagement: how many intended families the trial actually got to, and how fully they took part.

The study is a mixed-methods implementation study, mixing numbers with interviews and observation. Its period covers two hard stretches, the COVID-19 pandemic and the cost-of-living crisis, which strained the same families the trial served. Trial designers working with low-income communities can learn how such crises change who joins research and who stays in it.
plos-pone-0350672:
Ahasanul Karim and colleagues graded the water of Bangladesh's Halda River seven different ways, because the river is irreplaceable: the country's only natural spawning ground for major carp. Samples from dry and wet seasons were scored by seven established water quality index systems, from Canadian to Malaysian to a new entrant, to cross-check whether the verdict depends on the ruler.

It did not. Scores landed between poor and very poor on every system, with basic measures like turbidity, ammonia, and oxygen demand repeatedly breaching national limits. The dry season scored worst, when low flow concentrates factory discharge. A carp nursery failing every grading scheme at once leaves little room for methodological excuses. The authors frame the multi-index agreement as the evidence base for enforcement and cleanup planning.
plos-pone-0350772:
Erfurt and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a trial of ear surgery for cholesteatoma, a damaging skin growth inside the ear that must be cut out. One standard operation keeps the ear canal wall, which preserves anatomy but may leave disease behind. Filling the hollowed bone afterward, called obliteration, may cut the return of disease, yet surgeons disagree and evidence is thin.

About one hundred eighty adults will be assigned at random to the wall-preserving operation with or without obliteration. Disease return will be checked by ear inspection and special MRI scans at one, three, and five years, with surgery to confirm when scans suspect trouble. Hearing, complications, quality of life, and costs are also tracked. The five-year follow-up is deliberate, since returns can be slow. As a protocol, the paper sets the test; the verdict on obliteration awaits the trial.
plos-pone-0350972:
Siyuan Wei and Liu Xia published an economics study in PLOS ONE in 2026. They looked at what a new rail link between China and Thailand means for Thai trade with Guangxi, one of China's southern provinces. Rail lines can redraw trade maps by cutting the cost and time of moving goods.

Wei and Xia measured how trade flows shifted as the railway came into use. Their findings show a land link pulling two economies closer in practice, not just on paper. For readers in trade and transport policy, the study offers a concrete case of how one line can reshape who sells what to whom across a border.
plos-pone-0351072:
Víctor Vera-Ponce and six colleagues published a 2026 umbrella review asking whether intravenous vitamin C helps adults with sepsis or septic shock. Many earlier reviews had reached mixed conclusions, so the team gathered and graded the reviews themselves, focusing on deaths within about a month of treatment.

Across thirty-one reviews, combining vitamin C with steroids and thiamine did not lower deaths, and small improvements in organ scores seemed to come from the steroid. Vitamin C alone showed a possible benefit under narrow conditions. It looked best when started within a day, at moderate doses, for a few days. Still, the evidence was weak and the reviews overlapped heavily. Clinicians are left with a maybe for solo use and a no for the popular cocktail.
plos-pone-0351172: Gao and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE trial on clearing mucus from the lungs of very ill patients. The patients had ARDS, a severe lung failure, and were on breathing machines with set air pressure. The trial compared open and closed suction methods for effects on lung volume and oxygen levels. It used random assignment. Ventilator care details like this shape daily practice in intensive care.
plos-pone-0351672:
Taofeng Wu and colleagues built and tested a new questionnaire for people who receive dialysis to clean their blood. Eating well during long dialysis sessions is hard, and beliefs shape whether patients follow diet advice. The team drafted questions from a behaviour theory, refined them with nineteen experts, and gave the draft to more than four hundred patients in Suzhou.

Final form holds twenty one items across three parts: attitude, social pressure, and felt control over eating choices. Scores held together well when checked again and split in halves. Expert review backed the content, and factor checks matched the three part design. Clinics now have a tested tool to learn why a patient struggles with diet during dialysis.
plos-pone-0351772:
Zhicong Chen and four colleagues read seventy years of China's flagship newspaper for its portrait of the world. Their 2026 study analyses the People's Daily from 1950 to 2019. Foreign scholars have long studied how others portray China. The reverse view was rarely measured systematically. Word embedding techniques tracked how ninety-four countries were represented over time. The team then asked what predicts a country's image in the paper.

Favourability rose and fell with turning points in Chinese foreign policy. Countries' wealth, industrialisation, and military strength all predicted warmer coverage. The weight of economic factors shifted significantly across the decades. In other words, the paper's world map is strategic, not decorative. It flexes as China's own global position changes. Computational reading of a party newspaper exposes the logic of state narrative power, a method other countries' official media could equally be judged by.
plos-pone-0351872:
Yiwen Kang and co-authors worked on reading what a person sees from brain waves on the scalp. Raw scalp signals mix many brain areas at once. The team first projected the signals back onto a map of brain regions. They then pulled several kinds of features from each region. A classifier was trained for each person. Last, they checked which features and regions mattered most across people.

One simple feature carried the most useful information. It tracks how jagged the signal is over time. Shape-based and link-based features added less. Small, anatomy-based decoders have real appeal for brain-computer tools. They run fast, and doctors can explain how they decide.
plos-pone-0351972:
Caleb McMurray and seven colleagues test whether a quick visual checklist can stand in for laboratory water testing. Their 2026 study works on four urban streams in the southeastern American Piedmont. The checklist, a federal stream visual assessment protocol, scores what an observer can see: banks, canopy, channel shape, and similar features. Ten metrics produce one snapshot grade. The team compared those grades against instruments measuring depth, flow, temperature, and seven chemical and bacterial indicators.

Looks predicted looks. The visual scores correlated strongly with the streams' measured physical characteristics. Chemistry was another story. Few significant links appeared between the scores and actual water quality. A pretty stream can still carry invisible pollution. A scruffy one can run clean. The warning to managers and citizen monitors is direct. Use the protocol for habitat snapshots if you like, but never let it testify about water quality it cannot see.
plos-pone-0352172:
Yanqi Wu and four colleagues listen to the brain shift gears mid-melody. Their 2026 study uses Mozart's famous serenade for strings as the stimulus. Volunteers listened while scalp sensors recorded their brain activity. Two ten-second transitions were chosen with opposite characters. One moved from busy, hard-to-guess music to calm, steady music. The other reversed the journey. Rhythm metrics and network measures tracked what changed as segments turned.

The brain, it seems, budgets its effort. In stable passages it runs lean, favouring efficient frontal and rear handling. At a transition, the network reconfigures itself. Global efficiency briefly drops, and the right prefrontal region is recruited. The costlier, less predictable shifts delayed the brain's response measurably. Music feels effortless to hear. These recordings show the hidden labour: a brain that coasts through the expected and spends real resources the moment the pattern breaks.
plos-pone-0352372:
Aditi Sarker, Chanchal Kumar Ghosh, and Prodipta Chowdhury compare nutrition in adults with Crohn's disease at a large hospital in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Crohn's inflames the gut and often leaves patients underfed, yet detailed data from South Asia are scarce. The team measured body size, arm and calf thickness, skin folds, diet scores, and blood levels in just over a hundred patients, half with active disease and half in remission.

Malnutrition proved far more common when disease was active, affecting most of that group, while only a small share of remission patients met the same standard. Active patients also carried lower iron, zinc, and blood protein levels. Sarker and colleagues argue that nutrition checks should be routine in Crohn's care, with closer watch during flares.
plos-pone-0352472:
Readers should know upfront: this entry is not a research paper. It is an Editorial Note from the PLOS One Editors, issued in 2026, about an earlier malaria study from Dielmo, Senegal. That study asked whether malaria could be eliminated after seven years of insecticide-treated bed nets. It had already drawn an Expression of Concern. This note updates that warning after an investigation into its reported ethical approval.

The fieldwork ran from 2007 to 2015, using blood samples, daily home fever surveillance, and mosquito catches. The article reported consent and approvals but no approval reference number. The authors' university explained that Senegal's national ethics committee did not exist when work began, so approvals came from the health ministry. PLOS examined the documents supplied. They did not settle the matter: coverage of the full period is unclear, and approved study titles do not clearly match. The Expression of Concern therefore stands.
plos-pone-0352672:
Yayun Xiang and four colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One computational study on why depression and vitiligo so often occur in the same patients. Vitiligo destroys skin pigment, and the two conditions together worsen outcomes, yet shared mechanisms are unclear. Using public gene expression datasets, the team hunted for genes changed in both diseases and mapped how those genes interact.

Fourteen hub genes emerged, mostly tied to immune activity and inflammation. Machine learning narrowed the field to three candidate markers, with the gene MAPK14 singled out for follow-up, and immune profiling suggested distinct immune patterns in each disease. The authors stress that these are hypotheses from data mining, useful for choosing targets that laboratory experiments should test next.
plos-pone-0352772:
Yong Liu and seven colleagues explain how a school fitness programme actually played out in practice. Their 2026 paper is a process evaluation of PRO-HIIT in China. The programme swapped the usual warm-up in PE lessons for six to eight minutes of high-intensity interval training. The aim was fitter, sharper adolescents. This study asks how faithfully schools delivered it, and why.

Delivery was strong overall. Pupil retention and the dose students received both ran high. Slightly fewer sessions happened than planned, averaging about twenty-six across twelve weeks. Heart rate monitors confirmed that sessions truly reached high intensity. Training logbooks and focus groups filled in the human side. Following national guidance for complex interventions, the evaluation separates delivery problems from a weak idea, so the main trial's results can be read fairly.
plos-pone-0352872:
Zachary Neal and Jennifer Watling Neal charted where childfree adults live across the United States and whether state settings matter. Childfree adults, who neither have nor want children, form a large and growing share of the population. Their 2026 study used survey data from more than twenty thousand respondents covering every state.

Prevalence varied widely, from about one in five adults in California to under one in ten in Louisiana. Yet the pattern showed no clustering into multi-state regions. Being childfree ran somewhat higher in populous, costly states, but personal traits like age and education predicted it far more strongly. The authors say policy aimed at this group should follow people, not places.
plos-pone-0352972:
Md Jawadul Haque and seven co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One study of a digital vaccine registry in Rajshahi City, Bangladesh. Digital registries promise better tracking of children's shots. But user experience in such settings is rarely recorded. More than three hundred caregivers took part in mid-2024. A small group of health workers took part too. All answered surveys about the new system.

Caregivers and providers both viewed the registry well. Most reported being satisfied or highly satisfied with the services it supported. Providers valued easier record handling and quick data access. They did flag weak internet links and device limits. Sign-ups happened mostly at vaccine centers, with some house-to-house outreach. The authors stress the study measured views, not impact. Wider, harder tests are needed before a national roll-out.
plos-pone-0353072:
Steven Camilleri and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of cold spray manufacturing. Cold spray builds copper parts by blasting metal powder at a surface so fast it sticks, without melting. The team sprayed copper at four gas pressures. They then examined the deposits' structure, hardness, and electrical flow. They also tested strength.

Higher pressure drove particles faster, so they bonded better. It also refined the inner crystal structure. Hardness fell as pressure rose. The authors credit the metal partly healing its own deformation. Electrical flow and ductility both improved. High-pressure samples stretched almost like solid copper before breaking. The study maps a best pressure window for parts that need both strength and good electrical flow.
plos-pone-0353172:
Correa Orellana and colleagues mapped microbes living on red-eared slider turtles in Austin, Texas, in a 2026 study. The turtles are widespread invaders, yet their body microbes were little studied. Samples came from shell, skin, mouth, and rear opening of more than forty turtles in four urban waters.

Body site shaped the microbe mix most strongly, with habitat adding a second effect. Outer surfaces carried sun-loving and hardy groups, while mouth and rear samples held gut-like groups with more local variation. Knowing a turtle's normal microbes gives wildlife vets a baseline for spotting illness and may hint at what invaders carry into new waters.
plos-pone-0353272:
Masato Takeda and seven co-authors report this 2026 PLOS One eye study. It concerns a blistering cornea disease that strikes eyes with a very shallow front chamber. The team reviewed ninety-six eyes treated with a partial cornea transplant between 2015 and 2025. One group had damage from a common inherited dystrophy. The other group had shallow chambers. Some of those eyes had past angle-closure attacks or laser care. Others had no such history.

The shallow-chamber eyes had far less depth at the front of the eye. This held before cataract surgery and after it. The pattern supports the idea that the shallow space itself wears down the cornea over time. Transplant survival past five years topped nine in ten in both groups. The authors say that with careful surgical care, these hard eyes do just as well.
plos-pone-0353372:
Nanchatsan Sakunpong and four colleagues interview older LGBTQ+ adults in Thailand about how they look after their own mental health, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Thirty participants aged fifty to sixty-eight described their lives in depth. Most research on this topic comes from Western countries, so the team listened for what Thai culture, Buddhism, and family duty bring to the picture.

Self-care turned out to be woven into caregiving roles, religious ethics, and online peer support. Participants coped with stigma quietly, found pride and joy deliberately, and treated physical health as an anchor for the mind. Formal services were often hard to reach. The authors call for policies that build on this homegrown resilience rather than ignoring it.
plos-pone-0353472:
A. Malini and Gerardine Immaculate Mary build a guard for the internal network of a modern car, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Cars coordinate brakes, steering, and engine through a message bus that was designed without security, leaving it open to injected or replayed messages. Their detector combines two neural network types: one reads the shape of each message, the other follows sequences over time in both directions.

A training trick called focal loss forces the model to concentrate on rare, hard-to-spot attacks instead of drowning in normal traffic. Tested on a public car-hacking dataset, the system scored high on accuracy, precision, and recall alike. Such onboard watchdogs will matter as cars grow more connected.
plos-pone-0353672:
Wang Zhang and co-authors build in 2026 a light segmentation network that traces yak body outlines in messy high pasture scenes for automated livestock checks. Outline accuracy matters for later shape analysis, yet light networks often lose borders on soft, moving animals and must run on small edge devices. Their design pairs a slim image backbone with modules that adapt view size cheaply and rebuild outlines across scales.

On a custom high altitude yak dataset the network reached high overlap accuracy while running well above real time speed. The balance of speed and border care makes it practical for smart pasture tools that cannot carry heavy models.
plos-pone-0353772:
Jifeng Jing and four colleagues engineer a gel scaffold that both summons bone-forming stem cells and tells them what to become, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Bone repair fails when too few stem cells arrive at the defect, or arrive and drift into the wrong tissue. Their gel carries a molecular lure that captures the body's own marrow stem cells, and its stiffness rises across a gradient to a firmness known to favour bone.

Together the two cues outperformed either alone: enzyme markers of bone formation more than doubled, bone genes switched on strongly, and mineral deposits grew. Because the gel recruits the patient's own cells, it avoids the cost and risk of transplanting cultured cells — an appealing template for bone grafts.
plos-pone-0353972:
Wei and Wang, in a 2026 study, trace how feeling connected to school helps Asian students grow. They use a large OECD survey of social and emotional skills covering more than twenty-three thousand students. Feeling that one belongs at school is easy to praise and hard to use. The team modeled the pathways with a statistical method that tests chains of influence.

Belonging predicted positive development, but mainly through two skills in sequence: first getting along and engaging with others, then regulating emotions. Both skills also helped directly. Two relationships fed belonging itself: how students felt about classmates, and how they felt their teachers related to them. Energy, stress resistance, and optimism stood out as key skills, and the gains showed up as good feelings at school and engagement with it. The authors advise schools to build belonging deliberately, as the first link in the chain.
plos-pone-0354172:
Wichian Chanthanet, a single author, published this 2026 study of public parks in Bangkok, Thailand, surveying twelve hundred users across thirty parks. Tropical heat and humidity shape park life differently from temperate cities. The study combined ecological, expectation, and attachment theories into one model of park use and satisfaction. It paid attention to income and gender fairness.

Quality upgrades mattered more for satisfaction than simply adding space. Shade, heat protection, and evening access proved essential, and benefits were unevenly shared across social groups. Chanthanet feeds the results into Bangkok's fifteen-minute park policy.
plos-pone-0354272:
Su and colleagues, in a 2026 laboratory study, probe a protein that senses low oxygen in cells from infantile hemangioma, the most common benign tumor of infancy. These growths swell early, then usually shrink. Low oxygen signals may help drive them, but one sensor, EPAS1, had been little studied in the tumor's vessel cells.

The team treated the cells with a drug that blocks the sensor and, separately, switched the gene off. The blocking drug slowed cell movement and invasion under low oxygen. Switching the gene off slowed cell growth and shifted the cell cycle, and the gene activity pattern pointed to programs that copy DNA, tied to two well-known growth drivers. A related oxygen-sensing gene was lower in tumor tissue, which hints the sensor may stay active even without low oxygen. The authors note a limit: cells came from one tumor, so findings are exploratory.
plos-pone-0354372:
Zenebe and colleagues, in a 2026 interview study, ask rural parents in the Alle district of southern Ethiopia what helps and what blocks them from vaccinating daughters against human papillomavirus. The vaccine prevents most cervical cancer, yet uptake depends on parents, and Ethiopian evidence was mostly numerical. The team held group discussions and deep interviews with dozens of parents of eligible girls.

Three forces pushed parents toward the vaccine: knowing it prevents cervical cancer, seeing vaccination as part of a parent's duty, and trusting the advice of health workers. Six forces pulled the other way: plain lack of awareness, no reliable source of information, distrust of the vaccine, misconceptions, fear of side effects, and cultural and religious worries. The authors recommend that government and partner groups work together on information and trust, since the strongest lever, health worker advice, is already in place.
plos-pone-0354472:
Zhang and colleagues, in a 2026 study, model how posts spread on social media, using data from Sina Weibo, a major Chinese platform. Likes, comments, and reposts do not just add up; each post competes with others on the same hot topic for limited attention. Forecasting that contest helps explain how online attention moves.

Their model blends two tools. A self-exciting process, which captures how each burst of activity sparks more, estimates how strongly posts excite or drain each other. Those estimates then feed a transformer, the deep learning design behind modern language tools, which makes the forecast. Reposts strongly amplified spread. Comments, by contrast, could slow a post by pulling attention away. Parallel posts on one topic tended to split attention rather than boost each other. The authors say the blend keeps the forecast sharp while staying readable, a help for anyone studying how platforms steer public attention.
plos-pone-0354672:
Yasin Demircan and five colleagues published this 2026 study of thirty-six sedentary adults aged thirty to forty-five. They completed an eight-week exercise program mixing endurance, strength, balance, and flexibility work three days a week. Fitness tests and blood measures were taken before and after, with no comparison group.

Weight and body mass index fell, while fitness, jumping, speed, agility, and balance all improved. Several blood cell counts rose too, though the authors warn those shifts may reflect fluid changes rather than true gains. With no control group, Demircan presents the changes as suggestive, not proven effects.
plos-pone-0354872:
Abdulaziz Ibrahem-Altwijri led a team of eight authors on this 2026 feasibility study of DizzyVR, an immersive virtual reality system for people living with balance disorders from inner ear problems. Standard balance exercises are repetitive and dull, so patients quit. Ten participants used the headset system weekly for eight sessions, with usability, satisfaction, sickness, and balance tests recorded.

Attendance and acceptance were high, the system scored well on usability, and early balance and walking measures looked promising. Ibrahem-Altwijri recommends larger trials with control groups before claiming the system improves recovery.
plos-pone-0354972:
Chucai Peng and three colleagues published this 2026 engineering study of soil pressure on slanted retaining supports built close to existing structures. Five laboratory model tests tilted the support from upright to twenty degrees, while cameras tracked soil failure and sensors read pressure. The team then built matching theory by dividing the soil into zones.

Measured and predicted pressures agreed well. Tilting the support further lowered the total soil push and generally moved its balance point upward, while rougher soil pushed it downward. Peng offers the formulas as design guidance for tight urban excavation work.
plos-pone-0355172:
Su Jin Lee and four colleagues published this 2026 hospital study of bone scans after falls. More than three hundred patients at a top-level trauma center had a bone scan after standard imaging such as X-rays, CT, or MRI. The team compared which broken bones each method found across six body regions.

The bone scan regularly surfaced injuries the earlier imaging had missed, and its injury counts tracked how severe the overall trauma was. Extra findings clustered in patients with the worst injuries. Lee suggests the scan earns its place as a second look when fall injuries may be hiding.
plos-pone-0355372:
Khoa Nguyen Dang Dinh and co-authors propose predicting a phone user's next cell tower before the network needs to hand over. In dense 5G small-cell areas, blocked or drained cells interrupt service and slow handovers. Their 2026 method trains a recurrent neural network on past movement to forecast both the user's path and data needs.

Forecasts feed a warning system that reroutes users away from flagged or unavailable cells in advance. In simulations of uniform and mixed networks, next-cell prediction reached accuracy above ninety-five percent at best. Service quality measures improved across both layouts. Dinh and colleagues argue prediction turns handover from a reaction into a planned move.
plos-pone-0355472:
Ru Zhang and co-authors extracted wolfberry sugars without heat and compared them with the conventional dried-fruit product. Wolfberry polysaccharides are prized bioactive ingredients, but fresh-fruit, cold-process versions were barely characterised. Their 2026 method adjusted pulp density and used strong alcohol to pull the sugars out without heating.

Total sugar and protein contents matched the conventional extract. The dried-fruit version held more bound phenolic compounds. The two differed in molecule size spread, sugar building blocks, shape, and thickness. The fresh extract protected liver cells better against oxidative damage in culture. It also provoked less nitric oxide release from immune cells. Zhang and colleagues say cold extraction yields a distinct, gentler ingredient.
plos-pone-0355672:
Lan Thi Vu and co-authors mapped how daidzin, a soy compound, might act against breast cancer using network pharmacology and molecular modelling. Soy isoflavones attract cancer interest, but this compound's routes were poorly defined. Their 2026 in silico study predicted the compound's protein targets and intersected them with breast cancer genes.

Ninety-seven shared targets emerged. Ten hub proteins sat at the network's centre, spanning inflammation, hormone signalling, and tissue-cutting enzymes. Docking placed daidzin snugly against all ten hubs, most strongly against a matrix-cutting enzyme tied to tumour spread. Its grip there beat the reference compound used for comparison. Vu and colleagues present the map as a prioritised hypothesis set for bench testing.
plos-pone-0355872:
Fatimah Albrekkan and co-authors measured the strain carried by family caregivers of people with severe, lasting mental illness in Saudi Arabia. Caregiving in this group is heavy, yet local studies of its mental cost were few. Their 2026 survey at a Riyadh medical city used standard scales for burden, low mood, worry, and quality of life.

Higher burden scores moved closely with higher depression and anxiety scores. Women caregivers and those living under the same roof as the patient carried significantly more burden. The severity of the patient's illness also mattered. Albrekkan and colleagues argue that services for severe mental illness should screen and support caregivers as patients in their own right.
plos-pone-0356072:
Geertje van Wijk and coauthors published a 2026 participatory study in PLOS ONE on neighborhood meeting places in four disadvantaged Dutch districts. The study asks what two often-overlooked groups need from them: teenage girls and women from non-Western migrant backgrounds. Meeting places can build social cohesion that protects health, but only if people feel welcome. Nearly one hundred participants contributed through walks, focus groups, photo methods, and interviews.

Both groups wanted clean, nearby, welcoming spaces with seating, greenery, safety, and design respecting gender and culture. Favorite activities ran from cooking and language learning to hanging out and sports, in familiar, culturally comfortable settings. The authors sort the findings into physical design, social use, organization, and perception, showing barriers in each layer, from poor lighting to unwelcoming programming. Their message to municipalities: ask intended users first, because small choices decide who a public space is really for.
plos-pone-0356172:
Arfeen Zahra and colleagues built a quantum computer emulator on an ordinary programmable chip. It lets students and engineers test quantum algorithms without quantum hardware. Their 2026 paper implements a universal two-qubit gate set. The set includes adjustable phase gates and the entangling CNOT gate. It runs on a mid-range FPGA board, exploiting the chip's parallelism and low energy draw.

They validated the emulator on a tour of famous circuits. The tour covered entangled Bell states, the Deutsch algorithm, and superdense coding. Grover's search and a quantum key distribution protocol were included. Every result was checked against IBM's noiseless simulator. Matching outputs across the suite certify the design. Emulators like this give quantum software developers a cheap, reliable workbench while true quantum machines remain scarce and fragile.
plos-pone-0356272:
Chengjun Wang and colleagues built a system that finds tiny surface flaws on steel wire ropes from three-dimensional scans. Wire ropes carry heavy loads, yet their defects are small, sparse, and hard to spot. Their 2026 paper first assembled a labelled point cloud dataset covering wear, protruding wires, and broken wires.

Their model mixes graph-based learning, which reads local shape, with a transformer that tracks long-range patterns. Extra modules sharpen edges, spatial layout, and feature blending across scales. On the new dataset the system scored well above eighty percent on a standard overlap measure. Wang and colleagues present the dataset and model as a base for finer, automated rope inspection.
plos-pone-0356472:
Barbara Metzler, Martin Fleischmann, and Daniel Arribas-Bel ask whether pictures from space can substitute for costly ground data when mapping inequality in England, in this 2026 study. They compared three ways of predicting two very different targets, air pollution and house prices, across a fine grid covering the country. One approach used census and land data, another used compact summaries extracted from satellite images by a foundation model, and a third mixed both.

Traditional data still won overall. Even so, image-only models predicted air pollution surprisingly well once rough regional context was added, suggesting the images carry real environmental signal. For house prices, much of the images' apparent power turned out to reflect broad location rather than visible detail. The authors conclude that satellite summaries are a promising low-cost complement, especially where conventional data are scarce or outdated.
plos-pone-0356772: Fu and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on the working lives of Chinese university faculty. The focus is a national drive called Double First-Class that pushes set universities toward top rank. The authors argue that the drive claims teachers' time in clashing ways, pulling them between research, teaching, and service. Their deconstruction speaks to debates about pressure and priorities in higher education.
plos-pone-0356872:
Mohamad Siarudin leads a team of eight measuring what smallholder forests store in Ciamis, West Java, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Indonesian families manage these woodlands three ways: single crop tree stands, mixed tree lots, and agrisilviculture that weaves trees with farm crops. Across one hundred fifty plots in three elevation bands, the team counted species and measured trunks to estimate the carbon held above ground, testing whether management or altitude matters more.

Mixed lots and agrisilviculture held richer species mixes, while tree crop stands were dominated by few species. Carbon stocks shifted with cropping pattern and with the stand's growth stage, but not with elevation. Mixed lots stored the most on average, tree crops the least among the patterns measured. For climate policy, the message is that how a family farms its forest outweighs where on the hillside it sits, so incentives should reward mixing over monoculture.
plos-pone-0357272:
Shoulin Gao and colleagues published a 2026 engineering paper in PLOS ONE on making emergency braking in commercial buses both safer and smoother. Conventional automatic braking switches between warning and braking stages abruptly, so deceleration jumps and passengers feel a hard jolt. The team redesigned the controller in layers: a smarter time-to-collision estimate on top, an optimizer choosing the ideal braking force with a comfort adjustment. A tracking controller below follows the chosen force faithfully.

They also built the software on the automotive AUTOSAR standard so the code generates cleanly for real vehicles. In hardware-in-the-loop rigs and real bus tests, the new strategy still met collision-avoidance demands while cutting the longitudinal jerk the older staged strategy produced. Passengers, in other words, get a firm stop without the whiplash feel. The approach is presented as ready groundwork for bus makers refining emergency braking.
plos-pone-0357372:
Jiaojiao Deng and colleagues compare three doses of a newer pain drug for women recovering from womb removal done through small cuts. Patients controlled their own pain relief through a vein pump for two days after surgery. The trial lost its planned comparison arm using a classic pain drug, because many patients refused a chance of getting the older option, so only the three dose groups finished.

Middle and higher doses eased pain during coughing and cut how often patients pressed the pump, compared with the low dose. The middle dose gave the best overall recovery picture, balancing pain control against side effects. Deng and colleagues frame the middle range as the sensible starting point, while noting the missing comparison arm limits how far the findings reach.
plos-pone-0357572:
Chelsea L. Kracht and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for a study of how daily stress swings while people try to lose weight, and whether those swings predict success. Stress and poor coping can quietly undo diet and activity plans, but most studies measure stress once. Adults with obesity entering a community weight loss program will be followed for six months, with intensive measurement bursts at the start, early weeks, midpoint, and end.

During each two-week burst, participants answer brief phone surveys several times daily about stress, coping, and mood, while devices track activity and sleep and saliva captures the stress hormone cortisol. The central question is whether stress variability, rather than average level, forecasts weight change. The patterns, they hope, will point to moments when a well-timed phone prompt could rescue a struggling day.
plos-pone-0357672:
Yuan Mao, Wei Zheng, and Qian Chen built a small lighthouse-shaped gadget that tells a strong cleaning fluid apart from plain water in seconds. Hospital cleaning units use the fluid to disinfect tools, but mixing it up with tap or purified water can quietly ruin the cleaning process. Their 2026 device reads how well a liquid carries electric current, a trait where the fluid differs sharply from water.

A pocket controller and sensor light one lamp for the cleaning fluid and another for water, and tests at ten hospitals sorted every sample correctly. Battery life covered about a week of use, and the sealed body survived a month soaking in the fluid. Technicians rated it far above paper test strips for accuracy and ease.
plos-pone-0357772:
Chang-Seok Yoon and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on a tuberculosis question. When a chest scan shows a lung cavity, should drug treatment run longer than standard to prevent relapse?? Cavities mark higher relapse risk, but hard evidence for extending therapy is thin. Using a multicenter Korean cohort, they compared patients with cavitary, drug-susceptible tuberculosis treated a standard span against those treated longer.

Relapse was rare in both groups, a handful of patients, and did not differ meaningfully between them. The longer-treated group had started sicker by one measure, yet cleared the bacteria at the same speed. Stopping treatment because of drug side effects was somewhat more common with extended therapy, though overall side effect rates were similar. A cautious adjusted analysis hinted longer treatment might lower relapse, but the signal was not firm. A cavity alone, they say, may not justify routinely prolonging treatment.
plos-pone-0358472:
Guo Liu led a team of eight authors mapping shared biology between psoriasis and metabolic syndrome, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The two conditions occur together far more often than chance explains. The team studied their shared genetic basis and built a spatial cellular atlas spanning both.

Liu's atlas shows where the biology of the two diseases overlaps, tissue by tissue and cell by cell. Shared genes can explain why one disease raises the risk of the other. They can also reveal drug targets that help both at once. Patients with psoriasis are often screened for metabolic problems late; a shared map strengthens the case for early checks and joined-up care between skin and metabolic clinics.
plos-pone-0358572:
Laura van Dussen led a team of six authors studying Fabry disease and gene testing, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Fabry disease is an inherited condition that is often missed for years. As labs add the GLA gene to broader gene panels, more cases surface, including milder or unusual ones.

Van Dussen's team examined how that wider testing changed the known range of the disease's symptoms. The shifting picture suggests Fabry disease is more varied, and perhaps more common, than once thought. For doctors, broader panels mean finding patients earlier, when treatment can do more good. For genetic counselors, the wider spectrum complicates advice, making studies that map it carefully all the more valuable.
plos-pone-0358772:
Isamu Yamakawa leads a team of eight hunting for a gentler warning sign of breathing failure in ALS, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Carbon dioxide retention is what kills in this disease, and catching it early guides ventilator support. The standard check, arterial blood gas, means an arterial puncture patients dread repeating. The team tested whether a number hiding in routine blood work, the sodium chloride gap, tracks carbon dioxide in eighty-eight patients.

It tracks well. The gap correlated strongly with both bicarbonate and carbon dioxide pressure. A cutoff value flagged retention with about eighty-five percent sensitivity, and a negative result was right nearly nine times in ten. A higher cutoff was rarely wrong when positive. Patients whose breathing capacity had fallen below half showed the raised pattern too. A number from blood already drawn could decide who truly needs the needle.
plos-pone-0358872:
Xianwei Zhu, He Chao, and Yahui Zhang upgrade a popular detection network to find cracks in bridge concrete, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Cracks are thin, faint, and irregular, and busy surface textures fool automated eyes. Their version of the YOLOv8 detector first cleans the image with filtering and contrast equalization, then adds attention modules that respect direction and mix fine and broad features across scales.

The redesign jumped detection quality dramatically over the stock network on their benchmark, while keeping the model small enough to run at roughly seventy-six frames per second. Step by step removal tests showed each added part contributed, rather than one trick doing all the work. Tests with different random seeds and on an independent outside dataset held up, supporting the claim that the system generalizes. For inspection teams, it promises fast first pass scans that flag slender cracks human reviewers can then verify.
plos-pone-0358972: Mukhia and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study of the Ethereum blockchain, the public ledger behind a major digital currency. They mapped number patterns across two kinds of accounts: plain user wallets and self-running contract accounts. Their focus was the network of ERC20 tokens, the most common token type on the chain. Such maps help spot odd trading, fraud risk, and how value moves through the system.
plos-pone-0359072:
Matthew Incha and seven colleagues published this methods article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents a laboratory protocol for changing the genes of diverse yeasts using Agrobacterium, a bacterium that naturally moves DNA into other cells. Their version works without a membrane, using a spot-plating approach.

A simpler protocol matters because many yeast species are hard to transform with standard methods. Removing the membrane step cuts equipment and handling, which can open genetic experiments to more species and more labs. Researchers who study yeast diversity, fermentation, or fungal biology are the likely users of a cheaper, broader transformation method.
plos-pone-0359272: Abi Zeid and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on COVID-19 among older Syrians who had fled to Lebanon. They drew on a survey run in several waves over time. The goal was to find which traits or living conditions raised the odds of infection. Such knowledge helps health teams aim vaccines, testing, and advice at displaced older people in crowded settings.
plos-pone-0359572: Darusman and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on eye screening for school children in Indonesia.
