Their platform, called CERMATA, is digital and works through referrals, so children flagged at screening get sent for full care. The team built the platform and ran a first rollout in primary schools. Catching vision problems early can protect learning for children far from eye clinics.
plos-pone-0359872:
Abel Walekhwa and colleagues examined in 2026 what helps and what hinders farmers in Uganda from reporting abortions in their livestock. Such reports are an early warning system for Rift Valley Fever, a viral disease that spreads from animals to people and announces itself through waves of livestock abortion. Community based reporting only works if farmers actually file the reports.

The authors organize their findings with the COM-B framework, which sorts influences into capability, opportunity, and motivation. That structure turns a pile of field observations into a checklist for fixing the system: train what is missing, supply what is lacking, motivate what is weak. Better reporting in Uganda would speed detection of outbreaks across the region.
pmc-13196172:
Shoko Kubota and colleagues published a 2026 review of past lung cancer surgery cases. They asked whether hip muscle size before surgery predicts problems after surgery in older patients. Muscle loss with age is called sarcopenia, and it may raise surgical risk.

The study covered 584 patients aged 70 or older who had part of a lung removed. Staff measured hip muscle area on scans at the lower back. About one in five patients had notable problems after surgery. Patients with muscle area below a set cut-off had more problems, even after other factors were weighed. Common problems were long air leaks and fast, uneven heartbeat. The scan measure may help flag high-risk patients early.
pmc-13197572:
Zongxueni Deng and colleagues built a 2026 forecast model for rectal cancer response to radiation. Radiation is a main local treatment for rectal cancer, yet some tumors resist it and outcomes suffer. The team mined public gene datasets to find markers of that resistance.

They combined bulk gene data from close to one thousand patients with single-cell data from six samples. A risk score built from gene patterns linked to immune cell mix, drug sensitivity, and growth pathways. Five key genes stood out as tied to radiation response. Protein checks in databases and animal tissue backed the picks. The genes may serve as markers and drug targets, pending clinical tests.
pmc-13200172:
Fan Yang and colleagues mapped the research field on gene-based markers for ascending aortic aneurysm in a 2026 bibliometric study. An aneurysm is a dangerous bulge in the body's main artery. It often stays silent until it tears, and size alone poorly sorts risk, so gene findings that change care are prized.

The team searched three databases for work from 1997 to 2025 and analyzed close to thirteen hundred fifty papers. Output grew fast, at about fifteen percent a year. The United States led in papers and citations, with a tight Western European cluster and fast-rising output from China. Core themes center on inherited aorta syndromes and two gene pathways. The field seems to shift from gene hunting to reading variants for care.
pmc-13202872:
Sugars that fungi secrete could become programmable industrial materials, and a 2026 review authored by Hassan AH Ibrahim lays out how to get them there. The article integrates what is known about fungal exopolysaccharides, from the genes that build them to the factories that might produce them at scale.

The review links biosynthesis and molecular structure to function across major polymer classes, using gene-cluster case studies. It then maps cultivation and purification workflows that could deliver consistent product specifications for medicine, food, materials, and environmental uses. Bottlenecks including strain variability, purification cost, and quality standards are weighed honestly, and the authors offer a roadmap from laboratory promise to manufacturing.
pmc-13241672:
Mansour and colleagues in Houston introduce a new radiographic angle for the lower half of tibial slope deformity. Excess posterior slope threatens ACL grafts, yet its below-tubercle share went unmeasured. Three hundred knee patients formed cohorts without tears, with primary tears, and with graft tears. Full-length lateral tibia films supplied every measurement.

The new infratubercle angle averaged highest in the graft-tear cohort, near ninety-two degrees. Three-quarters of graft-tear patients with elevated slope showed an elevated angle. The measure correlated with overall slope in all three cohorts. Mansour recommends pairing it with existing angles to localize deformity before osteotomy.
pmc-13242472:
Arwel Jones and colleagues tested whether a single day of bovine colostrum could blunt the immune dip that follows hard exercise. Their randomized crossover trial appeared in the European Journal of Nutrition in 2026. Sixteen healthy, active men each completed two long cycling sessions, once with colostrum doses and once with a matched placebo drink. Blood and saliva samples tracked white-cell activity and mouth-level defenses around the ride.

Colostrum raised the oxidative burst of neutrophils, a front-line germ-killing response, by roughly fifteen percent over placebo. A lab sub-study showed that plasma taken after colostrum intake boosted neutrophil action in fresh blood too. Salivary lysozyme, an antibacterial protein, also ran higher after exercise in the colostrum trial. Some other immune measures did not change. The authors credit compounds in colostrum that reach the blood after drinking it.
pmc-13246872:
Saegner and colleagues analyzed walking in Parkinson's disease as a whole-body network problem, in this 2026 Journal of Neurology study. Twenty-nine patients and twenty-nine healthy controls walked at three speeds while sensors recorded how each body segment accelerated. The researchers turned those signals into network maps, where segments are nodes and their coordination forms the links, then looked for where coordination breaks down.

Patients showed coherence deficits concentrated in the core body segments, trunk and pelvis, most clearly at their preferred speed and in the forward direction. Healthy walkers adjusted their coordination as speed changed, while patients largely could not, shifting what adjustment they had to their legs. The authors suggest trunk-focused training with varying speeds, and using the network maps to personalize rehabilitation.
pmc-13248972:
Beckman, Syed, and Gromacki argue for earlier, more active care of keratoconus in this 2026 perspective. In this disease the cornea thins and bulges, blurring vision over time. Care once meant glasses early and a transplant late, neither of which slowed the disease itself. Cross-linking changed that by stiffening the cornea and halting progression.

A newly approved version works through the intact surface layer with added oxygen, and its approval does not require waiting for worsening. The authors sketch a community pathway where optometrists and general eye doctors spot cases early and refer fast. They say acting sooner preserves sight and cuts the long-run costs of advanced disease.
pmc-13249172:
Tang and Mei publish the plan for a review of leakage risk after anal fistula surgery, in a 2026 PLOS One protocol. Losing bowel control is the complication patients fear most from these operations, and reported rates swing widely. The authors will search five databases plus grey literature, without language limits, for cohort and case-control studies reporting new or worsened incontinence months after surgery.

Pairs of reviewers will screen papers, extract results, and grade each study's bias risk with established tools. Pooled estimates will be explored by fistula complexity, operation type, and follow-up length. The authors aim to give surgeons firmer numbers for counseling patients and choosing procedures, and the protocol is already registered publicly.
pmc-13250172:
Ratnayake and Wild comment on a Sudanese study of abdominal war wounds to make a wider point about research in conflict zones. Their 2026 Trauma Surgery and Acute Care Open commentary praises local clinicians who collected casualty data during Sudan's war, which began in April 2023. Such settings rarely preserve what their teams learn.

The Sudanese data showed mostly civilian patients, long delays before admission, and worse courses for combat injuries. The authors contrast this with wealthy militaries, whose trauma registries preserve hard-won lessons in detail. They describe toolkits and volunteer networks that help local teams publish, and they ask journals to respect austere conditions without dropping standards. Building local research capacity, they argue, improves care far beyond one war.
pmc-13250472:
Samiee and co-authors ask whether genes help explain why frequent blood donors run low on iron. Their 2026 Health Science Reports study recruited regular male donors at Iran's national blood service during 2023. Three gene variants tied to oxygen sensing, iron control, and blood group were tested against blood iron measures.

One variant, in the oxygen-sensing gene HIF-1 alpha, stood out: donors carrying one form kept clearly higher ferritin, the main iron storage marker. The other two variants showed no reliable link to iron status in this group. The authors suggest screening for this variant could personalize donor care, such as spacing donations or adding iron support. They call for larger, more varied studies that also weigh diet and environment.
pmc-13250872:
Izhar and co-authors map phone-based tools that help community health workers trace the contacts of tuberculosis patients. Their 2026 Global Health Action scoping review covers studies from countries with heavy tuberculosis burdens, published through October 2024. Finding and testing patients' contacts is a key step in stopping the spread of the disease.

Nine studies qualified, most using hybrid phone tools for messaging, case registration, health records, and decision support. Workers generally found the tools acceptable and workable in daily practice. Barriers included worker skills, unreliable systems, and service delivery snags, while training, community engagement, and patient-centered design helped. The authors say success needs stronger worker capacity, dependable technology, and ongoing checks during rollout.
pmc-13251772:
Issdisai and colleagues trace how a histamine drug stops melanoma from spreading to the lungs in mice. Their 2026 ImmunoTargets and Therapy study starts from a gene switched on by histamine dihydrochloride in human immune cells. The gene makes thrombospondin-1, a protein found where tumors prepare to seed new growth.

The drug raised thrombospondin-1 output across several myeloid cell types, working through histamine's type-2 receptor and a known signaling chain. Human melanoma data linked higher gene levels with better survival, and tumor tissue showed reduced levels. In mice, the drug raised lung thrombospondin-1 and cut metastasis, but only in animals able to make the protein. The authors name it a key messenger of the drug's anti-spread effect.
pmc-13252772:
Jananee Rasiah and colleagues profile hospital use by frail home care clients in Alberta, Canada, in this 2026 study. Older adults receiving long-term home care often live with frailty, a state of low reserve that turns small upsets into hospital trips.

The cohort held 10,107 people aged 65 to 104 followed from 2015 to 2017. Most were women, and the biggest group was aged 75 to 84. Arthritis and high blood pressure were the most common conditions among frail clients. About four in ten frail clients visited emergency departments one to three times, and hospital stays averaged about 17 days. Being pre-frail or frail raised the odds of hospital admission.
pmc-13253772:
Lindsay Jibb and co-authors map family reports after limb surgery for childhood cancer in a 2026 review. Children with bone or soft tissue tumors may get limb salvage, which saves the limb, or amputation. The review gathered studies where children, survivors, or caregivers rated life after surgery.

Twenty-seven studies met the rules. Body function was the most rated area, with mostly fair to good results and small gaps between surgery types. Pain stayed common months to years later, and school, play, and body image were trouble spots. Only four studies covered caregivers, who reported worry, low mood, and money strain.
pmc-13253872:
Mohamed Abdel-Basset and co-authors present SIFA, a solar forecasting system, in a 2026 study. Solar plants need good forecasts of sunlight, since output tracks it directly. SIFA first picks the most useful input features with a hybrid method, then blends three machine learning models with tuned weights.

A manta ray-inspired optimizer, improved with chaotic maps, tunes both stages. Tested on data sets from San Diego, Islamabad, and NASA, SIFA gave lower average forecast errors than rival models across repeated runs. The authors present it as a strong option for solar plant planning, with stable results across sites.
pmc-13254072:
Yuki Kametani and co-authors create a new class of copolymer in a 2026 study. Copolymers combine different building blocks, and only four basic layouts were known: random, sequence-controlled, block, and graft. Their new bundle copolymers link several different chains side by side in parallel.

The team made them by growing vinyl chains inside the one-dimensional channels of a metal-organic framework, a porous crystal scaffold. Cross links between the aligned chains can be spaced by changing junction density. The authors say this tying method opens a fresh design space for soft materials.
pmc-13257372:
Diana Carvajal and her co-authors report a mixed-methods study of contraceptive care in Baltimore, published in 2026. Their focus is Latine patients, who say they want care built around their own needs and preferences. The team asked whether such patient-centered care actually happens during clinic visits.

They surveyed patients aged fifteen to forty-five, recorded visits, and coded how clinicians communicated. Most patients gave top ratings for counseling and satisfaction. Trained coders, though, scored the same visits lower, especially for Spanish-preferring and uninsured patients. Follow-up interviews help explain the gap between warm personal impressions and observed practice.
pmc-13259572:
Brian Kuzik, a retired Canadian pediatrician, reflects in French on medical certainty in an essay titled Mais êtes-vous certain? The CMAJ humanities piece reaches back to his fourth year of medical school in the nineteen eighties. A hereditary bowel disease anchors his memory.

He recalls learning about familial polyposis, where hundreds of intestinal polyps sprout in adolescence. Left alone, they turn cancerous, and patients of that era could expect death from colon cancer in their forties. Families watched relatives follow the same path before them. The only hope then was removing the colon and rectum before cancer appeared.
pmc-13261372:
Sergiy Boiko and co-authors present a 2026 study of genetic structuring within populations of the fungus Schizophyllum commune in Poland and Ukraine. This widespread wood-decay fungus serves as a model for genetic and evolutionary processes. The team used highly informative SSR DNA markers, short repeating DNA stretches, to map gene flow.

Clustering and network analyses pointed to substantial gene flow across the whole population, with a single network covering 44%. A Mantel test showed a weak but significant correlation between genetics and geography (r = 0.1415, p = 0.001). The Vor and Olex subpopulations held the most unique genotypes. The Sha and Kyiv subpopulations showed intensive gene flow. The authors conclude the Dnipro River and Carpathian Mountains shape the structure. Genetic material appears to spread from western Ukraine into Poland, then from the north into central Ukraine.
pmc-13262572:
Li-jun Han and co-authors distill the best Chinese evidence for treating acute pancreatitis with rhubarb. The medicinal root is a traditional Chinese medicine staple for this dangerous pancreatic inflammation, but dosing practice varies widely. Their 2026 synthesis hunts guidelines, consensus statements, and systematic reviews through October twenty twenty-five.

Fifteen documents survived quality screening, yielding twenty-seven evidence statements. The team sorts them into how rhubarb works, whether it is feasible, how to evaluate it, and how to give it. Used well, the evidence supports faster gut recovery in these patients. Caution flags remain, since the source base is narrow and uniform protocols are still forming.
pmc-13263272:
Mauro Podda and co-authors look for admission signs that predict death in flesh-destroying infections in a 2026 journal article. Necrotising soft tissue infections are rare but kill quickly. The team reviewed 379 adults with surgically confirmed infections at four large Italian referral centers from 2010 to 2024, comparing survivors and non-survivors on data available at arrival.

About one in six patients died in hospital. Mortality was similar in necrotising fasciitis and in Fournier's gangrene, a form affecting the groin area. In adjusted models, older age and higher creatinine, a kidney function marker, at admission predicted death across all patients. In limb cases, chronic kidney disease also mattered. A simple chart using age and creatinine predicted death with fair accuracy and calibration.
pmc-13264572:
Sohila Mostafa and colleagues present a 2026 paper on a sensor system built to find tiny traces of cancer DNA in blood. The target is KRAS, a gene often changed in tumors, and the test must tell apart a single letter change in the code. Their method joins an enzyme copying step with two light-based readouts.

One readout uses glow tracking during the copying cycles, and the other uses a laser method that reads a molecular fingerprint on special chips. The laser readout found far lower amounts than the glow readout in lab tests. Both stayed steady on repeat runs and worked in diluted blood serum. The authors call it a proof of concept that cross-checks results to cut false positives.
pmc-13264972:
Dongdong Yu and colleagues present a 2026 study of an AI model that spots spinal infections on plain CT scans. These infections are rare but serious, and their signs on cross-section images are easy to miss. The team trained a transformer model, a modern image-reading design, on scans from one hospital and tested it at a second.

The study held 157 patients with primary spinal infection. On held-out scans at the home hospital, the model sorted slices with very high accuracy, catching 96.2 percent of infection signs. At the second hospital it did as well or better. The model beat two human radiologists on accuracy and sensitivity, and both doctors improved when given its help, while also reading faster. The authors note that abscess presence and germ type affected results.
pmc-13270572:
A. Modrek is lead author of a 2026 journal article on protecting carbon steel from acid damage with a shop-bought chemical called lauramidopropyl amine oxide, shortened to LAO. The tests used a weak hydrochloric acid mix. That is a common setting where steel parts corrode fast.

Using metal-release measures and three electrical tests, the team found LAO slowed steel dissolving more as its dose rose. It reached about 95 percent or higher protection in the electrical tests at the top dose. Results pointed to a thin layer stuck to the steel surface. Under far harsher hot, pressurized gas tests, protection fell sharply, so room-temperature success did not carry over.
pmc-13270872:
Can Chen is lead author of a 2026 journal article on shikonin, a natural compound, against diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, a fast-growing blood cancer. Earlier work showed shikonin can kill these cancer cells, but how it does so was unclear, so the team traced the process in cells and in mice.

Shikonin raised iron build-up and fat damage inside the cells, pushing them into an iron-driven form of cell death called ferroptosis. A long non-coding RNA named ADPGK-AS1 normally protects the cells against that death through a partner protein and gene. Shikonin weakens that protection by lowering the RNA, and tests in a mouse tumour model supported the findings.
pmc-13272672:
Neerav Shukla leads a 2026 letter on detecting drug resistance in acute leukemia from free DNA in blood plasma. Menin inhibitor drugs work for some leukemias, but changes in the MEN1 gene can stop them binding. Finding those changes now relies on bone marrow samples, which are invasive to take.

The team describes a sensitive sequencing assay, MSK-ACCESS MEN1, that looks for resistance changes in plasma free DNA. They compare its results with marrow sequencing in patients on menin inhibitors. Such blood testing would allow repeated checks with less burden, which matters in children who often need sedation for marrow sampling, and could flag resistance before relapse shows.
pmc-13273072:
Nadezda Ignatyeva leads a 2026 study of how cholesterol imbalance inside heart cells drives dilated cardiomyopathy, a disease where the heart stretches and weakens. The team used stem-cell-derived heart cells, patient heart tissue, and living adult heart cells. Mutations in muscle fiber proteins were the disease model.

They found abnormal cholesterol in the mutant cells, linked to distorted shape and poor function of the endoplasmic reticulum, a cell network that handles proteins and fats. Loss of contacts between muscle fibers and this network drove the changes. Restoring cholesterol balance repaired the network, the contacts, and cell contraction, suggesting a new treatment target for failing heart cells.
pmc-13274572:
Augusto Azuara-Blanco and a large team present 2026 results from CHAMP-UK, a trial of weak atropine eye drops to slow short-sightedness in children. Myopia is rising fast, and low-dose atropine is a candidate treatment. The double-masked trial ran at five United Kingdom centers, randomly assigning 289 children aged six to twelve to nightly drops for two years.

One hundred ninety-two children got atropine 0.01 percent and ninety-seven got placebo drops, and 235 finished the study. After two years, the atropine group's eyes had worsened less, by a mean of 0.33 dioptres, the unit of lens power. Their eyeballs also lengthened less, by 0.14 millimeters on average. Benefits did not differ by age, sex, ethnicity, or starting severity.
pmc-13274872: Catalina E Gardella-García and co-authors issued a 2026 correction notice for their article in PLoS One on a proteomics-based assessment of living indicators in Mexican water bodies. Proteomics means reading the full set of proteins in a sample. The notice concerns only the article's title, which was published in a garbled, doubled form: an extra phrase was wrongly included. The corrected title is 'A Preliminary proteomics-based assessment of biotic indicators in Central Mexican water bodies.' The notice gives the correct citation for the article.
pmc-13275772:
Amina Ahmady and co-authors report a 2026 laboratory study on mouth antiseptics that kill viruses. Such products could slow the spread of flu and the virus behind COVID-19. The team tested single agents and paired mixes, including two common antiseptic salts and thymol, an oil from thyme.

In test tubes, each agent weakened influenza A and SARS-CoV-2 more as the dose rose. Pairing either salt with thymol killed far more virus at much lower doses than any agent alone. The mixes were also gentler on cells. Mucin, the slimy protein in saliva, weakened the pairs a lot. Certain gel-like polymers, which help products cling to the mouth, partly kept the mixes working. The authors link these effects to how the chemicals attract and bind.
pmc-13275972:
José Alcides Almeida de Arruda leads a South American team reporting a 2026 case series on oral melanoma. This rare cancer grows inside the mouth and can lack dark pigment, which makes it easy to mistake for a harmless sore. The series gathers cases from five centers in four countries.

The team reviewed twenty-one cases diagnosed between 2003 and 2025. Patients averaged about sixty-three years old, and just over half were women. Most felt no symptoms at diagnosis. Lesions sat most often on the palate or upper gum, and most tumors carried dark pigment. Surgery removed the cancer in most cases. Still, over half the patients died during follow-up. The authors stress early recognition as the best hope against this fast-moving cancer.
pmc-13276272:
Marian Zeibak and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on a surprising driver of obesity and diabetes in mice. The protein, CD59, sits on cell surfaces and normally shields cells from the complement system, part of the immune defenses. Its role in metabolism had not been explored.

Mice missing the mouse version of this protein were fed a high-fat diet. Unlike normal mice, they were protected from obesity, fatty liver, and insulin resistance, the core defect in type 2 diabetes. Their blood sugar control stayed better and their insulin stayed lower. Cage studies suggested they ate less and moved more on running wheels. Liver gene readings showed far less inflammation and scarring activity. The authors say this immune protein plays an unexpected part in diet-driven metabolic disease.
pmc-13276372:
Seina Miyamoto and Takeshi Komino present a 2026 physics article on turning a light-killing effect into a light-boosting one. When glowing molecules sit near metal, waves running along the metal surface, called surface plasmons, usually drain their energy and dim the glow. That loss wastes a large share of power in modern light-emitting diodes.

The authors trap those surface waves inside a tiny ring-shaped resonator, a whispering gallery device that keeps waves circling. Trapped waves form standing patterns, like vibrations on a guitar string. When those patterns resonate with the glowing molecules' own transitions, the molecules can release their energy as brighter light instead. The paper proposes and develops this route to stronger photoluminescence, light emitted after absorbing light, for future devices.
pmc-13276572:
Chenggong Ma and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on cellular sponges that soak up inflammatory signals in arthritic joints. Osteoarthritis degrades cartilage while inflammation fans the damage. Two messengers, shortened to IL-1β and TNF-α, drive much of that process, and current treatments only ease symptoms.

The team wrapped tiny gel spheres in engineered macrophage membranes, borrowing the immune cells' own signal receptors. The sponges neutralized both target signals in lab tests. They also nudged macrophages toward their healing state. In lab-grown cartilage models and in rats with joint disease, the sponges reduced cartilage breakdown. Building genes switched up while breakdown markers switched down. The authors present the design as a strong candidate for disease-targeted care.
pmc-13276772:
Mike Jentsch and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on a blood and urine test panel for diagnosing major depression. Depression is now diagnosed by interview, which is subjective and overlaps with other conditions. Earlier work by the team suggested a set of body chemicals could flag the disorder objectively.

They tested thirty-four biomarkers in one hundred sixty patients and one hundred twenty controls across three cohorts. A machine learning model scored each chemical against reference ranges and summed the scores. After internal validation the combined score separated patients from controls well. When each cohort was scored on models built from the others, accuracy fell to modest levels. The authors say a biomarker panel could add value to the diagnostic toolkit one day, but it is not clinic-ready and needs further research.
pmc-13277072:
Suju Liu and colleagues report a 2026 case report of an unusual eye finding two years after glaucoma surgery. Glaucoma is eye damage tied to high pressure inside the eye. A 53-year-old man had an operation that placed a fine suture, a surgical thread, through a drainage channel called Schlemm's canal.

At a routine follow-up exam with a special lens, doctors saw the retained suture moving back and forth in a steady rhythm. The eye was quiet, with no active inflammation, and no more surgery had been needed. Earlier imaging work hinted that this eye region may pulse with pressure or heartbeat. The suture may simply make that hidden motion visible, the authors suggest.
pmc-13281472:
Anna-Lena Wien and Angeliki Stamtsis-Datsi reviewed cell therapies for skin cancer in a 2026 paper. Melanoma that shrugs off standard drugs remains a hard problem. Most patients in time resist the main drug classes. Tumors often lack enough cancer-fighting immune cells and keep the rest shut out. Cell therapies aim to supply fresh fighters or train new ones. The review weighs five paths, from cancer vaccines to lab-built cells.

Vaccines made from the patient's own alarm cells were safe and sparked broad, lasting responses. But alone they did little in advanced disease. Cells pulled from the tumor itself helped even after other drugs failed, though making them is slow and harsh. Built-to-order cells face target choice, harm risks, and short lives in solid tumors. Killer cells from donors could be shelf-ready but need polish. The authors favor pairing vaccines with cell transfer.
pmc-13281872:
Ziqiao Yan and colleagues used gene data to test a gut-to-disc link in back pain in a 2026 study. Worn spinal discs are a major cause of low back pain. Gut germ mixes have been tied to disc wear in loose studies. The team used genes as fixed levers to test cause. Gene sets covered gut germs, swelling signals, and disc cases from a Finnish bank. It held near thirty thousand cases. Two-step checks asked whether swelling signals carry the effect.

Eleven germ groups hinted at a causal tie to disc wear. Only one neared the strict proof bar. Seven swelling signals also hinted at ties, but none cleared strict checks. The carry-through test found no sign that blood swelling signals pass the gut effect on. The authors say a gut-disc axis may still exist. Its path likely runs through germ chemicals or local immunity.
pmc-13282172:
Jacob Brain and co-authors published a 2026 test of twelve dementia risk prediction models in a large British cohort. A risk model combines factors such as age, blood pressure, and lifestyle to estimate future dementia odds. Models often work worse outside the group they were built on, so outside testing matters. The Norfolk cohort held more than twenty-five thousand people, followed for up to thirty years.

Five models could be fully tested and seven only partly. Two heart-risk models kept good accuracy for dementia, showing the weight of blood vessel health. One British dementia model kept strong sorting power despite partial testing. Some dementia models lost moderate accuracy, and performance was generally lower in women. Several models were too small in events to judge firmly. The authors favour simpler models built on core vessel and lifestyle factors for clinic use.
pmc-13282272:
Gurpreet Jhally and co-authors present a 2026 food science study turning two medicinal plant juices into a shelf-stable powder by spray drying. Aonla is a sour, vitamin-rich fruit, and giloy is a herb used in Indian traditional practice. Their fresh juices spoil fast and lose active compounds. The team varied feed flow, air heat, juice share, and a drying aid to find the best settings.

The drying aid share mattered most, followed by air temperature. The best settings used seventy percent aonla juice and a moderate aid level. The resulting powder kept high levels of vitamin C and plant phenols, the protective compounds. It dissolved and dispersed well, tasted acceptable to panellists, and held low moisture. Recovery of powder, though, was only about a fifth of the feed. The authors see real potential for long-life health food powders, if yield can be improved at scale.
pmc-13282372:
Feng Ni and co-authors describe a 2026 materials study on an ultrathin polymer membrane that harvests energy from salt differences in water. Such osmotic power systems need narrow, charged channels that let one ion type pass. The team's membrane is about fifty nanometres thick and fully crystalline. Its layers are staggered, forming aligned triangular channels just over one nanometre wide, lined with charged sites.

Against a non-staggered version, the staggered membrane more than tripled the electric double-layer coverage, a measure of how fully channel walls control ion flow. It combined strong selectivity for negative ions with very high current density. Simulations showed the staggered charges create a screw-like path that speeds ions across. Fitted into small test generators, the membrane reached a peak power density among the highest reported for such systems. The authors present staggered stacking as a design lever for blue energy devices.
pmc-13282672:
Geronimo Garcia and co-authors report a 2026 case of anaesthesia for surgery on a giant aneurysm of the ascending aorta in an elderly woman. An aneurysm is a ballooning of the aorta, the main artery; ones over eight centimetres are exceedingly rare and can rupture or crush nearby structures. Their patient, aged eighty-three, had an aneurysm pressing hard on her right ventricle and lung artery.

The team treated her physiology like that of a patient with a chest mass, where losing natural breathing or blood return can cause collapse. Heart bypass through an armpit artery was set up before opening the chest, given the rupture risk. Ultrasound imaging through the oesophagus guided the work and checked the repair. Surgery proceeded under deep cooling with circulation paused, and she recovered without major complications. The authors stress anticipation, fast bypass readiness, and tight team coordination for these rare cases.
pmc-13283172:
Apprentices in Geneva who face orientation-based abuse early leave training more often, Lavinia Gianettoni's longitudinal team found in 2026. The study tracks sex-based and orientation-based abuse over time. It asks whether early abuse raises the chance of leaving vocational training.

A cohort of 1,370 first-year apprentices in Geneva was followed from 2020 to 2023. Abuse was measured at three points, and dropout meant absence from class rolls the next year. Abuse tied to sexual orientation at the start raised dropout risk the next year. The effect held after checks for sex, field type, and hiding orientation. Sex-based abuse showed no clear link. Early protection is the key lesson.
pmc-13283372:
Morning gallbladder surgery consumed more opioid than afternoon surgery in Zhe Li's 2026 timing study at a Beijing hospital. Daily body rhythms shape pain sense and drug handling in people. The team tested whether morning and afternoon surgery differ in opioid use.

A total of 45 patients had gallbladder keyhole surgery under general anesthesia. Groups were split by start time: 24 in the morning and 21 in the afternoon. Sedation and pain control were kept equal by monitored targets. Morning patients needed higher total and weight-based opioid doses in surgery. Stress hormone levels were also higher in the morning group at all checks. Timing may guide dose planning for anesthesia teams.
pmc-13283572:
Lesion size steers treatment and recovery in children's knee cartilage defects, Edmund Corcoran's twelve-year series shows in 2026. Such defects can harm long-term joint function in young patients. Lesion size may shape treatment choice, recovery speed, and final outcomes.

Records covered 112 patients treated with surgery from 2012 to 2023 at one center. Mean age was about 16 years, and most patients were male. Large lesions were more common in males than in females in the cohort. Ligament injuries arose more often in the small lesion group by contrast. Outcomes were tracked with standard knee scores for two years after surgery. Return timing was modeled with lesion size and ligament injury together.
pmc-13284172:
Plants threatened at home yet invasive abroad form a paradox mapped globally by Ramiro R Ripa and colleagues in 2026. Eighty-nine plant species fit that rare double status under strict cross-database rules. Alien flora lists were merged with conservation assessment lists for the count.

Threatened plants proved far less likely to settle or invade than non-threatened peers. That gap makes the paradox outcome genuinely uncommon in the data. Paradox species cluster in the Americas and East to Southeast Asia regions. Human uses dominate their profiles, with farming and overuse as persistent threats. Success abroad splits from survival at home, driven by shared human pressures.
pmc-13284472:
Gabriel Fernando Todeschi Variane and co-authors report a 2026 multicenter study of brain bleeding in preterm newborns in Brazil. The prospective study followed 268 infants born under 32 weeks or under 1500 grams in four neonatal intensive care units from September 2023 to September 2024. Head ultrasound results and short-term outcomes were tracked.

Normal scans were seen in just over half the infants, while mild bleeding and severe bleeding were less common, the authors report. Infants with severe bleeding or death before a scan had lower birth weight and gestational age, lower Apgar scores, and more intensive early care. Severe bleeding also linked to higher death before discharge and longer stays. The team urges a standard prevention bundle in Brazilian units.
pmc-13284872:
Kamal Abi Mosleh and co-authors present a 2026 case report of a rare benign uterine tumor that looked like a cancerous growth. A healthy 29-year-old woman came in with sharp belly pain three months after delivery. Scans found a fast-growing 10 cm blood-rich mass from the womb corner reaching behind the belly organs, raising fear of sarcoma.

Keyhole surgery was switched to open removal with a multi-team approach due to deep spread. A quick frozen test gave no clear answer, so the uterus was removed. Final tissue study showed a benign angiomyolipoma made of muscle, vessels, and fat. Recovery was smooth. The authors stress how hard such cases are when cancer cannot be ruled out.
pmc-13285372:
A beefed-up antibody drug for HER2-positive breast cancer is reported by Yuqi Zhang and co-authors in a 2026 mouse study. This cancer type grows fast and often learns to resist trastuzumab, the antibody that targets HER2. The team hung a light-active dye carrying a radical source onto trastuzumab, making a conjugate with several payloads.

After vein dosing, the conjugate gathered at tumor sites in mice. Shining near-infrared light on it freed gas and radicals through heat, adding a burn-like attack to the antibody aim. Growth of HER2-positive tumors shrank markedly under this paired strike. The authors pitch the design as a broad template for exact cancer treatment paired with imaging.
pmc-13285672:
A rare inherited fat-storage illness shows wide faces in Iraq, Rabab Farhan and co-authors chart in a 2026 single-center study. Acid sphingomyelinase shortage stems from faults in one gene and spans three types, from fast infant harm to slower adult forms. Forty-seven patients seen since 2007 had their call confirmed by gene reads and enzyme tests.

Family history showed in two thirds of cases, and near all came from kin marriages. Big liver and spleen showed in every patient, with low blood counts common and face quirks in a quarter. Thirteen gene variants turned up, three of them new to science. The authors urge doctors to suspect the illness in children with big organs and anemia.
pmc-13286072:
Johanne Mensah Gourmel leads a 2026 European survey study on why rehab teams use digital tools with children. Robots, virtual reality games, and telehealth apps all promise livelier motor therapy, yet clinics adopt them unevenly. The survey asked professionals across Europe what drives real use, testing the answers with a standard acceptance model.

Of nearly fourteen hundred replies, 635 met the rules for study, and the model fit the data well. Plain access to the gear beat every other factor for all three tool types, far ahead of plans to use them. Belief that a tool truly helps children drove the wish to use it more than peer pressure or ease did. The authors say proof of benefit plus gear on site matter most, and family views should shape the next round of rollout work.
pmc-13286172:
Andrea Bernasconi and colleagues compare two child health data systems in Adamawa State, Nigeria, in a 2026 retrospective analysis. A tablet tool that walks clinic staff through sick-child care also logs each visit, while the state routine system still leans on hand counts. Quarterly facility data from 2017 to 2021 let the team lay the two tallies side by side for four common childhood illnesses.

The tablet system logged far fewer malaria, gut, and lung cases than the routine system across the five years. Measles ran the other way, with the tablet tool counting more cases than the paper-based tally. The gap grew wider as the tablet tool spread to more clinics over time. With no perfect count to judge against, the authors avoid crowning a winner and instead urge shared case rules and merged data flows.
pmc-13286572:
Melquesedek Ferreira da Silva Almeida, Suellem Zanlorenci, and Diego Augusto Santos Silva link reported discrimination to body discontent in Brazilian teens in a 2026 survey analysis. School adolescents aged 14 to 17 in São José answered standardized questions about unfair treatment and whether they wished their weight were different. Models accounted for social background and split the results by sex.

Teens reporting discrimination carried higher odds of wanting to gain weight and, separately, of wanting to lose it. The direction split by sex in striking ways. Boys who felt discriminated against leaned toward wanting to weigh less, with odds near two-thirds higher. Girls leaned the opposite way, wanting to gain, with odds roughly tripled. The authors read the split as social pressure bending body ideals along different tracks for each sex, and call for protective responses in schools.
pmc-13288872:
Julian Mutz and co-authors test if mental illness speeds body aging in 2026. Their study uses UK Biobank data. Blood profiles fed a metabolomic aging clock. The set held 225,212 people. Nine diagnosis groups were compared. Forty-five single disorders were also checked.

Substance use disorders came with older readings. Psychotic, mood, and anxiety disorders did too. Psychosis showed the largest gap. Obsessive-compulsive disorder pointed the other way. Eating disorders also read younger. Some links ran stronger in men. They also ran stronger under age sixty-five. Genetic risk sometimes clashed with clinic patterns. Life circumstances may shape much of the signal.
pmc-13288972:
Kate Mallory Anderson leads a 2026 protocol for a child well-being tool in Australia. The tool is for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children. The children are aged 5 to 11 years. No tool now fits their culture well. Pictures will sit beside each question.

The plan has five phases in all. Local groups will co-design each step. Children will help shape the pictures. The goal is a strength-based set of questions. It asks what helps a child thrive. Ethics boards across the nation have approved it. Results will go to journals and partner groups. The team hopes services will use the tool widely.
pmc-13289172:
Emilie Leblong and colleagues sketch a 2026 trial plan on robot walking aids in MS. The trial deals with home use of an exoskeleton. MS often cuts walking and drains energy. Life quality falls as a result. Home robots may boost training and freedom.

The trial will enroll 28 patients in all. Three rehab centers in France will host it. Each phase will last eight weeks. One phase uses the robot at home each day. One gives activity advice with no device. A wash-out gap will split the phases. Life quality is the main outcome. Walking tests and fatigue scores will also be tracked.
pmc-13289372:
James Hollister headed a 2026 cohort study in Arizona on whether PFAS chemicals blunt COVID-19 vaccine response in children. PFAS are long-lasting industrial chemicals found in blood, and earlier work linked higher levels to weaker vaccine antibodies for other shots. Whether that holds for COVID-19 vaccines in youth was unknown before this study.

Children aged 6 months to 17 years in the AZ-HEROES Kids cohort qualified under set rules. They had finished the Pfizer primary series and gave blood 14 to 60 days after dose two. None had prior infection before vaccination. Labs measured 13 PFAS types and antibody binding to two spike protein parts. Models adjusted for age, sex, and region within Arizona. The setup lets readers see if everyday chemical exposure tracks with early vaccine response.
pmc-13289772:
Ulrike Beilenhoff, Christoph Schlag, and Dörte Wichmann report a 2026 multinational survey on hidden workflow costs in endoscopy units. Nurses handle many tasks inside and outside the unit, and wasted time drives cost. An anonymous 23-question online survey went out through nursing groups in 33 countries in several languages to capture daily reality.

Answers from 456 nurses in gut and lung endoscopy entered the analysis, mostly from large, busy, experienced centers. Full scope reprocessing fell to nurses in 51 percent of reports, and moving equipment towers was frequent each week. Delays from missing scopes were seen regularly by 62 percent of respondents overall. Single-use scopes were praised most for safety and availability.
pmc-13289872:
David Elmenhorst headed a 2026 randomized brain scan study on whether lost sleep raises a synaptic marker in humans. Sleep is thought to trim synapses strengthened during waking, restoring balance. The marker SV2A, seen with a PET tracer, serves as a stand-in for synapse density, letting the team test that idea directly in living brains.

Forty healthy adults with a mean age of 27.5 years had two scans on back-to-back days. Half slept normally and half stayed awake about 28 hours before the second scan at the same clock time. Deprived brains showed higher marker binding in the thalamus, hippocampus, and parietal cortex, while controls showed no change. Gains tracked with deeper recovery sleep pressure.
pmc-13290572:
A ratio built from waist size, triglycerides, and cholesterol predicts bad outcomes after stroke better than older markers, Yue Wang and colleagues report in 2026. Their subject is the Cardiometabolic Index, tested in patients with acute ischemic stroke who received clot-busting therapy.

The retrospective study enrolled 588 thrombolysis patients and compared the index against traditional biomarkers for long-term adverse cerebrovascular events. The index outperformed the conventional measures, and a high value, at or above 0.80 in the analysis, was independently tied to more major adverse events. Part of that predictive power ran through systemic inflammation, which the authors found partially mediated the link. Wang and colleagues present the index as a cheap way to sharpen risk sorting after stroke, pending larger cohort checks.
pmc-13290672:
Smaller treatment zones in overnight contact lenses slowed eye growth slightly more in teenagers, Lu Lai and colleagues report in a retrospective study from 2026. Orthokeratology lenses reshape the cornea during sleep to control myopia, and the size of the optical zone may tune how well they work.

The study followed 84 adolescents who wore the lenses for over 12 months, comparing a 5-mm zone group with a 6-mm group. Axial length grew by 0.25 mm on average in the 5-mm group against 0.29 mm in the 6-mm group, a small edge for the tighter zone. Older age meant less elongation, and a wider peripheral power ring predicted more growth, suggesting a one-month ring measurement could forecast control. Corneal safety measures did not differ between groups.
pmc-13291072:
Smart dumbbells that name the exercise being done, using a model tiny enough for cheap wearable hardware, are presented in a 2026 study led by Yifeng Xu. Many activity recognition systems rely on heavy designs with attention or memory layers, which drain power and block real-time use on small devices.

A purely convolutional design called DeM-FCN adds physics-aware inputs built from movement angles and signal strength, plus noise training and a loss that favors hard cases. Tested by leaving one person out at a time on data from 15 people doing four resistance exercises, the model scored high accuracy while holding under 74 thousand parameters. Extra checks on a public dataset support its use in everyday fitness tracking gear.
pmc-13291272:
Tiny chips need smart models that fit their limits. René Groh leads a 2026 study presenting EdgeVolution, a full design platform. It searches model shapes with real hardware in the loop. Many goals are balanced at once, like speed and energy.

Most edge tools ignore the true target chip. That gap leads to weak, hard-to-repeat results. This platform picks, tunes, and installs models end to end. Four use cases show its wide range. Each case ties data, task, and chip limits together. Open access to the pipeline is a core aim. Small teams can thus build fit models without deep chip skill.
pmc-13291372:
Loose joints may raise the risk of a second knee ligament tear. Jakob Lindskog leads a 2026 registry study of athletes after surgery. Players who return to sport can tear the graft or the other knee. A simple bend test, the Beighton Score, grades looseness.

Data came from a rehab registry in January 2026. Patients were aged 15 to 50 at surgery. All played hard knee sports before injury. Each extra positive looseness test lifted second tear risk. The pattern held after age and graft checks. Split looks covered graft tears and other-knee tears apart. A count, not just a yes-no label, carries the warning. Rehab plans could use that finer signal.
pmc-13291572:
A hormone coil buried deep in the womb wall is removed safely. Qingmei Wang leads a 2026 case report of this tricky surgery. The patient had adenomyosis, a painful womb condition. Her levonorgestrel coil had sunk fully into muscle.

Three scan types first located the lost device. Plain X-ray, CT, and MRI each played a part. Live ultrasound then pinned its spot in the wall. A scope through the cervix guided the removal. The womb was stitched closed after extraction. Stepwise imaging plus scope guidance is the lesson. Such planning can spare patients a larger operation. Prevention tips for tricky insertions close the report.
pmc-13292472:
Marjan De Graef and co-authors sum up a 2026 review of what pharmacy technicians actually do on hospital wards and what changes when they do it. Five databases were searched to November 2024 for studies with countable results from technician drug work on general wards. Screening and quality checks ran on their own, summed up in words because studies varied too much to pool.

Twenty-one studies qualified. Medication history taking and reconciliation topped the task list in eleven studies, ahead of preparation support, supply work, and discharge teaching. Thirteen studies found fewer medication errors where technicians worked, catching omissions and dosing mistakes. Pharmacy and nursing efficiency each improved in several studies, staff satisfaction rose in five, and cost analyses looked neutral to positive. One study found patients understood their medicines better after technician-led discharge education.
pmc-13292772:
Yasin Öztürk leads a 2026 lab study of shop-bought chicken-based dry food for cats sold in Italy. The team tested 29 kibbles for drug traces, industrial chemicals, toxic metals, bisphenol A, and plastic particles.

Drug traces were rare, found in only a few samples, while metals appeared in 28 of 29 products. Bisphenol A and plastic fibers or fragments appeared in every sample tested. PFAS chemicals appeared in 7 of 29 samples at low levels. Since no legal limits cover many of these substances in pet food, the authors warn that daily feeding could mean long-term mixed exposure for cats and call for closer checks.
pmc-13294172:
Firat Korkmaz and coauthors test how long ram sperm should rest in protective fluid before freezing in a 2026 study. Semen from five healthy Merino rams was pooled and held for 3, 24, 48, or 72 hours, then frozen and thawed. Checks covered movement, membrane health, energy signals, oxidative damage, and calcium entry.

Short holds of 3 to 24 hours kept movement and membrane health high while limiting damage signals. Long holds of 48 to 72 hours brought toxic and oxidative harm. The 3-hour group thawed best, with the highest motility in the reported figures and the lowest lipid damage. Breeding centers gain a clear timing guide.
pmc-13294272:
Huali Zhang and coauthors summarize nursing care around keyhole cleanup surgery for infected pancreatic necrosis in a 2026 case series. Severe pancreatitis with infected dead tissue can kill, and video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement is a favored low-impact route. Records covered 41 straight cases at one center from July 2024 to June 2025 under a standard nursing protocol.

The group held 30 men and 11 women with mean age 52.9 years. Operations averaged about 134 minutes with low blood loss and no transfusions. A second cleanup was needed by 14.6% of patients, and one person bled inside the abdomen afterward. No new organ failure appeared in the reported follow-up.
pmc-13294372:
Rudi Mao and colleagues uncover a staging trick for inflammasome assembly in a 2026 cell study. The speck protein ASC must gather into one bright dot to fire inflammation, yet fast gathering in living cells was unexplained. Protein fishing found the RNA helicase DDX6 as a partner, and tests covered two inflammasome types in immune cells and mouse infection.

DDX6 uses its unwinding activity to ferry ASC to sensors and seeds specks inside processing bodies through phase separation. When downstream bursting is blocked, specks later shift into stress granules. Macrophages lacking DDX6 left mice more open to Listeria. Ordered staging suggests new drug footholds for runaway inflammation.
pmc-13294972:
Peng Qu and colleagues build a smart patch that delivers replacement mitochondria to injured hearts in a 2026 study. Damage after a blocked heart artery is reopened ties closely to failing mitochondria in heart muscle cells. One cell subtype with high HEY1 activity kept its mitochondria in unusually good shape.

Healthy mitochondria from those cells were packed into tiny vesicles and loaded into a microneedle patch that answers to local metal ion changes. In Bama minipigs with heart injury, the staged release improved heart function, shrank damaged area, and reduced cell death. Treated mitochondria also kept better structure and energy output, supporting timed delivery as a precision strategy.
pmc-13295072:
Dimitra Iosifina Papageorgiou leads a 32-country survey of breast cancer screening in Europe in a 2026 study. Screening finds cancers earlier, yet national programmes differ in ages invited, spacing, and who organises invitations. The part played by family doctors in each system was especially unclear.

Expert informants in each country answered structured questions, refined through rounds of shared checking. Most countries ran population based programmes, while four relied on chance-based screening when women sought it. Family doctors had little or no role in 15 countries and some role in 13 countries. Uptake tended to run highest where organised programmes gave family doctors little involvement.
pmc-13295472:
Nawaf Khayal Alkhayal and colleagues map ear research in Saudi Arabia across nearly five decades in a 2026 scoping review. Output from 1978 to 2024 was charted by topic, design, institution, and funding to expose gaps. Topics were sorted using the ICD-11 disease classification for comparability.

From 2,227 records, 510 studies qualified for the map. Yearly output grew steadily and sped up sharply after 2017, while first authors clustered at few institutions led by King Saud University. Watching-style studies dominated and experiments were rare. Ear and mastoid topics plus health service contact topics took the largest shares, guiding where broader, bolder studies are needed.
pmc-13295872:
Philips Edomwonyi Obasohan and co-authors ask, in 2026, how much the individual therapist matters in Denmark's national osteoarthritis programme, GLA:D. Similar therapist effects are known in other care fields but had not been sized for joint rehabilitation.

Records covered 23,021 adults with hip or knee disease treated by 657 therapists, and about half reported a solid drop in pain at three months. The share of outcome differences tied to which therapist a patient saw was under one percent and barely moved after adjustments. Standard training and delivery, the authors suggest, leave little room for therapist-level gaps.
pmc-13295972:
Han Li and co-authors set out a 2026 trial protocol testing personalised magnetic brain stimulation for stubborn nerve pain in the limbs and face. Standard stimulation helps some patients, but target choice is crude, so the team will aim treatment using each person's brain connectivity maps.

Across four hospitals, 152 adults will get either guided or conventional stimulation in ten sessions over two weeks, with neither side knowing which. Pain scores lead the outcomes, backed by mood, quality-of-life, blood, stool and brain scan measures. The design should show whether personal targeting beats the usual hotspot method.
pmc-13296172:
Alex Oscco and co-authors add, in 2026, fresh anatomical and genetic data on a parasitic flatworm living in the gut of a Peruvian coastal fish. Detailed imaging and DNA reading were used to confirm the worm's identity and place it among relatives.

The work confirms the species and reveals body details not described before. Genetic comparisons suggest some supposed relatives may not form one natural group, unsettling current classification. The authors say better knowledge of such parasites supports marine resource management and a fuller account of ocean biodiversity along South America's Pacific coast.
pmc-13299172:
Three popular programs for labeling horse DNA variants agree far less than users might assume, show Jillian L Marlowe and colleagues in a 2026 comparison. They ran Ensembl-VEP, SnpEff, and ANNOVAR over more than 58 million variants from 1,065 horse genomes and measured how often the tools concurred.

Once the programs' differing vocabularies were standardized, agreement exceeded 90%. Without that step it collapsed to anywhere from 0% to 67%, and exonic and loss-of-function variants disagreed most. ANNOVAR also demanded about twenty-eight times more memory than the leanest rival. The authors advise choosing annotators by study needs and computing budget, not headline accuracy.
pmc-13303672:
Zhen-yu Gu, Yan Chen, and A-jian Zhou analyze how Western news outlets frame traditional Chinese medicine in a 2026 cross-national study. Coverage shapes what the public believes about health and what policies gain support.

News from the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, France, Spain, and Italy between 2010 and 2024 was coded into four frame types across 360 country-quarter units. Risk and safety angles led in the United States and United Kingdom, while science and benefit angles led in Germany and France. The pandemic lifted overall tone but also raised risk framing. Tailored messages by country are advised.
pmc-13303772:
Serena Y. Kuang proposes a new way to organize whole-body function in a 2026 theory article on integrative physiology. Bodies are usually taught in layers from molecules to the whole person, but key jobs such as heat control span many layers at once.

Starting from how cell fluids work together inside the shared fluid around cells, five working domains are derived. Processes are sorted by how they operate rather than where they sit in the body. A companion platform arranges math-based rules of function, such as oxygen binding curves, into one ordered system. Both tools aim to make cross-level links easier to teach and use.
pmc-13305172:
Martina Ludewig leads a 2026 study using a commercial enzyme mix to strip antibiotics from waste milk in Austria. Milk from treated cows cannot be sold, and breaking down the drugs could make it fit for calves.

Both heat-treated and raw milk were spiked with two common cow antibiotics, pure and as farm products, then treated at varied heat, time, and acidity. Farm product forms resisted breakdown more than pure drugs, though several recipes cleared tests fully. Raw treated milk still carried high germ counts, so it stays unfit for calves without acid treatment or heating afterward.
pmc-13305272:
Uma P Reddy, Gerilyn Boyle, and Robert Carpenter describe a pilot class that prepares medical students for patient death in a 2026 report from Texas A&M College of Medicine. Facing a patient's death ranks among the hardest moments in care work, yet training covered it only informally.

Students helped build a formal session mixing a physician video with a live mixed-team panel for second-year students in spring 2024. About sixty students took part across two campuses. Dallas survey replies showed felt readiness rising after the session, with every respondent calling it clinically relevant and worth recommending to others.
pmc-13306472:
Hee-Jin Jun tracked daily stress in LGBTQ+ young adults with phone surveys and smartwatches in a 2026 pilot study. Twenty people aged 18 to 27 took part for fourteen days, answering four surveys daily while watches recorded body signals.

A body stress score came from heart rhythm change in the hour before each survey, alongside good and bad mood ratings. Four stress measures covered daily discrimination, identity-based slights, logged events and felt stress in the reported design. Most measures moved in expected directions within each person, linking higher stress to stronger body response and worse mood.
pmc-13307172:
Ghizlane Akhouy blew nanofibre mats carrying mastic tree oil for active food wrapping in a 2026 study. Polycaprolactone mats, plain, gelatin-blended and oil-loaded at 5, 10 and 20 percent, were spun by solution blowing for comparison.

All mats showed smooth, bead-free fibres, with width rising from 239 nm to 320 nm once gelatin joined in reported measures. Oil shares barely shifted fibre width, yet antioxidant power climbed with oil content. Active compounds named include β-pinene, terpineol and verbenol, supporting greener packaging that slows food spoilage. Such mats could wrap fresh food and slow loss while still breaking down after use at home.
pmc-13308172:
Norah M Alyahya and co-authors explore in 2026 how nurses talk with patients who struggle to grasp health information, drawing on interviews with 18 nurses in Saudi acute care units. Units spanned emergency, intensive care, surgical, and specialist wards, and themes were drawn through a six step method.

Nurses named language gaps, clashing beliefs, and thin base knowledge as core blocks to clear talk with patients. Helpful moves spanned plain words, shown steps, teach back checks, and kin involvement in the talk. Short time, thin resources, and vague rules held nurses back, and the work took an emotional toll as well. The authors frame poor talk as a system fault more than a personal one.
pmc-13308972:
Emilia Rotstein and co-authors measure in 2026 the perineal body, a key pelvic floor support, in Swedish women who have never been pregnant, using three dimensional endoanal ultrasound. Their group held 148 women with a mean age of 31 years, and raters of mixed skill scored each scan by a shared method.

Mean length was 17.5 millimetres, front to back height was 9.7 millimetres, and mean area was 120 square millimetres in this cohort. Agreement between raters ran from fair to excellent, with length the most steady of the three scores. Heavier women held longer and larger bodies by a fair margin. Shared scan rules can thus yield base values for future pelvic work.
pmc-13309372:
Jiazhi Song and co-authors report a 2026 lab study on what happens inside brain cells after traumatic brain injury. After injury, lactate builds up in the brain and nerve cells often die. The work traces how that buildup may switch off a key protective enzyme.

Cell and mouse work showed that lactate adds a chemical mark to the enzyme SOD2 and lowers its activity, so harmful oxygen byproducts rise. Two other proteins add and remove that mark. Turning on the removing protein in injured mice restored enzyme activity and cut nerve cell death. The authors point to this pathway as a possible target for limiting later brain damage.
pmc-13309472:
Kenta Anraku and co-authors study a small char fish in dam-split Japanese rivers in a 2026 ecology article. Below small dams, the southern Asian Dolly Varden shares water with two rival fish. Above the dams it lives alone. The team asked what release from rivals does to growth, survival, and body shape.

Fish sharing reaches grew slower, stayed in poorer shape, and showed lower survival than fish living alone. Shared-reach fish also grew mouths set lower and smaller eyes, suiting bottom feeding. Lone fish grew denser, fed more on land insects, and kept forward mouths with larger eyes. The authors show how rivals can reshape both numbers and bodies of a fish.
pmc-13309572:
Mart Sillen and colleagues test a friendly yeast as a live treatment for vaginal yeast infection in a 2026 study. The illness, driven by Candida albicans, brings tissue damage and an overstrong immune response that adds harm. A related yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, was checked for calming both sides of that problem.

One yeast strain, Sc3458, slowed Candida growth, grip on surfaces, and shape shifting into threads, which together weakened its surface films. Gene activity in Candida shifted toward stress and away from harm traits. In mice, the yeast eased swelling while keeping immune cells able to fight. The authors present Sc3458 as a candidate live therapy for this common infection.
pmc-13309672:
Walid A Al-Qerem and co-authors survey diabetes knowledge among adults without diabetes in Iraq in a 2026 study. Knowing warning signs and prevention steps helps people lower their own risk and seek care early. Views from the general public, not clinics, were the target here.

A culturally adapted questionnaire reached 874 adults across regions of Iraq in mid to late 2025. Nearly half reported a family history of diabetes. Classic signs like frequent urination and strong thirst were widely known, at 89.9 percent and 84.2 percent awareness in the reported figures, while subtler signs lagged. Knowledge of complications ranged from high for dramatic outcomes to moderate for kidney and eye harm. The authors call for teaching that fills the quieter gaps.
pmc-13310772:
Caitlin S Frazee led a 2026 lab study on why engineered immune cells fade after cancer care. CAR T cells can clear blood cancers, but few infused cells settle into long lived memory form, so relapse is common. Approved products use one of two booster parts, and each part shapes cell fate in a distinct way.

When a parent cell splits unevenly, daughters can take different paths. One booster type made surface traits more uneven yet inner programs more alike, which linked to weaker staying power. The other type did the reverse and yielded one fighter daughter and one lasting daughter. Tuning the split may build longer lasting cell therapy.
pmc-13311172:
Sara Parviz and co-authors test scan measures for a harsh womb cancer subtype in a 2026 study. Endometrial cancer with abnormal p53 protein fares worse, and tissue tests remain the gold standard. Magnetic scans offer a noninvasive hint if water motion in the tumor splits the subtypes well.

Records covered 115 patients scanned on standard machines, with subtype set by tissue stains. Mean water motion values ran notably lower in the abnormal group. Other scan traits showed no clear link. A cutoff value sorted subtypes with full sensitivity and strong specificity in this set. Joint models named water motion and tissue type as the key drivers.
pmc-13311572:
Alastair Fung and co-authors build a 2026 prediction model for serious illness in young babies in Dhaka, Bangladesh, using signs gathered by community health workers on home visits. The aim is to beat the current eight danger signs.

The study followed 1906 healthy newborns through eleven home visits in their first 60 days. About 9.2 percent were hospitalized or died in this cohort. Two models, a time-based regression and a random forest, used visit patterns such as repeated fever rather than one-off signs. Their accuracy and calibration were set against a model using the standard danger signs alone.
pmc-13311972:
Daisy Shepherd and colleagues present a 2026 Australian study mapping speech sound development in children to help doctors spot true speech disorder. No fresh English normative data had appeared in over twenty years.

The team assessed 1179 children aged two to just under thirteen at 24 sites in New South Wales and Victoria. Skill varied widely up to age six, and by age seven 90 percent could make all sounds. Errors flagged as disordered included sound swaps, vowel errors, and backing sounds. Against old norms, sounds now arrive more slowly. The fresh benchmarks tell clinicians which errors can be watched and which need referral.
pmc-13312972:
Afnan A. Nassar and co-authors survey, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, what kinds of face and mouth pain bring patients to a university dental hospital in Makkah, Saudi Arabia. The survey also asks how that pain weighs on their daily lives. One hundred four adults with orofacial pain received standardized diagnoses and completed the OHIP-14 questionnaire on oral health's impact on quality of life.

Pain from inside the tooth, endodontic pain, dominated at 80.8 percent of cases, followed by decay-related problems at 12.5 percent and gum pain at 3.8 percent. The median impact score of 28 signaled a moderate drag on quality of life, with functional limits, physical pain, and psychological discomfort reported most often. The authors urge earlier diagnosis and targeted care, while noting the one-clinic sample and lopsided sex mix limit how far the findings travel.
pmc-13313272:
Sachin Aryal and a large team report in 2026 that gut microbes can lower blood pressure through a bile acid. Gut bacteria and bile acids both shape blood pressure, but the chain of cause was not clear, so the team probed the bile acid receptor TGR5.

Using gene editing, they made rats that lack TGR5 on a salt-sensitive background prone to high pressure. Those rats had lower blood pressure than control rats, a shifted gut microbe mix, and more of one bile acid, glycodeoxycholic acid. Feeding that acid to normal rats copied the microbe shift and lowered pressure as well. Moving gut contents by transplant also carried the effect, as the report has it. The work ties microbes, bile acid, and pressure into one testable path.
pmc-13314472:
Quan He and colleagues screen for long non-coding RNAs tied to hepatitis B passing from mother to baby, in a study put out in 2026. Even with antibody shots and vaccines, some babies of mothers who carry the virus surface antigen still get infected, and why prevention fails is not understood.

The team took blood immune cells from babies where prevention worked, babies where it failed, and healthy controls. Full RNA sequencing flagged genes and long non-coding RNAs that differed between groups. Function and pathway maps then hinted at what those RNAs do. A co-expression network linked the long RNAs to partner genes in antiviral defense. Chosen candidates were checked further, as the authors describe. The work may yield early markers of babies at risk and fresh ways to block transmission.
pmc-13314572:
Ana Pilar Javierre Miranda, Coro Sánchez Hernández, and Jose Javier Gómez Marco weigh the pros and cons of making the official vaccine calendar mandatory, in a Spanish paper published in 2026. Vaccination is among the most effective public health tools, and the World Health Organization credits it with saving millions of lives a year.

The authors cite the WHO estimate, given in the text, that shots prevent roughly 3.5 to 5 million deaths a year from diseases such as diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough, flu, and measles. Vaccine calendars set doses by age and sex and by personal traits such as chronic disease, travel, or job. Spain set its first child calendar in 1975, as the report notes. The piece weighs forcing compliance against the aim of the widest cover for the target group, guarding even those who cannot be vaccinated.
pmc-13314772:
Tiantian Song and colleagues grade the flood of death-risk models for acute-on-chronic liver failure in their 2026 review. This liver syndrome races ahead and kills many in weeks, so doctors lean on scores to triage care, yet the worth of scores on offer was murky.

The team searched four databases to the end of 2025. They screened 9447 studies, keeping 185 that covered 241 outside test cohorts and 75 distinct models, by the report counts. Standard tools judged study quality and bias risk. Nearly all study units, at a share near 99.51 percent as stated in the report, carried a high bias risk. Pooled accuracy scores were also worked out. The harsh verdict urges care in picking a model for real bedsides.
pmc-13315172:
Palla Ranga Prasad and many co-authors review progress in 2026 toward building a replacement windpipe in the lab. Damage from swelling, injury, birth defects, or tumors can block breathing, and current options such as stents, grafts, and repair surgery often fail for long damaged sections.

The review weighs cell sources, scaffold materials, and printing methods, with close attention to 3D bioprinting. Multi-material printing that places several cell types in set patterns looks most promising for copying the windpipe's mix of tissues and strength. No fully working printed human graft exists yet, and the authors stress blood supply, nerve growth, and lasting function as the main hurdles.
pmc-13315572:
Ahmed N. Hegazy comments in 2026 on new work that finds a brake on a key gut inflammation signal in inflammatory bowel disease. In this disease, macrophages gather in the gut lining and keep making cytokines that damage tissue, and oncostatin M is one signal that also predicts failure of anti-TNF therapy.

The study under discussion shows the enzyme USP9X trims a specific ubiquitin tag from STAT1, which limits STAT1 entry to the nucleus and lowers oncostatin M output. Losing that brake in myeloid cells worsened lab colitis, and blocking oncostatin M reversed the harm. The pathway may offer a fresh treatment target.
pmc-13315672:
Zhaoying Liu and colleagues developed a new dental filling resin in 2026 to fight film buildup and water breakdown, two long-standing weaknesses of standard composites. They made a fluorinated polyurethane monomer and added surface-treated PEEK filler at levels from zero to 7.5 percent by weight to build test resins.

Checks confirmed both new parts. More filler lowered curing depth and conversion, yet every mix still met ISO standards, and water uptake did not differ between groups. Strength, stiffness, polish, early bacterial sticking, and cell safety were all measured before and after aging. The blend aims for a tougher, longer-lasting filling material.
pmc-13316272:
Huan Zhang and a large team deleted the mitochondrial transporter gene Sfxn5 in mice in 2026 and traced the fatal fallout. Mitochondrial disorders often strike through liver metabolic crises, so the team combined biochemical, metabolomic, tissue, and ultrastructure analysis in a global knockout model.

Every pup lacking the gene died after birth amid metabolic collapse and growing multi-organ failure. The liver was the main injury site, with damaged mitochondria and wide disruption of the energy cycle, fat burning, and ammonia cleanup, causing high blood ammonia. Restoring the gene only in liver partly rescued metabolism and eased organ damage.
pmc-13316372:
Hendrik Eismann and colleagues ran a 2026 randomized study with German advanced paramedic teams, asking whether yearly training should stress hands-on technical skills or teamwork skills instead. Teams were split by lot, trained with one focus, then tested six months later in a simulated emergency.

Scoring of timing, key steps, and finished tasks showed no clear edge for either training focus, and use of incident management methods also matched between groups. Checklists were rarely used by anyone. Worryingly, over half the teams missed a quarter or more of the needed steps in the scenario. The authors argue teamwork skills are still not routine and that checklists could lift care, whatever the training theme.
pmc-13317672:
Hanadi Qeyam, Ahmed Al-Rusan, and Robert Dellavalle grade, in a 2026 content analysis, ChatGPT's answers to common sun protection and skin cancer questions against dermatology academy guidelines. The public increasingly asks chatbots for health advice, so its accuracy deserves checking.

Nine standard questions went to the free GPT-4 tier in one session in May 2025, and two senior dermatologists scored replies on accuracy, completeness, clarity, and relevance. Accuracy and clarity hit perfect marks, relevance nearly so, and the overall mean reached 4.75 out of 5.0 in the panel scoring. Completeness lagged, with gaps from missing details rather than wrong claims. The raters agreed strongly. Chatbots may support, never replace, professional advice, the authors caution.
pmc-13317772:
Fathima Anooshiya Mohamed Hassan Abdul Razak and colleagues weigh, in a 2026 study, how to choose between upfront surgery and chemotherapy first for advanced ovarian cancer. Clearing every visible tumor is the strongest survival lever there. Their data come from 818 patients treated at Qilu Hospital between 2014 and 2023.

Chemo-first patients carried heavier tumors yet achieved full clearing more often, at 56.40 percent versus 39.90 percent for upfront surgery in the reported rates. Overall survival ran slightly longer after upfront surgery, while time without progression matched. Age, a marker called CA153, blood calcium, and incomplete clearing predicted survival on their own. Models joining CA153 to a standard score predicted clearing well, aiding case-by-case choices.
pmc-13318672:
Leizhen Xia and co-authors present a 2026 retrospective cohort study of fertility treatment. They ask whether adding luteinizing hormone helps women of advanced reproductive age. The study covers assisted reproduction cycles from 2015 to 2024. It includes 2,316 women in three stimulation groups.

One group used follicle stimulating hormone alone. Others added recombinant LH or human menopausal gonadotropin. Matching balanced the groups before comparison. The combined LH group reached a cumulative live birth rate of 61.31 percent. The hormone-alone group reached 51.48 percent in the matched comparison. Adjusted models also favoured added recombinant LH over both alternatives. Fresh transfer results did not differ, and the authors warn against causal claims.
pmc-13318872:
