Alberto Jarrin Lopez, Hanmin Lee, and Sunghoon Kim report a 2026 chart review of freezing-based pain relief during chest wall repair in young children. The Nuss procedure corrects sunken chest but hurts afterwards. Cryoanalgesia is approved only above age twelve, so its use below that age is off-label. Outcomes in younger children were poorly known.

Ten children treated between August 2019 and July 2023 met the criteria. Their mean age was 10.1 years, and most were boys. Median opioid use was 0.96 morphine-equivalent units per kilogram during the stay. Median hospital stay was two days, and pain scores fell to zero by day one. Two complications occurred, neither blamed on the freezing technique. No lasting numbness or pain appeared by nine months.
pmc-13318972:
Qiongqiu Zhao and colleagues present a 2026 randomised comparison of Tai Chi and brisk walking for older adults with peripheral neuropathy. Nerve damage dulls feeling in the soles and ankle position sense, raising fall risk. Thirty-eight participants were assigned to one practice or the other. Each programme ran eight weeks with three hour-long sessions weekly.

Tai Chi produced larger drops in touch detection thresholds at the forefoot and heel. Lower thresholds mean sharper sensation. Ankle position sense during downward movement also improved more with Tai Chi. Both practices improved upward ankle sensing over time. Exercise intensity was held at 55 to 65 percent of maximum heart rate in both groups. The authors rate Tai Chi as the stronger option here.
pmc-13319172:
Mira L. Katz leads a large team reporting a 2026 randomised trial of a streamlined genetic counselling model for women at raised breast cancer risk. The Know Your Risk programme swaps a pre-test session for online videos. It adds direct access to testing and optional post-test counselling. Conventional counselling formed the comparison arm. In total, 866 women were randomised between 2022 and 2024.

Knowledge scores rose in both groups. The programme group reached a mean of 8.66 on a twelve-point scale after counselling. The conventional group reached 8.56 in the same window. Risk accuracy, attitudes, and satisfaction also met the non-inferiority bar. The authors argue the lighter model makes counselling and testing more accessible and patient-driven without losing quality.
pmc-13319372:
Jinyu Wang and co-authors study blood flow in the brain for people with Parkinson disease in a 2026 article. Many in this group feel dizzy on standing because blood pressure drops, a fault that may also starve the brain and harm thinking. Sound wave checks were used to watch flow speed in a main brain vessel while people lay flat and stood up.

Those with the standing drop plus a weak flow response scored lower on a thinking test and showed more thinking decline than other groups. Flow speed also fell as scores fell. The authors read the standing drop as a sign of wider strain in the body, one that tracks with weaker thinking.
pmc-13319972:
Xuyong Zhao and co-authors probe a plant compound as care for heart harm from diabetes in a 2026 study mixing computer maps and lab tests. The compound has guarded heart cells in past work on blood flow harm and cell death, but its path in sugar linked heart disease stayed murky. Network maps first flagged likely targets, then cell tests checked those leads.

In heart cells stressed by high sugar, the compound cut scar markers, swelling signals, and a fiery form of cell death. Two targets stood out in the maps and bound the compound well in docking tests. One target was then silenced in cells to confirm its part in the death path. The results name fresh leads for drug design against sugar linked heart harm.
pmc-13320272:
Julia Brake and co-authors study how type 1 diabetes changes the duel between immune guard cells and tuberculosis germs in a 2026 lab study. Diabetes raises the risk of active lung tuberculosis around the world, yet the cell level reasons stay hazy. Guard cells grown from blood of people with type 1 diabetes and healthy peers were infected with the germ and read on both sides at once.

Defense gene switches flipped in much the same way in both groups, but one key alarm signal ran lower in diabetes cells at both gene and protein levels. Germs inside both cell types showed stress and shut down their metabolism. Tight links between host defense genes and germ wall genes seen in healthy cells mostly vanished in diabetes cells. The paired data set opens new hunts for the fault.
pmc-13320672:
Philip J. Wilson offers a deliberately simple climate model for the general public in a 2026 article. Full climate reports from the IPCC use complex models that most readers find hard to follow. Wilson instead takes the straight trend line in recent global warming data and extends it forward as the forecast.

Over 1974 to 2023, warming ran close to a straight line at 0.20 degrees per decade on average. Shorter recent windows gave similar or slightly higher rates, up to 0.27 degrees per decade for 2005 to 2024. Extending that latest line puts 1.5 degrees of warming in 2029 and 2 degrees in 2047. The exercise is one readers can repeat themselves.
pmc-13322172:
Aina Pons and colleagues link social life, habitat, and gut germs in a sea fish in a 2026 field study near Mallorca, Spain. Tracking free living fish and sampling their gut germs at once is hard, so the team used fine acoustic tracking on the pearly razorfish, Xyrichtys novacula. Movement paths were logged for 232 fish over many days.

A recaptured subset gave gut samples sorted into core and non-core germ groups. Fish living nearer seagrass meadows held richer non-core germ mixes, above all larger fish. Overall germ makeup did not differ clearly by size, territory, social ties, or sex, though core germs weakly tracked harem structure. Local habitat, more than social rank, seems to shape the gut mix.
pmc-13323172:
Chi-Hsin Chen and a large team test machine learning against rule-based selection for extracorporeal resuscitation, in a 2026 study of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in Taiwan. Records came from four tertiary centres between 2016 and 2024, covering adults with non-traumatic arrest attended by emergency services.

After matching on shockable rhythm and witnessed arrest, a causal forest built on boosted trees estimated each patient's treatment effect and likely survival gain to discharge. The team compared real benefit across model thresholds with entry rules drawn from the ARREST, PRAGUE OHCA and INCEPTION trials. Their aim was a selection method that captures varied treatment response, rather than treating all rule-eligible patients as equal candidates.
pmc-13323872:
Lee and colleagues hunted for skin anti-aging peptides in 2026 inside microbes that survive extreme radiation. Sunlight's ultraviolet rays flood skin with reactive oxygen, breaking down collagen and driving photoaging. The team profiled gene activity in two radiation-hardy microbes, built peptide libraries from the stress-response data. Ranked candidates with a seven-model machine learning screen plus docking simulations against a key antioxidant control pocket.

Forty-eight sequences passed the docking test, and the team made the top 21 in the lab. Seven blocked collagenase, the enzyme that chews collagen, at the test dose. Four raised a collagen building marker in ultraviolet-damaged skin cells in step with dose, lifted the main collagen gene, and cut two breakdown enzymes at gene and protein level. The authors offer the pipeline, joining omics, learning models, and docking, as a reusable route to stress-based peptide discovery.
pmc-13324672:
Josefina Peláez Zuberbuhler and colleagues ask whether good leadership softens the harm of workplace violence for Swedish health staff in a 2026 survey study. Violence at work can push staff toward harmful drinking and later burnout.

Two survey waves from the Longitudinal Occupational Health Survey in Healthcare Sweden covered 2,446 workers. Violence, drinking, and leadership climate were rated first, with burnout measured later. Violence linked to heavier drinking, but the link weakened where leadership climate was strong. The path from violence through drinking to later burnout showed only under weak leadership. No firm split appeared between doctors and nurses. Supportive leaders may offer modest shelter in violent workplaces.
pmc-13325072:
Zhaoyi Liu and co-authors build a neural system that forecasts shale gas fracturing pressure in real time in a 2026 study. Wellhead pressure reveals formation changes and risks such as sand blockage during hydraulic fracturing.

The design pairs a multiscale one-dimensional convolutional network, which reads both sudden jumps and slow trends, with a temporal fusion transformer for timing patterns. A gentle online learning step updates the model as conditions drift, using a first-in buffer and smoothed weights. On field data the static model already beat rivals, with mean error of 3.21 MPa on the pressure scale. Online updates cut error to 1.98 MPa, a gain of about 38 percent.
pmc-13326572:
Xinyu Shi and colleagues survey how coercive care feels to psychiatric inpatients in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Restraint, forced medication, and seclusion are common on such wards and can wound a patient sense of control.

A total of 161 patients on wards for children, teens, and adults at a Chengdu hospital completed Chinese scales for coercion, resilience, and social support. Lower schooling linked to stronger felt coercion. Resilience correlated with lower coercion scores at r of minus 0.355, and support at minus 0.178 on the reported scales. In joint models, resilience stayed a firm negative predictor. Building resilience may soften harsh ward experiences.
pmc-13328272:
Argajit Sarkar, Epsita Ghosh, and Surajit Bhattacharjee use generative AI to run a gum disease forecast in a 2026 study. Working from records of 416 dental hospital patients, a prompted AI pipeline handled cleaning, correlation checks, and building six learning models for periodontitis severity from body-wide and personal indicators alone. Severe disease meant the top community periodontal index score.

Models separated cases only modestly, with AUC values from 0.48 to 0.57 across the set, though logistic regression hit 72 percent accuracy and the support vector machine caught 89 percent of severe cases. Age and blood sugar ranked as the strongest predictors, matching known risk factors. In low-resource clinics, such screening could flag who needs a full dental exam first.
pmc-13329872:
Yiran Rong and co-authors compare heart ablation outcomes with and without advanced imaging in a 2026 study of Medicare records. Patients aged 65 or older had catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation. One group had intracardiac ultrasound plus three-dimensional mapping during the procedure, while the other did not.

The group without advanced imaging held 35,490 patients, and the group with it held 170,762 patients in the reported counts. After weighting to balance traits, problems within 30 days were far more common without imaging guidance. Heart puncture, a rare food pipe injury, and death were each higher in that group as well. The authors link imaging guidance to safer ablation in older patients.
pmc-13330572:
Rosemary Muk Ting and colleagues test a positioning aid for men receiving radiotherapy to the upper thigh in a 2026 report. The Ting-Sling holds the external genitalia clear of the treatment zone for sarcoma care. Patients and therapy staff rated the device on a five-point scale for positioning, modesty, and overall experience, with written comments also gathered.

Nearly all patients, 98 percent in the reported ratings, judged the device good or excellent. Staff approval reached 87 percent in those summaries. Patients valued genital covering and preserved modesty during treatment. Limb positioning for thigh tumours is hard to standardise, the authors note, and genital handling had no prior guidance. A simple sling may fill that gap.
pmc-13330672:
Yulan D Chen and colleagues sum up findings from the ABCD Study on thinking skills and youth mental health in a 2026 review. The study follows children across five waves from ages 9 to 14 with long-term, multi-type data. Symptoms covered range from low mood and anxiety to conduct problems, psychotic-like experiences, and substance use.

Weak planning and working memory tied most steadily to outward behaviour problems and attention disorders in the summed work. Links for inward symptoms varied more. Psychotic-like experiences showed firm, lasting ties to thinking skills. Brain and gene data pointed to shared pathways within some conditions. Effects were mostly small, as expected in community groups. Early thinking marks may guide targeted help.
pmc-13331172:
Takahiro Morita and colleagues report rescue use of clazosentan for brain vessel spasm after bleeding in a 2026 case. A 61-year-old man bled from a ruptured fistula in the front skull base. After surgical closure, preventive drug care failed to stop severe spasm in both front and middle brain arteries by day 10, with growing drowsiness.

Direct artery drug doses helped only briefly. Clazosentan then ran for 4 days as rescue care, and vessel imaging showed marked widening, most of all in small far vessels. Fluid build-up was handled with diuretics without breathing decline. No brain infarction arose, and the patient transferred out with a near-normal function score.
pmc-13331772:
Soyeon Jeon and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study on what happens when aged plastic particles, closer to what people actually breathe, reach the lungs. They made polystyrene nanoplastics in round and broken shapes and weathered some under ultraviolet light to mimic time outdoors.

The broken and light-aged particles carried more surface oxidation and stronger chemical reactivity than smooth new spheres. After a single dose placed into the airways, the weathered broken particles caused sharper lung inflammation, with immune cell counts 3.9-fold higher at the top dose than for plain spheres. The early inflammation mostly faded, yet broken particles cleared from the lungs far more slowly, with a half-life of 27.4 days against 13.5 days for spheres. The authors conclude that real-world aged nanoplastics may carry greater breathing risks than the fresh particles usually tested.
pmc-13333772:
Trina Sengupta, Hruda Nanda Mallick, and Raj Kumar Yadav wrote a 2026 full review of MSG safety for infants and breastfeeding mothers. Regulators keep coming back to MSG, so the team pulled together the research and agency record.

Following PRISMA 2020 guidance, five sources were searched through August 2025 and two readers screened 3,800 records. Thirty-five studies and agency reports qualified, spanning randomized trials, observational work, animal studies, and agency reviews. Human evidence consistently showed fast MSG metabolism and stable MSG levels in breast milk whatever the mother ate. Findings were summed up in words because the studies differed too much to pool. The review gives parents and officials a balanced, current account of a long-debated flavor enhancer.
pmc-13336372:
Jian Du and co-authors identified a host protein that Japanese encephalitis virus exploits to keep cellular recycling running in its favor in a 2026 virology study. The virus threatens people and livestock, and the RNA-modification tricks behind its replication were little known.

The zinc-finger protein ZNF33B recruits METTL14 and steadies the m6A writer complex, raising global m6A levels. It then binds modified sites on the antiviral transcript Trim25 and speeds its decay. TRIM25 normally tags the autophagy protein ATG7 for destruction, restraining autophagy. With TRIM25 gone, autophagy flows freely and the virus replicates in a friendlier cell. Delivering ZNF33B into mouse brains raised m6A and lowered Trim25 there too, confirming the proviral circuit in vivo.
pmc-13336472:
Yuxin Ke and co-authors learned to control the intergrowths that form when two zeolite frameworks grow together in a 2026 catalysis study. Silicoaluminophosphate zeolites earn their keep as catalysts, but mixed and intergrown crystals blur results and defy tidy synthesis.

The team varied pH, silicon content, and the amount and ratio of structure-directing agents. They mapped where pure SAPO-5 forms versus SAPO-34/18 intergrowths and mixtures, and framed selectivity as a race between thermodynamics and kinetics. Low-dose electron microscopy then imaged the beam-sensitive intergrowths at atomic resolution, exposing their stacking order and how silicon level and agent ratio rearrange them. The joined recipe, synthesis windows plus atomic pictures, offers a template for mastering other finicky framework solids.
pmc-13337372:
Min Wei and co-authors follow a hard course of a rare lung cancer in a 2026 case report. A 42-year-old woman had EBV-linked pulmonary lymphoepithelioma-like carcinoma, first at stage IIIB. Surgery plus follow-up chemoradiation left no clear local return, yet neck lymph nodes were involved soon after and the disease reached stage IV with liver spread.

Pembrolizumab with chemotherapy first shrank the disease partly. Later, persistent high fever resisted antibiotics and repeatedly interrupted treatment; tumor fever was judged most likely, though hidden infection could not be fully excluded. Blood EBV-DNA levels rose and fell in step with disease activity throughout. The case shows how fever and fast spread can stall even promising combined therapy.
pmc-13337772:
Wilma Grönroos and a large team follow breathing infections in pro ice hockey during one Finnish season in 2026. Three elite league teams were tracked for seven months in 2022 to 2023. Players gave nose swabs when symptoms began, and one team also gave monthly swabs without symptoms.

Among 81 players, 93 percent had at least one respiratory illness and 17 percent had three or more in the reported counts. A virus was found in 65 percent of 129 cases, spanning 23 different viruses. Coronavirus, rhinoviruses, and influenza A were most common. Cluster patterns hint at spread within teams, including cases without symptoms that still carried virus.
pmc-13339772:
Antonella Cutrupi and colleagues measure the free-carrier share in layered perovskites from light output in a 2026 study. Whether light creates bound pairs or free charges decides how solar and light devices should be built. Simple power-law reading oversimplifies the middle ground.

Full analysis tied power-dependent peak glow to the Saha balance equation. Layered crystals of varied thickness covered wide binding energies as test cases. Recovered binding energies matched known values, confirming the method as reported. Mapping showed the free share varies across a sample, giving device builders a simple probe of excited-state character.
pmc-13341472:
Blocking the protein BRD4 attacks stomach cancer through its MYC engine, in a 2026 study by Xu-Liang Liao and colleagues. MYC is hyperactive in gastric cancer but hard to drug directly, so the team targeted BRD4, a co-activator that keeps MYC-driven survival programs running.

Large datasets showed BRD4 raised in tumors and tied to MYC activity, later stage, and shorter survival. Deleting BRD4 or breaking it down with the PROTAC drug ARV771 cut the survival protein BCL2 and slowed tumors. Mouse xenograft tests checked both benefit and safety. The work positions BRD4 as a reachable weak point in advanced disease.
pmc-13342172:
Protein-folding stress gone wrong drives diabetic kidney damage, in a 2026 review by Hao Zhang and colleagues. Diabetes floods kidney cells with glucose, fat, and protein load, keeping the unfolded protein response switched on until its three branches, PERK, IRE1α, and ATF6, turn from repair to harm.

Chronic activation in podocytes and tubule cells feeds inflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial failure, and scarring, while cross-talk with apoptosis, ferroptosis, pyroptosis, and other death routes decides cell fate. The review closes with therapeutic strategies aimed at retuning this response. Since diabetic kidney disease leads global kidney failure statistics, its stress circuitry is prime drug territory.
pmc-13342972:
Marta Musidlowska, Michiel Fierens, and Isabela Maria Rosal examine the European Health Data Space in a 2026 legal analysis. The European Union is building shared data spaces to spur innovation and personal services. Yet the authors see tension between Europe's push for digital autonomy and its founding values of solidarity and cooperation.

Health data rules rest on an internal market treaty article, which limits broader global aims and engagement with non-EU countries. The authors propose data cosmopolitanism, an extension of solidarity, as a frame for worldwide health data sharing grounded in social justice and equal access to care. Their argument offers a path beyond a closed single market for data.
pmc-13343272:
David Higgins and co-authors offer a 2026 practitioner's view on why machine learning donor selection for stem cell transplants stalls before reaching clinics. Models keep improving on paper, yet wards barely use them, so the team draws lessons from a federally funded Berlin incubation project run from 2021 to 2023.

Registry data, they argue, was never built for learning algorithms and needs rethinking from the ground up, with shared multi-center infrastructure as a prerequisite. Teams should gather broader clinical measures and test tools in forward-looking studies tied to standard care. The authors also warn about regulatory load, true resource costs, and market incentives that quietly block adoption.
pmc-13343472:
Laura A. Hillmann, Thomas D. Sharkey, and Todd C. Einhorn explain apple fruitlet drop through sugar status in a 2026 orchard study. Young apples compete for tree carbohydrates, and the weakest usually fall, so the team tracked sugars, starch, and growth in Gala and Honeycrisp fruitlets across two seasons after chemical thinning.

Small fruitlets carried lower soluble sugars and slower growth before dropping, while larger ones kept higher sugars and piled up starch, marking stronger sinks. King fruitlets beat side fruitlets on sugar, though size explained most of that edge. Once size entered the picture, flower position stopped mattering: weight and sugar together foretold which fruitlets the tree would keep.
pmc-13345472:
Ryo Yoshikawa and co-authors test whether three-dimensional knee gap measures beat flat X-ray measures at foretelling arthritis worsening in 2026. Using the Multicenter Osteoarthritis Study, the team measured joint space width on standing CT scans and standard radiographs for 425 knees and tracked structural change over 24 months.

In the 302-person analysis set, plain radiograph width predicted inner knee narrowing better than a basic demographic model, while the 3D measure added nothing on that side. Side and cartilage outcomes scored nearly identically for both methods. Most knees lacked clear radiographic arthritis at the start, and the authors leave standing CT a promising tool still hunting for its best role.
pmc-13345672:
Hosameldin Abdelrahman Ahmed and co-authors chart a treatment revolution for bowel disease in the United Arab Emirates in a 2026 registry study. The cohort holds 508 patients, 333 with Crohn's disease and 175 with ulcerative colitis, treated at one tertiary center across 2015 to 2025 as drug options widened past anti-TNF agents.

Three quarters received advanced therapy. First-line anti-TNF use in Crohn's fell from 76 percent before 2023 to 42 percent after, while anti-IL-23 drugs claimed 32 percent of first starts. Time to first advanced drug collapsed from 23 months to 2 months in Crohn's, and anti-IL-23 therapy stuck longest with a far lower stopping risk. Early surgery stayed rare in both eras.
pmc-13345872:
Baitong Chen and co-authors characterize a killer bacterium pulled from farmed snakes in China in 2026. The strain, named NM-11 and confirmed as Morganella morganii by gene and genome checks, came from diseased and dead snakes and had never been documented in Chinese snake stocks before.

Challenge tests in the rat snake Ptyas mucosus produced depression, loose stools, and bleeding across the belly, lungs, and gut, with heavy organ damage under the microscope. The strain resisted many drugs at once, including polymyxin B, tetracycline, and several cephalosporins. Infection also reshaped the snakes' gut microbe mix and boosted diversity. The report gives reptile vets a diagnostic foothold and a public health warning.
pmc-13346672:
Océane Boulais and colleagues test whether playing healthy reef sounds draws young reef fish toward new habitat, in a field study from 2026. Autonomous cameras, speakers, and water microphones were set on sand at 5 m depth in Kāneʻohe Bay, Hawaiʻi, across three spawning events in 2023 and 2024. Active and silent sites were swapped between runs.

Larval counts peaked near the new moon at both sites. Yet the sound site drew 4 to 14 times more larvae in the reported counts, while adult fish numbers stayed alike. Camera watching without divers let the team follow the pattern over long parts of the lunar cycle, supporting sound as a restoration aid.
pmc-13347672:
Mosoka P. Fallah and a large team report how ethics review ran during an African mpox study, in a multicountry account from 2026. Cases rose across 20 member states in 2024, prompting a continental emergency call. A joint response team set up a research pillar that produced a master plan plus ten country plans within a month.

Approvals still took 3 to 11 weeks across countries, with most finishing in 4 to 8 weeks in the reported timelines, well above the speed an outbreak demands. Routine review can take 2 to 9 weeks even outside emergencies, so the authors press for deeper fast-track reform so trials can start while data matter most.
pmc-13349772:
Shijie Jiang and colleagues compare tumour shelling against standard partial kidney removal, in a meta-analysis from 2026. Six databases to May 2026 gave 17 studies with 5,249 patients with localised, mostly early kidney tumours. Pooled outcomes covered kidney function after surgery, margin safety, and major complications under random-effects models.

Shelling kept higher kidney function, with a mean edge of 5.64 units and a smaller drop from baseline in the reported pools. Major complications fell with an odds ratio of 0.48 for the shelling group. Margin risk did not rise, surgery ran shorter with less blood loss, yet long-term cancer control could not be pooled, leaving that question open.
pmc-13351572:
Jing Chen leads a 2026 single-centre cohort study of growth hormone treatment in children with Turner syndrome. Real-world guidance on when to start treatment and how safe it is remains limited. The study followed 50 children aged 3 to 14 years who received recombinant human growth hormone for at least 6 months.

Children were seen twice a year across as many as 36 months, with height scores and safety measures tracked. Mean height rose from 114.50 cm at baseline to 132.82 cm after 36 months, and height scores improved. Blood sugar control stayed stable in the safety group. Longer treatment and higher starting height linked to better outcomes, and children who started earlier gained height faster in the first year.
pmc-13353072:
Gaurav Jain leads a 2026 lab study of ceftaroline against MRSA isolates at a North India tertiary hospital. MRSA resists many standard antibiotics, and local data on the newer drug ceftaroline are scarce. Non-repeat MRSA samples from patients aged 1 year or older were gathered over two years and typed by an automated system, with E-test strips giving ceftaroline potency.

Of 180 patients assessed, 167 isolates entered the final analysis, with mean patient age of 34.51 years and 61.7 percent male. Surgical departments supplied 59.3 percent of isolates, and most patients were ward-based. Surgical site infections led diagnoses at 36.5 percent, followed by skin and soft tissue infections at 18.0 percent.
pmc-13353172:
Monireh Sadat Seyyedsalehi leads a 2026 pooled analysis of cadmium exposure and pancreatic cancer risk. Pancreatic cancer is highly lethal with few treatment options, and heavy metals may feed its causes. Following PRISMA guidance, three databases were searched, yielding 18 studies with 20 risk estimates for pooled random-effects analysis.

Overall, cadmium exposure linked to higher pancreatic cancer risk, with a relative risk of 1.69. Workplace exposure gave the steadiest link at 1.38, followed by urine and blood markers. Risk ran higher in men than women and in case-control than cohort designs. No straight dose-response trend emerged. Bias checks were mostly reassuring, with some asymmetry in urine studies.
pmc-13354872:
Ximenes and colleagues test a targeted antioxidant, called mitoquinone, in rats after a heart attack. The drug goes straight to mitochondria, the cell's power units. Those units leak harmful oxygen forms after an attack. The team gave the drug by mouth for seven days. Treated rats kept more body weight. Their hearts pumped with better force. Heart muscle strips also pulled with near normal strength.

In single heart cells, the drug cut swelling and kept shortening strong. It also cut harmful oxygen forms in the cells. One harm-linked protein fell, while guard proteins held steady. The team says guarding mitochondria early may stop later heart failure.
pmc-13355272:
Gregory M Hemenway and Daniel M Geynisman write a 2026 commentary on final results from the CheckMate 9ER trial in advanced kidney cancer. The trial tested nivolumab plus cabozantinib, an immune drug paired with a targeted drug, against an older single drug. Follow-up ran for a median of 5.6 years, among the longest for such pairings.

The pairing nearly doubled the time before cancer grew and added about eleven months to median survival versus the older drug. Gains held across most risk groups, though not clearly in the lowest-risk group, and no new safety issues arose. The writers say the durable gains confirm the pairing as a front-line standard.
pmc-13360472:
Aishwarya Devanand led a 2026 study of software that helps doctors read capsule endoscopy videos. Patients swallow a tiny camera pill that films the small bowel, but watching the footage takes long and tires readers. The TOP100 tool uses artificial intelligence to flag the key frames. The team compared its finds with expert human reading on cases done from January 2023 to August 2025.

Out of 1,382 exams, 1,374 had full data for the check. The most common reason for the exam was inflammatory bowel disease. Two blinded passes, one by experts and one with the tool, let the team weigh how well the software caught key findings across many reasons for testing. Tools that safely shorten reading time could ease a real bottleneck in bowel care.
pmc-13362072:
Lei Sheng and co-authors mined 218 rapeseed transcriptomes to study the microbes living in rapeseed seeds in a 2026 paper. Rapeseed is a top world oil crop, and its seeds carry microbes that pass to the next generation. Those passengers shape the young plant's growth, yield, and quality. Yet the seed microbiome as a whole lacked systematic study, so the team reused published gene-activity data from 218 seed samples.

They compared microbe makeup in seeds grown normally, under biological attack, and under stresses like drought. The work maps how the community shifts and what functions change with conditions. The authors note a caveat: the source data had no surface-sterilization control, so some reads may come from the seed coat. Even so, the sweep gives breeders a first atlas of the seed's inner life.
pmc-13362672:
Yasemin Ünver and colleagues describe a 2026 chemistry study of four new sulfonate compounds built with triazole and hydrazone parts. The team made the compounds, proved their shapes with standard spectra, and used computer models to map their charge patterns and light behavior. They then tested the set against brain tumor cells, other cancer cells, healthy cells, and germs.

One compound stood out: it hit neuroblastoma and glioblastoma cells hard while sparing healthy fibroblast cells far more. Two others worked well on a mutant glioma line. Computer checks suggest the shapes move charge in ways that suit both drug action and light-based uses. Lab tests in animals or patients remain future work, but the lead compound gives drug hunters a clear start.
pmc-13362872: The journal Molecules, through its Editorial Office, issued a 2026 expression of concern about a 2020 paper by Ahsan and colleagues on silver nanoparticles made with Parthenium hysterophorus, a weed plant. The notice flags Figure 3 of that paper: the size spread shown does not match the particle size the text reports. The authors have been asked for the raw data and an explanation. The inquiry is still open and no verdict has been reached, so readers are warned to treat the results with care until the journal updates the notice.
pmc-13363672:
Jing Wang and colleagues present a 2026 study on a greener way to extract saponins, prized medicinal compounds, from the herb Panax japonicus. Instead of methanol, they used deep eutectic solvents, safe liquid blends, helped by ultrasound. After screening 26 blends, a choline chloride and urea mix won, and step-by-step tests tuned the ratio, water share, heat, and time.

The tuned method pulled a saponin yield about an eighth higher than the official methanol method. Computer simulations showed why: the solvent's hydrogen bonds pry saponin clumps apart so they dissolve freely, with one target saponin solvated more strongly than the other. The authors propose the recipe as an industrial, lower-harm extraction route.
pmc-13363772:
José María Vadillo and colleagues present a 2026 study adapting a crop growth model, VegSyst, from greenhouses to open fields in Spain's Extremadura region. The model forecasts dry matter growth and nitrogen uptake, the two numbers that guide fair fertilizer dosing and curb nitrate pollution. They calibrated it on five seasons of field data for processing peppers and broccoli at varied nitrogen doses, building nitrogen dilution curves for each crop.

pmc-13380972:

pmc-13389072:

pmc-13390972:

pmc-13391372:

pmc-13391472:

pmc-13393072:

pmc-13393272:

pmc-13394472:

pmc-13394872:

pmc-13396872:

pmc-13398872:

pmc-13405072:

pmc-13408072:

pmc-13409272:

pmc-13436572:

pmc-13436672:

Ions that grip wall charges, such as sodium and uranyl, curbed skin reshaping and nudged cells toward wire-led uranium capture. Other ion mixes favored skin bubble release instead. The authors warn that broth ions can flip study results, so clean-up tests must match field water with care.
pmc-13443172:
Maxime Amoyel and colleagues review the stomach as a small but real microbe home in a 2026 paper. Acid once led doctors to call the stomach sterile, yet gene reads show a shaped microbe set. The hard task is to split true residents from mouth or food passers-by.

Healthy stomach walls host five broad microbe phyla, with Streptococcus and kin among the steady finds. Fat states shift stomach acid, empty speed, and bile wash, each with microbe marks of its own. The ulcer germ H. pylori rules the niche where it lives, while acid-blocking drugs push the mix toward a mouth-like cast. Mouse work hints that weight surgery reshapes the stomach crew, yet no human study has mapped that shift yet.
pmc-13443672:
Shaheer Saeed and colleagues teach machine vision to reason by mixing fast and slow thought in a 2026 paper. Human minds pair snap calls with slow rethinks, while vision models stay stuck with what training taught. Their frame pairs a fast module that drafts and checks answers with a slow module that refines them through self-play.

Extra think time at run time, not more labeled data, drives the gains in this design. Steps propose rival answers, pit them, and polish the winner in loops. Tests span vision benchmarks and cancer spotting in five organs. Longer thought beat large supervised models, foundation models, and human experts on those tasks. The authors pitch run-time thought as a new lever where labeled data run thin.
pmc-13444472:
Liang Jin and colleagues coat bile duct stents with a licorice compound that fights tumor growth in a 2026 study. Blocked ducts in bile cancer need stents, yet plain coated stents lack tumor punch and clog again with time. Their coat loads the licorice flavonoid licochalcone A into a PTMC film for slow local release.

The film sheds water better, holds the drug steady, and stays kind to cells in their tests. Treated bile and colon cancer cells grew less, and tumor growth slowed in their models. The drug works through a CYP19A1-led path into GPR30 and AKT signals in the report. Coat fouling also eased in the checks. The authors pitch the dual coat as a stent upgrade that drains and treats at once.
pmc-13444672:
Seung-Hwan Kim presents a math model of how childhood leukemia changes over time under the limits set by growth and treatment, published in 2026. The model joins Ornstein-Uhlenbeck drift, where cell states wander yet get pulled back toward a mean, with branching trees of cells that split, die, or vanish. Plain random drift serves as the base case for contrast.

Kim tested the joined model against gene data tracked over time in 16 children with a rearranged form of acute leukemia. No single model won for all children: the pulled-back model, the joined model, and plain drift each fit best for a share of cases. That spread supports care plans that match each child's own pattern of change.
pmc-13447272:
Jiacheng Liu and Wei Chen search for a gene signature tying faulty cell recycling to star cells in Alzheimer's disease in 2026 data work. Faults in both may drive disease, yet a shared molecular marker set was missing.

Several public brain datasets were mined with machine learning and network tools, plus checks in single-cell data and donated tissue. An eight-gene signature sorted patient subgroups and supported a prediction model. One gene stood out as a hub, raised in Alzheimer's tissue and concentrated in astrocytes. Computer screening then nominated an existing compound that might reverse the signature by acting on that hub, though lab and clinical proof remain ahead.
pmc-13447372:
Ha Eun Na and co-authors report a 2026 case where dehydration worsened involuntary movements in diabetic striatopathy, a rare movement disorder tied to high blood sugar. The condition causes jerky one-sided movements and bright spots on brain scans, and sugar control usually settles it. Less is known about other triggers that can flare symptoms after early gains.

A seventy-seven-year-old woman arrived with acute jerky movements and received sugar control plus anti-movement medication, with initial improvement. Her movements later worsened as she became dehydrated, then eased again after full fluid replacement. The authors present dehydration as an added aggravating factor worth watching in such patients. Their account also reviews why the disorder can be mistaken for stroke or bleeding in the brain during its acute phase.
pmc-13448472:
Chen and co-authors formally describe a new plant species in this 2026 taxonomic paper. It is Astragalus baimaensis, a member of the milkvetch genus in the pea family. The team found it during field surveys around Baima Mountain in Deqin County, Yunnan, China. New species claims in such a huge genus need both visible differences and genetic evidence, and the team supplies both.

The authors single out hair presence on the ovary as a stable, trustworthy trait for telling Astragalus species apart.
pmc-13448672:
Shizhou Ma and co-authors examine in 2026 how warming changes the climate balance of temperate inland wetlands. Wetlands store carbon dioxide yet also release methane, a much stronger warming gas. The team asked whether the cooling benefit wetlands have long provided will survive a hotter century.

They combined about 19,000 chamber measurements of methane from 202 wetlands with burial rates from sixteen dated sediment cores in the Prairie Pothole Region. Methane output rose across the past two centuries and could near 950 kilograms per hectare per year by 2100 under high emissions, while carbon uptake slipped. The result points to wetlands shifting from a net cooling role toward a lasting source of warming.
pmc-13448872:
Ruya Abdulsalam and co-authors track in 2026 how women's weight and heart-metabolic markers evolve after a pregnancy complicated by gestational diabetes. Using primary care and hospital records for births from 2001 to 2021, they matched each of 43,572 women with gestational diabetes to four women without it, by age and delivery date. Trajectories were followed for fifteen years after birth.

Women with prior gestational diabetes stayed about 5.5 kilograms heavier and carried higher blood sugar, blood pressure, and LDL cholesterol throughout follow-up. Most markers climbed more slowly in that group over time, but blood sugar was the exception, rising far faster than in the comparison women. Later progression to type 2 diabetes reshaped several trajectories. The authors argue the early years after birth offer a window for risk checks and targeted prevention.
pmc-13449072:
Katharina Bünzel and colleagues set out in 2026 to relate long-term energy expenditure to glucose sensor readings in adults with type 1 diabetes. Step counts are the usual stand-in for activity, but they say little about metabolic demand, and fear of low blood sugar still keeps many patients from exercising. Energy expenditure, in kilocalories per week, offers a fuller measure to set against sensor data.

Their retrospective analysis draws on the Syntactiq Cockpit database, anonymized records donated between 2018 and 2024 by users of a diabetes app that merges data from Apple Health, Nightscout, and glucose monitors. Steps, exercise minutes, and calories burned were aligned with continuous glucose metrics over six months in a physically active group. The aim was to characterize how total energy outlay tracks with time in range and related measures, informing safer exercise guidance.
pmc-13449472:
Ronald Man Yeung Wong and colleagues survey in 2026 the arrival of robotics and AI in orthopaedic trauma surgery, writing for a journal devoted to translating such advances into practice. Robots already assist joint replacement and spine work, but trauma is the newer frontier. A surgical robot pairs computerized navigation with arms that guide the paths of screws and other fixation hardware. The newest systems can even perform a full closed reduction, pulling broken bones back into line before fixing them.

Pelvic and hip-socket fractures show the stakes: complex breaks in fragile elderly bone, with one-year mortality reported as high as 15.5 percent. Reported advantages of robotic help include shorter operations, less X-ray exposure during surgery, and less blood loss. Because many steps can run through small incisions, recovery may come faster. The authors frame trauma robotics as a shift from navigation aid to active surgical partner.
pmc-13449772:
Anna Lorencz and co-authors argue in 2027 that antibiotic resistance in the bacterium Corynebacterium striatum did not slowly pile up but flipped state around 2020. Textbooks usually picture it as gradual accumulation of traits. The team worked with records spanning 2013 to 2025. They applied segmented regression, variety measures borrowed from ecology, and Markov chain analysis to test whether the pattern looked like buildup or reshuffling.

A sharp breakpoint sat near 2020. Before it, resistance patterns built around aminoglycoside antibiotics were common. Afterward those architectures collapsed, replaced by fluoroquinolone-linked configurations without aminoglycoside resistance. Overall pattern variety shrank a lot, and the Markov analysis showed the system settling toward a stable end-state dominated by two related architectures. The authors say resistance surveillance should watch for such structural shifts, not just rising shares.
pmc-13449972:
Yalong Deng and co-authors run in 2026 a large factorial feeding trial to untangle how energy, protein, and one amino acid interact in the first two weeks of a Pekin duckling's life. They placed 2,304 day-old ducks into 36 diet combinations spanning four energy levels, three protein levels, and three lysine levels. Growth, feed intake, conversion efficiency, and carcass yields were measured at day fourteen. Feed is the dominant cost in poultry, so these interactions carry money.

Raising lysine from 0.8 to 1.05 percent lifted breast and leg meat yields sharply. Protein only helped growth when lysine was adequate; under lysine shortage, extra protein actually cut growth and intake. Energy's pull on intake likewise depended on lysine level. Fitted curves put the growth optimum near 2,995 kilocalories of energy per kilogram with 18.65 percent protein and 1.20 percent lysine. The authors conclude starter diets must balance the trio jointly, not nutrient by nutrient.
pmc-13451872:
Franziska Griessenauer, Franziska Pfannerstill, and Thomas Probst test in 2026 whether a virtual safe place beats plain eyes-shut imagery for calm. The safe place drill, where a person pictures a spot of total ease, is a common stress tool. Sixty adults were split by lot into a group that later rested inside an AI-built virtual copy of their own safe place, or a group that pictured it with eyes shut.

Calm was scored at four points in one lab visit, then daily for five days online. The team also scored how vivid the imagery felt and how present users felt inside the virtual scene. The trial asks whether tech adds real calm or just a new wrapper.
pmc-13452272:
Abhishek Tripathi and Manoj Hudnurkar lay out in 2026 a hybrid filter that cleans speckle grain from radar images while keeping edges sharp. Radar speckle blurs the texture reads that land and sea studies need. Classic smoothers clean flat zones yet smear edges, while edge-keeping flows are slow and balk at this noise kind.

Their method joins a Bayesian smoother with a guided flow filter, switched by a flow rule from a known speckle method. All settings are given as plain formulas, from look counts to edge thresholds. On two test radar images across a grain range, the hybrid was scored against four named filters on sharpness and likeness scales.
pmc-13452872:

Their 2026 study, called ANGEL-J2, ran at 20 sites in Japan with 131 patients split into three groups by their starting pressure. Two groups used sepetaprost alone, and the third added timolol, a second pressure drop, twice a day.

Pressure fell fast in every group and stayed down across the 52 weeks. The drops at week 52 were 4.40 points for the mild group, 6.38 for sepetaprost alone at higher pressure, and 7.51 for the pair of drops. Side effects showed in about six of ten patients, led by longer eyelashes and mild eye redness. The team presents the drop, alone or paired, as a sound long term option.
pmc-13453072:
Ludwig and a large team create metal-bearing versions of classic worm medicines in this 2026 study. Attaching an organometallic fragment, a metal-containing chemical group, is one strategy to refresh old drugs. Some derivatives matched the parent drugs' activity against several targets, including the rat parasite Strongyloides ratti, the hookworm Ancylostoma ceylanicum, and the blood fluke Schistosoma mansoni in laboratory tests. Others hit a tapeworm relative and the Leishmania parasite. The metal attachment did not systematically boost potency, the authors note, but the results give a starting point for new antiparasitic compounds and for studying how these drugs work.
pmc-13453572:
Marichal and colleagues worked in 2026 on synthetic CT scans for breast radiotherapy planning. A synthetic CT is a computer-made scan built from a cone-beam scan taken during treatment. The cone-beam view is narrow, so tissue outside it can be missing and dose sums can go wrong. The team added surface scan data from three cameras into their image-matching method and tested it on 20 patients.

Each patient had a wide-view scan as reference and a narrow-view version from the same raw data. The surface-guided version matched the reference better on all nine image measures tested. Its average image error fell sharply, and it removed false hot spots in some dose maps.  The authors say surface guidance can rescue narrow scans and plan tests on other body sites next.
pmc-13453672:
Christian Omar Ramos Peñafiel and five co-authors compare daily iron pills with every other day pills for women with iron shortage anemia. Their 2026 study follows 171 women aged 18 to 70 at a referral center from January 2023 to June 2024. Most cases traced to fibroids, the benign womb growths that drive heavy bleeding.

Starting hemoglobin, the blood's oxygen carrier, averaged 9.02 in the group as a whole. At six weeks the daily group averaged 10.91 and the alternate day group 11.26, a gap too small to count as real. By three months both groups averaged near 12.7, and about three quarters of each group had cleared the anemia bar. More alternate day patients moved up to intravenous iron, though that call rested on doctor judgment. The authors advise tailoring the schedule to each woman.
pmc-13454572:

A second score folded in gene patterns from related traits using a boosting method. Joining the two scores sharpened prediction further. The authors argue that ancestry-aware, trait-aware scores can make genetic screening fairer and more useful for people outside European samples.
pmc-13455272:
Jaiyeoba-Ojigho and team reviewed accuracy studies of blood tests for early Alzheimer's disease. Such tests are an appealing alternative to costly brain scans and needle-based spinal fluid sampling. It shows the ADNP-derived peptide preventing abnormalities in ovariectomized mice, hinting at therapies for postmenopausal bone and muscle loss.
pmc-13457472: Root-invading fungi of Chinese grassland plants — inventoried by culture and sorted into functional guilds. Tong Tong Wang, Bo Yang, and others do the fieldwork. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is fungal ecology. It catalogs root-associated fungi across multiple Chinese regions and studies their ecological roles.
pmc-13459172:
Hanna Jung and co-authors describe a limited repair technique for the most dangerous aortic emergency, an acute type A dissection, where the inner wall of the body's main artery tears. When the tear is confined to one of the three pouches at the aortic root, replacing the whole root is extensive surgery. Their 2026 case series reports seven such patients treated between 2015 and 2021. The repair rebuilds only the single affected sinus using two rings of reinforcing stitches, preserving the patient's own valve and root shape.

The seven patients had a median age of 59 years at surgery. None needed reoperation for bleeding, and none died in hospital. Follow up lasted a median of eight years. No patient developed more than mild leakage of the aortic valve over that time. The technique is a feasible, durable option for carefully selected patients, the authors say.
pmc-13459272:
Yanyan Zhou and co-authors compared two forms of menstrual migraine, attacks tied to the menstrual cycle, in women attending a headache clinic. Their 2026 study used online questionnaires from 430 women at a Soochow University hospital clinic. It classified 43 as pure menstrual migraine, 322 as menstrually related, and 65 as unrelated to menstruation, then compared symptoms and drug responses.

The pure group had lived with migraine for a shorter time, 6.8 years on average against 11.1 years in the related group. They also reported fewer warning symptoms before attacks, 58.1 percent versus 75.5 percent, and less nausea, eye pain, and smell sensitivity. Common anti inflammatory painkillers worked strikingly better for the pure group, relieving 96.4 percent of their attacks around menstruation against 72.8 percent in the related group.
pmc-13459572:

These rare cancers of the bile duct lining are usually found late, and no third-line standard has been proven in randomized trials. Among patients whose tumors lacked a drug-targetable alteration, median survival on third-line therapy was a little over ten months. Paclitaxel outperformed the FOLFIRI combination, giving median survival of thirteen months against seven months, with slightly longer time before the disease progressed. The authors present paclitaxel as the stronger option here and call for research on which patients benefit most.
pmc-13460172:
Feiyang Zhong and co-authors built in 2026 an interpretable machine learning model to predict early recurrence after surgery for stage IA lung adenocarcinoma. Even the earliest stage returns in some patients, and follow-up scans hold clues: radiomics extracts numerical patterns from tumor images, while delta-radiomics tracks how those patterns change between scans. Only 23 patients, five percent, recurred early. A fusion model blending clinical features with both imaging scores discriminated excellently in validation, and explanation tools showed which inputs drove each prediction. Survival analyses confirmed the score separated patients meaningfully. The authors aim the tool at choosing who needs closer surveillance or extra treatment after surgery.
pmc-13461172:

Promoters differed in how much they leaked expression into dendritic cells, and leakier designs drove stronger early T cell activation.
pmc-13461472:
Zhang and co-authors reviewed a 2026 narrative review of lifestyle factors in sudden cardiac death, which kills an estimated four to five million people yearly. Untreated sleep apnoea carried notably higher risk in one subgroup analysis, though evidence varied across studies. Brief bursts of vigorous daily activity cut cardiovascular death by about a third, while Mediterranean style eating cut major events by roughly thirty percent. The authors propose adding lifestyle measures to routine risk assessment, aided by wearable devices.
pmc-13461972:
Nathalie Aladjidi and the French CEREVANCE network ask how to cut long term deaths in children whose immune systems attack their own blood cells. Standardizing what counts as secondary disease, and hunting aggressively for inborn immune errors behind childhood cases, would redirect children toward definitive treatments such as targeted drugs or transplantation. The letter marshals accumulated French registry experience into a plea for earlier genetic and immunological workups.
pmc-13462172:

pmc-13462572:

Larvae on 30 percent lees grew heaviest, at about 83.7 milligrams dry weight, and cleared the most feed. Protein content peaked near 48 percent at moderate inclusion, while fat rose steadily as lees increased. At 40 percent and above, growth stalled, gut microbe diversity fell, and harmful types gained ground, Zhao reports.
pmc-13462872:

Newborns were exposed most, at over thirteen percent, with older children next. Transfused children died within thirty days far more often than others, an adjusted link the study reports. pmc-13463872:

Only two patient studies exist, and both drew on one shared group of patients. Whether microbe shifts help cause the wasting or merely follow it stays unresolved, the authors stress.
pmc-13464772:

Worked cases cover serial heart attack blood tests, where extra draws help only mid-risk patients, and a sepsis path shown step by step. pmc-13465172:

Bigger trials must now pick the form and dose worth pairing with standard therapy.
pmc-13465272:

A biopsy-first habit, they argue, can cut needless resections and speed the right therapy.
pmc-13465372:
Wu and co-authors pooled trials in 2026 on placing curcumin or turmeric preparations directly into gum pockets as an add-on to deep cleaning for periodontitis. Twenty-nine trial reports entered the review, and 27 gave usable pocket-depth data.

The add-on helped modestly in studies with inactive comparison treatments. Pocket depth shrank by about two thirds of a millimeter more in whole-mouth trials. In split-mouth trials, where each patient hosts both treatments, the extra gain was about half a millimeter. The results varied a lot between trials, though. Prediction ranges crossed zero, and evidence certainty was rated low. Trials were small, formulations differed, and reports clustered in a few countries.
pmc-13465572:
Duanyang Zhai and colleagues report a multicenter prospective cohort study, published in 2026, on finding sentinel lymph nodes after chemotherapy given before surgery. Ultrasound findings matched the dye mapping closely, and the scans also gave extra clues about whether nodes held cancer. The authors present the pairing as a practical option worth testing further in selected patients.
pmc-13465672:
Zhang and co-authors compared three mantis shrimp species in 2026 to learn how feeding style splits a food niche. Gut lining folds were widest in the first species and smallest in the third. Microbe types totaled 8,273 across the samples, yet only 17 were shared by all three. One species' gut was dominated by a single microbe group at about 89 percent. The most widespread species carried the richest gut community, which may aid its flexible lifestyle.
pmc-13465872:
Ge and co-authors used three omics layers in 2026 to learn how the heart drug nicorandil protects against reperfusion injury in rats. pmc-13466372:
Zouhair Essahli and colleagues survey research on health-active compounds from cyanobacteria and microalgae, in a 2026 review. The most studied organisms were the spirulina group, followed by Chlorella and two other algae genera. Most papers tested crude extracts or whole biomass rather than purified ingredients, with pigments and fats next in line. The authors present these tiny photosynthetic organisms as renewable factories whose chemistry could feed both supplement and medicine pipelines.
pmc-13466772:

pmc-13467272:
