pmc-13467572:
Oswaldo Junior and a large Brazilian team report a mouse study, published in 2026. It tests short bursts of intense exercise as treatment. The setting is an animal model of multiple sclerosis. The mice had experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis. This is the standard model of that brain and spinal cord disease. Some mice stayed sedentary. Some trained once daily. Others did brief high-intensity sessions three times a day. This is the exercise snack pattern.

The three-times-daily group showed a clear drop in disease scores. The drop was significant. Shifts in inflammatory messengers backed it. Tissue examination backed it too. Frequent short sessions reprogrammed the autoimmune response, the authors say. It moved toward a calmer, nerve-protecting state. They propose the pattern for clinical research in multiple sclerosis.
pmc-13468072:
Xingchen Yu and colleagues refine in 2026 how optical fiber sensors embedded inside polymer composites report strain. Fiber Bragg gratings, short etched sections of optical fiber, are widely treated as simple one-direction strain gauges with a fixed sensitivity. Inside a real composite under multiaxial load, that assumption produces significant errors. The team built a general framework that calculates the true sensitivity from the local three-dimensional strain state.

Their model joins an analytical strain transfer principle with the optical-mechanical behavior of the grating itself. Tests under hydrostatic pressure and two-directional compression and tension confirmed the predictions. The work further shows how strongly the bonding quality between fiber and host material shapes the reading. Better strain math means embedded sensors can flag real interface damage in aircraft and wind turbine parts instead of crying wolf.
pmc-13468172:
Sheila Genoveva Pérez Bravo and colleagues map in 2026 what is known about emerging contaminants in Mexican waters, from drug residues and hormone-disrupting compounds to PFAS, farm chemicals, and personal care products. The authors screened studies from 2004 to 2025 on rivers, groundwater, sediments, and sewage plant flows. Research within Mexico itself remains limited, which is part of the point.

The Apatlaco, Cuautla, and Santa Catarina rivers showed the widest diversity of contaminants. Well water carried traces of medicines, phthalates, bisphenols, and triclosan that had seeped in from urban, industrial, and tourist discharges. River mud held some compounds at trace levels, while phthalates reached thousands of nanograms per gram. The review also covers how these substances transform in the environment, where testing falls short, and what removal methods can and cannot do.
pmc-13468272:
Sanchooli and de la Presa built a 2026 hybrid nanostructure that heats under both a laser and a magnetic field for hyperthermia therapy, which cooks tumour tissue with heat. Gold nanorods absorb near-infrared light, while iron oxide nanoparticles respond to alternating magnetic fields. A chemical linker joins the two into one stable unit.

Under combined laser and field exposure the hybrid's temperature rose fast and sharply, beating either part alone, Sanchooli reports. A simple loose mixture heated about as well within the margin of error in the same combined setup. Linking changed the gold's light absorption and may slow the iron particles' motion, yet heating efficiency did not drop. The linked form adds magnetic guidance and delivers both parts as one unit, which a mixture cannot offer, the authors note.
pmc-13469072:
Zhang and co-authors measure what domestication traded away in a Chinese tree. Their 2026 paper grows fifteen Gleditsia sinensis germplasms, fourteen cultivars and one wild control, in a single common garden, removing environmental differences that bedevilled earlier comparisons. Pods and seeds were measured for form and for quality components, from saponins and polyphenols to sugars and protein.

Cultivars out-yielded the wild type on pod dry weight, thousand-seed weight, and total saponins. The wild type countered with significantly higher total polyphenols and flavonoids, the defensive chemistry breeding left behind. Bigger, heavier pods and seeds correlated negatively with those defensive compounds and with sugar and fibre, but positively with pectin, ash, and soluble protein, a growth-versus-defence pattern. A combined evaluation grouped the germplasms into four clusters and singled out three cultivars, JD9, YJ2, and YJ10, as the most balanced overall.
pmc-13469272:
Zakia Harmak and co-authors construct in 2026 a seven-gene signature, drawn from mitochondrial genes, that grades the prognosis of glioma, the most common and aggressive adult brain tumor. Mitochondrial failure is increasingly tied to cancer behavior, yet glioma lacked a mitochondrial risk marker set. Using the large TCGA tumor cohort, the team assembled the signature from ACSL1, NOX4, ALDH3A2, ALKBH4, FASTK, FDX1, and ACADVL, then validated it in the independent Chinese CGGA cohort.

High signature scores clustered with high-grade tumors, the IDH wild-type molecular class, aggressive tissue features, and poor survival. The authors also profiled the tumor immune microenvironment across signature levels, since mitochondria-linked states may shape immune infiltration and therapy response. A compact seven-gene readout that survives validation in a second population gives clinicians a candidate tool for sorting glioma patients by risk and for research into metabolism-targeted treatment.
pmc-13469372:
Gravante and colleagues used ultrasound in 2026 to watch blood flow change after foam injection treatment for hemorrhoids, a sealing of swollen veins from inside. Thirty-seven patients with all grades of disease were scanned before treatment and at 7 and 30 days after. Doppler ultrasound measured flow speeds and resistance, symptom scores were tracked, and patients split into mild and advanced groups.

The two groups diverged sharply: in mild disease, peak flow speed and resistance fell significantly by day 7 and stayed down at day 30. In advanced disease, neither measure budged, and a secondary flow measure even rose by day 30, hinting at worsening congestion. Symptoms mirrored the scans: everyone felt better at one week, but advanced cases slipped back by one month. The authors conclude foam works durably in mild disease, while advanced disease gains only a brief reprieve. Ultrasound, they argue, can sort patients accordingly.
pmc-13469872:
Ren and co-authors report a 2026 multi-omics study of heart damage from doxorubicin. The drug is a widely used chemotherapy agent whose toxicity limits treatment. Working with cultured heart cells and mice, the team combined gene-expression profiling, lipid measurement, and spatial mapping of molecules in heart tissue. Their goal was to find what changes first.

Gene and lipid profiling showed that doxorubicin suppresses the PPAR pathway. That pathway is a control system for burning fat for energy. With it suppressed, toxic long-chain acylcarnitines and ceramides build up in heart tissue. Chlorogenic acid, a plant compound, restored PPAR activity and lowered acylcarnitine levels. It reduced oxidative stress and cell death, and improved heart function in treated mice. Blocking the PPAR alpha receptor erased the protection. Adding acylcarnitines back did the same. The result confirms that this fat-burning pathway sits at the center of the injury.
pmc-13470572:
Kim and colleagues report a 2026 population study of fracture risk in lung cancer survivors in South Korea. Using the national health insurance database, they followed 33,292 survivors treated with curative-intent surgery and nearly one hundred thousand matched controls without cancer, accounting for death as a competing risk.

Survivors faced higher fracture risk than controls across the follow-up. Spine fractures stood out: risk peaked in the first year after surgery at about eighty percent above controls. Hip fracture risk pointed the same way in year one without reaching significance overall. Cancer treatment, inactivity, and bone loss converge after lung surgery, so the early window matters. The timing argues for bone checks and fall prevention starting at discharge, not years later when survivorship care usually turns to bones.
pmc-13471172:
Fortuin and colleagues asked Dutch schoolchildren in 2026 what they think of routine health checks from the youth health service, a voice rarely heard in service design. Six focus groups gathered 41 children aged 9 to 12 who had a check in the past year, covering experiences, whether parents should sit in, and how checks could improve. Themes were drawn from the conversations.

The children surprised with enthusiasm: their first theme was a demand for more, wanting checks more often and more thorough. They asked for kind professionals who hold a genuine two-way conversation, making them feel safe. Parents split opinion: children valued their knowledge but admitted parents do not know everything, and sometimes their presence inhibited honesty. Finally, children wanted the service organized more attractively. The authors say designing with children, not just for them, would fix much of this cheaply.
pmc-13471272:
O'Sullivan and a large team mapped sleep problems in 2026 across children with rare genetic syndromes, including several never profiled for sleep before. Caregivers of 251 children aged 1 to 18 filled in surveys on sleep and on features like anxiety, behavior, and epilepsy. Sleep profiles were compared with typically developing children, and modeling untangled how features relate while controlling for each other.

Most syndromes showed raised night waking, bedtime resistance, disordered breathing in sleep, unusual sleep behaviors, and short sleep, yet each kept its own signature pattern. Across syndromes, worse sleep traveled with anxiety and low mood, and tracked with autism-related traits, overactivity, and more severe epilepsy and physical illness. Family income status mattered too. The authors argue sleep should be checked routinely in these children, sitting as it does at a crossroads of mental and physical health. Syndrome-specific profiles can guide what doctors ask first.
pmc-13471372:
Inpan and colleagues pooled animal and human studies to test whether curcuminoids, the active compounds in turmeric, ease allergic rhinitis, the hay-fever condition that inflames the nose. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis drew on seven animal studies with 189 subjects and three human studies with 371 participants. Searches covered PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library through December 2024.

In animals, curcuminoid treatment clearly cut nose rubbing and sneezing, with effect sizes around −2.2 and −2.4 standard units respectively, and lowered IL-4, an immune signal that drives allergy. Human evidence was far thinner, resting on only three trials with mixed designs. The authors judge the overall case for clinical benefit uncertain and call for larger, better standardized trials with longer follow-up.
pmc-13471572:
Yang and colleagues modeled the chain from short sleep to depression in older Chinese adults, asking whether self-rated health and frailty carry the effect step by step. Their 2026 cross-sectional study used the 2018 wave of a national aging survey covering 5,111 participants aged 60 and older, with bootstrap mediation analysis.

Sleep duration acted mostly directly: its direct path to depressive symptoms accounted for 63.3% of the total effect in the model. The routed paths still mattered, with self-rated health carrying 14.2% of the total effect and frailty 12.5% along their separate channels, making 36.7% mediated overall. Subgroup analysis found the mediation only among those sleeping six hours or less, sharpening the case for targeting very short sleepers.
pmc-13471672:
Le Peng, Zhiliang Chen, Lei Li, and Shiwen Zhang combine in 2026 five long running cohorts to test how frailty, and changes in frailty, relate to later cognitive impairment. The cohorts span China, Korea, England, Europe, and the United States. Close to forty seven thousand participants fed the baseline analysis, and about eighty eight hundred developed cognitive problems over follow ups of four to ten years.

Compared with robust peers, pre frail participants carried about a quarter higher risk of cognitive impairment in the pooled estimate. Frail participants carried roughly seventy percent higher risk. A second analysis of about twenty two thousand people traced frailty paths over time using growth models, asking whether worsening or improving paths changed the outlook. The authors present frailty screening as an early warning the five regions share.
pmc-13473072:
Claudia Schildböck and colleagues show in 2026 that a simple additive can restore toxin testing in human blood serum. Tests for bacterial toxins often fail in serum because blood proteins hide the toxin from the assay. The team screened five candidate additives with growth tests and a standard toxin assay. One compound, dextran sulfate, stood out for freeing the toxin signal.

At a tuned dose, dextran sulfate brought toxin recovery back into the accepted range for three kinds of bacteria. Its results matched heparin, the older additive, while avoiding animal-sourced material. Batch quality was steadier and cost was lower as well. The finding gives labs a defined, non-animal option for more reliable toxin checks in blood.
pmc-13473272:
Wang and colleagues report a fatal 2026 case involving vascular Behçet's disease, an inflammatory vessel disorder, combined with infective endocarditis, an infection of the heart's inner lining. The patient underwent complex heart surgery and then needed two mechanical support devices, a balloon pump and a membrane oxygenation machine, to sustain circulation.

While on that support, the patient developed extensive clotting in both the arteries and veins supplying the gut. The clots rapidly caused intestinal necrosis, meaning death of bowel tissue, followed by perforation. The authors stress that patients with vascular Behçet's disease already tend strongly toward clotting because inflamed vessel walls promote it. Adding mechanical circulation support may raise a catastrophic gut clotting risk that clinicians currently under-recognize.
pmc-13473672:
Govindasamy and co-authors tuned a shunt active power filter, a device that injects corrective currents to cancel electrical distortion, using a hybrid optimizer that crosses sand cat swarm search with zebra optimization. Their 2026 simulations target autonomous three-phase microgrids feeding nonlinear loads, the electronics that dirty a clean sine wave.

The tuned controller held voltage steady between 145 and 150 volts across all three phases and cut total harmonic distortion to 2.11% under standard conditions, settling in 0.07 seconds after disturbances. Under unbalanced and extreme test cases distortion stayed low at 2.50% and 2.85% respectively, both under the 5% target the field aims for. Training data spanned voltage sags of 10 to 25%, swells, and harmonics up to the 13th order, split 70% for training and the rest for validation and testing.
pmc-13473972:
Payne and colleagues used a genetic trick in 2026 to ask how low oxygen shapes the building of coronary vessels, the heart's own blood supply, during development. Rather than starve embryos of oxygen, they fixed the oxygen sensor HIF in its active state in heart muscle, mimicking hypoxia. They then read gene activity cell by cell and tracked vessel growth from each source tissue.

The mimic hearts switched on sprouting genes and expanded the pathway that drives sprouting from the heart's inner lining, and sprouting from that source grew. The vessel web from the sinus venosus, an early vein, barely changed, and its pathways stayed quiet. Early artery identity changed little, yet the assembly of mature coronary arteries ran late. The authors link the oxygen pathway directly to lining-derived sprouting and suggest it also guides how arteries come together.
pmc-13474372:
K. Yu. Slashchuk and a large team study thyroid cancer in children that stops answering radioactive iodine care in 2026. This cancer is rare in youth and often spreads, yet long-term outlook is good for most. Care records covered 278 patients aged five to eighteen treated with surgery plus one or more iodine courses. Close watch lasted a median of four years.

Thirty-nine patients had advanced disease, and among them four reached full remission while most stayed stable. Six showed clear worsening on scans or blood tests. Survival without worsening held at a high level, and no deaths occurred over five years in the resistant group. The results help families weigh hard choices when standard iodine care fails.
pmc-13474672:
Luyang Zha and co-authors study womb lining thickness and pregnancy results in 2026 across more than sixteen thousand frozen embryo transfers. Each transfer used a single thawed blastocyst at one center. Cycles were sorted into five thickness bands, from seven millimeters or less up to above ten. Models weighed age and body mass as possible modifiers of any link.

The thinnest band faced far lower live birth odds and higher loss and early birth odds than the middle band. The thickest band showed higher live birth odds with no rise in adverse baby outcomes. One mid band raised loss risk for women aged thirty-five and above. Lining checks can help time transfers and set expectations.
pmc-13474772:
Fawole and colleagues surveyed physiotherapy researchers across Nigeria in 2026 about patient and public involvement, often shortened to PPI, which means planning research with patients rather than only about them. The team asked how these researchers view PPI when they design health studies, and what training they would need to use it well. Their survey followed the INVOLVE framework, a British guide for working with patients as partners, and drew 50 replies from 58 invited researchers.

Nearly all respondents said PPI helps pick the right study outcomes, with 94 percent agreeing on that point, and every respondent called it part of improving health systems. Support weakened for later stages, since 64 percent disagreed that patients should help analyze data, and many opposed help with writing reports. Training stood out as the clear gap, because 82 percent said they need support to run PPI well, while 98 percent said they would join training programs if offered.
pmc-13474972:
Annapareddy and co-authors measured the natural twist of the thigh bone in Indian patients in 2026, since hip replacement planning still leans on Western reference values. The twist, femoral neck anteversion, is the angle between the neck of the thigh bone and a line through the knee. Using robotic surgery planning scans, the team measured 742 hips from patients scheduled for primary hip replacement across several centers.

The average twist was minus 2.6 degrees, meaning a slight backward twist, with values spanning minus 42 to plus 41 degrees across the hips. More than half, 53.2 percent of hips, twisted backward, a pattern called retroversion, while 43.1 percent twisted forward and the rest sat neutral. Men leaned toward backward twist and women toward forward twist, and 94.7 percent of hips fell below the 15-degree figure often quoted as normal in Western texts.
pmc-13477372:
Marita Knudsen Pope and coauthors published a 2026 cohort study on how repeat heart events change the risk of sudden cardiac arrest. The work follows patients who survived a first heart attack syndrome or a first heart failure hospital stay. Researchers tracked later repeat events and sudden arrests over time, then checked the pattern in the long-running Framingham Heart Study.

Among 2,946 patients after a first coronary event, a repeat event more than tripled the arrest risk. Among 6,711 patients after a first heart failure stay, a repeat heart failure event raised risk by about four fifths. The Framingham check confirmed the coronary pattern but not the heart failure one. The authors argue that risk should be updated as new events occur, not set once at discharge.
pmc-13477572:
Nicholas A. Krasnow and coauthors published a 2026 protein design study asking whether computer-built enzymes make better starting points for laboratory evolution. The team used an AI design tool to rebuild three botulinum toxin proteases, enzymes that cut certain proteins. Redesigned versions kept full cutting power while growing more stable.

Side-by-side evolution campaigns then ran the redesigned and natural enzymes through phage-assisted nonstop evolution, a method that runs many rounds per day. Campaigns starting from redesigned enzymes again and again yielded stronger proteases. Mutations found in redesigned backgrounds often failed when moved back into natural enzymes. Redesign had opened paths that the natural enzymes could not reach. A final campaign evolved a protease aimed at ataxin-2, a protein tied to disease, with the redesigned start again reaching better cutting power.
pmc-13480072:
Figen Bezci Aygün and co-authors report a 2026 study of eye blood flow in people who need regular transfusions for beta-thalassemia. Repeated transfusions load the body with iron, which may harm the retina and the layer beneath it. The team compared 66 eyes from 33 patients with 66 eyes from 33 healthy adults, using detailed scans of the eye and blood and imaging tests for iron in liver and heart.

Flow in the finest vessel layer under the retina ran lower in patients than in healthy adults. Within the patient group, higher ferritin levels tracked with thicker central retina and denser flow in two vessel layers. Signs of heavier liver iron pointed toward a thicker choroid, though that link faded after strict correction for many tests. Eye measures may offer a painless way to watch how iron burden affects the body over time.
pmc-13481472:
Barbara Filar and co-authors report a 2026 case of a child cured of a second cancer sparked by treatment for the first. Brain tumour care had ended when acute myeloid leukaemia appeared, the most common second cancer of childhood and one with grim odds after brain tumours. Prior drug doses, heavy on heart-straining agents, ruled out standard double rounds of chemotherapy.

Doctors gave a single cycle of a liposomal drug pairing that parcels two agents at a fixed ratio, then moved to a stem cell transplant. The child came through the plan with success. Adult data backed the pairing, while child data stayed thin beyond relapse settings. The case adds a data point for gentler paths in second cancers, where past treatment boxes doctors in from every side.
pmc-13481572:
Jude Zziwa Byansi and co-authors present a 2026 study ranking upkeep risks for school toilets in Kampala City, Uganda. Head teachers and sanitation teachers from 205 schools scored 33 upkeep indicators across six areas, judging how rundown each stood and how likely and how badly each might fail. The method adapted a World Health Organization safety planning frame.

Near half the indicators rated low risk and none rated very high, while thirty percent rated high. The sharpest risks sat in supply handling, toilet cleanliness, planned preventive upkeep, menstrual hygiene supplies, and use of the sanitation budget line. Monitoring items scored low risk thanks to strong current performance rather than low worth. The message is blunt: habits and resource handling, not missing buildings, threaten steady school sanitation most.
pmc-13481672:
Asthana and colleagues examine who got a seat at the table during COVID-19 decision-making. Their 2026 comparative study covers six countries: Singapore and Nigeria, Jordan and Bangladesh, plus South Africa and the United Kingdom. Through interviews and focus groups with 64 stakeholders, the team assessed how civil society organisations and universities participated in pandemic governance.

Civil society groups were active in the response everywhere, but mostly worked independently of government, especially early on. Some governments brought these groups in only after new transmission clusters appeared, and then mainly for risk communication and services such as vaccine delivery, not for shaping policy. Universities, in contrast, were more often used to gather evidence for decisions. The authors identify practices for giving both groups genuine governance roles in future health crises, rather than delivery roles alone.
pmc-13482172:
Masud and co-workers in Bangladesh and Australia ran in 2026 joint design workshops to curb antibiotic misuse at rural drug shops. Germs that shrug off antibiotics are a world scale threat, and in rural Bangladesh most antibiotics are sold over the counter with little advice. Sellers, doctors, patients, drug reps, and health staff met in two rural regions to craft fixes that fit local life.

Their plan spans four layers. At the top, they want stronger public care, clear rules for informal sellers, and tight watch on sales. In shops, they back clear pack labels and coaching to finish each course. In towns, they urge school lessons and public drives. For patients, they push advice seeking before any use. All sides warned that no lone fix will work. Gains need all layers to move at once, backed by real funds.
pmc-13482472:
Bang and colleagues examine a chromosome-handling protein called KIF4A in gastric cancer in 2026 and find, unusually, that having less of it marks the dangerous tumors. In many cancers KIF4A runs high and acts like an accelerator, but its role in stomach tumors was unsettled. The team stained tumor samples, measured the protein with digital image analysis, and cross-checked gene data from public databases.

Low KIF4A tracked with the adverse features clinicians fear, and it ran opposite to HER2 amplification, the growth signal targeted by a major drug class in this cancer. Patients whose tumors carried little KIF4A survived worse, matching the gene-level pattern, though the protein lost independent force once other factors entered the model. Tumors low in the protein switched on an invasion program, while high ones looked proliferative and immune-inflamed, a split needing care before clinical use.
pmc-13482572:
Reyes-Saldaña and Rivera present a dehazing network in 2026 that clears indoor images by borrowing real texture from a clean reference photo instead of inventing detail. Indoor haze from smoke demands faithful recovery, since hallucinated patterns would corrupt the scene. Their system matches patches between the hazy input and the reference, aligns them with deformable convolutions that bend to fit, and sharpens edges with a gradient module.

On the RESIDE-indoor benchmark the method reached a structural similarity score of 0.992, the best among the methods compared in the study's tests. Its signal quality score, 36.59 decibels, stayed competitive while the model kept a favorable balance between quality and computing complexity for practical use. Stress tests with imperfectly matched reference images held up, supporting the claim that borrowed texture plus flexible alignment restores structure better than generation alone.
pmc-13482872:
Duong and colleagues used computer calculations to ask how plant chemicals from the tree Syzygium nervosum might disarm hydroxyl radicals, highly reactive molecules that damage cells. Their 2026 study examined thirteen terpenoids, a large family of plant compounds, and compared several ways each one could react with a radical. The method, called density functional theory, estimates reaction energy without any laboratory bench work.

One route, where the radical sticks onto the molecule, had the lowest energy hurdles and looks like the main pathway. Dehydroisolongifolene stood out with the lowest barrier, needing only 14 kilojoules per mole of energy to react. Carotol performed steadily across several routes, suiting broad use. Larger terpenoids also passed electrons to radicals more easily than smaller ones did. Duong offers the ranking as a guide for which compounds deserve real laboratory testing first.
pmc-13483172:
Miriam M. Calkins and co-authors present a 2026 study of chemical traces in the urine of firefighters who tackle blazes where homes meet wildland. Such fires burn houses and cars beside brush, mixing smoke types. The team enrolled 250 Southern California firefighters in 2019 and compared urine from sign-up with samples after fires, with 125 post-fire samples from 89 crew members.

All seven tracked smoke markers from one chemical family rose after fires, as did eleven solvent markers. A flame-retardant marker and two metals climbed as well. Peak values for two markers passed workplace guide levels used for industry. Crews defending structures gained more smoke markers than crews on wildland tasks. Gear use went unrecorded here, a gap the team flags for follow-up work on wash-down routines.
pmc-13486072:
Magdalena Płódowska quantifies how much of the cell-to-cell scatter in radiation damage response is pure biological noise. Published in 2026, the experiment uses two-nucleus cells from a human bone tumor line, where sister nuclei share one cytoplasm and therefore one environment. Photon exposure at 2 Gray is followed by counting repair focus markers at four time points.

Sister nuclei resembled each other far more closely than random nucleus pairs, proving that shared environment damps scatter. Noise contributed 28 percent of total variation for one repair marker and 50 percent for the other, with the remainder reflecting randomly placed damage itself. Even identical cells in identical conditions respond unevenly to the same dose. Radiobiology models that assume uniform cellular response will understate real spread.
pmc-13486672:
Xuerui Zhu and colleagues ask what combinations of conditions turn forest ecological value into real income in China. Published in 2026, the study builds a capital circulation framework and grades 43 official cases with a coordination model. A fuzzy-set comparative method then finds which condition recipes produce high-level value realization.

Sampled regions reached only initial coordination between protection and earnings, with a clear east-west gap favoring the east. Several distinct recipes led to high realization, mixing capital investment, value enhancement, institutional design, and market mechanisms in different proportions. No single factor dominated. Current models still diversify poorly and lack benefit-sharing rules that keep value flowing to local stewards, which the authors flag as the weak point for durability.
pmc-13487172:
Anastasia I Palamarchuk tests whether a longevity enzyme quietly disarms the suicide switch engineered into therapeutic killer cells. Published in 2026, the study modifies natural killer cells with hTERT to extend their growth, plus an inducible caspase gene meant to kill the cells on chemical command if trouble arises. Gene activity comparisons separate resistant survivors from sensitive cells.

Modified cells resisted the kill command significantly, and a catalytically dead enzyme version resisted just as well, proving the shield works through a side job rather than telomere lengthening. Resistant cells shared a signature of revved cell-cycle genes and muted splicing machinery. One transcript stood out, since BIRC3 makes a direct caspase-9 blocker and ran high in every resistant group. Safety switches for cell therapy need auditing against exactly this kind of interference.
pmc-13487472:
Yoshimura and co-authors hunt for drugs that destroy, rather than block, a leukaemia-driving enzyme. Their 2026 paper targets LCK, a kinase switched on in about 40 percent of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia cases. Blocking drugs such as dasatinib work at first, but resistance emerges, and related degrader drugs built from those blockers inherit the same weakness.

Screening 3,424 compounds, the team found molecular glues, small molecules that stick LCK to the cell's disposal machinery. Five hits degraded most of the LCK protein within a day. The glues engage the disposal protein CRBN through an unusual loop feature on LCK, away from the drug-binding pocket. Because of that separate grip, the glues kept working in cells resistant to inhibitors and inhibitor-based degraders, suggesting a route around kinase drug resistance.
pmc-13487972:
Eric Kerns and co-authors report outcomes for patients in intensive care whose cirrhosis was paired with sudden kidney failure, in a 2026 single-center cohort study. All were treated in the medical intensive care unit of a liver transplant center and had started dialysis. Severity was scored with liver failure measures taken on admission, and survival was tracked from the start of kidney replacement therapy.

Only about one in five of the 131 patients was alive one month later, and fewer still at six months, with median survival of five days from starting dialysis. Overall liver failure severity predicted death better than kidney or transplant factors did. Differences by dialysis type likely reflected how sick patients were, not the method itself, the authors caution.
pmc-13489572:
Fariba Ahmadi, Mostafa Amini-Rarani, and Alireza Jabbari present a study protocol, published in 2026. It plans a worldwide scoping review of family physician training. Family medicine is taught in many different ways. No shared global criteria exist. The planned review aims to map that experience. Countries could then learn from one another.

The team will follow Joanna Briggs Institute guidance. They will search databases and search engines. Related websites will also be searched. Sources will be screened with the PRISMA process. Content will be analysed across several themes. These include admission criteria, curriculum, and core skills. Training length is another theme. As a protocol, the paper presents no results yet. The finished review should help policymakers design training for their health systems.
pmc-13490372:
Isiksel and co-authors cooked up hybrid nanoparticles of copper oxide and zinc oxide using plant extracts, then wrapped them in polymers for infection fighting and drug delivery. Pairing two metal oxides can outperform either alone, but harsh chemical synthesis limits medical use. Their 2026 study brewed the particles with extracts from three plants, stabilized them in chitosan and acrylic copolymer matrices, and characterized the results with microscopy and spectroscopy.

Particles measured between about 62 and 138 nanometers across, with mostly disordered, glass-like internal structure. Nanochitosan versions packed tighter and varied less in size than the plain chitosan ones. Computer docking showed the carriers gripping a model transport protein and key bacterial and fungal virulence proteins strongly. Dish assays confirmed antimicrobial action matching the docking predictions. Isiksel presents the green-made complexes as dual-purpose medical candidates.
pmc-13490872:
Frank E. Garcea and colleagues show that brain areas for hand action shape how vision areas respond to tools in a 2026 lesion and brain imaging study. Using a tool well requires joining what an object looks like, handled by the brain's lower visual stream, with how it is grasped, handled by the upper action stream. The team studied 109 neurosurgical patients with left-brain lesions who viewed pictures of handheld objects, animals, faces, and places during functional scans.

Damage to two left parietal zones dulled visual stream responses to handheld objects specifically. Those zones are known for grasping and manipulation. Responses to places in the same visual zone held steady in the reported mapping. The lesion evidence is causal in flavor, since the damage came first. Connecting pathways are explored next.
pmc-13491772:
Zekun Ma and seven colleagues compare in 2026 two fusion operations for patients whose two lower spine levels have both slipped and narrowed. Posterior and transforaminal lumbar interbody fusion reach the disc space from different angles, and which serves double-level disease better was unsettled. The retrospective study covered forty-four patients treated between 2013 and 2021, with checks out to two years.

Both groups improved markedly in back and leg pain and in disability scores at every follow-up point. X-ray measures of alignment and slippage also improved in both groups, with no major complications or implant failures anywhere. The transforaminal group showed slightly larger alignment gains that did not reach significance. The authors judge both operations effective and decline to crown a winner.
pmc-13491972:
Erik K R Hanko and Naglis Malys dissect in 2026 how the bacterium Cupriavidus necator eats itaconate, a valuable building-block chemical also known as an immune modulator in animals. The microbe can grow on itaconate as its only carbon source, and the team deleted candidate genes one by one to find the machinery responsible.

Several backup copies of three enzyme steps together carry the breakdown pathway, and a regulator protein named ItcR1 switches the response on when itaconate appears. Gene activity scans showed wider reactions to related five-carbon acids, hinting at a broader metabolic web. By inserting a foreign enzyme, the team then coaxed the bacterium to manufacture a mixture of these acids from carbon dioxide and hydrogen alone. The work advances this species as a factory for sustainable chemicals.
pmc-13493672:
Theresa Klinger and four colleagues mine German insurance claims in 2026 to learn whether the harm from steroid tablets in eczema grows with exposure. Two measures of exposure compete: how long people take them, and how much they swallow in total. Guidelines limit these drugs to short bursts, yet real-world use drags on. The cohort followed people with atopic dermatitis who started systemic glucocorticosteroids, tracking new diagnoses over time.

Each extra quarter-year of therapy raised the hazard of mental disorders, stomach inflammation, bone thinning, high blood pressure, and diabetes by meaningful margins. Bone risk climbed fastest, at roughly a third higher hazard per quarter. Total swallowed dose predicted harm less consistently than sheer duration did. The authors say doctors should watch the calendar, not just the milligram count, and switch patients sooner to steroid-sparing treatments.
pmc-13494172:
Hasset Tamirat Molla and co-authors report a 2026 study of folate levels in pregnant women in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Defects of the spine and brain in newborns are among the most common in the world there. Folate, a B vitamin, is vital in the first weeks of fetal growth, and low levels raise the risk of these neural tube defects. The team asked which diet and life factors shape folate status at a first pregnancy visit.

Among 404 women at three public health centers, 61 percent had blood folate below the level thought to guard against these defects, and supplement use was rare. Folate fell step by step with each prior pregnancy, which fits the idea that repeated pregnancies drain the mother's stores. Levels were higher later in pregnancy than in the first three months. The authors urge action before conception, through supplements, fortified food, and wider spacing between pregnancies.
pmc-13495472:
Jette Henriksen and Ingrid Villadsen Kristensen explore, in a 2026 interview study, how mentors and leaders view the onboarding of newly graduated nurses. The jump from student to registered nurse is steep, with high demands and fast skill growth expected. Structured programs are spreading, yet the view from those who run them was little heard. The team spoke with eight mentors and leaders across medical, surgical, and cancer wards.

Four themes came out. Early weeks shape confidence and whether a nurse stays. Programs must blend fixed expectations with support shaped to each newcomer. Good mentors stay present yet fade back, building safety while letting independence grow. The program also forges a professional identity, not just skills. The authors read onboarding as a human, growth process far beyond paperwork, and urge hospitals to fund it well for the sake of retention and care quality.
pmc-13499672:
Thakkar and colleagues designed and synthesised a family of molecules aimed at tuberculosis, one of the world's deadliest infections. The compounds join a triazine core, a ring carrying three nitrogens, to a piperazine unit. They were built to block dihydrofolate reductase, an enzyme the tuberculosis bacterium needs to make DNA building blocks. The 2026 team screened the series against the standard lab strain, checked toxicity on immune cells, and modelled how the best compounds grip their targets.

Two leads, coded FP3 and FP8, stopped bacterial growth at a low concentration that the authors class as potent, while showing acceptable safety margins in toxicity tests. Computer docking placed them in the target enzyme and in a second bacterial enzyme, and dynamics simulations found those grips stable over time. Small greasy additions to a side ring boosted activity, while bulky halogens hurt it.
pmc-13500372:
Shushi Yamamoto and co-authors report in 2026 the first case of ampullary carcinoma, a cancer at the junction where the bile duct meets the intestine, in a dog. Tumour-caused blockage of bile flow outside the liver is rare in dogs, and this tumour type was never described in the species. Their patient was an 11-year-old spayed mixed-breed dog with months of jaundice, and imaging showed a lesion running from the lower bile duct to the intestinal opening.

Surgeons removed the duct opening through the intestine. They then cut away part of the intestine including that opening and rerouted the gallbladder into the bowel to restore bile drainage. Tissue analysis confirmed adenocarcinoma invading the intestinal muscle layer, with clean margins. More than two years after surgery no spread had appeared and the dog stayed clinically well, which the authors cite to support the operation for relief and staging.
pmc-13500472:
Muni Lakshmi G K and Mokesh Rayalu G build in 2026 machine learning forecasts of the Air Quality Index for Kolkata, India, where fine particle pollution threatens public health. Their dataset blended weather variables and pollutant readings, cleaned through a multi-step method for filling missing values. Many individual algorithms were tried, from linear regression and decision trees to neural networks and a sequence model. Combined ensemble methods that average or stack several learners were tried too, alongside simple baselines for reference.

A voting ensemble achieved the best overall error and fit scores in the temporal test split, while a stacking ensemble led on two other error scores in the reported results. Sequence modelling captured time patterns yet trailed the ensembles. Removing the two particle readings degraded every model clearly, and checks confirmed those particles as the dominant predictors, with stability checks supporting the framework.
pmc-13500672:
Irfan Tito Kurniawan and co-authors dissect in 2026 how a four-legged robot can walk naturally without endless reward tuning, by building its gait on a biological rhythm generator. Pure learning controllers often settle into ugly, wasteful gaits, so the team coupled a central pattern generator, which produces rhythmic stepping, with a learned policy. Two extras with unclear roles were then added, terrain sensing ahead of the feet and direct posture corrections at the joints, and removed each in turn.

Terrain sensing enabled energy-saving anticipation and faster balance recovery but could not reshape the rigid rhythm in the ablation tests. Posture adaptation supplied that flexibility, letting awareness become stable, accurate movement. Distinct strategies emerged, sensing favouring precise shorter steps and adaptation favouring low, efficient steps with quick reactions. Together they beat a plain learning baseline, trotted naturally with no gait-shaping rewards, and held up on unfamiliar terrain.
pmc-13501572:
Mahdi Jafarlou leads a nine-author team with a 2026 review of why immune therapy fails against colorectal cancer and what might beat that resistance. Most colorectal tumours are microsatellite stable, so they respond poorly to checkpoint drugs. The minority with faulty mismatch repair and high microsatellite instability respond better, thanks to many mutations and an inflamed tumour setting, yet resistance still develops. The review sorts resistance into causes inside the tumour, such as lost antigen display, and causes outside it, such as suppressive stroma and gut microbe imbalance.

Rather than listing therapies one by one, the authors map each plan to the barrier it best targets. Options covered include checkpoint combos, targeted drugs, adoptive cell treatments, CAR-T cells, bispecific engagers, vaccines, oncolytic viruses, microbiome methods, and cytokines. A biomarker section weighs MSI status, tumour mutational burden, contexture, Immunoscore, circulating tumour DNA, and microbiome profiles to guide choices.
pmc-13501672:
Qiufei Wu leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 genome study of MADS-box genes in oil palm, the high-yielding crop behind much of the world's palm oil. These genes encode transcription factors that steer flower development, which drives fruit set and yield. Scanning the oil palm genome, the team found 61 family members and sorted them by evolutionary analysis into two major types and 15 subfamilies. The genes sit across 14 chromosomes, and 17 pairs of segmentally duplicated copies explain much of the family's expansion.

RNA sequencing pointed to type II genes as the floral players, and targeted expression tests confirmed distinct patterns for six genes across flower organs. Two genes, EgMADS3 and EgMADS45, were tested functionally by overexpressing them in the model plant Arabidopsis. Transgenic plants flowered early and produced abnormal flowers, supporting a regulatory role in flowering. The authors nominate these genes as breeding targets for yield improvement.
pmc-13504272:
Gut, Kleinschmidt, and Lemmin probe in 2026 what smart protein shape tools have truly learned, by feeding them fake kin lists built to order. The tools, like AlphaFold, read a protein's kin in a stack to guess its fold. But many proteins work in two folds, and the tools show one. The team built fake stacks whose marks spell a set fold. Three top tools took the bait in fold switch tests.

Fake stacks pushed each tool to the spelled fold, at times one no true kin list could reach. Clash tests, where the base chain and the stack spelled rival folds, showed how each tool weighs the two calls. All three lean to tight, stock folds from their school sets. Mixed stacks, half fake and half true, steered calls to set states. The team frames fake stacks as a probe kit.
pmc-13504972:
Paula Gisely Costa Silva leads a team profiling health literacy in river communities of the Brazilian Amazon, in a 2026 study. Riverine families reach care mostly by boat and face weak services and deep social hardship. Knowing how they find and judge health facts can guide fairer programs.

The team surveyed 200 residents of two islands in Pará state with a many-sided literacy questionnaire, then grouped like answers. Seventeen distinct profiles emerged, a sign of wide variety rather than one community level. The sharpest gaps sat in social support for health, hunting down trustworthy facts, and finding one's way through services. Scores on other skills, like grasping health advice, varied less. The authors call for targeted steps, above all on service navigation and judging information.
pmc-13505072:
Shenghua Zhang leads a team tracing how fine air particles and a tobacco chemical team up to drive colon cancer, in a 2026 study. Both exposures are common, and each has been tied to metabolic disorder and cancer growth. The chain that links them inside tumors was missing.

In mouse and cell models, the pair gave tumors a metabolic-syndrome-like state with high sugar uptake. Immune cells that sit inside tumors took up extra sugar through two transporter proteins and released a growth factor. That factor switched on a receptor in cancer cells, which moved into the nucleus and turned on a gene that helps tumors hide from immunity. Blocking sugar use, removing those immune cells, or blocking the hiding signal each slowed tumor growth. Patient samples showed the same markers high.
pmc-13505472:
Oussama Benhar and colleagues report a large eye tumour found by chance in a 27-year-old woman who had no symptoms. A routine eye examination revealed a dark mass at the back of her left eye. Layered imaging showed a mushroom-shaped growth roughly nine and a half millimetres wide and nearly eleven millimetres thick, with fluid lifting part of the retina.

A whole-body scan then found two small nodules in her right lung, raising concern about spread. The tumour's size, position, and extent ruled out treatments that save the eye, so the eye was removed urgently. Choroidal melanoma is the most common cancer arising inside the eye, yet it rarely appears before age thirty and often grows silently. The authors stress that a look at the back of the eye during ordinary check-ups remains the best way to catch this dangerous tumour while treatment can still help.
pmc-13506172:
Kalliopi-Kleio E Gotti and co-authors review treatment evidence for median arcuate ligament syndrome. In this disputed condition, a fibrous band above the gut's main artery squeezes it and the nerve bundle beside it. Many people show the squeeze on scans without symptoms, so picking true cases is the central difficulty. Their search covered major databases up to June 2026, favouring guidelines, systematic reviews, and multi-centre work.

Diagnosis, they conclude, should rest on matching symptoms plus imaging that shows the squeeze changing with breathing, after other causes are excluded. Cutting the ligament, often with treatment of the nerve bundle, remains the main therapy, and keyhole approaches tend to bring fewer complications and faster recovery. Widening the artery from inside without releasing the ligament is not advised. Evidence stays weak, built on retrospective series with varied definitions, so the authors call for prospective studies and standard reporting.
pmc-13508272:
Celeste Nicola leads a twelve-author team studying breast tumors tied to rare autoimmune nerve syndromes, in 2026 work. In these syndromes, called Yo and Ri types, the immune system attacks nerve tissue in the setting of cancer. Why tolerance breaks down is unknown. The team compared twelve Yo-linked and ten Ri-linked breast tumors with matched tumors lacking the syndromes. They used a panel reading 760 genes, plus tissue staining checks.

Twenty-seven genes differed in both syndrome groups compared with their controls. One shared change pointed to more lymph vessels, and staining confirmed lymph structures in both tumor types. Yo-linked tumors showed a more mesenchymal, spread-ready character and lower activity in low-oxygen response genes. Ri-linked tumors lacked that second pattern. The authors suggest lymph vessel growth may be part of the setting that lets autoimmunity start, while each syndrome keeps its own tumor fingerprint.
pmc-13508372:
Sanjoy Kumar Mukharjee, Faruk Hasan, and Biswanath Sikdar present the genome of a plant-linked bacterium found around taro roots, a species first known from hospital wastewater in Australia, in 2026 work. Genome checks confirmed the strain's identity and sized its DNA at 4.68 million letters. Gene reading spotted equipment for gathering nutrients, making plant hormones, hauling iron, and weathering stress. Seed and pot tests then checked whether those hints held up in practice, using rice under salty conditions.

Rice treated with the strain grew clearly better under salt levels that normally stunt it. The strain carried a few resistance genes but no plasmids, showed no blood-breaking activity, and stayed sensitive to major antibiotic classes in lab tests. Family-wide comparison suggested the species keeps an open, flexible gene pool. The study extends this species' known range into farm soils and marks a plant helper, with safety checks reported alongside.
pmc-13511772:
Sai Yin and four co-authors review hydrogels made from chitosan, a natural material from shell waste, for pulling antibiotics and dyes out of water, in 2026 work. Leftover antibiotics and dye pollution threaten ecosystems and human health together, so recyclable, gentle cleaners are in demand. Plain chitosan dissolves poorly in acid, breaks easily, and is hard to recover from treated water.

Hydrogels fix much of that with a water-loving, sponge-like cross-linked network full of pores that speed contact with large pollutants. The review covers design routes from chemical grafting and cross-linking to magnetic and stimulus-responsive builds that react to heat or acidity. Uptake behavior is traced for three antibiotic families and for dyes, through forces such as electric attraction. The authors map how structure choices drive cleaning power to guide better designs.
pmc-13515672:
Cao and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how a small protein tag called ubiquitin controls the copying machine of influenza A virus. The virus copies itself with a three-part enzyme. Host cells add or remove these tags, and a tag can help the virus or block it, depending on where it lands.

The review gathers what is known about the cell enzymes that add or cut these tags, the exact sites they mark, and the kinds of tag chains they build. Some tags steady the viral enzyme and aid copying, while others mark viral parts for disposal or trigger immune alarms. The authors argue that drugs aimed at these host enzymes could back up current antivirals. The virus can mutate its own proteins to escape drugs, but it cannot change host targets as fast.
pmc-13518872:
Dun Fu and five colleagues pair a green tea compound with iron chemistry in 2026 to strip toxic arsenic(III) from groundwater. Mining regions face rising arsenic risk, and the trivalent form is both more poisonous and harder to remove than arsenic(V). Their system activates peroxydisulfate, a strong oxidant, using iron(III) plus epigallocatechin gallate, or EGCG.

The tea compound grabs iron and speeds its cycling between oxidation states, which fires off reactive oxygen species that convert arsenic(III) to arsenic(V) for capture on iron aggregates. Removal hit 98.2 percent within 10 minutes, an 84.4 percent improvement over the iron system without EGCG. Treated water met China's national limit in their tests.
pmc-13520072:
Nathan Schedler, Manaal Saqib, Chenan Huang, and Steven Feldman present a research letter, published in 2026. It measures how quickly dermatologists adopted biosimilar versions of adalimumab. Adalimumab is a major inflammatory skin disease drug. Biosimilars are cheaper copy versions. They reached the market only in 2023 after years of patent disputes. The team counted United States Medicare claims through that first year.

More than fifty thousand dermatology adalimumab claims were counted in 2023. Biosimilars made up only a small share. It was about three percent. The originator product took the rest. Adoption was similarly low in other high-prescribing specialties. No geographic pattern appeared. National uptake was slow in the first year after launch.
pmc-13520172:
Ailian Guo and a large team hunt for a drug target in 2026 in acute megakaryoblastic leukemia, a rare, aggressive blood cancer subtype with few options. pmc-13520872:
Firas Al Majarfi and colleagues present in 2026 a 36-year-old man who bled heavily six weeks after surgical fixation of a lower leg fracture, due to a torn artery behind the knee. Vessel injury with shin fractures is rare, while delayed rupture from a shifted bone fragment is rarer still.

Bleeding traced to a cut at the artery branching point, caused by a fragment from the broken upper fibula. Surgeons repaired the artery directly and restored flow quickly. Severe muscle death in the rear calf compartment and foot drop followed despite repair. The case warns teams to watch for late vascular trouble after complex leg fractures.
pmc-13521472:
Saegusa reviewed the molecular pathology of morules, cell clusters found in endometrial carcinoma, cancer of the uterine lining, in a 2026 article. A three-protein axis involving EBP50, S100A4, and myosin heavy chain 9 completes the change, especially under low oxygen. pmc-13522272:
Xiaohang Qi and colleagues hunt in 2026 for key protein targets of curcumin in triple-negative breast cancer. Curcumin is a turmeric compound. This cancer type lacks targeted drugs and acts with force. Network maths overlapped curcumin-linked proteins with disease-linked proteins.

Three targets passed the overlap test. Jobs cover cell division checks, growth signals and DNA damage checks. Docking runs showed good binding, on par with known blockers. Long motion simulations showed stable pairs. Energy maths favoured the checkpoint protein most. All proof is by computer only. Cell and animal checks must come before any care claims can stand.
pmc-13522572:
Anni Li and co-authors build a system for controlling how many copies of a plasmid yeast cells carry in a 2026 synthetic biology study. Tunable control existed in bacteria but not in yeast, where common plasmids are either few in number or unstable.

The new platform, based on a natural yeast plasmid, held up to twenty copies per cell with improved stability and much higher gene expression than genes placed in the chromosome. Adding further elements let copy number switch widely and climb still higher under selection. Demonstrations ranged from producing useful compounds to preserving strains, giving yeast engineers a quantified dosage toolkit.
pmc-13523372:

Only studies using the current Sepsis-3 criteria were included, drawn from five databases through late 2025. Eleven studies covering more than two thousand people met the criteria.

The authors conclude the marker is useful for ruling out, yet shared threshold standards are needed before wide clinical adoption.
pmc-13523472:
Chen Chang and colleagues describe, in 2026, a nasal vaccine strategy against pseudorabies virus, a herpesvirus causing acute febrile disease in animals. pmc-13523972:
Yunuo Zheng and colleagues combine, in a 2026 study, transcriptomics and single-cell RNA sequencing to find prognostic features linked to lactylation in cervical squamous cell carcinoma. Prognostic gene expression rose in later stages of that path.
pmc-13524072:
McNelly wrote a 2026 commentary on new work linking male sterility in red sage, Salvia miltiorrhiza, to starch making in pollen. The gene's code was the same in both lines, but it was switched on more strongly in fertile plants as starch built up. Engineered plants with the gene boosted or knocked out backed its role. McNelly notes the work may aid breeding and sterile lines for hybrid seed.
pmc-13526872:

Liver enzymes normalized quickly, and fibrosis genes declined gradually. pmc-13527972:
Yesim Demirel Karaduman and three colleagues compare dental bonding agents in a 2026 network meta-analysis. The team searched three databases for lab studies.

Of 1,677 records, 82 studies entered the pooled analysis, covering 22 adhesives. Rankings put G2-Bond Universal and Scotchbond Universal near the top in self-etch mode, both fresh and aged. Zipbond Universal led in the rinse mode at both time points. Most comparisons carried high certainty. The authors conclude that application strategy and material makeup matter more than any single ingredient. They add that clinical trials should confirm the lab rankings.
pmc-13528072:

They call for work on how the whole network goes wrong.
pmc-13528172:
Stefania Della Vecchia and five colleagues review mental and behavior signs in neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses in a 2026 paper. pmc-13531872:
Yuhan Jin, Yiran Liang, and Mahsa Maghsoudy Kasvaei review in 2026 how alternative splicing rewires breast cancer. Splicing lets one gene yield several protein versions by shuffling its segments. Tumors exploit that flexibility to drive spread, energy shifts, immune escape, and drug resistance.

Tumor variety and blunt drug targeting remain the chief obstacles.
pmc-13534572:
L Nate Overholtzer and colleagues use in 2026 the ABCD study to examine how ADHD medicines relate to brain structure in preadolescents. Stimulant medicines showed effects opposite in direction to the ADHD pattern in several regions, suggesting a shift toward the control pattern. Non-stimulant effects looked weaker, and some stimulant effects extended beyond the disorder pattern.
pmc-13536572:
Ayşe Öztürk and colleagues compare in 2026 children rights awareness among Turkish students and Syrian migrant students in Turkiye. Surveys reached over 870 pupils, with interviews and drawings from smaller groups.

Turkish pupils scored slightly higher on some rights, while both groups shared several ideas and sometimes confused duties with rights. Lived experience and social setting shaped which rights children named first. The authors call for context-sensitive rights teaching that includes migrant children voices in programme design.
pmc-13536672:
Yue Gao and colleagues present a 2026 analysis of United States survey data linking liver scarring scores to a combined heart, kidney, and metabolic syndrome. The team used health records for 8,592 adults collected between 2005 and 2018. Five of the six scores were tied to more advanced syndrome, while all six were tied to higher risk of death from any cause. Four scores also tracked deaths from heart and vessel disease in a steady dose pattern. The results held in follow-up checks. The authors suggest these simple scores may help flag adults who need closer monitoring and earlier care.
pmc-13538372:

The hybrid beat every baseline on accuracy, precision, recall, and combined score, reaching top marks near ninety-eight percent. Explanation maps showed predictions driven by meaningful feeling words rather than noise. The authors present the hybrid as a strong balance of accuracy and openness for large-scale opinion tracking on social platforms.
pmc-13540072:
Xiao Chen leads a 2026 laboratory study searching for the best settings when a dental laser removes porcelain veneers, thin shells bonded onto front teeth. Laser removal is gentler than grinding, yet settings that free the bond quickly might heat the tooth pulp or spoil the veneer for reuse.

Three energy and pulse combinations at a fixed power were timed and monitored for temperature inside the tooth. The team also checked bond strength on reattachment, surface shape, light transmission, and hardness after laser work. Their aim was a practical recipe clinicians can copy with confidence.
pmc-13540872:
Áron Sztaniszláv and four colleagues link, in a 2026 Swedish register study, schooling level with later heart events in people first hospitalised with atrial fibrillation, the common irregular heartbeat. Social position shapes cardiovascular health, and education is a clean marker of it.

The cohort held 263,172 patients diagnosed between 1995 and 2008 and followed for up to five years. Compared with primary schooling only, secondary and academic education both came with lower adjusted risks of heart failure and heart attack in men and women alike. Stroke risk fell clearly only for the academic group. Lower-educated patients also carried heavier illness burdens at the start, the authors note.
pmc-13542172:
Simon Ladouce and C R Gillebert track walkers in a 2026 study. Twenty young adults wore eye trackers and foot sensors. GPS units rode along as well. Routes mixed flat pavements, cobblestones, and dirt paths. Rough surfaces drew more downward glances. Heads tilted down more deeply on those surfaces. Walking slowed on rough ground too. Strides grew shorter, and step rate fell. Eye changes and gait changes correlated tightly. The authors say city structure steers movement strategies.
pmc-13543072:
Brian Chu and colleagues published a 2026 case report of a severe blistering skin reaction that looked like Stevens-Johnson syndrome but followed ingestion of a supplement containing black seed oil, Nigella sativa. pmc-13543372:

Combined, they caught every patient who needed referral, a sensitivity of 100 percent, with specificity near 73 percent and strong overall accuracy. pmc-13543472:

Normal and diabetic mice got the particles by mouth over a subchronic period at several sizes. Exposure raised immune signals, tipped liver oxidative balance, and suppressed a key insulin signal axis while lowering the glucose transporter GLUT4. Diabetic mice showed stronger oxidative and immune responses, marking them as the hosts most at risk. Models tied the oxidative-immune imbalance to the liver signal failure.
pmc-13543572:
Zhenyu Luo and colleagues published a 2026 report of two cases, with a literature review, of a rare extra ligament in the knee. This anterior medial meniscofemoral ligament runs from the front horn of the medial meniscus to the notch between the thigh-bone knuckles. Normally that horn anchors firmly to the shinbone; this variant leaves it mobile, which may invite tears and degeneration. Both patients were women with knee pain and no injury.

Keep or cut depends on impingement and joint wear, the authors conclude.
pmc-13544772:
Jiahao Li and colleagues published a 2026 review of hydrogel technologies for musculoskeletal disorders, the bone, cartilage, disc, tendon, and muscle conditions that lead global disability tables. The review surveys laboratory work, animal studies, and products already reaching patients, organ by organ.

pmc-13545572:
Xiao-Ying Qi and co-authors followed brain growth in preterm babies in 2026 using repeated head ultrasound scans from birth until the age they would have been born at term. The study covered 117 newborns, 57 born early and 60 born at term, with 719 scans in total. Measurements focused on the corpus callosum, the bridge between brain halves, and on its spatial relationship with the cerebellum.

At term-equivalent age, preterm babies had a shorter, smaller corpus callosum and cerebellar vermis, plus a wider angle between the bridge and the cerebellum. Growth of the bridge slowed after 35 weeks of corrected age in the early-born group. The authors support ultrasound monitoring of these structures during the newborn period.
pmc-13546572:
Daniel Reinhorn and co-authors ran a small prospective trial in 2026 in locally advanced rectal cancer. Twenty-one patients had scans before treatment and again at two weeks, and their tumors were later graded under the microscope after surgery. The authors present the work as a pilot that narrows which scan measures deserve larger trials.
pmc-13548572:
José Luis Ubago-Jiménez and colleagues test whether short movement breaks inside lectures sharpen university students' attention, in a 2026 quasi-experimental study. Long seated classes promote inactivity, and teacher trainees are a natural audience for classroom strategies they may later use themselves. A single group of 224 students took a standard attention test before and after fifteen weeks of weekly ten-minute breaks filled with physical and mental games, choreographed boxing, and movement play.

Modeling also showed the links among concentration, stability, and overall performance growing stronger, while the push and pull between concentration and variability shifted. With no comparison group, the authors stay cautious, yet they present active breaks as a promising habit for teacher education courses.
pmc-13550472:
Jared Boasen and colleagues record brainwaves and eye movements while people watch a live stage performance with surtitles, the opera world's captions, in a 2026 exploratory study. Twenty-five attendees viewed the show while researchers compared periods when text was projected against periods without it, and related the signals to how absorbed each person felt.

Brain activity told text periods apart mainly through theta rhythms and beta-band connections among visual areas. Two changes, a theta rise near the frontal eye fields and stronger coupling between two visual hubs, did not vary with self-reported absorption. pmc-13550572:

pmc-13552572:
Christina Lamb and Sophie Bertaud present a 2026 perspective on ethics in care for dying children. They argue that the usual adult model, built on four broad principles, fits this work poorly. The authors propose blending that older model with an ethics of care, which stresses bonds, empathy, and response to need.

Readers find a case example, a comparison of the two approaches, and advice for training staff. Justice receives fresh treatment, since what a child is owed looks different inside a caring family and team. The piece gives clinicians a way to honour a child's voice, weakness, and place among others when choices grow hard.
pmc-13554172:
Zahra Karimian and three colleagues build and test a questionnaire on how medical students judge online versus in-person learning in a 2026 study. Peer contact and group learning carried the strongest weight among the six themes. Together the themes explained about seventy percent of what the tool measures. Scores for consistency and expert approval both ran very high. The authors say blended courses should mix methods and judge students in varied ways. Warm, low-stress settings matter for both formats.
pmc-13554272:
Xiaoye Gao and three colleagues measure eye damage from diabetes in northern Xinjiang in a 2026 survey. The study enrolled 3,253 people in chronic diabetes care across six areas. Eye photos were graded with software help and expert review. About 2,972 participants had photos clear enough to grade.

After age adjustment, close to one person in five had diabetic eye damage. About one in eleven had damage severe enough to threaten sight. Longer diabetes, higher fasting sugar, high blood pressure, and insulin use each raised risk. Younger age and male sex also raised risk for damage overall. The authors urge regular eye screening, above all for patients matching those risk signs.
pmc-13554572:
Junhwan Kwon leads a five-author team estimating bladder volume from a single ultrasound view in a 2026 feasibility study. Standard volumetry multiplies three diameters and applies a shape guess, needing two views taken at once. Their learning model reads one lengthwise image plus an expert outline of the bladder. True volumes came from catheter drainage right after each scan.

On fifty-three held-back cases, estimates tracked true volumes closely. Average error stayed small for low volumes, and percentage error stayed modest for larger ones. Attention maps showed the model studying the bladder wall and nearby tissue texture. The authors say one view may nearly match two-view accuracy while simplifying the scan and dropping fixed shape guesses.
pmc-13554672:
Kock and colleagues report in 2026 a longitudinal study of anxiety and depression among people in a public smoking cessation program in Tubarão, southern Brazil. It asks whether psychological symptoms predict who manages to quit tobacco.

Eighty participants were assessed with nicotine dependence, anxiety, and depression inventories at entry, thirty days, and ninety days. Forty percent quit; about a quarter dropped out and a third kept smoking. Those who failed to quit were older, averaging about fifty-nine against forty-nine for quitters, and carried far heavier lifetime tobacco exposure. Dependence scores fell nearly to zero among quitters. Anxiety measured at ninety days was clearly higher in those who had not quit, while depression showed the same direction without reaching significance. The authors argue cessation programs should build in psychological assessment and multidisciplinary support.
pmc-13554772:
Kim and colleagues track three-year results for people who had a heart attack type called NSTEMI. They sort more than fifteen thousand patients by kidney function. Stent care linked to lower risk in patients with mild, moderate, or severe kidney loss. The gain showed in deaths and in major events alike. In patients with the best kidney function, the gap was small and not clear. The results help doctors weigh stent care when kidneys are weak.
pmc-13555872:
Quynh Nguyen and three colleagues gather stories from Vietnamese mothers of children born with cleft lip or palate in a 2026 study. Talk covered vitamins in pregnancy, access to scans, doctor advice, and traditional practices.

Doctors stressed folic acid and early detection as the keys to prevention. Mothers described poverty, thin knowledge of prenatal nutrition, and stigma clouding their pregnancies. Old customs sometimes clashed with modern medical advice. The authors call for health education built with communities, wider access to care, and action on social barriers, arguing that leaflets alone will not shift outcomes for these families.
pmc-13556072:

Six independent fellows then rated the finished system on accuracy, adaptability, realism, and educational value, each on a five-point scale. Every domain scored above four points, with educational value rated highest across 160 evaluations. Panel members scored the system higher than the first testers had. The authors present simulation as a repeatable supplement to ward experience.
pmc-13558272:

At discharge their independence scores were lower, and among patients admitted from home they more often failed to return home and more often gained long-term care certification. Early swallowing screening, the authors suggest, sharpens discharge planning.
pmc-13558672:

pmc-13558772:

That chemical, CXCL2, summons suppressor cells that smother killer T cells, and tumours with the axis active resisted PD-1 therapy while excluding defenders. pmc-13558872:
Sofie D Wahyudi and five colleagues followed pregnant women in 2026 to test whether two routine blood measures can warn of early delivery. pmc-13559972:

Shared standards, they stress, keep fifty state systems from becoming fifty incompatible ones.
pmc-13560272:

pmc-13562172:

pmc-13562572:

pmc-13563672:

pmc-13563772:

pmc-13566372:

pmc-13568472:

pmc-13569672:

pmc-13571372:

pmc-13572172:

pmc-13574772:

pmc-13575172:

pmc-13578272:

pmc-13579772:

pmc-13579972:

pmc-13583372:

pmc-13583572:

pmc-13584372:

pmc-13585772:

pmc-13587672:

pmc-13591672:

pmc-13593572:

pmc-13595772:
