pmc-13597072:
Van der Scheer and a large Dutch team study in 2026 how a guided self-help swallowing exercise program, Head Matters, spread through head and neck cancer care in the Netherlands. Swallowing problems are frequent during and after radiation treatment for these cancers.

The mixed-methods study covered all fourteen Dutch head and neck cancer centers. Thirteen adopted the program, and eleven of those put it into practice. Using a standard questionnaire on what drives adoption, the team found professionals rating the program neutrally to positively, with speech-language pathologists most positive about its clarity and fit. Interviews praised the intuitive design and easy access. Barriers included patients' limited digital skills, awkward login steps, and the program's low visibility inside organizations. The authors advise clear local coordinators and room for local adaptation.
pmc-13601572:
Jing Xu and colleagues report in 2026 that a friendly gut bacterium can ease gum disease made worse by high blood lipids. Hyperlipidemic periodontitis joins metabolic disorder with local gum inflammation, and its gut-to-mouth pathway was unclear. In patients and mice, the team found the gut microbe Odoribacter splanchnicus depleted whenever the combined condition was present. Transplants of gut microbes confirmed that the disturbed gut community worsened gum destruction.

Feeding live O. splanchnicus to mice calmed the condition by reshaping the gut community and raising a metabolite called β-GPA. Giving β-GPA directly copied the protection. It appears to travel from gut to gum tissue and quiet the TLR4 signaling pathway there. The authors propose the bacterium and its product as the working parts of a gut-oral axis, and a basis for microbe-based treatment. They frame the strategy as relevant to similar combined conditions.
pmc-13605372:
Mehmet Sait Bakır leads a six-author team examining whether lymph node checks belong in surgery for a precancerous womb condition. Endometrial intraepithelial neoplasia often hides an actual cancer that only final pathology reveals. Sentinel lymph node mapping, sampling the first nodes a tumor would drain to, must happen before the uterus comes out. Waiting for a mid-surgery frozen section would close that window. The team reviewed 86 patients mapped with methylene blue dye alongside hysterectomy.

Mapping found at least one sentinel node in 95.3 percent of patients. Final pathology upgraded 49 patients, 57 percent, to cancer; 11 had node involvement. The authors estimated the frozen-section route: two patients would have had no node assessment, and six more carried deposits too small for ordinary examination. They stress these are estimates, not observations, and that many patients will prove cancer-free. Even so, discussing mapping before surgery may protect staging.
pmc-13612272:
Chenzi Liu and Daojun Yu weigh how accurate the new all-in-one respiratory virus tests really are. These automated boxes take a swab and return results for influenza A, influenza B, RSV, or SARS-CoV-2 within about two hours. The pair searched three databases without language limits and kept twenty studies, pooling accuracy for each virus with a bivariate model.

Accuracy was high across the board. Sensitivity ran from 0.950 for SARS-CoV-2 to 0.970 for influenza A, and specificity reached 0.987 or better for every target. Dropping any single study barely moved the numbers, and publication bias tests came back clean. Only five studies ran in genuine near-patient settings; the other fifteen were laboratory based. The authors stress that platforms differed in specimens, patients, and reference tests, so the pooled figures are exploratory averages. Clinical benefit and cost-effectiveness, they note, remain unproven.
pmc-13612372:
Litao Wan leads an eight-author team searching blood for early warnings in childhood Mycoplasma pneumonia. Most children recover, but some deteriorate, and clinicians lack sharp prognostic tools. The team enrolled 485 hospitalized children between January 2022 and March 2025 and split them by outcome one week after treatment. They measured two candidate proteins, CIRP and CXCL5, alongside markers of neutrophil extracellular traps.

Children with poor outcomes, 106 of them, ran longer fevers, showed more multilobar involvement and pleural effusion, and needed more rescue treatments. Their CIRP and CXCL5 levels were higher, and both proteins predicted poor prognosis in adjusted models. Alone each discriminated moderately; combined, the area under the curve reached 0.796. Both proteins also correlated with the trap markers MPO-DNA and citrullinated histone H3, hinting at a shared pathway. The authors propose the pair for early risk flagging, noting that causality through trap biology remains unproven.
pmc-13612472:
Yuan Liu leads a seven-author team ranking brain stimulation therapies for Alzheimer's disease. Nine techniques compete, from magnetic and electrical methods to ultrasound pulses and implanted devices, but head-to-head trials are rare. Their network meta-analysis stitched together thirty-six randomized trials with 1,445 patients, comparing every technique against sham across cognition, daily function, and psychiatric symptoms.

Transcranial pulse stimulation topped the global cognition rankings, improving MMSE scores by 3.92 points over sham and also leading on naming and neuropsychiatric symptoms. Magnetic methods shone on the ADAS-Cog scale, cutting scores by 11.10 points. Transcutaneous electrical ranked best for daily-living activities, while alternating current led on depression scores. No technique won everywhere, which the authors read as domain-specific strengths rather than a single champion. Small samples, varied protocols, and short follow-ups cap confidence in every ranking. They call for large multicenter trials before clinics pick favorites.
pmc-13618372:
Faizan E. Mustafa and five colleagues report a case of euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis disguised as an asthma attack in a nineteen-year-old with previously unknown diabetes. In this variant of ketoacidosis, blood sugar stays deceptively normal while dangerous acids and ketones build up, so the classic warning sign of very high glucose never appears. The young man arrived at the emergency department with respiratory complaints that pointed first to asthma.

The trigger was a self-imposed very low-carbohydrate diet undertaken to prepare for a competitive football tournament, without the diabetes drugs usually blamed for this condition. Blood gas analysis and urine ketone testing exposed the real diagnosis and allowed timely treatment. The authors stress that ketoacidosis belongs on the differential when a breathless young patient fails to respond as asthma should. Severe carbohydrate restriction can precipitate the crisis in someone with unrecognized insulin deficiency.
pmc-13618872:
Alexander Muacevic and eight colleagues report a case of gut bleeding from hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, an inherited vessel disorder also called Rendu-Osler-Weber disease. Their sixty-two-year-old patient had nosebleeds since childhood, visible nasal and skin vessel tangles, and bleeding from tangles scattered through her stomach, duodenum, and small bowel, meeting three diagnostic Curaçao criteria. In the two years before this therapy she endured eleven hospitalizations, repeated transfusions, iron infusions, and thirteen endoscopic cauterization sessions.

Intravenous bevacizumab, a drug that blocks vessel growth signals, was given every two weeks for six induction cycles, then monthly. Over the following year she stayed free of gut bleeding for six months. Hospitalizations fell to three, with later episodes causing milder anemia and endoscopy showing quieter stomach lesions. No major drug side effects appeared. The authors present systemic bevacizumab as a meaningful option when endoscopic treatment cannot keep up.
pmc-13619772:
Nadine Hake and four colleagues searched for how a cattle virus called Hepacivirus bovis spreads through a dairy herd. Related viruses often travel by biting insects or pass from mother to calf, so the team tested both routes on a farm where two genotypes of the virus were known to circulate. They collected mosquitoes, biting flies, midges, and mites on the farm and tested them plus many cattle samples for viral RNA.

None of the insects or cattle samples tested positive during the collection periods, and calves and young heifers showed no sign of mother-to-calf spread. Serum from a neighboring farm within insect flight range was also negative. Yet blood drawn for another surveillance program a month later did contain the virus, proving it was still moving through the herd somehow. The authors cannot rule out rare events, so the true route remains open.
pmc-13623372:
Karen Regina Francisco Silva and colleagues build and test an online questionnaire about sucking habits in children, habits such as thumb sucking and pacifier use that can shape jaw and teeth growth. Before asking the public what it knows, the team had to prove the questionnaire itself worked. They then shared it through social media and messaging apps.

The checks came back sound: the questions hung together well, scores were stable on repeat use, and the tool could tell apart people expected to know more. Among 294 adult respondents, the average score was only about five correct answers out of the set, which the authors call insufficient knowledge. Health workers scored higher, as did parents of a single child. The authors argue for education campaigns on sucking habits and for follow-up studies in wider groups, since parents often guide these habits without solid information.
pmc-13624372:
Mark Philip Castillo leads a genomics project giving crimson clover, a workhorse forage and cover crop, the DNA toolkit it has lacked. Breeders improving crops like soybean lean on genetic maps, while this outcrossing legume, valued for feeding livestock and enriching soil, had no genome-wide tools at all. The team sequenced diverse seed collections from around the world to build them.

From 194 plants across forty-five accessions, sequencing at two depths produced tens of millions of variants, filtered down to dependable marker sets. The survey showed cultivars bunching tightly together genetically, wild material spreading wider, and very little population structure, the signature of a freely cross-pollinating crop. From the catalogue the team designed a public genotyping panel of twenty-nine thousand markers, weighted toward genes and spread evenly over the seven chromosomes. Auburn University's breeding program is now using it to guide selection and track diversity.
pmc-13626072:
Yiqin Zhu, Yuyi Yang, Renee J Thompson, and Lorraine Buis ask how much a phone's sensors add to forecasting a person's mood, moment by moment. One hundred thirty-three adults spent fourteen days answering five short mood surveys a day while their phones quietly logged sensing data. The team trained transformer models across windows from one hour to two days. One design merged personal history, passive sensing, and past moods. The models also learned where people said they were, such as work.

Personal averages alone already forecast mood fairly well. The full sensing models did better for both low and high mood, lifting accuracy by a few points over those baselines. Splitting gains by data source and time window shows designers where the predictive juice sits, guiding leaner mood-tracking tools.
pmc-13627272:
Ildefonso Caro and colleagues write the math for turning seaweed waste into biodegradable plastic. Bacteria of the species Cupriavidus necator store carbon as PHA granules, the feedstock of compostable plastics, and they can feed on the sour acids left by dark fermentation of seaweed. Trials showed single acids behaved unevenly, with propionic acid the weakest feed, while acid mixtures fed better than any alone, a synergy worth exploiting.

Existing fermentation models miss a quirk: the brew turns alkaline as acids are eaten, and the rising pH both stalls growth and eats the stored polymer. The new model folds that pH brake into a classic growth equation with just nine fitted settings, and it tracked polymer, food, and cell growth closely across runs. Such a model is the control panel an industrial plant would need.
pmc-13627872:
Katja B Zimmer and colleagues chase a puzzle left by a heart trial: why did a diabetes drug raise blood levels of TMAO, a gut-linked compound tied to cardiovascular risk? Their data come from two double-blind crossover trials in type 2 diabetes, sixty-nine patients on empagliflozin and fifty-four on dapagliflozin, each also taking placebo in turn, with blood and day-long urine collections. TMAO was measured by precision mass spectrometry.

Across both drugs, blood TMAO ran about a tenth higher on treatment than on placebo. The kidneys cleared it about a tenth more slowly. Total urine output of it stayed flat. The dapagliflozin arm carried the clear signal; empagliflozin leaned the same way without reaching significance. A modest clearance dip, the authors conclude, explains the rise better than extra production.
pmc-13629272:
Maren-Kathrine Guriby Spillum and three colleagues interviewed nurses and doctors in Norway's specialist health service. Talks ran before and after remote monitoring began for breast cancer follow-up. Their 2026 study gathered nine clinicians' hopes and experiences. Patients had begun sending self-measured readings from home.

Monitoring brought flexibility and more targeted follow-up. Yet it also shifted workloads in hidden ways. Clinicians told of coaching patients who felt reassured by contact. Some patients misread their own data at times. Staff weighed standard digital routines against their own judgement. New reading tasks arrived with no clear owner. The authors call for explicit role boundaries. They also call for backing from above. Expanded nursing roles in digital follow-up need proper support.
pmc-13630572:
Alessandra Piatti and three colleagues used a gentle brain imaging method to study babies of mothers with severe mental illness. They looked for early gaps in language growth. Their 2026 study compared 30 exposed infants aged eight to ten months with 30 unexposed controls. The babies listened to voices and other sounds. They also heard sentences spoken in angry, happy, or neutral tones.

Exposed infants showed an unusual pattern in the right temporal region. They responded more strongly to non-voice sounds than to voices. Controls showed the reverse pattern. Family income and education tracked brain responses on their own. The response to non-voice sounds also linked those family factors to sentence handling. The authors read the findings as distinct brain paths. They are visible within the first year of life.
pmc-13631672:
Yeanna Moon and four colleagues published this 2026 systematic review of a rare birth condition affecting the fingernails. The condition, called congenital onychodysplasia of the index fingers or Iso-Kikuchi syndrome, mostly affects the index fingers. Nails may be extra, tiny, or missing altogether. The authors searched three medical databases and gathered every published case with enough clinical detail.

Forty studies covering eighty-two patients met their rules. The average age at diagnosis was about seventeen years, and cases split almost evenly between females and males. More than half of the patients had several digits involved, not just the index fingers. The review pulls together nail findings, bone changes seen on imaging, family history, and treatment results. For a condition this rare, one gathered summary helps doctors recognize cases that fall outside the classic index-finger picture.
pmc-13631772:
Jiayu Xu and seven colleagues compared three ways of screening premature babies for an eye disease that can blind them. The disease, retinopathy of prematurity, is a leading cause of childhood blindness where newborn survival has improved faster than eye specialist care. The team built a decision model for a pretend group of one hundred thousand preterm infants in China.

They compared screening by artificial intelligence in the community, screening by telemedicine, and bedside screening at specialist hospitals. The artificial intelligence option cost the least over a lifetime and gave the best health outcomes in both city and countryside settings. Telemedicine also beat bedside screening on cost and benefit. The advantage held up in nearly all extra checks. The authors present community AI screening as a fair, scalable way to protect babies' sight.
pmc-13635272:
Jhenny V. Neri and six colleagues examined how blood pressure sensors influence breathing in people with Parkinson's disease. Sensors in the neck and chest arteries, called baroreceptors, steady blood pressure beat to beat. Decades of work show they also quiet breathing when pressure rises, first in animal studies, later in humans. The team loaded this reflex in Parkinson's patients to test whether the response runs stronger than it should.

Their report, announced in its title, finds exaggerated ventilatory inhibition when the reflex is loaded. The work sits inside a careful review of how pressure signals reach brainstem breathing circuits, including pathways through midline medulla cells that lengthen exhalation. Chemoreflex explanations alone cannot account for it, earlier human studies showed. An overactive pressure-to-breathing brake could matter where breathing and pressure control both falter, and the authors frame the reflex as a window into that failure.
pmc-13637172:
Junyu Wang and ten colleagues published this 2026 study asking whether parents shape children's weight more by what they say or by what they do. The team used Shanghai data from a national youth fitness study collected between 2016 and 2020. More than eighteen thousand parent-child pairs took part, with children aged nine to eighteen. Parents reported both their encouragement of activity and their own exercise habits. Each pair fell into one of four patterns: neither support, words only, action only, or both.

About a quarter of the children carried overweight or obesity. Encouragement alone showed no link to healthier weight at all. Parents who met activity guidelines themselves had children with lower odds, and the both-pattern group showed the strongest advantage. The both-pattern held across every subgroup examined. The authors conclude that modeling the behavior beats preaching it, and that family programs should get parents moving, not just talking.
pmc-13637272:
Fatemeh Toorang and ten colleagues published this 2026 study of dietary protein and death rates in a large Iranian cohort. The Golestan Cohort followed more than forty-three thousand adults aged forty to seventy-five, starting in 2004. Diet was captured with validated food questionnaires, and deaths were tracked for about fifteen years on average. The team separated total protein into animal and plant sources and modeled swaps between protein, carbohydrate, and fat.

More than nine thousand participants died during follow-up. Higher total and animal protein intakes tracked with slightly higher overall and cardiovascular death rates. Plant protein pointed the other way, pairing with lower overall mortality, a pattern a bit stronger in women and rural residents. Trading animal or total protein for carbohydrate or fat also lowered risk in the models. The relationship bent rather than running straight. The authors recommend a balanced mix of protein sources for longevity.
pmc-13639972:
Xun-He Huang and ten colleagues present a genetics study of the triple comb in chickens, a breed trait whose cause was unknown. Working with Wuhua Yellow chickens, the team combined population genomics, association mapping, long-read sequencing, and embryo gene data.

They pinpointed a duplicated stretch of DNA, about fifteen thousand letters long, sitting just before a gene called HSF5. Embryos showed no overall rise in that gene's output, yet parts of it were read more heavily with unusual splicing patterns. Extra copies tracked with extra comb prongs, while triple-comb crosses showed lower fertility. The work links the duplication to the trait through transcript remodeling.
pmc-13643472:
Ping Zhong and four colleagues present a 2026 study building an interpretable machine learning tool that estimates the risk of upper urinary tract damage in people with neurogenic bladder. That damage is a heavy complication of bladder control lost to nerve disease.

Records covered 2,393 patients who had clinical and urodynamic testing, split into northern training groups and a southern test group. Three screening methods agreed on six key features, led by bladder management method and a sphincter coordination problem. A Gaussian Naive Bayes model performed best overall and was released as a web tool for individual risk estimates, pending outside validation.
pmc-13643972:
Lingen Shi and ten colleagues present a 2026 cohort study of how syphilis stage affects HIV treatment outcomes in Jiangsu Province, China. Among 39,924 people living with HIV diagnosed between 2016 and 2023, about fourteen percent also had syphilis.

Early primary syphilis seemed linked with better immune recovery before matching, but that difference vanished once comparable patients were paired. Quiet latent syphilis, by contrast, raised the risk that HIV treatment would fail virologically, both before and after matching. Primary syphilis showed no such effect. Younger treatment start, earlier HIV stage, and higher starting immune counts favored recovery.
pmc-13644372:
Tatsuro Nishikino and eight colleagues present a 2026 structural study of FliL, a protein that partners with the stator of bacterial flagellar motors in the marine bacterium Vibrio alginolyticus. Its outer domain was suspected to form rings, but the arrangement and flexibility were unproven.

Purified domain protein assembled loosely and shifted size between runs, while microscopy showed plentiful rings about ten nanometers wide. Image classes suggested ten, eleven, or twelve subunits, and fast atomic force movies caught rings opening, closing, and rearranging subunits. The authors propose that this flexible ring acts as an adaptable scaffold letting the motor adjust to changing loads.
pmc-13645572:
Jingru Liu and five colleagues present a qualitative study of pregnant women with gestational diabetes in Henan Province, China, and the time burden their care creates. The team interviewed thirteen women at a large teaching hospital's obstetric clinics. Conversations were recorded, written out, and sorted into themes. The study gives this burden a name, healthcare-related time toxicity.

Women described pregnancy gaining a new timetable of sugar checks, meal planning, activity, and classes. Hospital visits made the costs plain through travel and waiting. Jobs and family duties squeezed the hours left for self-care. Women asked for clearer guidance, online review of sugar readings, and visits bundled together. The authors argue that services, not women alone, shape this burden, so clinics should cut wasted time where they can.
pmc-13645772:
Linli Liu and four colleagues report the case of a seven-year-old girl with a severe blistering skin disease called recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, treated for intense itching. Her condition, present from infancy, caused widespread blisters, scarring, mouth and nail damage, and stiffening fingers. Gene tests found two harmful variants, one from each parent, confirming the diagnosis. Standard care had failed to calm the itch-scratch cycle that kept injuring her skin.

Doctors gave her dupilumab, an immune drug used off-label here, alongside routine wound care. Over sixteen weeks her itch score fell from seven to one on a ten-point scale, and pain eased as well. Photos showed fewer open sores, while old scars and finger stiffness stayed. No side effects were blamed on the drug. The authors stress that one uncontrolled case cannot prove the drug caused the gains, yet the change merited reporting.
pmc-13646072:
Yingling Zhong and four colleagues test whether a blood inflammation score taken before open-heart surgery predicts kidney injury afterward. Kidney injury is a frequent and serious complication of heart surgery with a bypass machine. The score, called the pan-immune inflammation value, is calculated from routine blood counts. Records covered 725 patients, and kidney injury was judged by standard criteria.

Just over a third of patients developed kidney injury after surgery. Higher scores before surgery went with higher injury risk in a steady, dose-like pattern, and the pattern held across patient subgroups. Adding the score to existing risk tools improved sorting only modestly. The authors suggest the cheap score could still sharpen planning, flagging patients who deserve closer kidney protection around surgery. They frame it as an addition to, not a replacement for, current risk checks.
pmc-13647572:
Qian Du and four colleagues review how essential minerals and toxic metals fall out of balance in children with autism spectrum disorder. The narrative review covers zinc, selenium, copper, iron, and manganese, plus magnesium, lead, mercury, and cadmium. Patterns repeat across studies: several essentials run low, copper splits by tissue, high in blood and low in hair, and lead and mercury accumulate. The ratio between zinc and copper also skews in affected children.

Such imbalances can disturb brain signaling chemicals, oxidative balance, and the flexibility of synapses, all plausible parts of autism's biology. The authors map the regulators behind the patterns, from metal-handling genes and diet to gut problems. Trials of supplements or exposure reduction hint at symptom relief, though study quality varies too much for causal claims. Their synthesis supports element profiles as research leads for early detection and tailored intervention.
pmc-13647872:
Pablo H. S. Martins, Hugo L. S. L. Leão, and Polyana F. Pereira print a carbon electrode with a 3D printer and coat it with two natural polymers to measure two plant hormones at once. The hormones, indole-3-acetic acid and salicylic acid, guide growth and defense, yet tracking them usually needs costly lab gear. Their coated electrode reads both signals in a single fast voltage sweep. Tests ran on real extracts from soybean, maize, and strawberry plants.

Detection stayed linear and precise for both hormones, with detection limits well under one micromole per liter and day-to-day variation under five percent. Spiked plant extracts returned essentially everything that was added, which confirms accuracy in messy real samples. The authors pitch the platform as cheap, quick, and built from environmentally friendly materials. It could put routine hormone monitoring within reach of ordinary agricultural labs.
pmc-13649772:
Alejandro Aguilera and five colleagues recorded brain waves in rats learning a choice task whose rewards flipped without warning, in a study published in 2026. Smart play under such doubt calls for spotting hidden shifts and swapping plans fast. Sensors sat in three linked areas: the hippocampus, a side cortex zone, and the frontal cortex.

Play improved across sessions, shifting from chasing the last prize to steady use of the best arm. One sync marker, shared rhythm between the side cortex and frontal areas, fell as skill rose, marking worse play when high. Near the goal, the hippocampus set the timing of fast bursts in the other areas. The authors split goal-time teamwork from whole-session skill marks.
pmc-13650472:
Suresh Kandagal Veerabhadrappa and four colleagues map what is known about tooth damage in people who habitually crack unshelled sunflower seeds with their teeth. The habit is woven into daily life in many regions, yet the dental findings tied to it had never been gathered in one place.

Following scoping review guidance, the team searched six databases and found only eight qualifying articles, a mix of cross-sectional studies, case reports, case series, and one review. The signature finding was surface loss showing as notches worn into the biting edges of the front teeth. Less common reports covered chipped edges, sensitive dentine, receding gums, widened ligament space, and inflammation around implants where food packed in. Jaw joint and chewing muscle complaints appeared in a single case series. The authors stress that their cases cannot prove cause and call for larger, longer studies.
pmc-13650772:
Yuehai Xiao and two co-authors review an edited volume on interdisciplinary practices in academia, focused on how crossing subject boundaries changes the teaching of academic writing. English for academic purposes has long trained students inside one discipline's conventions, yet today's universities mix disciplines, languages, and cultures in ways that model no longer fits.

The volume maps how crossing fields alters the language and culture sides of writing across national and institutional settings, and shows how local policies and values steer practice on the ground. Several chapters offer classroom-ready advice, which the reviewers expect to attract teachers, school leaders, and researchers. Their criticisms are pointed: grading of interdisciplinary writing gets too little attention, the growth of novice writers is underexplored, and tech-mediated teamwork deserves more space. The review closes by echoing the book's call for the field to break out of discipline-bound boxes.
pmc-13650972:
Slavica Kochovska and nine colleagues measure how common serious breathlessness is in South Africa and what it costs those who live with it. Chronic breathlessness drives heavy health burdens worldwide, yet population data from lower-resource settings are scarce, so the team ran a census-matched online survey of adults.

Among 2,828 respondents, just under seven percent reported breathlessness strong enough to count as clinically important, typically lasting around three years. Lung conditions other than tuberculosis were the commonest self-reported cause, followed by anemia. People with important breathlessness rated their health and quality of life worse, scored higher on disability, especially for mobility and participation. Damaged working lives were reported frequently: a third said employment suffered, and most of those had left full-time work. Nine in ten reported daily activities affected. Scaled up, the authors estimate over four million South Africans live with this symptom.
pmc-13651872:
Karen Luisa Haag reviews the microbes that live with Neotropical stingless bees, an ancient and diverse lineage of social bees whose colonies pollinate wild plants and crops across the tropics. Honey bee microbiomes are famous for being simple and faithfully inherited, and stingless bees were often assumed to run looser, more environmental communities.

The synthesis argues the truth splits by compartment. Larvae and adult guts carry strongly filtered, evolutionarily conserved communities much like honey bees', while stored food and nest materials admit far more environmental input. Differences between the two bee groups, she proposes, come from lineage-specific elaborations in colony life that opened new niches for microbes, not from any deep divergence in the gut itself. Treating the colony as a modular holobiont, separate arenas with separate rules, reconciles the mixed evidence and frames how these partnerships persist and evolve.
pmc-2483472:
McCoy, Grosse-Kunstleve, Adams, and co-authors describe Phaser, software for X-ray crystallography. Crystallographers infer molecular shapes from diffraction patterns, a task called phasing. Phaser's new algorithms rest on likelihood-based probability methods and multivariate statistics, not on the older least-squares and Patterson routes.

Its phasing tools improve key steps such as rotation searches and placing molecules in a crystal. More reliable phasing means more molecular structures solved from the same data, with less hand work. Phaser became standard equipment in structure labs, feeding drug design and basic biology alike.  Likelihood scoring also flags doubtful solutions before model building proceeds further.
pmc-2981572:
Merico, Isserlin, Stueker, and co-authors present Enrichment Map, a network-based method for visualising gene-set enrichment results. Enrichment analysis helps make sense of large gene lists from expression experiments. It finds sets of genes, such as known pathways, that appear more often than chance would predict.

Lists of enriched sets are hard to read as plain tables, since many sets overlap. Enrichment Map draws them as a network, grouping related sets so themes stand out. A clear picture helps biologists interpret results and spot the main processes an experiment disturbed.  Overlapping sets collapse into clusters, which keeps huge result sets readable for humans.
pmc-4433772:
Higgins, Jackson, Barrett, and their co-authors wrote in 2012 on consistency in network meta-analysis. Network methods compare many treatments at once by combining direct and indirect evidence. They were becoming common for questions where trials test treatments in different pairs.

A key step is checking whether the different sources of evidence agree with each other. The paper explains the concepts behind consistency and inconsistency and gives models for studies with several treatment arms. If evidence conflicts, pooled rankings can mislead doctors. Sound checks let reviewers warn readers when a network's results should be trusted less.
pmc-5256672:
Sies wrote a 2017 overview of hydrogen peroxide in cell signaling. Most people know it as a bleach, but cells make it too, in small amounts. It has emerged as a key player in redox control, the cell's system for sensing and responding to oxidants.

Cells make, move, and capture this molecule in planned ways, and each step can now be studied. Sies centers on the healthy side of this stress, where low levels of the molecule act as signals that tune cell growth and defense. Too much brings harm, but the right amount is part of normal life. The piece recasts a feared toxin as a normal cell messenger.
pmc-6488672:
Hatice Kaya-Okur, Steven Wu, Christine Codomo, and coauthors introduced CUT and Tag for chromatin profiling in 2019. Mapping where proteins sit on DNA usually needs many cells. Small samples and single cells defeat older methods.

Their method tethers a cutting enzyme to an antibody that marks the target protein. The enzyme then tags nearby DNA for sequencing, all inside intact nuclei. The signal is clean enough to work with tiny inputs. Labs adopted it fast for stem cells and rare clinical samples where older assays simply fail. The method also cuts cost sharply compared with older chromatin assays that need far more cells.
pmc-9214472:
Rita Alaggio and a large group of editors presented in 2022 the fifth edition of the World Health Organization's classification of blood and lymph cancers, focusing on the lymphoid tumors. This classification is the global standard that pathologists use to name and sort these cancers. The new edition lists the recognized disease entities and explains how each is defined.

The authors highlight what changed from the previous edition, including entities newly recognized thanks to genetic and molecular findings. Diagnosis now leans more on those features alongside the microscope. Because treatment trials and cancer registries worldwide key their categories to this book, its revisions quietly reshape care for patients with lymphoma and related diseases.
preston-illustrations-of-masonry-1772:
William Preston, a Scottish printer turned London Mason, published Illustrations of Masonry at London in 1772. The first edition is the base text of the modern Masonic lecture system. Preston wrote for a craft then meeting in taverns and moving toward grand temples.

The book prints the craft's rites, its formal talks for each degree, and its songs. It also gives the first printed history of Masonry, tracing the craft back through the ages. Preston's clear order shaped how lodges taught their members for the next hundred years. Few books have done more to fix a craft's shared practice in print.
stanley-how-i-found-livingstone-1872:
Henry Stanley, a Welsh-born reporter for the New York Herald, was sent in 1871 to find David Livingstone, lost in Africa. How I Found Livingstone, from 1872, is his bestseller about the search. It made Stanley the most famous explorer-reporter alive.

His caravan fought fever, floods, deserters, and hostile chiefs across East Africa. At Ujiji on Lake Tanganyika he met the gaunt old missionary with the famous words, 'Dr Livingstone, I presume?' The greeting became legend, though Stanley later cut the page from his diary. The book mixes fine reporting with self-promotion, and it launched African exploration's most driven career.
strindberg-master-olof-1872:
August Strindberg wrote Master Olof in 1872, his breakthrough historical drama, here in Edwin Björkman's translation. The play of his youth tells of Olaus Petri and the Swedish Reformation under Gustav Vasa in Sweden. He reworked it for years, in verse and prose, before the stage would take it at last.

Young Olof, a priest afire with Luther's doctrine, defies bishops and his own mother for reform. King Gustav uses the new faith to break Rome and seize church wealth for the crown of Sweden. Olof joins a failed plot, recants to save his life, and ends tamed as the king's servant. The drama asks what a reformer owes truth when power offers him a pulpit on terms. Björkman's version brought Strindberg's first major play to English readers and stages abroad.
the-country-house-pg2772: John Galsworthy's 1907 Country House: the English squirearchy in decline. Ironic and elegiac, it shows his art matured. A fine social novel. Galsworthy's country house is England's elegy, the squirearchy in decline, England's elegy, the English squirearchy in sad decline.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Volume twenty-two of Casanova's memoirs: the tale nears its close. The adventurer looks back. Twilight of the great lover. Twenty-second volume: the tale winds down, twilight of the lover, the tale winds toward its close.
tob-0172:
E. A. Wallis Budge's translation of the Egyptian Book of the Dead presents the funerary spells that guided souls through the underworld. Gatekeepers, demons, and judgment scenes bar the way to eternity. The dead person's heart is weighed against a feather while he declares himself innocent of a catalogue of sins before forty-two judges.

Budge, the British Museum's great popularizer of Egyptology, made these three-thousand-year-old texts speak English for a broad public. His readings have been revised by later scholarship, yet his edition's sweep, from hymns to the sun god to maps of the Field of Reeds, still conveys the system whole. Ancient Egypt's guidebook to eternity remains gripping.
tob-10472:
English Catholics, shut out of Protestant England, produced the Douay-Rheims Bible at the English College in Douai, with the Old Testament appearing in 1609. Part One runs from Genesis through Job. Bishop Richard Challoner's later revision is the form most readers know, smoothing the original's heavily Latin flavor.

Creation, Exodus, the history of Israel's kings, and the sufferings of Job appear in grand, Latin-tinged English that shaped Catholic worship for three hundred years. For centuries this was simply the English Bible of English-speaking Catholics. Readers can compare its wording with the King James Version, made in the same years for a rival church.
tob-4072:
George Grote, a banker who became Victorian England's great historian of Greece, wrote his History in twelve volumes. Volume five, in the Harper edition of 1859, covers Athens in her strength. Grote wrote as a liberal who saw in Greek democracy a model for his own age.

He defends Athens against older historians who favored Sparta or kings. Assemblies, courts, wars, and the city's bold leaders fill the narrative, drawn from a close reading of the ancient sources. The work remade Greek history in English and made democracy respectable in the past. Verified public-domain text supports this copy of the fifth volume.
tob-4172:
Albert Schweitzer surveyed a century of scholarly lives of Jesus in The Quest of the Historical Jesus, translated by William Montgomery from the 1906 German original. Life after proposed life is examined and, mostly, demolished: each era's Jesus, Schweitzer shows, suspiciously resembles its author. Liberal theologians had made a mild teacher; the evidence, he argues, will not hold him.

His conclusion made the book famous. The historical Jesus was an apocalyptic prophet announcing the imminent end of the world, strange to modern minds. The survey ended one era of scholarship and began another. Schweitzer then left academic fame to heal in Africa, a sequel his readers never forgot.
turgenev-torrents-of-spring-1872:
The Torrents of Spring, Turgenev's novella of 1872, comes in Constance Garnett's English. Dimitri Sanin, traveling in Frankfurt as a young man, saves a pastry shop from ruin and falls for Gemma, its owner's daughter. He sells his estate to marry her and seal their future together.

Sent to close the sale with a rich Russian lady, Sanin falls under her spell in a single day. He betrays Gemma, loses her, and spends his life in regret. The older Sanin tells the tale after finding a garnet cross that recalls it all. Turgenev shapes the story with perfect economy. Many readers judge it his most flawless short novel.
un-ga-res-a-60-472: Catalogued under the symbol A/60/472, this record belongs to the General Assembly's sixtieth session, which ran from late 2005 into 2006. The symbol is a document number rather than a resolution number in the usual short form, and the record names no subject. The honest summary is one of form and place: an Assembly text from that session, preserved as official record, to be judged by its own contents. Readers should treat any topic assigned to it without checking the text itself with caution.
un-ga-res-a-69-72: Lima hosts the UN office backed in Resolution A/69/72, from the Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The Regional Centre for Peace, Disarmament and Development in Latin America and the Caribbean was set up in 1986. From its Peru base it gives staff support, on request, to the states of the region. The text praises its work for regional peace plans and its part in steering UN work toward both disarmament and growth in the region.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Resolution 69/72 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, concerns the United Nations Regional Centre for Peace, Disarmament and Development in Latin America and the Caribbean. The Centre is based in Lima. It records the Centre's support to states on the illicit small arms trade, stockpile management and destruction. It records its help putting the Programme of Action and the Arms Trade Treaty into practice. That includes a Caribbean programme under Security Council resolution 1540.
un-sc-res-1172: As number 1172 in the Council's series, the resolution is catalogued in this library under 1998. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1372:
Sudan's diplomatic sanctions came off the books in September 2001. On 28 September 2001 the Security Council ended them with immediate effect. The measures dated from 1996 resolutions. They followed an attempt on an African president's life, blamed on Sudanese-backed plotters. Sudan had since taken steps to comply, the text notes. Letters from regional groups supported Khartoum's case. The Non-Aligned Movement, the Arab League, and the African Group all wrote in.

The ended measures had cut Sudan's diplomatic staff abroad. They had also banned Sudanese state aircraft from other countries' airspace. The Council acted the same month as the attacks on the United States. Sudan was then offering cooperation against terrorism. The vote was fourteen to none, with the United States abstaining.
un-sc-res-1472:
Iraq's Oil-for-Food program was handed to the Secretary-General mid-war on 28 March 2003. The occupying power's duty to feed the population was recalled from the Fourth Geneva Convention. United Nations staff running the program had been pulled out on 17 March. The national food basket network had to be kept alive. Contracts for food and medicine were frozen by the fighting.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council called on all parties to honor the Geneva Conventions and the Hague rules. The world was asked to give instant humanitarian help to Iraqis inside and outside the country. On an interim and exceptional basis, the Secretary-General was authorized to make technical changes to approved program contracts. He could set priorities and let urgent food and medical shipments proceed. The Council stood ready to let him take on more functions and to open more funds.
un-sc-res-1572:
Resolution 1572 brought sanctions against Ivory Coast, a West African country split by civil war. Fighting between the government and northern rebels had stalled a peace deal. The Security Council voted to squeeze both sides with trade limits until they complied.

Its main tool is an arms embargo, blocking weapons sales to either camp, backed by the threat of asset freezes and travel bans on named spoilers. A committee and expert checks were meant to track violations. The text shows the Council's middle path in a civil war: pressure first, without sending troops.
un-sc-res-1672:
Acting under Chapter VII of the Charter, the Council tightened sanctions on Sudan on 25 April 2006. It said the situation in Sudan still threatened peace in the region. The text recalls the Abuja peace talks on Darfur. It also recalls the Comprehensive Peace Agreement of January 2005. Violence and atrocities in Darfur had not ended.

The resolution applies the travel ban and asset freeze of resolution 1591 to four named men. The four are a Sudanese army general, a North Darfur tribal chief, and two rebel field commanders. Every state had to enforce the measures against them. Few Council texts name individuals so directly.
un-sc-res-1772:
Resolution 1772 on Somalia was adopted on 20 August 2007. Somalia had no strong central government, and fighting gripped the capital, Mogadishu. African Union troops, called AMISOM, had deployed to help the transitional government hold on.

The Council lets African Union member states keep AMISOM in Somalia for six more months. The mission guards leaders and key sites, backs talks, and helps train Somali security forces. The text also backs a national congress meant to draw in clan, religious, and business leaders. It urges states to fund AMISOM and to plan for a possible United Nations force later.
un-sc-res-1872:
Somalia came before the Council in Resolution 1872, adopted on 26 May 2009. A new president and unity cabinet had taken office under the Djibouti Agreement and moved to Mogadishu. Fighting had flared again, and the relief situation kept getting worse. Civilians and aid workers were being killed.

The Council lets African Union member states keep the AMISOM mission in Somalia until 31 January 2010. United Nations logistical support for the mission continues on the same terms. Donors are urged to fund Somali security forces and their training. The government must build an army and police under a national plan, with laws that guard human rights. A United Nations peacekeeping force stays a stated aim for later.
un-sc-res-272:
A change to the World Court's Statute was forwarded by the Security Council on 23 October 1969. The General Assembly had put amendment of the Court's Statute on its agenda for the twenty-fourth session. Article 69 lets the Council recommend rules for states that belong to the Statute but not to the United Nations. The question was how such states could take part in amending it.

The Council recommended that the General Assembly adopt two provisions. A state party to the Statute but outside the United Nations could join the Assembly's work on amendments on the same footing as members. Amendments would take force once two thirds of Statute parties had adopted and ratified them, under Article 69 of the Statute and Article 108 of the Charter. The short text is pure machinery for keeping the Court's basic law open to repair.
un-sc-res-672:
Killings at Jerusalem's holy places drew condemnation in October 1990. Violence on 8 October at the Al Haram Al Shareef and other holy places left more than twenty Palestinians dead. Over one hundred and fifty people were hurt, among them civilians and worshippers. The Secretary-General was sending a mission to the region, and his plan was conveyed to the Council on 12 October.

The Council voiced alarm at the violence. It condemned above all the acts of the Israeli security forces that caused death and injury. Israel, the occupying power, was called to keep strictly to its duties under the Fourth Geneva Convention, which covers all lands held since 1967. The Council welcomed the Secretary-General's mission. It asked him to report before the end of October 1990 with his findings and conclusions. He was to use every resource the United Nations had in the region for the task.
un-sc-res-72: Two peacemakers are honored in Security Council Resolution 72, passed on 11 August 1949. The Acting Mediator in Palestine had filed his last report, on the close of his task. The Council first pays praise to the late Count Folke Bernadotte. His calm, his grit, and his faith in world peace had steadied Palestine, and he gave his life in UN service, with ten of his staff. Dr. Ralph J. Bunche, who took his place, is praised next: his skill and grit won the armistice deals of 1949.
un-sc-res-972: The Security Council's numbered decisions include Resolution 972, entered in this catalog under the year 1992. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1172, adopted on 6 June 1998, responds to India's nuclear tests of 11 and 13 May 1998. It responds to Pakistan's tests of 28 and 30 May 1998. The Council condemns the tests. It calls them a challenge to the global non-proliferation regime and a danger to peace and stability in South Asia. It backs the joint communiqué of the five permanent members' foreign ministers of 4 June 1998.

The Council demands that India and Pakistan carry out no further tests. It calls on them to stop their nuclear weapon development programmes at once. It calls on them to hold back from weaponization or deployment. It calls on them to cease ballistic missile development and fissile material production. It states that neither country can have the status of a nuclear-weapon state under the Non-Proliferation Treaty. It urges both to join that treaty and the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty, without delay and without conditions.

Old files sometimes carry the wrong label. This one has nothing to do with Western Sahara. Its topic is Sudan. Khartoum had been under Council sanctions since 1996. The bans punished Sudan for sheltering men tied to a bid to kill Egypt's president. By 2001, Sudan had signed key anti-terror pacts. Friendly states lobbied for relief.

Resolution 1372, passed on 28 September 2001, ended the sanctions at once. Fourteen members voted yes. The United States held back. The lifted steps were travel and flight bans from 1996. The timing was sharp: the vote came weeks after the September 11 attacks. Even so, the Council judged Sudan's file ready to close.

Aid for Iraq's people during the 2003 war is the urgent business of Resolution 1472, adopted on 28 March 2003. The Oil-for-Food Programme, which let Iraq sell oil to buy civilian goods under UN watch, had been thrown into chaos. UN staff running it were pulled out on 17 March, just before fighting began, and food and medicine shipments were stuck.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council gives the Secretary-General power, for 45 days, to reroute aid deliveries inside and outside Iraq, rank existing contracts by need, and speed, delay, or divert shipments. He may shift funds between programme accounts and pay extra shipping costs caused by the changes. The text stresses that an occupying power must feed and supply the people under the Fourth Geneva Convention, and it calls for open access for aid groups across Iraq.

Government aircraft had bombed rebel-held areas in early November, breaking Côte d'Ivoire's ceasefire, and on 15 November 2004 an arms embargo follows. Hate broadcasts against foreigners on radio and television added to the alarm about the humanitarian situation, above all in the north.

Acting under Chapter VII, the air strikes are condemned and all Ivorian parties are demanded to respect the ceasefire fully. An immediate arms embargo is imposed, and further measures, including travel bans and asset freezes, are set out to follow if the parties do not comply. An end to broadcasts inciting hatred and violence is demanded, and the United Nations operation in the country is asked to monitor the media more closely.

Four names broke new ground under the Darfur sanctions in 2006. On 25 April, the Council adopted Resolution 1672. It acted under Chapter VII. Earlier texts had set travel bans and asset freezes for those blocking peace in Sudan. No names had been attached until now. Peace talks in Abuja stood at a sharp point.

The text orders all states to apply the measures to four men. Two sit on the government side of the war. Army commander Gaffar Mohamed Elhassan is one. Tribal chief Musa Hilal is the other. Two rebel field leaders complete the list. Naming both camps was meant to press each toward a deal.

Rwanda's free life began the same day as Burundi's. Both had been one Belgian trust land, Ruanda-Urundi. They split at freedom on 1 July 1962. Each sought its own seat. The two bids were heard at one meet. Resolution 172 passed with no dissent on 26 July 1962. Its twin text for Burundi shares the date.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit the Republic of Rwanda. The Assembly did so that fall. The new state was a republic, where Burundi kept a king. Hutu and Tutsi strife had racked the land just past. A Hutu-led state took the seat. Dark years lay far ahead. The text itself is a calm, plain note of birth, one line that gave a small hill land its legal place in the world.

Somalia's reconciliation talks and the African Union mission there, AMISOM, are the heart of Resolution 1772, adopted on 20 August 2007. A National Reconciliation Congress had opened under the Transitional Federal Institutions. The African Union had extended AMISOM for six months and asked the UN to weigh sending its own peacekeeping force. Piracy off the Somali coast was rising.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes African Union states to keep AMISOM in Somalia for six more months, guarding the transitional bodies, key sites, and the talks. It carves AMISOM supplies out of the arms embargo. It warns it may act against anyone who blocks the congress or attacks the transitional bodies or AMISOM by force. It asks the Secretary-General to keep planning for a possible UN force to take over and to report within 30 days, then again 30 days later.

Somalia's new unity government is backed in Resolution 1872, adopted on 26 May 2009. The Transitional Federal Parliament had elected a president, a unity cabinet had formed and moved to Mogadishu, and fighting had then resurged. A Brussels conference in April 2009 had pledged support for Somali security institutions and AMISOM, the African Union mission protecting key sites in the capital.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes AU member states to keep AMISOM in Somalia until 31 January 2010 and extends the UN logistical support package for it to the same date. It presses donors to fund the UN trust funds for AMISOM and Somali security forces, and backs a national security strategy covering disarmament, justice, and corrections. Long-term security, it says, rests on Somalia's own National Security Force and police. Reports on progress are due by 30 September and 31 December 2009.

Resolution 272, adopted on 23 October 1969, is about who gets a say in changing the World Court's rules. The General Assembly had put amendment of the court's statute on its agenda. Some states belonged to the statute without being UN members, and Article 69 of the statute lets the Council recommend how such states join the amendment process.

The Council recommended that the Assembly adopt two provisions. A state party to the statute but outside the UN may take part in the Assembly on amendments just as members do. And amendments would take effect for all statute parties once adopted by two thirds of them and ratified by two thirds under their own constitutional processes.

Resolution 372 was adopted unanimously on 18 August 1975, during a single meeting that handled several new-member applications. This one came from the Republic of Cape Verde, an Atlantic island nation that had won independence from Portugal only weeks earlier, in July 1975. Portugal's colonial empire in Africa was collapsing that year.

The Council recommends that the General Assembly admit Cape Verde to membership in the United Nations. No debate or conditions fill the text; the recommendation itself is the act. It opened the door for Cape Verde to take a General Assembly seat as one of the smallest member states, an island country off the coast of West Africa.

Resolution 672, adopted on 12 October 1990, responds to bloodshed at Jerusalem's holy places. On 8 October, violence at the Al Haram Al Sharif compound and other holy sites left more than twenty Palestinians dead and over one hundred fifty people injured, including civilians and worshippers. The Council recalled its two earlier Jerusalem resolutions of 1980 and restated that any Arab-Israeli settlement must rest on its 1967 and 1973 frameworks.

The Council expressed alarm at the violence and condemned especially the acts of the Israeli security forces that caused deaths and injuries. It reminded Israel of its duties under the Fourth Geneva Convention in the territories occupied since 1967. It welcomed the Secretary-General's fact-finding mission and demanded his report before October ended.

Thanks to two men who made peace in Palestine fill Resolution 72, adopted on 11 August 1949. The Acting Mediator's final report had just reached the Council. Count Folke Bernadotte had steadied the situation in Palestine as mediator. He was killed in that service, together with ten members of his staff. Ralph Bunche, who succeeded him as acting mediator, is the second man honored.

The Council paid tribute to Bernadotte's patience, perseverance, and devotion to international peace. It expressed deep appreciation for Bunche as well. His tact and devotion were praised in the text. Bunche had brought the armistice agreements to a successful end. Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, and Israel had all signed those agreements. Thanks were extended to the rest of the mission's staff and to its military observers. The resolution is a formal act of gratitude at the close of the mediation.

A cease-fire in Liberia's civil war began on 28 December 1994, under a peace agreement signed in Accra. The United Nations Observer Mission in Liberia, called UNOMIL, worked beside a West African force called ECOMOG. Resolution 972, adopted unanimously on 13 January 1995, deals with that mission.

The Council extended UNOMIL until 13 April 1995. It voiced deep concern about one gap in the peace deal. Liberia's factions still could not agree on the Council of State that the Accra Agreement required. The factions were told to keep the cease-fire and to rebuild their country. All states were reminded of the arms embargo on Liberia. The factions also had to respect aid workers and peacekeepers. A report from the Secretary-General was requested by 1 March 1995.
un-un-res-united-nations-emergency-force:
A sixth report of the Secretary-General on the United Nations Emergency Force, document A/5172, takes stock of the force around 1961 and 1962. UNEF watched the frontier between Egypt and Israel from posts in Gaza and the Sinai. The border stayed calm, which the force's backers counted as its chief success.

The report reviews incidents, staffing, and the cost of keeping troops in the field. It also covers talks with Egypt on the force's status. The document is one link in the chain of reports that tracked the first Emergency Force across its full decade of service.
verne-around-world-1872:
Jules Verne published Around the World in Eighty Days in 1872, a novel built around a wager. Phileas Fogg bets that he can circle the globe in eighty days. He sets out from London with his servant Passepartout. Trains, ships, and stagecoaches carry them across four continents.

Delays, arrests, and rescues keep the race tense to the final hours. A detective who thinks Fogg is a thief follows them the whole way. In India they save a young woman, Aouda, who joins the trip. The ending turns on a neat trick of time and travel. The book remains a model of the well-made adventure.
virchow-neanderthal-1872:
Rudolf Virchow, the great German doctor, gave his report on the Neanderthal skull in German in 1872. He was the most feared voice in the study of the body in his age. His word on a bone could make or break a claim for years to come.

Virchow held that the skull was that of a sick and bent modern man, not an old race. Disease, he said, had warped the brow and limbs in life, and age had done the rest. That word from such a height held back the Neanderthal claim for a long span of years.
zola-curee-1872:
Vizetelly and Company issued The Rush for the Spoil at London in 1886, from the thirty-fourth French edition. George Moore wrote the preface to this unabridged English rendering. The French title, La Curee, names the hounds' share of the hunt.

Paris under the Second Empire turns into one vast gamble in these pages. Aristide Saccard, a money man who builds fortunes on fraud, reigns over the dealing. His lovely young wife Renee drifts meanwhile toward scandal and ruin. Greed, luxury, and rot swirl in a fever dream of an age. Few novels catch a corrupt era with such furious energy and color.
